description: This course surveys contemporary evidence from archaeological and art discoveries on elaborate rituals surrounding death and dying, economics of being a nomad, warrior culture, shamans, and the transmigration of gold and treasure in ancient Central Asia.

title: Cavemen, Mammoths, and Sabertooths: Stone Age Archaeology in Eurasia
description: This course will examine the archaeological record of Eurasia, starting with the earliest archaeological sites outside of Africa around 1.8 million years ago and ending with the period just before we begin to see the first signs of agriculture around 10,000 years ago.

title: Laboratory Methods in Archaeology
description: This course introduces students to scientific methodology central to the reconstruction of human lifeways through material remains left by past peoples and societies. Students will learn basic analysis methods relevant to the study of different material types, such as pottery, stone tools, and bones. Through these analyses, we will explore questions about past human identity and behavior: who they were, what they were eating, in which environments they were living, and how the answers to each of these questions can change over time.

title: Introduction to Medical Anthropology
description: This course examines the interaction between biology, culture and health, as well as how health is viewed cross-culturally. Material from this course is applicable to a range of fields including anthropology, medicine and public health.

title: Health, Illness and Society
description: This module introduces students to social theory in medical sociology and medical anthropology. It does this by exploring sociological factors that impinge on health status, health chances and health care.

title: Nomads: Around the world and through time
description: This course explores six regions of the world where nomadic populations have succeeded amidst climate change and cultural revolutions in the driest deserts, highest and treacherous mountains, and the coldest, bleakest reaches of the arctic. Through a global survey, the course examines the essential role nomads have played in the formation and transfer of culture, language, and power. Content will also include how Central Asian nomadic societies compare cross-culturally, and how they have impacted globalization and world empires from prehistoric times to the present day.

title: Foundations of Cultural Heritage Studies
description: What is heritage, and why does it matter? This course introduces students to the interdisciplinary field of heritage studies, exploring how societies define, preserve, and contest physical and immaterial aspects of past and living cultures. We will explore tangible (e.g., artifacts, monuments), intangible (e.g., oral traditions, performance), and natural heritage (e.g., ecosystems, geologic formations) through global and Kazakhstani case studies. We will consider issues surrounding identity, power, and decolonization to help us understand who decides what should be preserved and what is ignored. We will also examine risks to heritage, including the impacts of conflict, excessive tourism, and climate change, but also the ways in which heritage is becoming more inclusive through digital methods and community inclusion. By the end of the course, students will possess a foundational understanding of the field of heritage studies and be able to analyze the complex political, ethical, and cultural facets present within these dialogs about the past and future of heritage.

title: Anthropology of Religion and Secularism
description: This course examines the ways that anthropologists and other scholars of culture and society have explored the cultural experiences and social processes associated with religion and the other social systems in which religion is included or excluded. Case materials will be drawn primarily from Eurasia, broadly defined, while the course also aims to show how the experience of Eurasia -- particularly, post-Communist Eurasia -- can be better understood in a broad comparative perspective.

title: Political Anthropology
description: Political Anthropology is being proposed to replace “Anthropology of COnflict”--312. Political Anthropology shares similarities with Anthropology of COnflict in terms of human political organization, but it will serve as a more expansive exploration into the variety of human political organizations recorded by anthropologists, and it will focus on how anthropologists conceive of politics as they theorize political studies in combination with grounded ethnographic research projects.

title: Museum space: collections, collectors and society
description: The role and purpose of museums in contemporary society has been the subject of intense debate in recent decades. This course situates those discussions within a broader historical and theoretical framework, examining both the development of museums and the key concepts that shape current museum practice. Drawing on perspectives from art history, anthropology, and sociology students will engage critically with the question of what museums and collections are—and what they can become—in today’s world. Central to the course is the analysis of exhibitions as sites where societal values, identities, and norms are negotiated and communicated. Equally important is the critical study of collections and collectors: how collecting practices have been shaped by historical-political conjunctures, how they reflect shifting ideologies and hierarchies of value, and how individual collectors and institutional agendas have influenced what is preserved, displayed, or silenced. Special emphasis is placed on how (de)colonization, globalization, digital and AI transformation continue to reshape museum work and collecting strategies.
prerequisite: ANT 101 Being Human: An Introduction to Four Field Anthropology (2960) (C and above) OR ANT 140 World Prehistory (227) (C and above) OR ANT 110 Introduction to Sociocultural Anthropology (501) (C and above) OR WLL 171/ANT 175 Introduction to Linguistic Anthropology (4417) (C and above)

title: Archaeology of Power and Inequality
description: This seminar surveys the emergence of power and inequality in the ancient world through the lens of archaeology. Both dense urban centers and geographically dispersed ruins will be covered to examine interactions between the ‘powerful’ and ‘powerless’—and how this shaped world civilizations. Comparative case studies will provide material for our in-class discussions where we will deliberate how humans have built complex organizational structures to assert their power, take it from others, and to shape various modes of identity through agency. Anthropological literature that explores and questions traditional notions of civilization and complexity will provide a theoretical framework for broaching these topics intellectually and with a critical mind.

title: Method and Theory in Archaeology
description: This course will examine the origins of archaeology, the evolution of archaeological thought, and the current theoretical paradigms that shape archaeological investigations and interpretations. Theory is the foundation upon which questions, methodologies, and analyses are planned and formed, and we cannot conduct archaeology without it. Students will engage with the different approaches in theory and read widely among archaeology’s greatest works where interpretations rely on diverse theoretical underpinnings and intellectual positions regarding what about Homo sapiens is important to explore, explain, and understand.
prerequisite: (Subject "ANT" BETWEEN 100 and 199 AND Subject "ANT" BETWEEN 200 and 299) OR (Subject "ANT" BETWEEN 100 and 199 AND Subject "ANT" BETWEEN 200 and 299)

title: Human Evolution: Bones, Stones and Genomes
description: This course examines the evidence for the emergence of the human species, with an emphasis on the fossil or paleontological record. We will address questions such as: Why do humans have such large brains, and lack tails? How have technology and culture influenced human evolution? Are humans still evolving? In answering these questions, students will learn about the fossil, genetic and behavioral evidence of how we became human over the past several million years.

Inner Asian Frontiers of China: A Cultural Perspective
description: This course is a seminar designed to acquaint students with peoples around the Inner Asian periphery of China, especially those that are included today within the three large border regions – Xinjiang, Tibet, and Inner Mongolia. In each case, we will examine the life of peripheral peoples as part of the Sinocentric world; at the same time, we will attempt to hear not just the voices of the Chinese observers and overlords, but the voices of the local people as well.

title: Linguistic and Cultural Diversity in Contemporary China: From Beijing to Xinjiang
description: This seminar is an overview of the sociolinguistic and anthropological study of contemporary China, with a special focus on the speakers of Turkic languages in Xinjiang – mainly Uyghur and Kazak. The first goal of this course is to build a multifaceted understanding of daily life for China’s diverse population – especially Turkic speakers in Xinjiang – throughout this period. A second and related goal is to learn to identify and compare the different methodological and theoretical approaches that anthropologists and sociolinguists have developed to study social change in ordinary life.

title: Postcolonial Theory and its Applications in Eurasia
description: In this course, we will use postcolonial lenses to analyze Central Asia, its literature, and cultural production (film, songs, and videos). While postcolonial studies and postcolonial theory have been a part of the canon of several disciplines such as anthropology, comparative literature, and cultural studies in the West, the degree of its application to Eurasian Studies has been limited and its applicability has been questioned. We will read some classical theoretical texts in postcolonial studies and then see how this theory that has been so productive elsewhere can be applied to Central Asian cultural phenomena.
department: Languages, Literature and Linguistics, Sociology and Anthropology

title: Fundamentals of Social and Cultural Data Science with Python
description: With the expansion of electronic sources such as cell phones, social media, and other online platforms, researches now have abundant data about almost every aspect of human behavior – from what we buy to what we believe in. Coupled with the mass digitalization of historical texts, artwork, and scattered family archives, this unfolding influx of data is ushering a revolution in methods of social and cultural analysis. This course provides a hands-on, non-technical introduction to the ideas and tools of Social and Cultural Data Science. This multidisciplinary research field sits at the intersection of social sciences, humanities, statistics, informatics and computing. We will explore key methods of classical supervised and unsupervised machine learning, text analysis, computer vision, and the basics of deep learning (ANN). Every week, we will learn how to apply advanced research methods to analyze real world social and “business” problems through hands-on data collection and analysis.
department: Sociology and Anthropology, Sociology and Anthropology

description: In this seminar, we will explore the historical trajectory of global development as a set of ideas and practices. Using both anthropological and sociological approaches we will examine the shortcoming and failures of development as we know it today and think about new ways in which the problems of development can be approached and tackled.

title: Materiality and Eurasian Society
description: Objects have substantially more power than we give them credit for. This idea lies at the heart of studies of ‘materiality’ – the two-way relationship between people and things. This course is about uncovering the social life of manmade materials that have shaped Eurasia through time, across millennia: clay, glass, metals, fibers, stone, paint, plastic, steel, concrete, and more. Anthropological and Archaeological case studies will be introduced to reveal those aspects of our social life that we often ignore and to discover the many relationships that materials hold to human culture.

title: The Archaeology of Ritual
description: Nearly every human society participates in some form of ritual practice, including those from the past. Data recovered from archaeological sites of ancient cultures are sometimes described as “ritual” items when no other explanation is available. Carefully considering context and using multiple lines of evidence makes it possible to move beyond a blanket designation of “ritual” to understand what these data tell us about ancient religious beliefs and ritual practices. Using approaches to rituals grounded in religious studies and archaeological theory and physical evidence from past societies around the world, students will learn about different forms of ritual practices, what evidence they leave in the archaeological record, and how to interpret them when no written evidence is available to explain complex and symbolic behaviors. Students will develop their existing archaeological knowledge and interpretive skills by examining sacred space, artifacts, and additional lines of evidence presented in readings, lectures, and discussions. They will also gain confidence using terminology associated with religious and ritual practices, such as liminality, the sacred, and belief systems. They will apply their knowledge by describing, comparing, and interpreting materials from ritual sites.
department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, Sociology and Anthropology

title: Skeletal Materials for Archaeologists
description: This course will offer hands-on training for students in human and mammalian skeletal anatomy and introduce different ways in which archaeologists collect, analyze, and interpret these data across temporal and geographic contexts. Students will learn how to identify the different bones of the skeleton, distinguish between the bones of different mammalian taxa (including humans), determine sex and age from skeletal remains, strategies for human osteological and forensic analyses, and qualitative and quantitative methods for analyzing an archaeological site. Students will also learn about the processes that affect skeletal materials after burial and how to reconstruct the taphonomic history of the bones.

description: This course explores contemporary understandings of gender and sexuality in South Asia from a post-colonial feminist perspective. title: Applied Public Heritage
description: Heritage is a global matter. In the broadest sense, heritage includes both the tangible and intangible elements of cultures—languages, local history and archaeology, special technologies, traditional arts and performances, architecture, cultural practices and beliefs. Such diverse areas are enriched by incorporating insights from multiple disciplines, such as anthropology, archaeology, history, museum studies, political science, public policy, human geography, and others. Now more than ever, academics and governments are supporting approaches which foster greater collaboration when it comes to heritage. Public heritage aims to bring together multiple voices from researchers, institutions, and public stakeholders to ensure a greater appreciation for and understanding of heritage. Learning how to make heritage meaningful to the public is key to its protection and preservation. This course aims to provide students with the opportunity to bridge the gap between academics and the community to have meaningful conversations about shared heritage and what its role might be in today’s world. Students will connect with local or international institutions, cultivate skills for communicating heritage matters, and develop their own heritage-specific projects to present publicly either on a digital platform or through an in-person event.
prerequisite: ANT 101 Being Human: An Introduction to Four Field Anthropology (2960) (C+ and above) OR ANT 110 Introduction to Sociocultural Anthropology (501) (C+ and above) OR ANT 120 Anthropology Theory (137) (C+ and above) OR ANT 120 Sociology Theory/Anthropology Theory (135) (C+ and above) OR ANT 140 World Prehistory (227) (C+ and above) OR ANT 160 Introduction to Biological Anthropology (161) (C+ and above)

title: Capstone Seminar I
description: ANT 498 is the first part of the year-long capstone seminar taught to senior students majoring in Anthropology. During this course students will design their research projects, develop research instruments, review relevant literature, obtain ethics review approval from the SHSS ethics review committee, and start data collection. There will be two types of capstone projects: Track One: An independent academic research and undergraduate thesis. Track Two: Community-engagement participatory research project and project report.

title: Capstone Seminar II
description: ANT 499 is the second part of the year-long capstone seminar taught to senior students majoring in Anthropology. The goal of this course is to help students consolidate your analytical, writing, communication, and presentation skills as well as learn new practical skills that allow students to communicate their work to both academic and nonacademic audiences. Students will engage in systematically analyzing data, writing their findings, and revising their work through feedback and comments with the guidance of the teaching faculty member, peers, research advisor, and other experts brought into assist in the process of constructing an original product.

title: Data Analytics for Business
description: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to data analytics tools, techniques, and applications, emphasizing their relevance in managerial decision-making

title: Environmental, Social and Governance Factors (ESG) for Business
description: In this course, students will learn and analyze the concept of sustainable development and its relevance for business across its governance, social and environmental dimensions.

title: Fundamentals of Marketing
description: This introductory course provides a comprehensive overview of core marketing concepts, strategies, and practices

title: Entrepreneurship
description: This undergraduate Entrepreneurship course offers a comprehensive overview of entrepreneurial fundamentals, including the nature of entrepreneurship and its economic/societal significance, particularly focusing on entrepreneurial activities in emerging markets, such as Kazakhstan

title: Strategy
description: Strategic Management is a cornerstone course in the business curriculum, designed to equip students with the essential knowledge and skills to formulate and implement effective strategies in organizations

title: Operations Management
description: Operations Management is designed to provide students with a foundational understanding of the principles and practices involved in effectively managing business operations

title: Digital Marketing
description: This course introduces students to the core concepts, tools, and strategies of digital marketing. It combines theoretical foundations with hands-on applications, enabling students to design, implement, and evaluate digital marketing campaigns across multiple channels.

title: Project Management
description: The concepts and use of project management tools, techniques and methodologies are becoming all pervasive. The course addresses project management in a general context and not specifically focusing on any one type of project such as construction or software projects. Using the framework of project life cycle, the course covers various aspects pertaining to (i) project valuation and selection, (ii) project planning and scheduling, (iii) project monitoring and control and (iv) risk management. Scheduling of projects with resource limitations, role of incentives in project management, and project contracting are also included. Moreover, an overview of Agile Project Management, Organization Structure and project management approaches are covered.

title: Internship
description: This course provides undergraduate business students with the opportunity to gain real-world experience through an internship experience

title: Special Topics in Corporate Finance
description: This course is designed to enhance students’ analytical and critical thinking skills so that they are able to effectively: • Address advanced and specific challenges of corporate financial management. • Analyze a real-world advanced corporate finance case. • Solve advanced quantitative and qualitative corporate finance problems.

title: Capstone
description: The Business Capstone (Practicum) is the culminating experience for senior undergraduate students in the business major, providing an opportunity to integrate and apply knowledge gained throughout their academic journey to solve real-world business challenges.

title: Occupal and Environment Health and Safety
description: This course is an introduction to Risk Management: Hazards Identification, Risk Assessment and Risk Control.

title: Programming for Engineers
description: The module would focus on the development of programming skills that can be directly applied to solve engineering problems where the computer is part of the system, or is used to model a physical or logical system

title: Mechanics of Fluids and Thermodynamics
description: This course provides to the engineering student an introduction to the basic principles of Thermodynamics, Fluid Mechanics and how to apply them to analyze an engineering problem. It includes an introduction to engineering thermodynamics (fluid properties and first/second laws of thermodynamics), basic Fluid Mechanics (conservation laws applied to fluid flow, Bernoulli equations, dimensional analysis and flow visualization and integral flow analysis).
prerequisite: BENG 124 Engineering Mathematics I (101) (D and above)

title: Engineering Thermodynamics
description: Engineering Thermodynamics is module which is dedicated to study the matter of different substances and their forms during work energy transformation.

title: Engineering Mathematics III
description: This module will deepen and extend the first year engineering mathematics programme by considering the important field of differential equations and the equally applicable field of probability and statistics. Many of the most important mathematical methods and techniques used in either of these fields will be presented and developed.
prerequisite: BENG 124 Engineering Mathematics I (101) (D and above) AND BENG 225 Engineering Mathematics II (48) (D and above)

title: Interdisciplinary Design Project
description: It is designed to place students in a simulated work situation and provide them with an awareness of the roles and responsibilities of the other parties involved in large-scale engineering projects.

title: Introductory Biology
description: The course introduces basic concepts of biology including molecular biology, genetics, basics of human anatomy and physiology, evolution, ecology and modern biotechnology for non-science majors. The overview aims to develop in students critical thinking and scientific reasoning applied to biology in their everyday life and in the different fields of their main study areas. Many new discoveries are the result of integrated knowledge, and understanding the basis of life is a bonus for future professionals.
antirequisite: BIOL 110 Modern Biology I (1070) (C- and above)

title: General Biology
description: The course “General Biology” will introduce students to the basics of structure and function of the living organisms.

title: Modern Biology I
description: Modern Biology I focuses on the fundamental principles of molecular biology, cell biology, biochemistry and evolution. The course provides students with a foundation that is essential to understand the basic mechanisms of life on cellular level with further implications for health/disease and biotechnology.

title: Modern Biology I Laboratory
description: Modern Biology I Laboratory gives students an opportunity to explore biological technologies as practical applications of fundamental concepts learned in the lecture course.
corequisite: BIOL 110 Modern Biology I (1070) (C and above)

title: Modern Biology II
description: Modern Biology II introduces students to the fundamental principles of molecular biology, cell biology, genetics and biochemistry. The course helps students to relate structural and chemical properties of molecular players to their functions inside of a cell.
prerequisite: BIOL 110 Modern Biology I (1070) (C and above)

title: Modern Biology II Laboratory
description: Modern Biology II Laboratory allows students to obtain hands-on experiences of modern molecular biology technologies. The practical experiences gained enhance the understanding of fundamental concepts learned in BIOL 110 and BIOL 120 lectures.
prerequisite: BIOL 110 Modern Biology I (1070) (C and above) OR BIOL 110L Modern Biology I Laboratory (5448) (C and above)
corequisite: BIOL 120 Modern Biology II (1195) (C and above)

title: Introduction to Microbiology
prerequisite: (BIOL 110 Modern Biology I (107) (C- and above) OR BIOL 110 Modern Biology I (1070) (C- and above) OR PREM 110 Pre-med Biology I with lab (1071) (C- and above)) AND (BIOL 120 Modern Biology II (177) (C- and above) OR BIOL 120 Modern Biology II (1195) (C- and above))

title: Human Anatomy and Physiology I
description: BIOL 230 covers the normal structures and functions of human organ systems.
prerequisite: BIOL 110 Modern Biology I (107) (C and above) OR BIOL 110 Modern Biology I (1070) (C and above)

title: Human Anatomy and Physiology II
prerequisite: BIOL 230 Human Anatomy and Physiology I (72) (C and above)

title: Special Topics in Synthetic Biology I
prerequisite: (BIOL 110 Modern Biology I (107) (C- and above) OR BIOL 110 Modern Biology I (1070) (C- and above) OR PREM 110 Pre-med Biology I with lab (1071) (C- and above)) AND BIOL 120 Modern Biology II (177) (C- and above) AND CHEM 101 General Chemistry I (113) (C- and above) AND CHEM 102 General Chemistry II (232) (C- and above)

title: Special Topics in Synthetic Biology II
Biology Internship - 1A
description: Biology Internship - 1A is a 1 credit experiential learning endeavor where students work in a "real-life" biological sciences environment

title: Biology Internship - 1B
description: Biology Internship - 1B is a 3 credit experiential learning endeavor where students work in a "real-life" biological sciences environment.

title: Molecular Biology of Cell with Lab
description: The main aim of this course is to familiarize students with the principals of structural and functional organization of the eukaryotic cell, its dynamics and interaction of organelles and cytoskeleton.
prerequisite: BIOL 120 Modern Biology II (177) (C and above) OR BIOL 120 Modern Biology II Lab (1445) (C and above) OR BIOL 120L Modern Biology II Laboratory (5443) (C and above)

title: Molecular Cell Biology Laboratory
description: The lab practicals allow students to learn essential basic techniques of mammalian cell lines where they will learn different features of cells like cell viability, cell toxicity, cell fixation followed by staining of different organelles.
prerequisite: BIOL 120 Modern Biology II (1195) (C and above) OR BIOL 120L Modern Biology II Laboratory (5443) (C and above)
corequisite: BIOL 301 Molecular Cell Biology (5809) (C and above)

title: Introduction to Microbiology
description: Introduction to Microbiology is a general survey course of selected topics in the field of microbiology. Successful completion of this course will prepare students for advance study in the various fields of microbiology including virology, bacteriology, food microbiology, medical microbiology, and parasitology.
prerequisite: (BIOL 120 Modern Biology II (1195) (C and above) AND BIOL 120L Modern Biology II Laboratory (5443) (C and above)) OR BIOL 120 Modern Biology II (1195) (C and above)

title: Introduction to Microbiology Laboratory
description: Introduction to Microbiology Laboratory will teach students on basic methods in bacterial growth, staining, and biochemical activities to be able to identify them by using methods learnt on the module.
prerequisite: BIOL 120 Modern Biology II (1195) (C and above) OR BIOL 120L Modern Biology II Laboratory (5443) (C and above)
corequisite: BIOL 305 Introduction to Microbiology (5789) (C and above)

title: Immunology
prerequisite: BIOL 301 Molecular Biology of Cell with Lab (1197) (C and above) OR BIOL 305 Introduction to Microbiology with Lab (1642) (C and above) OR BIOL 301 Molecular Cell Biology (5809) (C and above) OR BIOL 305 Introduction to Microbiology (5789) (C and above)

title: Developmental Biology with Lab
description: This course is focused on the study of the process by which organisms grow and develop. It includes studies of genetic control of cell growth and development and cell differentiation which give rise to different tissues, organs and systems.
prerequisite: ((BIOL 110 Modern Biology I (107) (C- and above) AND BIOL 110 Modern Biology I Lab (1444) (C- and above)) OR PREM 110 Pre-med Biology I with lab (1071) (C- and above) OR BIOL 110 Modern Biology I (1070) (C- and above)) AND (BIOL 120 Modern Biology II (1195) (C- and above) OR (BIOL 120 Modern Biology II (177) (C- and above) AND BIOL 120 Modern Biology II Lab (1445) (C- and above))) AND ((BIOL 220 Molecular Biology of Cell (477) (C- and above) AND BIOL 220 Molecular Biology of Cell Lab (478) (C- and above)) OR BIOL 301 Molecular Biology of Cell with Lab (1197) (C- and above) OR BIOL 231 Human Anatomy and Physiology II (479) (C- and above))

title: Bioethics
description: This course begins with a brief overview of ethics, values and principles relevant to ethics of biological sciences and biomedicine.
prerequisite: BIOL 120 Modern Biology II (1195) (C and above)

title: Introduction to Immunology Lab
prerequisite: (BIOL 110 Modern Biology I Lab (1444) (C- and above) OR BIOL 110 Modern Biology I (1070) (C- and above) OR PREM 110 Pre-med Biology I with lab (1071) (C- and above)) AND (BIOL 120 Modern Biology II Lab (1445) (C- and above) OR BIOL 120 Modern Biology II (1195) (C- and above)) AND (BIOL 220 Molecular Biology of Cell Lab (478) (C- and above) OR BIOL 301 Molecular Biology of Cell with Lab (1197) (C- and above) OR BIOL 210 Introduction to Microbiology Lab (71) (C- and above) OR BIOL 231 Human Anatomy and Physiology II (479) (C- and above))
corequisite: BIOL 310 Immunology (628) (D and above)

title: Human Anatomy and Physiology II
description: BIOL 331 covers the normal structures and functions of human organ systems.
prerequisite: BIOL 230 Human Anatomy and Physiology I (72) (C and above) OR BIOL 230 Human Anatomy and Physiology I (6217) (C and above)

title: Human Anatomy and Physiology II Laboratory
description: Human Anatomy and Physiology II Lab covers the Anatomy & physiology of organ systems.
prerequisite: BIOL 110 Modern Biology I Lab (1444) (C and above) OR BIOL 110L Modern Biology I Laboratory (5448) (C and above)
corequisite: BIOL 331 Human Anatomy and Physiology II (6218) (C and above) OR BIOL 231 Human Anatomy and Physiology II (479) (C and above)

title: Environmental Biology
description: The main aim of this course is to provide students with foundational material on Environmental Biology and related research methods.
prerequisite: BIOL 120 Modern Biology II (1195) (C and above)

title: Introduction to Applied Bioinformatics
description: Introduces students to concepts of organizing data, extracting, utilizing and manipulating information related to DNA, RNA, proteins and other biological macromolecules to build knowledge and generate new insights on molecular and/or cellular levels in terms of depths and scale.
prerequisite: (BIOL 120 Modern Biology II (1195) (C and above) OR (BIOL 120 Modern Biology II (1195) (C and above) AND BIOL 120L Modern Biology II Laboratory (5443) (C and above))) AND MATH 310 Applied Statistical Methods (82) (C and above)

title: Biochemistry I
description: This course aims to describe and explain, in molecular terms, all the chemical processes of the living cell.
prerequisite: CHEM 211 Organic Chemistry I (154) (C and above)

title: Critical Research Reasoning
prerequisite: BIOL 120 Modern Biology II (1195) (C and above)

title: Structural Bioinformatics
description: The main aim of this course is to familiarize students with the principals of structural bioinformatics.
prerequisite: BIOL 341 Biochemistry I (2002) (C and above) OR CHEM 341 Biochemistry I (1058) (C and above) OR CSCI 235 Programming Languages (638) (C and above)

title: Genetics
prerequisite: BIOL 120 Modern Biology II (1195) (C and above)

title: Genetics Laboratory
description: This course will equip students with a set of skills to identify genetic traits from simple crosses and to observe genetic manipulations in multicellular organisms at multiple levels. The course will also provide students hands-on experience to observe the phenotype of a genetic trait through live cell imaging as well as to visualize and to analyze 4D data using advance computational image analysis techniques.
corequisite: BIOL 370 Genetics (1174) (C and above)

title: Biology of Behavior
description: Biology of Behavior covers the biological basis of human behavior and nervous system diseases.
prerequisite: BIOL 120 Modern Biology II (1195) (C and above)

title: Cell signaling: principles and mechanisms
description: After completion of the course the participants should have deep understanding of principles behind the cell signaling and know major pathways in control of gene expression and cellular metabolism.
prerequisite: BIOL 120 Modern Biology II (1195) (C and above)

title: Directed Study in Biology
description: Under the supervision of a faculty advisor, a student pursues independent research on a topic in Biology.

title: Biology Internship - 2A
description: Biology Internship - 2A is a 1 credit experiential learning endeavor where students work in a "real-life" biological sciences environment.

title: Biology Internship
description: Biology Internship is a 3 credit experiential learning endeavor where students work in a "real-life" biological sciences environment.

title: Biomedical Research Methods
description: The Biomedical Research Methods course covers a broad area of the basic and common methods instrumental for biomedical sciences including gene expression to purification of proteins and their complexes. The main purpose is to provide not only the fundamental knowledge how common methods work but also acquire the understanding of key practical steps required for completion of biomedical experiments.
prerequisite: BIOL 110 Modern Biology I Lab (1444) (C and above) OR BIOL 110 Modern Biology I (1070) (C and above) AND BIOL 341 Biochemistry I (2002) (C and above) OR CHEM 341 Biochemistry I (1058) (C and above)

title: Histology with Laboratory
description: Examination of basic histological and cytological techniques, including a comprehensive study of the ultrastructure of the eukaryotic animal cell.
prerequisite: BIOL 230 Human Anatomy and Physiology I (72) (C and above) OR BIOL 230 Human Anatomy and Physiology I (6217) (C and above)

title: Neuroscience
description: Introduction to key concepts in modern neuroscience.
prerequisite: BIOL 230 Human Anatomy and Physiology I (72) (C and above) OR BIOL 230 Human Anatomy and Physiology I (6217) (C and above)

title: Medical Microbiology
description: Medical Microbiology is an advanced course which will focus on studying microorganisms as pathogens and provide an insight on the molecular mechanisms by which microorganisms cause human infectious diseases, effectiveness of modern antimicrobial treatments and molecular methods in diagnostics of infectious diseases.
prerequisite: BIOL 305 Introduction to Microbiology (5789) (C and above) OR BIOL 305 Introduction to Microbiology with Lab (1642) (C and above)

title: Food Microbiology
description: The study of food microbiology including classification/ taxonomy, contamination, preservation and spoilage of different kinds of foods; pathogenic microorganisms, food poisoning, sanitation, control and inspection; as well as beneficial uses of microorganisms.
prerequisite: BIOL 305 Introduction to Microbiology with Lab (1642) (C and above) OR BIOL 305 Introduction to Microbiology (5789) (C and above)

title: Food Microbiology Lab
description: Food Microbiology labs will teach students to learn standard methods and apply basic techniques used in study of microorganisms found in food, both in its production and contamination.
prerequisite: BIOL 305 Introduction to Microbiology with Lab (1642) (C and above) OR BIOL 305 Introduction to Microbiology (5789) (C and above)
corequisite: BIOL 450 Food Microbiology (4609) (C and above)

title: Biology of Cancer
prerequisite: BIOL 231 Human Anatomy and Physiology II (479) (C and above) OR BIOL 301 Molecular Biology of Cell with Lab (1197) (C and above) OR BIOL 331 Human Anatomy and Physiology II (6218) (C and above) OR BIOL 301 Molecular Cell Biology (5809) (C and above)

title: Biotechnology
description: An upper-level undergraduate course that covers the principles and latest techniques in biotechnology.
prerequisite: BIOL 301 Molecular Biology of Cell with Lab (1197) (C- and above) OR (BIOL 301 Molecular Cell Biology (5809) (C- and above) AND BIOL 301L Molecular Cell Biology Laboratory (5678) (C- and above))

title: Biology Research Design
description: This course will provide students with an overview of research proposals and an immersion into the art of planning research and writing a research proposal.
corequisite: BIOL 355 Critical Research Reasoning (1000) (C and above)

title: Human Parasitology
description: Human parasitology is an advanced course which provides a foundation knowledge in the biology of parasites. Focus will be on the molecular mechanisms by which protozoan and metazoan parasites cause infectious diseases. Special emphasis will be placed on those parasites of major medical consequence in humans because parasites continue to be one of the primary causes of morbidity and mortality throughout the world.
prerequisite: BIOL 305 Introduction to Microbiology with Lab (1642) (C and above) OR BIOL 305 Introduction to Microbiology (5789) (C and above)

title: Integrated Cell Biology
description: The course will cover the structure and function of key cellular processes at a deep molecular level focusing on the integration of distinct cellular mechanisms and pathways toward maintaining cellular homeostasis.
prerequisite: (BIOL 110 Modern Biology I (107) (C and above) OR BIOL 110 Modern Biology I (1070) (C and above)) AND BIOL 120 Modern Biology II (1195) (C and above)

title: Advanced Cell Biology
description: An upper-level undergraduate course that covers in depth the latest advances in cell biology.
prerequisite: BIOL 120 Modern Biology II (1195) (C and above) AND BIOL 110L Modern Biology I Laboratory (5448) (C and above) AND (BIOL 341 Biochemistry I (2002) (C and above) OR CHEM 341 Biochemistry I (1058) (C and above))

title: Neuroimmunology
description: This course cover the interaction between the immune system and the nervous system that play an important role in the development of diseases such as sickness behavior, stress, autoimmunity, chronic pain, epilepsy, depression and others.
prerequisite: BIOL 310 Immunology (628) (C and above)

title: Honors Thesis Research
description: The course Honors Thesis Research is designed to monitor progress and develop understandings and skills to plan and conduct independent research at the Bachelor of Sciences level. Honors Thesis Research constitutes a partial fulfillment of the Honors Thesis and the research plan will be used as a basis for the assessment of the student's research progress.
prerequisite: BIOL 355 Critical Research Reasoning (1000) (B and above)

title: Honors Thesis
description: Research conducted under the direction of the thesis supervisor(s) culminates in the compilation of the research results in thesis format as prescribed by the Department of Biology and the defense of the thesis.
prerequisite: BIOL 490 Honors Thesis Research (1581) (C and above)

title: Research Experience in Biology
description: This course can be either an experimental learning endeavor with students conducting research in a biological sciences environment or an advanced theoretical or computational and content or data-based learning experience of biological mechanisms under the guidance and supervision of a Biology Department faculty member who agreed to offer a semester-long small research project.
prerequisite: BIOL 456 Biology Research Design (1217) (C- and above)

title: Research Methods and Bioethics
description: This course prepares students the fundamental skills and knowledge necessary for performing and managing their research works as well as training them to deliver high-quality technical presentations to communicate their findings.

title: Structural and Molecular Biology in Health and Disease
description: This course will cover the complex biological mechanisms from a cellular and molecular perspective, stressing integration of concepts as a key component to understand the relationship between different biological processes.

title: Molecular Biology of Prokaryotic Cells
description: This course will expand the knowledge of prokaryotic cells gained by the students in undergraduate studies.

title: Advanced Biotechnology
description: This course will cover methods and applications of biotechnology, examines present and future developments in this area.

title: Advanced Cell and Molecular Biology
description: The course entails a graduate-level exploration of the field of cell and molecular biology, with a focus on recent scientific achievements in these areas.

title: Applied Bioinformatics
description: This course designed for biologists combines conceptual and theoretical underpinnings of biological data analyses and information extraction with bioinformatics tools.
prerequisite: BIOL 520 Statistical Methods in Life Sciences (1203) (C and above)

title: Research Design and Project Planning
description: This research based course prepares students theoretically and empirically for starting their own project that will lead to the successful completion and defense of the master's thesis.

title: Cellular Biophysics
description: This course will address topics in each of the three major divisions of Biophysics: bio-molecular structure, biophysical techniques, and biological mechanisms. The goal of the course is to introduce and critically discuss the central concepts of physical chemistry and their application to gain an in-depth understanding of the fundamental biological principles underlying cellular physiology.

title: Graduate Research Seminar
description: The Research Seminar provides graduate students with different points of view of latest research in biological sciences presented by faculty members and external speakers. Students are required to attend all seminars, participate in questions and answers sessions, and reflective discussion sessions led by students and moderated by the course coordinator and/or the speaker. Students who led the discussion will turn in a reflective summary.

title: Master’s Thesis Research
description: This course is designed to facilitate from the first Academic Year onwards the preparation for the Master’s Thesis Research Proposal and Master’s Thesis Research in the second Academic Year.

title: Graduate Seminar Series
description: This course is based a series of presentations / seminars given by invited faculty and external guests.

title: Radiation Biology
description: This course covers all the relevant aspects of radiation as a central discipline of modern oncology.
prerequisite: BIOL 520 Statistical Methods in Life Sciences (1203) (C and above)

title: Advanced Environmental Biology
description: This research-oriented course focuses on current state of knowledge in environmental biology, as well as a wide spectrum of methodology in the laboratory, and in the field studies.

title: Advanced Immunology
description: This course will provide comprehensive knowledge about how the immune system develops, is regulated, communicates, and how its functional impairment contributes to human diseases.

title: Advanced Neuroscience
description: This course will introduce students to the principle of nerve cell biology in the context of several clinically relevant neurological disorders. The main aspect is to demonstrate how defects at cellular and molecular levels will give rise to the features of the disorders, as we know them from clinical presentation.

title: Synthetic Biology
description: Topics of synthetic biology applications covered in the course include 1) metabolic engineering to produce biofuels and antibiotics, 2) biological macromolecule design for calculations, storing, retrieving and data processing, 3) biosensors, detectors of various analytes that contain a biological molecule and a physiochemical detector and 4)genomic DNA editing techniques and their applications.

title: Drug Discovery and Design
description: This course will provide comprehensive knowledge about discovery and design of low molecular weight drugs as well as protein-based biopharmaceuticals.

title: Advanced Cancer Biology
description: Students will acquire an in depth understanding of the underlying biology and clinical challenges of common and select cancer diseases including colorectal cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer and leukemia. The students will explore the central cancer cell signaling pathways and mutations driving the development of these cancers and discuss specific case studies of anti-cancer therapeutics development.

title: Fundamentals of Advanced Microscopy
description: Fundamentals of Advanced Microscopy will cover microscopic methods (light and electron microscopy in biology research) and flow and imaging cytometry.

title: Fundamentals of advanced microscopy
description: Course will cover microscopic methods (light and electron microscopy in biology research).

title: Research Thesis I
description: During this course the students are expected to conduct research toward completing their specific research thesis.

title: Master’s Thesis Research Proposal
description: The course Thesis Proposal is designed to monitor progress and develop understandings and skills to plan and conduct independent research at the Master of Science level. The student will develop under the guidance of the supervisor a thesis proposal that will state a research problem, question, hypothesis, its background, outline a research strategy, the experimental approach, method of data collection, interpretation and validation.

title: Master’s Thesis
description: The course Master’s Thesis Research encompasses independent research under the direction of the thesis supervisor and the supervisory committee. Students must adhere to scientific ethics and standards while performing their research and compile the research results in thesis format as prescribed by the Biology Department and defend their thesis.
prerequisite: BIOL 691 Master’s Thesis Research Proposal (5676) (B- and above)

title: Doctoral Thesis
description: This course is designed to facilitate before the end of the prescribed program period or approved degree deferral period the writing and submission of the doctoral thesis for review by the thesis examiners. The thesis must be completed according to the Format and Style Guidelines of the Biology Department.

title: Thesis Research
description: The course’s aim is to develop all the professional skills needed for independent research at the PhD level as well as to monitor the progression of the PhD thesis.

title: Radiation Biology
description: This course covers all the relevant aspects of radiation as a central discipline of modern oncology.
prerequisite: BIOL 820 Statistical Methods in Life Sciences (5304) (C and above)
antirequisite: BIOL 605 Radiation Biology (7185) (C and above)

title: Statistical Methods in Life Sciences
description: This course aims at providing an introduction to the most commonly encountered statistical models and methods, visualization and programming environment R.

title: Advanced Neuroscience
description: “Advanced Neuroscience” covers a current understanding of the nervous system and its common neurological disorders.

title: Synthetic Biology
description: This course will provide comprehensive knowledge about synthetic biology (SYNBIO), which is a new, powerful and rapidly developing cross disciplinary field involving biology and engineering.

title: Drug Discovery and Design
description: This course will provide comprehensive knowledge about discovery and design of low molecular weight drugs as well as protein-based biopharmaceuticals.

title: Advanced Cancer Biology
description: The course will provide students with a comprehensive and deeper insights into the molecular, biochemical, cellular mechanisms underlying cancer development with current frontier knowledge and practice.

title: Hot Topics in Life Sciences
description: To broaden the scientific horizon of PhD students Hot Topics in Life Sciences includes presentations of renowned speakers from academia and industry in different biological disciplines (Cellular and Molecular Biology, Systems Biology, Evolution, Environmental Biology, and Climate Change, Cancer Research, Neurobiology, etc.) who are invited from Nazarbayev University and from all over the world. The primary goal is to widen the scientific horizon of PhD students in life sciences and increase their level of expertise.

title: Advanced Optical and Electron Microscopy
description: This graduate-level course explores modern methods in Cell Biology, emphasizing microscopic techniques. Topics include light microscopy (theory, fluorescent microscopy, confocal microscopy, multiphoton microscopy, single-molecule microscopy, and superresolution microscopy) and electron microscopy (transmission and scanning electron microscopes, their limitations, tomography, and specimen preparation). A dedicated section covers principles of digital imaging.

title: Structural and Molecular Biology in Health and Disease
description: The Structural and Molecular Biology in Health and Disease integrates cellular, molecular and quantitative biology with the study of human diseases, and explores fundamental questions related to the cellular and molecular pathways leading to the disease development both in human and not-human biological models. Four additional laboratory modules in cytometry and imaging cytometry.

title: Molecular Biology of Prokaryotic Cells
description: This course will expand the knowledge about prokaryotic cells including the relationships among recombination, replication, and repair and the importance of organizing sequences in DNA, the mechanisms of regulation of gene expression, the newest advances in bacterial cell biology, and the coordination of cellular processes during the bacterial cell cycle.

title: Advanced Biotechnology
description: This course will cover methods and applications of biotechnology, examines present and future developments in this area.

title: Advanced Cell and Molecular Biology
description: The course entails a PhD-level exploration of the field of modern cell and molecular biology, with a focus on recent scientific achievements in these areas.

title: Gene Therapy
description: This graduate advanced course in gene therapy will cover different aspects of biology that are necessary to understand and design gene therapy strategies. These include aspects of molecular and cell biology, virology, immunology, genetics and medicine. Students in this course will learn about and critically discuss the strategies used in the latest gene therapy preclinical and clinical studies, and will also propose novel design strategies.

title: Applied Bioinformatics
description: This applied bioinformatics course combines the theoretical underpinnings of biological data analyses and information extraction with practical use bioinformatics tools at various levels of complexity to attain advanced user competencies.

title: Cellular Biophysics
description: This course will address topics in each of the three major divisions of Biophysics: bio-molecular structure, biophysical techniques, and biological mechanisms. The goal of the course is to introduce and critically discuss the central concepts of physical chemistry and their application to gain an in-depth understanding of the fundamental biological principles underlying cellular physiology.

title: Core Course in Business
description: Fundamentals of Finance and Entrepreneurship in two modules, thematically connected via a common case study, providing you with a solid introduction to financial statement analysis, management planning and control, corporate finance, and financial markets. The course then moves on to theories and practices of entrepreneurship and business and competitive strategy. The course has a capstone team project component, in place of a final exam.

title: Business Law
description: This course is an introductory course in business law, with emphasis on real world applicability in the field of business. Theory combined with practice-oriented exercises to develop a foundation in intellectual property, environmental law and corporate law.
prerequisite: BUS 101 Core Course in Business (5889) (C- and above)

title: University of Pittsburgh Component - Critical Care Medicine
description: The Critical Care Elective is offered to fourth year students interested in learning an organized approach to the diagnosis and management of acutely ill patients. The intensive care unit provides a unique educational environment where technology, basic science and multidisciplinary subspecialities are integrated. Students participate in daily rounds with CCM attendings and fellows.

title: Structural Mechanics I
description: This course will introduce students the basics of the structural mechanics.

title: Environmental Chemistry
description: The course teaches basic theories and background understanding to the undergraduate students who start civil and environmental engineering.

title: Environmental Engineering
description: This course will give the students fundamental science and principles of environmental engineering. It will include the control of water, soil and atmospheric pollution, provision of safe water supply, the proper disposal/recycle of wastewater.
prerequisite: CEE 201 Environmental Chemistry (4999) (D and above)

title: Structural Analysis
description: In this course, the students analyze statically determinate and indeterminate structures.
prerequisite: MAE 200 Structural Mechanics I (5010) (D and above) OR CEE 200 Structural Mechanics I (5005) (D and above)

title: Civil Engineering CAD and Surveying
description: This module will introduce the concept of civil engineering drawings and will impart the knowledge of surveying.

title: Structural Design – Concrete
description: The objective of this module is to prepare students for entry level structural engineering employment by providing them with abilities to design reinforced concrete structures. It is a direct application of preceding modules: Structural Analysis. This module will provide the basic design techniques for students to be ready for the succeeding module: Capstone Design. This module provides students with abilities to design reinforced concrete structural members such as beams, columns, slabs and foundations. The mechanics underlying the code design procedures are evaluated as well as their application to practical design problems.
prerequisite: CEE 203 Structural Analysis (5500) (D and above)

title: Structural Design – Steel
description: The objective of this module is to prepare students for entry level structural engineering employment by providing them with abilities to design steel structures. This module provides students with abilities to design steel structural members such as beams, columns, slabs and foundations.
prerequisite: CEE 203 Structural Analysis (5500) (D and above)

title: Geotechnical Engineering
description: In this course, the students will learn fundamental knowledge of geotechnical engineering (soil mechanics). This course involves the measurement of stress-strain, strength and permeability properties of soil and the development of theories based on these measured properties to predict the response of structures to static loading

title: Geotechnical Design
description: In this course, the students will learn how to design shallow and deep foundations (e.g., strip and spread footings, mats foundations). This course covers bearing capacity, settlement, and group effects of the various foundation types based on these measured properties to predict the response of structures to static loading. In addition, retaining structures, and slope stability, subsurface exploration, construction of deep foundations, and analysis of geotechnical structure are included.
prerequisite: CEE 302 Geotechnical Engineering (5896) (D and above)

title: Fluid Mechanics
description: This course aims to present the fundamentals of fluid mechanics for civil and environmental engineering students. Students will learn to calculate and design fluids at rest and movement and analyze fluid mechanics problems to implement them into the design of water infrastructure assets.

title: Hydraulics and Hydrology
description: The objective of this course is to present fundamental of hydraulics and hydrology for civil and environmental engineering students. Students will gain the skill of calculating and designing of pipe and open channel flow, and analyzing hydrological data to implement them into the design of water infrastructure assets.
prerequisite: MAE 300 Fluid Mechanics I (5926) (D and above) OR EME 275 Fluid Mechanics I (1988) (D and above) OR CEE 304 Fluid Mechanics (6348) (D and above)

title: Civil Engineering Materials
description: In this course, the students learn various types of civil engineering materials to apply civil engineering infra structures. The student can also learn engineering properties of various construction and materials testing specification.
prerequisite: ENG 102 Engineering Materials I (4708) (D and above)

title: Water and Wastewater Treatment Processes
description: The study and design of basic environmental unit processes to treat contaminants in water and wastewater for drinking and other different purposes.
prerequisite: CEE 201 Environmental Chemistry (4999) (D and above) AND CEE 202 Environmental Engineering (5499) (D and above)

title: Application of Geomatics in Civil Engineering
description: This course will teach students to work with Remote Sensing, Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) data, to process satellite data and apply data for the civil engineering projects. Students will be introduced to the Remote Sensing and GIS software tool to work with satellite data.
prerequisite: CEE 204 Civil Engineering CAD and Surveying (5002) (D and above) OR ECE 215 Surveying (3153) (D and above)

title: Engineering geology
description: This course aims to provide fundamental knowledge of the geological processes which lead to the formation of different types of minerals and rocks in nature along with their physical and mechanical characteristics; and, develop practical skills related to geoenvironmental engineering regarding soil and contaminant interaction, contaminated site characterization, and treatment approach selection.

title: Transportation Engineering
description: This course teaches applications of fundamental principles and methods of transportation engineering and planning in an urban and rural environment.
prerequisite: CEE 204 Civil Engineering CAD and Surveying (5002) (D and above)

title: Construction Technology and Management
description: This is a core course in the undergraduate Civil and Environmental Engineering program under the specialty of construction management. In this course the students will learn the technology and management of running the construction project. The main topics will be site operations, construction equipment, planning, scheduling, estimating and controlling in construction projects.
prerequisite: CEE 306 Civil Engineering Materials (5897) (D and above)

title: Behavior and Design of Structural System
description: The objective of this module is to provide students with abilities to conduct structural analysis and design as a whole system. It is a synchronization of previous modules: Structural Analysis, Structural Design Concrete and Structural Design Steel.
prerequisite: CEE 300 Structural Design – Concrete (5895) (D and above) AND CEE 301 Structural Design – Steel (6157) (D and above)

title: Foundation Engineering
description: In this course, the students will learn how to design different types of foundations. This course will focus on the selection of foundation type based on building site conditions and site constraints, determination of size and reinforcement of the foundation, and finally construction of foundation element.
prerequisite: ECE 306 Geotechnical Design (1043) (D and above) OR CEE 303 Geotechnical Design (6158) (D and above)

title: Solid and Hazardous Waste Management
description: The course aims to give civil engineering B.Sc. students the fundamental notions of solid waste management and manipulation techniques. It aims to make students, after being provided with a specific case accompanied by a waste characterization data, capable to propose an integrated waste management plan with appropriate elements.
prerequisite: CEE 202 Environmental Engineering (5499) (D and above)

title: Air Quality Management
description: This course provides an overview of air quality management to all the activities to help protect human health and the environment from the harmful effects of air pollution which will be illustrated as a cycle of inter-related elements.

title: Modern Information Technology in Construction
description: This course will introduce the theory of information systems, advanced spreadsheet modeling, relational database management systems, Building Information Modeling (BIM), and other state-of-the-art ICT tools relevant with construction and civil engineering. Students will be able to work with the basic and advanced BIM techniques for construction project planning, design, construction and operational phases; and will have a basic knowledge of mobile applications in the construction industry.
prerequisite: CEE 204 Civil Engineering CAD and Surveying (5002) (D and above)

title: Water Supply and Distribution Management
description: This course aims to present the fundamentals of Water Supply and Distribution Management. Students will learn to calculate and design Water Supply and Distribution systems and implement them into urban water infrastructure assets.
prerequisite: CEE 305 Hydraulics and Hydrology (6177) (D and above)

title: Pavement Design and Performance
description: This course is to provide students with an understanding of the analysis and design of highway pavements, including both flexible and rigid types. The students can design the pavement using the knowledge in both asphalt and Portland cement concrete materials, geotechnical engineering, and basic structural design obtained from previous courses.
prerequisite: CEE 306 Civil Engineering Materials (5897) (D and above) AND CEE 303 Geotechnical Design (6158) (D and above)

title: Individual Research Project in Civil & Environmental Engineering 1
description: This course will allow students to know how to conduct real research or practical engineering investigation. Students will learn the processes of research as well as research methods. The course will consider the effective management of research project.

title: Individual Research Project in Civil and Environmental Engineering II
description: This course is a continuation of “Individual Research Project in Civil and Environmental Engineering I” which allows more time to further develop knowledge and skills in the chosen topic. In line with the “Individual Research Project in Civil and Environmental Engineering I”, this course focuses on the application of knowledge and skill to the publication of research, patent, and conference proceedings.
prerequisite: CEE 463 Individual Research Project in Civil & Environmental Engineering 1 (6594) (C and above)

title: Structure and Properties of Concrete Materials
description: This course develops students' knowledge and skills required to appraise PCC engineering materials in order to be able to apply appropriate PCC material properties for PCC construction projects
prerequisite: CEE 306 Civil Engineering Materials (5897) (D and above)

title: Introduction to Finite Element Methods
description: This course will provide students an introduction to formulations and implementations of the Finite Element Methods and its application to solid and fluid mechanics. Various types of elements will be studied including trusses, beams, and plates.
prerequisite: CEE 200 Structural Mechanics I (5005) (D and above)

title: Building Information Modelling for Geotechnical Engineering
description: This course aims to acquaint students with the building information modelling for application in geotechnical engineering
prerequisite: CEE 303 Geotechnical Design (6158) (D and above)

title: Structural Design – Concrete II
description: The course aims to prepare students for entry-level structural engineering employment by providing them with abilities to design and analyze reinforced concrete structures.
prerequisite: CEE 300 Structural Design – Concrete (5895) (C- and above)

title: Pavement Materials
description: The pavement materials course gives the students a fundamental understanding of the behavior of soil, aggregate, and bituminous materials used to construct pavement structures. The characterization, tests, and engineering properties of these materials will be elaborated on in context with their field application and current practices and future trends in pavement materials.
prerequisite: CEE 302 Geotechnical Engineering (5896) (D and above) OR CEE 306 Civil Engineering Materials (5897) (D and above)

title: Chemistry Study Hour
description: Student study hour. Each session lasts 75 minutes and students are required to attend twice a week. Faculty will be supervising and available for assistance.

title: Survey of Environmental Sciences for Non-Science Majors
Introduction to Chemistry
description: It covers key topics essential for understanding the basic principles of chemical science, including matter and energy, atomic structure, gas laws, concentrations, chemical equilibrium, and organic compounds.
antirequisite: CHEM 090 Chemistry for Non-Science majors (152) (D+ and above)

title: General Chemistry I
description: This course begins by introducing the fundamental theories of quantum mechanics, in the context of atoms and molecules. Building on this foundation, the periodic properties of the elements are introduced in the context of electronic structure theory.

title: General Chemistry I lab
description: This course (which complements CHEM101) aims to provide students with basic laboratory skills, including (but not limited to): accurate measurement of mass, volume, temperature, and and pressure.
corequisite: CHEM 101 General Chemistry I (113) (C and above)

title: General Chemistry II
prerequisite: CHEM 101 General Chemistry I (113) (C and above)

title: General Chemistry II lab
prerequisite: CHEM 101L General Chemistry I lab (179) (C and above)
corequisite: CHEM 102 General Chemistry II (232) (C and above)

title: Introduction to Physical and Chemical Sciences
description: This course offers a foundational exploration of key physical and chemical processes occurring in everyday life. Students will examine atomic structure, nuclear and chemical reactions, as well as concepts related to motion and energy conversion, fostering a deeper scientific understanding applicable across disciplines.
antirequisite: CHEM 091 Survey of Physical Science (149) (D+ and above)

title: Introduction to Environmental Science
description: To understand current environmental problems, we need to consider physical, biological and chemical processes that are often the basis of those problems. This course will give you the skills necessary to address the environmental issues we are facing today by examining scientific principles and the application of those principles to natural systems. This course will survey some of the many environmental science topics at an introductory level, ultimately considering the sustainability of human activities on the planet.
antirequisite: CHEM 092 Survey of Environmental Sciences for Non-Science Majors (1149) (D+ and above)

title: Independent Study
description: This course provides an opportunity for a student to gain practical hands-on experience in a related field of interest.
