title: Advanced Applied Mathematics
description: This course reviews and deepens the advanced analytical and numerical methods to solve ODEs and PDEs. The whole course, lectures, and tutorials will be delivered through a mathematical software package capable to perform symbolical calculations. The module is designed for graduate students to cover their research needs concerning mathematical modeling via analytical, semi-analytical or numerical techniques.

title: Rocket Propulsion Fundamentals
description: This course is designed to introduce fundamental aspects of rocket propulsion to graduate students. The course builds on a basic knowledge of thermodynamics, including combustion and gas dynamics, all of which are initially reviewed. This is followed by the basic elements of rocket propulsion, introducing performance parameters and important components of a rocket propulsion system. Different types of propellants will be introduced and discussed, including the important non-chemical propellants. The performance of space flight for several flight regimes, namely atmospheric flight, near-space flight and deep-space flight are analyzed.

title: Modern Control Engineering
description: The course aims to provide a solid background for the understanding of modern control system concepts, analysis and design techniques. It helps in gaining advanced knowledge of control theory in manufacturing such as NC, CNC etc. It also works in developing hardware and software packages.

title: Computational and Unsteady Aerodynamics
description: The course provides deeper knowledge of applied aerodynamics by focusing on computational methods and unsteady flows. During the course, students first review fundamentals of ideal aerodynamics and then extend the scope to include computation of aerodynamic forces for arbitrary streamlined bodies using different panel methods. The course also covers boundary layer corrections to account for viscous drag. Corrections for high speed are also discussed by introducing various compressibility corrections. Unsteady ideal aerodynamics is introduced to examine the effects of sudden plunging, periodic heave and pitching of airfoils. PhD students will be required to develop an advanced numerical model for an applied problem either coupling unsteady aerodynamics with structures or vehicle motion.

title: Space Structure Design
description: The course aims to impart, via active project- and inquiry-based learning, advanced competencies in the design of bleeding edge space technologies, such as gyroscopic systems, vibration damping systems, satellite structures, composites, honeycombs, truss-cores and nanomaterials.

title: Computational Fluid Structure Interaction
description: The PhD level course aims to introduce the students to an important and complicated topic in engineering: Fluid Structure interaction (FSI) and its analysis by computational simulation. The students will learn to understand the physics, methods and models available for the study of FSI and how to apply them in engineering applications.

title: Advanced Manufacturing Processes and Strategies
description: This PhD-level graduate course aims to provide deep understanding of advanced manufacturing terminology and introduces principles, techniques and applications of abrasive and non-conventional machining processes as well as additive manufacturing. Course topic also includes philosophies, and practices developed by world-class manufacturers to meet current manufacturing challenges, such as lean production. Students are expected to carry out an independent study by project and term paper on the related topics.

title: Digital Transformation Concepts
description: This course focuses on developing a systematic understanding and knowledge of key concepts and principles for digital transformation and its current practices, tools and processes and future development. The course will also provide hands-on experience using digital transformation tools and methods to enhance product development and enterprises. The course topics include digital tools, methods to support continuous improvements, design for Industry 4.0, enterprise systems, smart product, virtual and augmented reality (VR&AR), digital twin for product development, model based definition/enterprise, lean digital workflow for product development, and digital transformation industrial case studies.

title: Advanced Materials and Composites
description: This course teaches the latest advances in engineered materials, with a particular focus on high-performance nanomaterials. Their applications in electronics, aerospace, automotive and human-machine interaction are being studied. The course discusses the properties and characteristics of nanomaterials, their integration with polymers, metals and fibre metal laminates and improving their mechanical performance and functional properties. It also teaches how to use machine learning tools and numerical modeling methods to predict mechanical behavior of composite materials.

title: Advanced Fluid Mechanics with Applications
description: This course aims to further enhance students understanding on the basic principles of fluid mechanics, alongside covering more advanced topics. These include turbulence modeling, microfluidics, fluid flow in porous media, multiphase flows, as well as fluid-structure interactions, and other developing fields of fluid dynamics. Students will study key and analytical concepts like boundary layer theory, order-of-magnitude analysis, time and volume averaging methods, modern fluid mechanics research computational methods, among others. Because of the diversity and scope of these topics, the course will focus one or two areas depending on students’ preferences and previous knowledge.

title: Strategic Management and Leadership
description: Today’s managers and leaders especially those in the public sector operate in an increasingly complex and challenging environment. The emerging socio-political, economic and technological developments demand that public managers reposition themselves, think and act strategically, and employ innovative methods in leading and managing organizations in order to meet the changing demands of various stakeholders. This module introduces the students with unique context within which public managers operate and challenges in leading and managing organizations in the public sector.

title: Organizational Behavior in the Public Sector
description: This course introduces GSPP and other graduate students to Organizational Behavior in the public sector. This course examines 1) the core functions of management and 2) the political socio-economic context in which today’s organizations operate. The course is designed to introduce accepted theories of management and real world applications. To achieve these goals, the course includes in-class group assignments, articles presentation, and final term paper. Lectures and class assignments given in the course are intended to help students understand the needs of modern public and private organizations, including emerging national and international trends. Students will read the assigned textbook as well as other readings posted on Moodle or distributed in-class.

title: Policy Tools for Addressing Inequality and Demographic Change
description: This course explores the interlinked domains of social policy, inequality, and demographic change through a public policy lens. Students will learn how to critically analyze income and non-income inequality, understand different welfare models, examine the design of family and labor policy, and assess the demographic challenges shaping future welfare systems. Using evidence-based tools and accessible data analysis (Stata, Python, Excel), students will be equipped to interpret key indicators and develop informed policy responses to inequality and social challenges in both developed and developing countries, including Kazakhstan.

title: Institutions and Development Policies
description: This course provides an analysis of the relationship between institutions and development policies. The impact of institutional frameworks in promoting development is the course’s core concern. Consideration will be given to key tensions between theory and practice that researchers and development practitioners have identified.

title: Circular Economy Strategy
description: This course is designed to introduce the circular economy (CE) to learners and provide insights and practice in applying CE strategy to a business context, be it in the private or public sector. Through a project-based learning approach, learners will work independently and in groups to apply CE strategies to organizational improvement.

title: International Political Economy
description: This course aims to introduce students at an advanced level with the contemporary issues in international political economy, theoretical frameworks, and research approaches to analyze the issues of international political economy.

title: Ethical Challenges in Governance
description: This is an advanced course that centers on normative values and ethical dilemmas in public policy.

title: Open Governance
description: The course is intended as an introduction to the emerging concepts of open government and open data from both theoretical and practical perspectives.

title: Public Policy and Health Issues
description: This course is an introduction to public policy in health and social issues, with special focus on countries and systems experiencing rapid demographic and epidemiological transitions. It will cover population health and development aspects, and the different approaches and methods of public policy in comparing present and future health-related challenges. It will examine the roles and relationships between public policies in planning, implementation and evaluation processes and different approaches of national systems in providing, regulating and paying for health care.

title: Good Governance and Corruption
description: The purpose of this course is to give students an opportunity to familiarize with such concepts, to understand how corruption and good governance promote development, to learn about what international organizations do to promote good governance and contrast corruption, and how they track their progress in both respects.

title: Political Economy of State-Building
description: This course examines processes, institutions, and functions that make the modern state. The course is designed to teach students to understand the theoretical concepts and empirical literature for the subject.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Governance
description: This course explores the intersection of artificial intelligence (AI) and governance, examining how AI technologies are transforming public administration, policy-making, and citizen engagement. Through case studies, theoretical readings, and practical tools, students will critically analyze the opportunities and challenges of AI adoption in the public sector.

title: International Financial Policy
description: This course focuses on selected analytical and policy issues relating to international financial markets and policies.

title: Globalisation and Public Policy
description: This course is designed for students working in public, private or non-profit sectors with some background in political economy and policy making. It introduces students to the analysis of globalization – widening and deepening of international interconnectedness –and its impacts on national policy making substance and processes. Some of the questions this course deals with include what are the major issues brought forward by globalization, how can we think about them analytically, and what kinds of policy options are available to policy makers under the opportunities and constraints placed by globalization.

title: Marketing Public Policy
description: This practice-based marketing public policy course will help participants understand complexity and communication theories, media management, public opinion and public consultation principles, and the application of effective communication strategies.

title: Communications for Public Leadership
description: This course provides practical techniques to improve student's spoken and written abilities, and helps them to practice these skills in challenging real-world situations, from winning over hostile audiences to writing punchy op-eds suitable for publication in global media outlets. Communication For Public Leadership will also provide students with a deeper understanding of the styles and theories of communication and persuasion needed to succeed in public life, in an exhilarating intellectual journey that moves from Aristotle and Cicero to the TED conference.

title: Public Sector Innovation
description: This class is for students who are interested in public sector organizations and their innovation and reform, especially for the MPP, MPA, and PhD students in public policy. This course examines core functions of public sector innovation (PSI) and management and the political, socio-economic context within which organizations operate in different sectors, focusing on innovation.

title: Science and Technology Policy
description: The course is intended as an introduction to the concept of science and technology politics from both theoretical and practical perspectives.

title: Agricultural Policy Analysis
description: The course examines the design, implementation, and impact of agricultural policies. Students will examine the role of agriculture in economic development and food systems by applying economic principles to analyze key policy instruments, such as subsidies, price supports, and quotas. Through exercises and case studies, students will gain a practical understanding of how agricultural policies influence market outcomes and rural livelihoods. The course also covers trade policy, regional integration, and contemporary challenges in the agricultural and food sectors. Topics include agricultural trade, non-tariff barriers, the EAEU and EU’s CAP frameworks, food security, land governance, and environmental sustainability. Case studies and guest lectures from regional experts will provide practical insights. Students will be assessed based on their class participation, a midterm exam, group presentations, and case study analysis.

title: Health System and Policy
description: This is an introductory course on health, healthcare system and health policy. The course provides an overview and application of healthcare and health policy related key concepts needed for policy analyst and managers. During this course students will apply critical concepts from Public Health, Healthcare Economics, Policy Analysis, and Systems Thinking to health policy challenges facing middle income countries.

title: Governance Through Networks: Theory and Practice
description: Network governance refers to inclusive and participatory approaches to policy-making, collective action, and implementation. This course is designed to addresses ways to work together across institutional, geographic, economic, and social boundaries in many different policy domains, such as natural resource management, public health, and community and economic development.

title: Game Theory and Public Policy
description: Game theory is a framework for analyzing strategic interactions between rational actors. The tools of game theory are employed widely to understand a variety of phenomena in politics, economics, business, and biology. This course will introduce the fundamentals of game theory and guide the student through some prominent applications of it, with special emphasis on applications in public policy. The course will also touch on basic social choice theory and the spatial model.

title: Development Assistance and Governance
description: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be equipped with knowledge of the foundations of and issues/challenges in development assistance and public administration reform. Topics will include an introduction to the key institutions of development assistance, the role of international organizations in promoting public administration reform, internal governance of international development organizations. The assessment strategy will include both open-book/takeaway assignments and in-class/controlled env. assessments in addition to class participation.

title: Urban Mobility Policy in the Age of the Smart City
description: This ‘applied public policy’ elective links public policy principles with key urban transport policy choices and the transport policy opportunities and challenges arising from recent technological change. While focusing on urban transport it also provides opportunities to apply concepts from other public policy courses. Although the course would provide an introduction for students hoping to go further on urban transport issues, the course is primarily aimed at policy generalists. Many policy-related professionals need to be discerning consumers of both urban transport policy analysis and of pitches from technology system and service vendors. This course will not make its participants urban transport experts but it will prepare them to engage in critical and constructive discussion with technical experts in urban transport and transport-related technology applications. The course draws on examples from a variety of places and situations around the world.

title: Sustainable Development and Environmental Governance
description: This course will provide a comprehensive overview of the sustainable development concept and entailing public policies through an inter-disciplinary framework.

title: Energy Systems and Climate Policy
description: This course examines the role played by various energy resources in fueling modern economic growth from early industrialization through present and provide a basic understanding of the technology, economics, social, and political aspects of various energy systems (non-renewable and renewable) for public policy analysis and the various energy options for climate change mitigation and adaptation. This course is organized into five broad sections: energy and economic development; non-renewable energy utilization and constraints; renewable energy policy and options; climate change science and policy; energy transition and sustainability. While the course is pitched in a larger international context, specific examples of energy policy issues relevant to Kazakhstan and the Central Asian region are covered in each lecture.

title: Global Energy Policy
description: This course applies the policy cycle to energy sector whereby a variety of approaches are analyzed at the stages of agenda setting, formulation, decision-making, implementation and evaluation. Drawing on cases from the Global North and South, including Central Asian region and Kazakhstan specifically, a mix of energy policies and associated instruments are critically examined. The perspective taken is that of a policy maker confronting decisions about the design and implementation of energy policy that is informed by the learning from practices in different contexts, while focusing on ways that public policy can affect social and environmental outcomes.

title: Water Resources Policy and Management
description: Understand the concept of integrated water resources management (IWRM) through an inter-disciplinary approach, apply holistic models on IWRM for the development of better policy decisions and incorporate the complexities of transboundary water systems on policy frameworks.

title: New Technologies and Public Policy
description: This module will focus on TECH FOR GOOD or how new technologies can be used to improve the welfare of societies and how to minimize their harm. This course is also known as ABCD-EFGHIJ. ABCD refers to new, disruptive technologies (AI, Autonomous Systems, Blockchain, Cloud and Quantum Computing, Cryptocurrencies (Bitcoin/Ethereum, Libra, etc), Data Analytics, 3D, 5G, etc). We will examine the benefits, risks and problems associated with ABCD in terms of EFGHIJ (Education, Energy, Economic Development, Freedom/privacy, Finance/Banks, Government/Governance, Healthcare, Jobs and Inequality, Inclusion etc).

title: Economic Applications for Public Managers
description: This subject provides a public sector manager's guide to key economic principles, and their applications to public sector activity. Public policy issues are addressed within an economic paradigm. The aim is to help public sector managers make better decisions when allocating scarce resources, when pricing and delivering public sector goods and services and when designing regulations.

title: Program Evaluation
description: Public resources are limited, and decisions regarding how to use these scarce public resources must be informed by an understanding of how well public programs and policies produce their desired outcomes. This course will introduce you to the art and science of evaluation. You will learn methods of collecting, analyzing, interpreting, and communicating information used in evaluation studies.

title: Developing Dissertation Research
description: This zero-credit rated course is to offer guidance and direction to PhD students on their dissertations across Fall, Spring and Summer semesters x 4 years

title: Microeconomics in the Public Sector
description: Microeconomics for new PhD in Public Policy students that an economic framework for the analysis of public policy.

title: Macroeconomics in Public Sector
description: This module examines the essential key macroeconomic policy instruments used in the attainment of policy objectives such as full employment, price stability, and economic growth.

title: Public Administration and Management
description: Combining historical, contextual and theoretical perspectives, this course gives students a comprehensive overview of the disciplines of Public Administration and Management and focuses on the practical implications of public administration theory.

title: Human Resource Management
description: Situated in the context of the public sector, this module invites you to ask how you can manage and lead people both internal and external to an organization and how you can create a high-performing workforce that is resilient in responding to external shocks and adaptable to dynamic environments. The module aims to expose you to various theories and perspectives from a wide range of academic disciplines, ranging from public and business administration to political science and psychology. Case studies are introduced to bridge theories and practices.

title: Statistics in Public Policy
description: The purpose of this course is to equip students with the necessary statistical tools and model building expertise that are related to the empirical analysis of public policy problems in a professional environment. Students can apply these tools for policy evaluation in particular and testing social science hypotheses and explaining relationships in general. The course begins with an introduction to statistical and probability theory, probability distributions, types of data, hypothesis testing, linear regression, logistics regression, modeling panel data, and ends with an introduction to time series analysis.

title: Research Design (qualitative and quantitative)
description: This module focuses on research design through the analysis of research papers using the various techniques of qualitative and mixed methods of empirical analysis.

title: Advanced Quantitative Methods
description: The content of this module includes: the identification of, access to and analysis of, social science quantitative data bases relevant to public policy issues. Statistical techniques to explore relationships among variables (correlation; partial correlation; multiple regression; logistic regression; factor analysis; structural equation modelling). Statistical techniques to compare groups (non-parametric statistics; t-tests; multi-analysis of variance). Use of the above techniques to interrogate existing social science data bases. Critical review of quantitative research used as the basis of evidence in public policy.

title: Law, Governance and Public Policy
description: The course exposes students to essential aspects of law of particular relevance to public policy, so as to equip them with the basic skills necessary to access, understand and use law in developing and implementing legitimate and effective policies. Students will compare, analyse and assess the interaction between law and public policy in different governance settings, particularly in development policy context.

title: Advanced Qualitative Methods
description: The Content of this module include the following: Identification of, access to and analysis of, social science qualitative databases relevant to public policy issues. Main research methods associated with qualitative research: ethnography / participant observation; qualitative interviewing; focus groups; language based approaches to the collection of qualitative data, such as discourse and conversation analysis; the collection and qualitative analysis of texts and documents. Sampling, reliability and validity in qualitative research. Contrast between qualitative and quantitative research. Critical review of qualitative research used as basis of evidence in public policy.

title: Public Policy and Analysis
description: This module will build on students’ understanding of the public policy process, It considers a number of fundamental questions including: 1) rationales for collective interference in private affairs; 2) limitations to collective action; 3) generic instruments of public policy; 4) how can social costs and benefits be measured; and 5) what are the appropriate roles of policy analysts in democratic societies.

title: Politics of Public Policy
description: The first part of the module explores the institutions, practices, cultures, interests, and actors of modern political systems, whereas the second part focuses on modern political theories and ideologies that have conditioned the possibilities and limitations of policymaking.

title: Comparative Policy-Making and Public Policy
description: This course will examine how different countries handle and address political, social, and economic problems in different policy contexts.

title: Behavioral Economics and Public Policy
description: This course presents and discusses behavioral regularities that are of potential importance for public policy.

title: PhD Qualifying Examination: Field Exam
description: The PhD field exam is designed to test whether the PhD students have mastered the required skillset to be proficient researchers in their area of inquiry.

title: Thesis Preparation and Writing
description: Years 3 & 4 will involve thesis preparation and writing where the students will work closely with allocated supervisors who will agree regular progress meetings (minimum of 2 per semester).
prerequisite: DPP 689 PhD Qualifying Examinations (4830) (P) AND DPP 699 Thesis Design and Written Proposal (4831) (B- and above)

title: Thesis Preparation and Writing
description: Years 3 & 4 will involve thesis preparation and writing where the students will work closely with allocated supervisors who will agree regular progress meetings (minimum of 2 per semester).

title: Fundamentals of Data Science
description: This course is a one-semester course intended for graduate students in Data Science graduate programs. It is designed to introduce object-based programming and programming concepts with Python, Algorithm analysis and design, basic data structures, and Scientific computation and visualization with Python. The course will include the following sub topics; Introduction to Python and its basic data types; Object-oriented programming with Python; Recursion; Algorithm analysis; Searching and sorting; Abstract data types such as linked lists, stacks, queues, priority queues, trees, hashes and their implementation in Python; Vectors and matrices in Python; Plotting and visualization with Python; Solving systems of linear equations with Python. Students will gain experience through assignments and projects, with an emphasis on proper data science practices with appropriate applications.

title: Probability and Statistics for Data Science
description: The fundamental concepts of probability are essential to solve the data science problem. This course will introduce a broad range of probability theory and mathematical statistics that emphasizes the probabilistic foundations required to understand probability models and statistical. The topics covered include fundamentals of probability theory, statistical inference and graph data structure, including probabilistic models, random variables, useful distributions, expectations, the law of large numbers, the central limit theorem, point and confidence interval estimation, hypothesis tests, basic data structure and algorithms for graphs.

title: Data Mining and Decision Support
description: The course will start with setting the context by exploring the relationships between data mining, artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, and statistics fields. It will then introduce knowledge representation, input preparation (preprocessing), fundamental data mining techniques (like probabilistic modeling, linear modeling, association mining, etc.), minimum description length (MDL) principle, validation techniques, decision trees, association rules, instance-based learning models, data transformations, data projections, Bayesian methods, and ensemble learning techniques (bagging, boosting, stacking, etc.) within the supervised, unsupervised and semi-supervised learning frameworks. Data visualization and warehousing methods along with examples from various application areas will also be visited to illustrate the use of data mining in decision support systems and processes.

title: Database Management Systems
description: This course is a one-semester course intended for graduate students in Data Science and Computer Science graduate programs. This course focuses on the design, analysis and implementation of database management systems. Most of the topics will be covered as case studies using commercial and open-source database components such that the students can learn a wide-range of tools and techniques and also assess the trade-offs. Student will implement their own database management system as the integrated course project. Therefore, strong programming skills are required. The course will cover topics such as relational, document, key/value data models, storage models and architectures, query languages (e.g. SQL), various types of indexing, transaction management and recovery, query processing, distribute/parallel database architectures, and big data and NoSQL database models and systems.

title: Information Retrieval
description: Information retrieval (IR) is a discipline concerned with processing, storage, and search of information in large collections of unstructured documents. With development of the internet IR techniques have become a key enabler for accessing the vast amount of online information, with strong social and economic impact. This course is intended for students interested in theoretical foundations of IR and practical experience in building IR systems. During this course, we will discuss a wide variety of IR tasks, approaches, and tools. The course is accompanied by a set of practical assignments that reflect the main steps of the IR pipeline: document processing, indexing, search, and evaluation of results. In addition, we will discuss key research papers in the field of IR in a series of seminars.
prerequisite: DS 501 Fundamentals of Data Science (5218) (C- and above) OR CSCI 501 Software Principles and Practice (2408) (C- and above)

title: Process and Project Management
description: This course is a one-semester course intended for graduate students in Data Science graduate program. In this course, students will learn the concepts of process and project management, professional practices, software lifecycle, process models, requirements engineering, and design. Students will be taught theoretical concepts, applications, tools, processes, and practical insights to help them understand how to successfully manage projects in a wide variety of industries including software development and information technology. Students will be exposed to study aids, real-time projects, and tools to provide plenty of hands-on practice.

title: Data-Driven Innovation
description: With the rapid advance of information technologies, data is emerging as the world's most important resource. Data-driven innovation offers a huge potential for economic, social and technological progress. In this course, students will learn and discuss concepts such as data-driven research and development, transforming traditional goods and services to data-intensive products, optimizing processes, logistics and delivery using data-driven techniques, and personalized marketing using data analytics, social networking and cloud computing. The course will also discuss how organizational evolution and optimization can be facilitated using data-driven techniques as an accelerator. The students will engage in a semester-long team-based project to create a data-driven innovation project proposal for a governmental or private organization.

title: Thesis Proposal
description: Students are led through the processes required to plan and initiate an independent research project that will eventually lead to a thesis. Early on, students are required to finalize their topic and secure the participation of a thesis advisor. They must then develop a research proposal based on a literature analysis of the chosen topic, defend the proposal, and then begin the execution of the project.
prerequisite: SEDS 591 Research Methods (3184) (C- and above)

title: Thesis
description: The student will conduct independent work under the direction of a supervisor on a research project in the student's designated area of inquiry. This work will culminate in a thesis document that the student must successfully defend. The project itself should demonstrate student mastery of the some or all of the stages of the Data Science life cycle, such as data acquisition, storage, preparation / cleaning, analytics & data mining, modeling & machine learning, and visualization.
prerequisite: DS 693 Thesis Proposal (5915) (P)

title: Advanced Data Mining and Decision Support
description: Today’s modern and digital world houses vast sources of data which are increasing exponentially as we shift to industry 4.0 practices and plan to have almost every electronic device connected by the use of Internet of Things (IoT) technologies. Analyzing data to identify patterns of interest and to make future projections is a very important feedback for improving processes and procedures. This course teaches modern data mining solutions and illustrates how they are used in decision support systems which are becoming increasingly ubiquitous in all business and industrial sectors. The topics to be covered include knowledge representation, input preparation (preprocessing), fundamental data mining techniques (like probabilistic modeling, linear modeling, association mining, etc.), minimum description length (MDL) principle, validation techniques, decision trees, association rules, instance-based learning models, data transformations, data projections, Bayesian methods, ensemble learning techniques (bagging, boosting, stacking, etc.), visualization, and warehousing within the supervised, unsupervised and semi-supervised learning frameworks.

title: Advanced Information Retrieval
description: Information retrieval (IR) is a discipline concerned with processing, storage, and search of information in large collections of unstructured documents. With development of the internet IR techniques have become a key enabler for accessing the vast amount of online information, with strong social and economic impact. This course is intended for Doctoral students interested in theoretical foundations of IR and practical experience in building IR systems. During this course, we will discuss a wide variety of IR tasks, approaches, and tools. The course is accompanied by a set of practical assignments that reflect the main steps of the IR pipeline: document processing, indexing, search, and evaluation of results. We will discuss key research papers in the field of IR in a series of seminars, and students will be working on and presenting their own projects at the end of the semester.

title: Beginning Dutch I
description: This course is for beginners. During the course we will focus on all 4 main skills of language-learning: reading, listening, writing and speaking.

title: Intermediate Dutch I
description: This course is for medium advanced students. During the course we will focus on all 4 main skills of language-learning: reading, listening, writing and speaking, starting on level A2 and moving towards level B1.
prerequisite: DUT 102 Beginning Dutch II (8073) (C- and above)

title: Introduction to Eurasia
description: This course focuses on major contributions to the development of study of the Eurasian region in a broad range of fields of scholarship.

title: General Methodology
description: This course covers the basic foundations of research training across different disciplines, instructing students on how to choose and refine their thesis topic, to plan field trips to archives and research sites, to take accurate and detailed notes, to plan their writing, and to present their work orally.

title: Disciplinary Methodology
description: This course is designed to support MAES students in the preparation of a literature review for their project, which can be used both in their research proposal at the end of the first year, and for the writing of the thesis throughout the second year. The course will focus on the development of graduate level academic reading and research skills, critical engagement with primary and secondary source materials, and the development of a theoretical frame, for the original empirical research which is expected of every student. Students will be working closely with course instructor and their future supervisors, who will advise on the specific readings most suitable for their topic.

title: Thesis I
description: Students must write a thesis of 24,500 words based on original research over two semesters in the second year of the MA in Eurasian Studies
prerequisite: EAS 500 Introduction to Eurasia (1632) (C- and above) AND EAS 501 General Methodology (1633) (C- and above) AND EAS 502 Disciplinary Methodology (1379) (C- and above)

title: Thesis II
description: Student must write a thesis of 24500 words based on original research over two semesters in the second year of the MA in Eurasian Studies.
prerequisite: EAS 500 Introduction to Eurasia (1632) (C- and above) AND EAS 501 General Methodology (1633) (C- and above) AND EAS 502 Disciplinary Methodology (1379) (C- and above) AND EAS 503 Thesis I (2141) (C- and above)

title: Research and Fieldwork Practicum
description: The summer research practicum is compulsory for students on the MA programme in Eurasian Studies, and also open to those on other MA programmes. Students will spend a minimum of 200 hours over the summer engaged in primary research for their thesis topic.

title: Viva-Voce Examination
description: Viva-Voce examination for the final thesis, with the student's thesis committee.
prerequisite: EAS 503 Thesis I (2141) (C- and above)

title: Independent Study in Eurasian Studies
description: This course prepares MA students for conducting independent research in Eurasian studies.

title: Topics in Eurasian Studies
description: This course is an elective course in Eurasian humanities. It meets with a lower-level course.

title: Critical Issues in Eurasian Studies
description: This course is an elective course in Eurasian humanities. It meets with a lower-level course.

title: Topics in Eurasian Social Sciences
description: This course is an elective course in Eurasian humanities. It meets with a lower-level course.

title: Introduction to Eurasia
description: The course introduces the multidisciplinary field of Eurasian studies.

title: Critical Issues in Eurasian Studies
description: The course is an intensive introduction to critical issues in Eurasian Studies.

title: Elective in Eurasian Humanities
description: This course is an elective course in Eurasian humanities. It meets with a lower-level course.

title: Elective in Eurasian Social Sciences
description: This course is an elective course in Eurasian social sciences. It meets with a lower-level course.

title: Elective 2 in Eurasian Humanities
description: This course is an elective course in Eurasian humanities. It meets with a lower-level course.

title: Elective 2 in Social Sciences
description: This course is an elective course in Eurasian humanities. It meets with a lower-level course.

title: Proseminar in Eurasian Humanities
description: This course is an intensive introduction to a discipline or field in Eurasian humanities.

title: Proseminar in Eurasian Social Sciences
description: This course is an intensive introduction to a discipline or field in Eurasian social sciences.

title: Independent Study in Eurasian Studies
description: This course meets with another lower-level course in Eurasian Studies or another subject.

title: Doctoral Seminar in Eurasian Studies I
description: This course is devoted to preparation of the outline for the student’s doctoral dissertation.

title: Doctoral Seminar in Eurasian Studies II
description: This course is devoted to preparation of the outline for the student’s doctoral dissertation.

title: Qualifying Examination
description: Preparation for and taking of the doctoral qualifying examination.

title: Human Rights and Cultural Differences
description: In this course you will acquire the tools to analyze rights-talk and learn to appreciate the relevance of history for our understanding of human rights as well as the purpose and relevance of normative theories.

title: Doctoral Thesis in Eurasian Studies
description: This course is designed to facilitate the writing and submission and defense of the doctoral thesis before the thesis examiners. The thesis must be completed according to the Format and Style Guidelines of the Ph.D. in Eurasian Studies Program.

title: Dissertation Research in Eurasian Studies
description: This course is devoted to research and writing of the student’s doctoral dissertation.

title: Advance Sensors and Actuators
description: Principles & practice of power systems: steady state analysis of AC & DC motors, electrical motor selection; motor performance & prediction; electro-hydraulic systems; pneumatic systems; simulation & modelling; mechanical power transmission; physics of sensing & sensor design; sensor specification & dynamics; experimental error analysis; measurement uncertainty

title: Artificial Intelligence in Medicine
description: This course is an introduction to statistical data analysis. Topics are chosen from applied probability, sampling, estimation, hypothesis testing, linear regression, analysis of variance, categorical data analysis, and nonparametric statistics.

title: Biology, Physiology and Human Anatomy for Engineers
Biomaterials
description: An introduction to the chemistry and physics of soft material systems (polymers, colloids, organized surfactant systems and others), emphasizing the connection between microscopic structure and macroscopic physical properties.

title: Biosensors
description: Review of biosensors in use and under development and their application in vivo and in vitro monitoring of humans.

title: Medical Imaging: Basics, Applications and Perspectives
description: This course provides discussions and insights into the Principles of medical ultrasound, basics of Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), X-ray diagnostics and X-ray computed tomography (CT), Contrast enhanced medical imaging, Devices for Diagnostics of function of inner organs and systems, Devices for Diagnostics of function of inner organs II: Electroencephalography (EEG) and Electrocardiography (ECG) and Image Processing techniques.

title: Medical devices for therapy
description: The course covers the broad topics on devices for intensive care, Surgical instrumentation, Implants & stents, Artificial organs and devices for organ compensation / handicap, Biophysical modalities for therapy and drug delivery and Image-guided clinical interventions.

title: Telemedicine
description: This course focuses on a systematic approach to the design of analog electronic circuits.

title: Biomedical Signal Processing
description: This course presents the fundamentals of digital signal processing with particular emphasis on problems in biomedical research and clinical medicine.

title: Geomatics
description: NA

title: Surveying
description: This module focuses on understanding and applications of surveying methodologies and technologies: topographic surveying, boundary surveying, exercises using state-of-the-art equipment and data capture and analysis techniques.

title: Civil Engineering CAD
description: This module introduces students to civil engineering theories, tools, and design process for infrastructure projects such as highways, bridges, dams and land development. Design projects include feasibility study, engineering evaluation of site, and layout design of lots, buildings, streets, sewers, etc. The concepts of the site-investigation and urban infrastructures issues will be introduced. The module includes design cases of civil infrastructure projects with an emphasis on technical solutions as well as project impact on the environmental, social and economic factors.

title: Structural Analysis I
description: The module provides the students with fundamental analysis methods which they can apply to analyze and design a range of statically determinate structures. More specifically students will be confident to analyze the beam, column and frame; to determine the deflection; and to perform stress/strain analysis.
prerequisite: BENG 117 Engineering Mechanics (740) (D and above)

title: Environmental Chemistry
description: This course aims to provide students with the skills and knowledge needed to understand chemistry and chemical processes, to enable students to be aware of environmental issues in the world and to stimulate interest in, and care for the environment.

title: Hydraulics
description: This course aims to introduce fundamentals of hydraulic systems and hydraulic systems design and to provide the skills needed to solve practical civil engineering problems related to hydraulic systems.

title: Civil Engineering Design
description: This module introduces students to civil engineering theories, tools, and design process for infrastructure projects such as highways, bridges, dams and land development.
prerequisite: BENG 102 Engineering Graphics and Models (727) (D and above)

title: Civil Engineering Materials
prerequisite: BENG 221 Engineering Materials (47) (D and above)

title: Construction Management and Practice
prerequisite: BENG 148 Engineering Practice (1073) (D and above)

title: Geotechnical Design
prerequisite: ECE 210 Soil Mechanics (862) (D and above)

title: Structural Engineering Applications I
prerequisite: ECE 213 Structural Engineering Analysis (863) (D and above) OR ECE 217 Structural Analysis I (3156) (D and above)

title: Structural Engineering Applications II
prerequisite: ECE 213 Structural Engineering Analysis (863) (D and above) OR ECE 217 Structural Analysis I (3156) (D and above)

title: Structural Design - Concrete
description: The objective of this module is to prepare student for entry level structural engineering employment by providing them with abilities to design reinforced concrete structures.
prerequisite: ECE 479 Structural Analysis II (2460) (C- and above)

title: Structural Design – Steel
description: The objective of this module is to prepare students for entry level structural engineering employment by providing them with abilities to design steel structures. This module provides students with abilities to design steel structural members such as trusses, beams, columns, and slabs.

title: Engineering Hydrology
description: This course aims to introduce the fundamentals of hydrology, modeling in hydrology, and applications for civil engineering and to provide the skills needed to solve practical civil engineering hydrology problems.

title: Construction Technologies and Processes
prerequisite: BENG 148 Engineering Practice (1073) (D and above) AND ECE 302 Civil Engineering Materials (1040) (D and above)

title: Environmental Engineering
prerequisite: ECE 473 Environmental Systems (1953) (D and above) OR ECE 218 Environmental Chemistry (3296) (D and above)

title: Highway Engineering
prerequisite: ECE 302 Civil Engineering Materials (1040) (D and above)

title: Modern Information Technology in Construction
description: The aim of this module is to help civil engineering students: 1) to learn and understand the relevant IT tools which can be applied in their professional careers in construction and civil engineering 2) to use these tools to evaluate and solve a variety of engineering problems 3) to create innovative engineering analysis and design solutions.

title: Behaviour and Design of Structural System
description: This module covers a wide range of critical topics in structural analysis and design including structural load resisting system; structural stiffness, stability and integrity; nonlinearity and plastic collapse mechanism; introduction to finite element methods and innovative structural systems.
prerequisite: (ECE 318 Structural Design - Concrete (3709) (D and above) OR ECE 314 Structural Engineering Applications I (1042) (D and above)) AND (ECE 319 Structural Design – Steel (4038) (D and above) OR ECE 315 Structural Engineering Applications II (1041) (D and above))

title: Prestressed Concrete Design
description: This course covers the basic theory and design methods of prestressed concrete structures. Principles of prestressing, constituent material, loading and allowable stresses, working and ultimate stress analysis and design, shear and torsion, deflections, prestress losses, continuous beams, composite beams, and two-way slab.

title: Structure and Properties of Concrete Materials
description: This course develop students' knowledge and skills required to appraise PCC engineering materials in order to be able to apply appropriate PCC material properties for PCC construction projects

title: Introduction to Finite Element Methods
description: This course will provide students an introduction to formulations and implementations of the Finite Element Method and its application to solid and fluid mechanics.

title: Water and Wastewater Treatment Processes
description: This course will give the students knowledge on softening, coagulation, flocculation, sedimentation, granular flirtation, adsorption, membrane separation, ion exchange, biological treatment, chlorination, ozonation, UV radiation.
prerequisite: ECE 218 Environmental Chemistry (3296) (D and above)

title: Environmental Systems
description: This course is the second environmental module and expands upon the Environmental Engineering module.

title: Advanced Structural Engineering
description: By completing this module, students will gain understanding of static and kinematic indeterminacy, structural flexibility and stiffness, matrix structural analysis, etc.
prerequisite: ECE 315 Structural Engineering Applications II (1041) (D and above)

title: Capstone Project II
description: School of Engineering Capstone project is designed to be reflection of a culminating set of personal, academic, and professional experiences.
prerequisite: ECE 401 Capstone Project 1 (1270) (D and above)

title: Structural Analysis II
description: The module provides the students with advanced analysis methods which they can apply to analyze and design a range of statically indeterminate structures. More specifically students will be confident to evaluate deflections, to analyze the statically indeterminate structural system, to evaluate the structure under movable loads and to apply different methods for structural analysis.
prerequisite: ECE 217 Structural Analysis I (3156) (D and above)

title: Individual Research Projects in Civil Engineering
description: This course will provide students detailed information about how and what to research in civil and environmental engineering.

title: Solid and Hazardous Waste Management
description: The course aims to give civil engineering B.Sc. students the fundamental notions of solid waste management and manipulation techniques. It aims to make students, after being provided with a specific case accompanied by a waste characterization data, capable to propose an integrated waste management plan with appropriate elements.
prerequisite: ECE 405 Environmental Engineering (1265) (C- and above)

title: Introduction to Chemical Engineering
description: This course is designed to introduce the Chemical Engineering students basic chemical engineering concepts and methods of system analysis.

title: Foundations of Unit Operations
description: The course focuses on the basic essentials of the typical unit operations required to provide the functioning of a chemical plant in a safe, efficient, and sustainable manner.

title: Engineering Fluid Mechanics
description: This course aims at developing and enhancing students' knowledge and awareness of fluid mechanics and its applications in chemical engineering systems namely unit operations performance, sizing, and selection.

title: Computational methods in Chemical Engineering-I

title: Separation Processes-I
prerequisite: ECHE 319 Chemical Engineering Thermodynamics (1218) (D and above)

title: Separation Processes II
description: Fundamentals of equilibrium-stage and continuous contacting operations. Applications of principles to distillation, absorption/stripping, extraction, absorption, and other separation technologies.
prerequisite: ECHE 126 Introduction to Chemical Engineering (33) (D and above) AND ECHE 225 Heat and Mass Transfer Operations (541) (D and above)

title: Research Practice
description: The course aims to provide students with the opportunity to apply research methods. The students will work in groups that will choose a research topic offered and work on this throughout the semester.

title: Chemical Plant Design and Optimization
description: This course addresses the conceptual and detailed design of chemical processes together with plant wide optimization and energy integration (pinch technology).

title: Chemical Reaction Engineering 2
description: This course presents the main concepts and principles regarding the design of non-ideal reactors and covers the fundamentals of heterogeneous reacting systems. Emphasis is given on algorithm development and problem solving.

title: Process Dynamics and Control
description: This course aims to introduce basic theories of control engineering with its application in chemical process design. Process dynamics modeling basics will also be presented.

title: Capstone project 1

title: Advanced Process Simulation
description: The main objective of this course is to introduce advanced tools to chemical engineering students to perform rigorous plant simulation and detailed optimization.
prerequisite: ECHE 323 Computational methods in Chemical Engineering-I (1272) (D and above)

title: Polymer Processing and Rheology
description: The objective of the course is to give Engineering students a working understanding of the salient features of polymeric materials, including structure, rheological properties and processing. This course will cover the application and the analysis of several key processing operations for polymeric materials, namely extrusion, injection molding and calendering. Prior to this, the structure of polymeric materials and their rheological behavior and characterization will be reviewed, as they relate to processing. As part of the course, the students undertake an individual research project of computational (simulation and analysis of some polymer processing operation, possibly outside those covered in the class) or experimental (measurement of an important property of a polymer system, such as viscosity or glass transition temperature) nature. The final grade is the result of a final exam, a project and eight homework assignments. The course is open to Engineering students outside CHE, with demonstrated competence in Fluid Mechanics or Computational Methods. Such students might undertake a project related to polymer processing from the point of view of their particular discipline.

title: Oil and Gas Engineering
antirequisite: BENG 442 Industrial Pollution Prevention and Control (1274) ( and above)

title: Introduction to Molecular Modeling Methods
description: This course offers an introduction to the basic theory, methodology, and applications of molecular modeling as a tool in chemical and materials research. Topics include random walk simulations, molecular dynamics, Monte Carlo, electronic structure calculations, and materials informatics. The methods and concepts are illustrated by extensive computer exercises.

title: Electrochemical Engineering and Corrosion Protection
description: This course aims to gain basic knowledge in eletrochemical processes, application of electrochemistry in the fields of fuel cells, batteries, electrolytic processes/metallurgy, corrosion and corrosion protection with focus on oil & gas industry; to provide knowledge and skills in electrochemical calculations and experimental methods in electrochemistry and corrosion protection.
prerequisite: ECHE 222 Chemistry I (731) (D and above)

title: Capstone Project II
description: This course is designed for chemical engineers to be a reflection of their personal, academic, and professional experiences.
prerequisite: ECHE 418 Capstone project 1 (1278) (D and above)

title: Chemical Reaction Engineering
description: This module covers the topics of Mole balances, Conversion and reactor sizing, Rate laws and stoichiometry, Isothermal reactor design, Collection and analysis of rate data, Multiple reactions, and non-isothermal reactor design.
prerequisite: ECHE 126 Introduction to Chemical Engineering (33) (D and above) AND BENG 124 Engineering Mathematics I (101) (D and above) AND BENG 225 Engineering Mathematics II (48) (D and above)

title: Computational Methods in Chemical Engineering-II
description: Simulation of unit operations is used for design and optimization of the operation parameters leading to increased unit efficiency and production site level.
prerequisite: ECHE 319 Chemical Engineering Thermodynamics (1218) (D and above) AND ECHE 333 Separation Processes-I (1271) (D and above) AND ECHE 383 Separation Processes II (1982) (D and above) AND ECHE 481 Chemical Reaction Engineering (1985) (D and above) AND ECHE 323 Computational methods in Chemical Engineering-I (1272) (D and above)

title: Chemistry II
description: This is an intensive course matching the content for Chemistry II for Engineers in order to be delivered during the summer term.
prerequisite: ECHE 222 Chemistry I (731) (D and above)

title: Multiphase Systems
description: The course will cover topics on Multi-phase flows in Chemical Engineering Applications.
prerequisite: ECHE 319 Chemical Engineering Thermodynamics (1218) (D and above) AND ECHE 270 Transport Phenomena-l (735) (D and above)

title: Introduction to Biochemical Engineering
description: Teach undergraduate students in Chemical and Materials Engineering the principle of Biochemical Engineering and Bioprocesses. The course includes both lecture and tutorial sessions and is designed for students interested to a career in Biotechnology.

title: Chemical Process Safety
description: To give Chemical Engineering students a working understanding of the safety and risk assessment and modeling and how to incorporate them in the design of chemical process systems.

title: Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics
description: This course introduces the application of engineering principles including thermodynamics, transport phenomena and reaction engineering in the atmosphere. The course is designed to facilitate student’s learning and help them to better investigate functioning of the atmospheric system.

title: Managerial Economics
description: The goal of this course is to learn how to apply microeconomic principles and quantitative tools to managerial decisions.

title: Economic Statistics
description: This course will introduce students to the analysis of economic data.
prerequisite: ECON 101 Introduction to Microeconomics (379) (C and above) OR ECON 102 Introduction to Macroeconomics (503) (C and above)

title: Research Assistance in Economics
description: The aim of this course is to allow students to assist in the research projects of faculty in the Economics Department.
prerequisite: ECON 101 Introduction to Microeconomics (379) (C- and above) AND ECON 102 Introduction to Macroeconomics (503) (C- and above) OR CSCI 151 Programming for Scientists and Engineers (192) (C- and above) OR CSCI 235 Programming Languages (638) (C- and above) OR CSCI 390 Artificial Intelligence (643) (C- and above) OR MATH 321 Probability (482) (C- and above) OR MATH 322 Mathematical Statistics (1165) (C- and above)

title: East Asian Economic Development
description: This course presents an overview of East Asian economic development.
prerequisite: ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above)

title: Applied Econometrics
description: Economists’ use of data to answer cause-and-effect questions constitutes the field of applied econometrics. The purpose of this course is to prepare students for their own empirical work by giving them hands on experience in applying the core methods of applied econometrics or econometric techniques. As such, the emphasis is on applications, not derivations, of methodology. To build an understanding of proper research design, we will explore common methods in modern econometrics through example.
prerequisite: ECON 301 Econometrics I (664) (C- and above)
antirequisite: ECON 336 Programming for Economists (7979) (C- and above)

title: Matching Theory and Applications
description: This course introduces the theory of matching and market design and discusses how the theory can be applied to various applications such as labor markets where employers match with firms, student placements in colleges and high schools, organ donation where patient and organ donor match. How to match people to other people or goods is an important problem in society. The economics of matching and market design has studied these problems in a great detail.
prerequisite: ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above)

title: Money and Banking
prerequisite: ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above)

title: Economic Growth
prerequisite: ECON 202 Intermediate Macroeconomics (207) (C- and above)

title: Natural Resources and Environmental Economics
prerequisite: ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above)
antirequisite: ECON 331 Environmental Economics (1687) (C- and above)

title: The Economic History of the Soviet and Post-Soviet Area
prerequisite: (HST 100 History of Kazakhstan (172) (C- and above) OR HST 103 Central Asian History I (to 1700) (197) (C- and above) OR HST 104 Central Asian History II (1700 - 1991) (1192) (C- and above) OR HST 121 World History I (to 1500) (1193) (C- and above) OR HST 122 World History II (from 1500) (1162) (C- and above) OR HST 131 European History I (to 1700) (201) (C- and above) OR HST 132 European History II (from 1700) (139) (C- and above) OR HST 152 US History II (from 1877) (465) (C- and above) OR HST 172 Middle Eastern History II (from 1800) (1194) (C- and above) OR HST 182 East Asian History II (from 1500) (213) (C- and above) OR HST 199 Freshman Seminar (241) (C- and above)) AND ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above)

title: International Trade
description: The course will cover microeconomic aspects of international trade. It will introduce the standard models of the theory of international trade: The Ricardian model, where trade is driven by the comparative advantage based on technological differences across countries, and the Heckscher-Ohlin model, where comparative advantage and trade are determined by the cross-country differences in the endowments of the factors of production. The course will also explore the new theories of international trade based on the increasing returns to scale and offshoring. The international trade policy issues discussed in the course will include tariffs, quotas, export subsidies, and international agreements on trade.
prerequisite: ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above)

title: The Economics of Financial Markets
description: The course is intended as an introduction to the economic analysis of financial markets. The main economic function of financial markets is the coordination of savings with investments. More generally, financial markets provide opportunities for the allocation of scarce resources over time and under risk. Time and risk are the two major themes of this course. Students taking this course will acquire an understanding of economists' approach to analyzing both how, and how well, financial markets organize inter-temporal allocation of scarce resources. Topics that can be covered in this course include: inter-temporal allocation by consumers and firms when future payments are certain/uncertain, portfolio theory, the capital asset pricing model, the efficient market hypothesis, insider trading, financial derivatives, and risk management.
prerequisite: ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above)

title: Energy Economics
description: This course will cover theoretical and empirical topics related to energy demand, supply, prices, and environmental consequences of energyconsumption and production. Tools of microeconomic analysis will be applied to the study of the international and national markets for oil, natural gas, coal, electricity, nuclear power, and renewable energy. In addition, students will examine public policies affecting energy markets including taxation, price regulation and deregulation, energy efficiency, and control of emissions.
prerequisite: ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above)

title: Labor Economics
description: This course will introduce students to the economics of labor markets. The first part of the course will focus on labor supply and labor demand, and some direct applications. Labor force participation rates of women, welfare and work incentives, earning gap across skill groups and technological progress, and fixed costs of employment are some of the topics that will be discussed in the context of this basic theory of supply and demand. The second part of the course will focus on a variety of labor market topics including human capital theory, household production, compensating wage differentials, quasi-fixed labor costs, job market signaling, labor mobility, and discrimination analysis.
prerequisite: ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above)

title: International Finance
description: This course studies issues in international macroeconomics (also known as international finance or open economy macroeconomics) and examines the interaction of national economies through international financial markets.
prerequisite: ECON 202 Intermediate Macroeconomics (207) (C- and above)

title: Environmental Economics
description: This course will introduce students to the economic study of the environment and related issues.
prerequisite: ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above)

title: Political Economy
description: This course covers the core concepts in game-theoretical models of Political Economy.
prerequisite: ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above)

title: Programming for Economists
description: This course introduces students to Python programming, with an emphasis on its economic and econometric applications. It will focus on numerical programming, data manipulation, data visualization, and relevant applications in economics such as web scraping, geospatial data, and standard econometric methods.
prerequisite: ECON 301 Econometrics I (664) (C- and above)
antirequisite: ECON 318 Applied Econometrics (6078) (C- and above)

title: Empirical Finance
description: This course provides an introduction to the empirical analysis of the results covered in more theoretical courses.
prerequisite: ECON 211 Economic Statistics (2280) (C- and above) OR MATH 322 Mathematical Statistics (1165) (C- and above)

title: Economic Simulation Modeling
description: This course will teach the principles of computable general equilibrium (CGE) modeling and introduce some applications in trade, environmental and energy economics. The course will teach how to build a CGE model using the GAMS software. CGE models are widely applied in international organizations (World Bank, IMF) and research institutions.
prerequisite: ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above)

title: The Economics of Family
description: This course aims to examine theoretical and empirical studies of economics structure and decision –making of families. Household dynamics will be studied with the emphasis on the concepts of family formation, intra‐household resource allocation, divorce, fertility, investment (human capital and physical capital), and labour supply decisions. Lastly, we will evaluate the effects of various governmental policies that affect fertility and family formation within these frameworks.
prerequisite: ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above)

title: General Special Topics in Economics
description: The course will cover rotating topics of current interest in economics consistent with the level of other general elective courses offered within the department.
prerequisite: ECON 102 Introduction to Macroeconomics (503) (C- and above)

title: Independent Study in Economics
description: Student will perform study and research independently on a topic agreed by the instructor

title: Research Assistance in Economics 2
description: It is an advanced course on the research in economics.
prerequisite: ECON 300 Research Assistance in Economics (3080) (P)

title: Advanced Macroeconomics
description: The course aims to provide students with a comprehensive theoretical and empirical foundation in modern dynamic macroeconomic analysis, progressing systematically from the representative agent RBC framework to the sophisticated HANK models.
prerequisite: ECON 202 Intermediate Macroeconomics (207) (C- and above)

description: In this course we are going to take a first look at the theory of incentives, which is the core of modern microeconomics, game theory, and mechanism design. We are going to cover principal-agent models and take a look at such applications of mechanism design as auction theory. Some formal instruments will be introduced including how to work with uncertainty and reminder of Nash equilibrium in static simultaneous games.
prerequisite: ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above) AND ECON 301 Econometrics I (664) (C- and above)

title: Behavioral and Experimental Economics
description: The aim of this course is to introduce students to the field of behavioural and experimental economics. The
prerequisite: ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above) AND ECON 301 Econometrics I (664) (C- and above)

title: Econometrics II Time Series
description: This course covers time series econometrics, with applications in forecasting, macroeconomic policy assessments and risk management.
prerequisite: ECON 301 Econometrics I (664) (C- and above)

title: Advanced Monetary Policy
description: The Course aims to equip students with a comprehensive understanding of the role of money, and how monetary policy influences economic activities and addresses its challenges.
prerequisite: (ECON 202 Intermediate Macroeconomics (207) (C- and above) AND ECON 301 Econometrics I (664) (C- and above)) OR (ECON 202 Intermediate Macroeconomics (207) (C- and above) AND MATH 322 Mathematical Statistics (1165) (C- and above))

title: Industrial Organization
description: The purpose of this course is to introduce students to the study of how firms and markets function in market economies. In doing so, we analyze behavior under realistic and/or complex market conditions, including the presence of barriers to entry, economies of scale, externalities, imperfect market conditions, etc. This will allow us to analyze how and why firms use different organizational and pricing strategies, such as vertical integration, mergers, collusion, price discrimination and advertising. We will also address policy issues including the rationale for government intervention into markets, different forms of intervention and the role of the antitrust laws.
prerequisite: ECON 301 Econometrics I (664) (C- and above)

title: Empirical Industrial Organization
description: This course aims to prepare graduate students to be a specialist in empirical Industrial Organization. After finishing this course, students are expected to: (1) have a firm understanding of the leading papers; (2) be able to conduct their own empirical research on IO topics.For this purpose, we will read and study major literature in empirical IO field - topics include (but not limited to) firm entry, demand estimation for differentiated products, and detection of collusive firm behaviors.
prerequisite: ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above) AND ECON 301 Econometrics I (664) (C- and above)

title: Development Economics
description: This course aims to make students familiar with a wide range of issues relevant to less developed countries and to demonstrate how analytical frameworks of economics (i.e. theories, concepts, research methods) can be used to examine some of these problems.
prerequisite: ECON 301 Econometrics I (664) (C- and above)

title: Corporate Finance and Governance
description: This course is an introduction to the essential tools of a corporate finance and governance. The material includes an introductory level approach to theoretical and empirical study of the financial structure of the firm
prerequisite: ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above) AND (ECON 301 Econometrics I (664) (C- and above) OR MATH 322 Mathematical Statistics (1165) (C- and above))

title: Wages and the Labor Market
description: The course presents theories of labor markets, and empirical evidence along with methodological techniques to test whether the theories work.
prerequisite: ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above) AND ECON 301 Econometrics I (664) (C- and above)

title: Econometrics II Panel Data
description: This is an Applied Econometrics course dealing with topics related to panel or ’longitudinal’ data sets.
prerequisite: ECON 301 Econometrics I (664) (C- and above)

title: Introduction to Big Data Analytics
description: Big data analytics is the process of examining big data to uncover valuable information such as market trends, customer preferences, and hidden patterns that can help us make informed policy or managerial decisions.

title: Topics in Macroeconomic Theory
description: Topics in Macroeconomic Theory is an elective course in macroeconomics. The purpose of the course is to provide deeper coverage of the selected topics in macroeconomics, which span one of the main areas of macroeconomic theory: economic growth, real business cycles, monetary economics, and macroeconomic policy.
prerequisite: ECON 202 Intermediate Macroeconomics (207) (C- and above) AND ECON 301 Econometrics I (664) (C- and above)

title: Public Finance
description: This course examines the institutions behind, and the economic rationale for, government policy relating to public expenditures and taxation. Topics include public goods; externalities; public expenditure theory and policy; tax and price theory and policy; and social welfare and social insurance
prerequisite: ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above) AND ECON 301 Econometrics I (664) (C- and above)

title: Quantitative Macroeconomics
description: This course has a dual aim. First, it provides an overview of workhorse modern dynamic equilibrium macroeconomic models that are relevant for actual empirical and quantitative policy analysis. Usually, these theoretical models do not have an analytical solution, and drawing their practical quantitative implications requires resorting to computational techniques. As the second aim, this course thus introduces computational methods for solving and simulating macroeconomic models.
prerequisite: ECON 202 Intermediate Macroeconomics (207) (C- and above) AND ECON 301 Econometrics I (664) (C- and above)

title: Topics in Microeconomics
description: This course introduces students to the advanced topics in microeconomics. The aim is to apply the tools from microeconomics and game theory to the analysis of diverse economic and social situations.
prerequisite: ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above)

title: Contemporary Issues in Economics
description: This course uses economic models to obtain a better understanding and insights into a number of pressing economic problems that currently are the subject of debate in a number of regions and countries worldwide.
prerequisite: ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above) AND ECON 202 Intermediate Macroeconomics (207) (C- and above)

prerequisite: ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above) OR ECON 202 Intermediate Macroeconomics (207) (C- and above) OR MATH 322 Mathematical Statistics (1165) (C- and above) OR MATH 321 Probability (482) (C- and above)

title: Microeconomics
description: The first part focuses on classical theories of consumer and producer behavior, market demand and supply, and on the theory of competitive equilibrium. Topics include, choice theory, preferences, utility maximization, decision-making under uncertainty, expected utility theory; cost minimization and profit maximization by competitive firms; classical demand theory, existence of a general equilibrium in an Arrow-Debreu economy, the First and Second Welfare Theorems, trading in sequential markets, Radner equilibria in sequential markets economies with financial assets, incompleteness of markets. The second part explores the principles of game theory dealing with strategic situations in which decision-makers’ payoffs depend not only on their own choices but also on the choices of others, covering static and dynamic games to analyze market structures and different models of competition.

title: Macroeconomics
description: Macroeconomics examines the aggregate behavior of an economy through macroeconomic data and theoretical models, emphasizing the role of policymakers in economic outcomes. Key topics include economic growth, consumption, fiscal policy, the neoclassical model, money demand, inflation, and real business cycle theory.
