By the end of the course, students will develop the confidence and ability to write small programs to accomplish practical goals, regardless of their field of study.
antirequisite: CSCI 151 Programming for Scientists and Engineers (192) (F) OR CSCI 111 Web Programming and Problem Solving (110) (F) OR CSCI 115 Programming Fundamentals (5257) (F) OR CSCI 152 Performance and Data Structures (489) (F) OR CSCI 408 Senior Project I (1481) (F) OR CSCI 409 Senior Project II (1483) (F)

title: Engineering Materials I
description: The module covers the fundamentals of materials science and engineering. These include the understanding of the material structure from the atomic to micro to macro levels. The effects of the structure and the processing techniques on the material properties will be discussed. These concepts will be illustrated using metals to allow students to utilize the knowledge for materials selection in common engineering applications.

title: Engineering Materials II
description: This course will introduce students in the field of Materials Science and Engineering. Fundamental aspects will be discussed first, and from this starting point, the course will highlight materials with special electrical, magnetic or optical properties. Materials with special features for specific applications will be discussed toward the end of the course, emphasizing the role of materials in electronic devices, in micro- and nano-mechanical systems, and in medical devices.

title: Engineering Mathematics III (Differential Equations and Linear Algebra)
description: Introduction to Differential Equations and Linear Algebra with the help of special computer software.
prerequisite: MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (C and above)

title: Applied Probability and Statistics
description: This course provides an introduction to basic probability theory and statistics.
prerequisite: MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (C- and above)

title: Numerical Methods in Engineering
description: Numerical methods are the basic algorithms underpinning computer predictions in modern systems science. Such methods include techniques for simple optimization, interpolation from the known to the unknown, linear algebra underlying systems of equations, ordinary differential equations to simulate systems, and stochastic simulation under random influences. Students will gain the knowledge from the lectures and consolidate the learned concepts by solving practical problemsin labs. The performance of the students will be assessed by assignments, quizzes, midterm, lab reports and the final exam.
prerequisite: ENG 200 Engineering Mathematics III (Differential Equations and Linear Algebra) (5009) (D and above)

title: Interdisciplinary Project
description: In this course students work in interdisciplinary teams toward a holistic approach to design projects; including problem definition, design proposal, implementation, and critical evaluation.

title: Capstone Project
description: The final year thesis project.

title: Air Pollution & Climate Change
description: Climate Change Atmospheric chemistry Air emissions from transportation, power generation, and industrial sectors Atmospheric dispersion modeling

title: Environmental Monitoring & Geoinformatics (elective)
description: Environmental Monitoring, Data Management, Early Warning Systems, Large Data Visualization, Analytics and Informatics

title: Environmental Science & Technology
description: Environmental Chemistry. Sources, reactions, transport, effects, and fates of chemical species in the air, soil, and water environments

title: Green Engineering & Product Design
description: Green products & services Design for recyclability (DfR) Life Cycle Assessment of products Pollution prevention & source reduction of potential pollution

title: Laboratory Methods II
description: Sampling, preservation & preparation of environmental samples Quantitative and basic quantitative analysis Experimental data analysis Process equipment studies Instrumental analysis

title: Risk Analysis & Management
description: This course will help students develop a working knowledge of risk terminology and reliability engineering, analytic tools and models used to analyze safety, environmental and technological risks, and social and psychological risk issues. The course covers organization risk analysis and management in natural hazards, threat assessment, transportation risks, industrial accidents, environmental pollutions, public health, and regulatory policy.

title: Risk Assessment & Loss Prevention
description: Prevention of accidents with the potential of serious environmental impact Safety of production systems in relation to the environmental impact related to plant operation Applied Computational Fluid Dynamics for process and plant safety Multi-phase flow, toxic release modeling, fluids leakage, overpressure in pipes & reactors, relief measures

title: Solid Waste Management
description: Municipal, Industrial & Hazardous Waste Waste treatment, recycling & disposal Thermal treatment of waste & waste-to-energy processes (biodrying, anaerobic digestion, incineration, gasification & pyrolysis, landfill gas, biomass and coal co-firing systems)

title: Sustainable Construction & Environmental Geomechanics
description: Buildings & Energy (inc. geothermal energy) Green buildings Building materials Sustainable infrastructure projects Mechanical behavior of natural geomaterials under various environmental conditions and applications to waste disposal, natural disasters & depollution/remediation. Landfills design

title: Sustainable Development
description: Historical background, Concept of sustainable development, sustainable policies (from local to international level), sustainability indicators, case studies.

title: Sustainable Urban Development
description: Concepts of the City and Environmental Change Climate Change and the Built Environment Financing Sustainability Transportation and Sustainability Land-use change and landscape management Demographic change and adaptation

title: Wastewater Treatment
description: I. Wastewater treatment plants II. Advanced Separation Processes. Adsorption, ion exchange, extraction, absorption, membrane separations. III. Sewage sludge management technologies (bio-drying, composting, anaerobic digestion)

title: Water Resources Management
description: Water Resources management (surface & underground water) Environmental fluid mechanics Potable water treatment

title: Introduction to Biology
description: Introduction to Biology provides an introduction of the biological sciences to students who have not studied biology before. The course will look at life from the global scale of the biosphere to the microscopic scale of molecules.

title: Introduction to Business
description: Introduction to Business is designed for Foundation Year students and covers the basic concepts of business.

title: Introduction to Chemistry
description: The Introduction to Chemistry course provides principal concepts and practical applications of chemistry through topics of current interest to society.

title: Foundation English for Academic Purposes 1
description: Academic English language dedicated for Foundation students.

title: Foundation English for Academic Purposes 2
description: The English for Academic Purposes course in the second semester continues to develop the skills that students require in order to produce effective academic English necessary in pursuit of their undergraduate degrees. It is structured around three core integrated subject areas: Academic Critical Literacy; Academic Listening and Speaking; Academic Reading and Writing. These core areas are linked thematically to the various content areas that the students pursue in semester 2. All students complete a research project which is firmly situated in their chosen pathway and acts as the focal point for developing the following skills: recognizing bias, assumptions and arguments in sources; writing in academic format and language. Critical academic thinking and analysis in reading texts and writing essays are taught with the aim of allowing students to become competent in academic discourse. The research project is continually assessed throughout the semester and includes three, way stages where grades are awarded. The research project is then defended in a viva examination. The viva aims to produce the following learning outcomes; Delivery of a confident and competent presentation; Effective communication in varied oral exchanges; Effective expression in a specified formal context. Developing the skills necessary to scaffold the viva is ongoing throughout the semester and culminates in an intensive two-week period of preparation after the research project has been submitted. There are two further components of assessment in semester 2: (1) an open book reading examination and (2) a listening and note-taking assessment. The open book reading examination revisits many of the skills developed during research project preparation.

title: Foundation English for Academic Purposes
description: The English for Academic Purposes course is structured around three core integrated subject areas: Academic Critical Literacy; Academic Listening and Speaking; Academic Reading and Writing. Assessment of the module is composed of an individual research project; a listening and note taking examination; an open book reading examination; and a viva in defense of the research project. The module is thematically linked and materials are relevant to subject areas. The module has a clear focus on equipping NUFYP students with the skills needed for undergraduate study.

title: Introduction to Geography
description: The course focuses on world regional geography as a means of understanding human geography. It will provide knowledge of many cultural regions of the world through small, interactive lectures that will highlight geography as a social science discipline.

title: Foundation Humanities
description: In Semester 2, the guiding themes of the Humanities and Social Science are the ‘Idea of Progress’ and the ‘Rise of Modernity’; that is, the extent to which the normative term ‘progress’ be applied to the historical development of human social institutions. The broad topic areas are: ‘Natural states’ → Nation states → Empires & Ideologies → Post-Colonialism & Post-Industrialism → Power & Power Relations → The Promise and Perils of Technological Change. The course concentrates on developing students’ skills in interpreting and critically analyzing source material in core HSS subjects, including anthropology, cultural studies, economics, environmental science, geography, history, international relations, literature, philosophy, political science, psychology, and sociology. Assessment comprises student-led seminars, an essay-based writing portfolio, and a final exam.

title: Introduction to Humanities and Social Science
description: The aim of this course is to introduce students to some of the major theories and concepts of the social sciences through the framework of the global environmental crisis.

title: Foundations of Humanities and Social Sciences 2
description: In Semester 2, the focus of the Humanities and Social Sciences remains on interpreting and critically analyzing source material in core HSS disciplines. Students will conduct and write-up their individual Primary Research Project or secondary research project in special cases. Assessment consists of the Research Project, weekly Moodle quizzes, student-led presentations, a portfolio of essays, and a final exam.

title: Leadership 1
description: The goal of this course is to mature students both academically and personally in preparation for their undergraduate studies and future careers. It focuses on developing leadership qualities that help students adapt to the rigors of university studies both in their personal development and academic skills. In this course students focus on time management and related skills along with independent learning, deep reading, and reflective practices. Students will study historical examples of leadership and apply them to modern scenarios, thus seeking to enhance in their own lives characteristics such as integrity, responsibility, confidence, and self-discipline.

title: Leadership 2
description: The primary goal of the Leadership course in the second semester is to deepen students’ understanding of personal development and social dynamics through projects that allow students to demonstrate critical thinking, enhance creative problem solving, practice teamwork, and show an understanding of both academic and personal integrity. Students will be given the opportunity to demonstrate leadership traits, apply decision-making principles, and become more thoughtful and independent leaders.

title: University of Pittsburgh Component - Family Medicine Preceptorship
description: This elective is intended to offer medical students the opportunity to experience Family Medicine in a community setting which is realistic to how Family Physicians practice. The student will focus on developing skills necessary to evaluate and treat patients in a community office setting. Degree of responsibility will be determined by the knowledge and skills of the student. The student will be exposed to the Community Family Physician's patient responsibilities, call schedule, community activities, family and life style.

title: Foundation Mathematics for engineers
description: The Foundation course, Mathematics for Engineers in Semester 2 requires that students have a good grasp of Pre Calculus from Semester 1. The structure and content of the course is based on the competencies, knowledge and skills set out for Level Zero in the European Framework for Mathematics Curricular in Engineering Education. As such it contains a significant amount of elementary Calculus. Material will be used with real world applications and students will be encouraged to develop problem solving skills.

title: Foundation Core Mathematics
description: The Core Mathematics course in Semester 2 is primarily a repeat of the semester 1 Pre Calculus module. All students should be able to reach a reasonable level of pre-calculus competence by the end of the Semester. The key theme of the Core course will be mastery of basic techniques and algebraic fluency. Students will focus largely on solving problems in seminars to strengthen their knowledge and understanding of the topic areas and to reinforce their problem solving skills.

title: Foundation Mathematics for Science
description: The Foundation Mathematics for Science course in Semester 2 requires that students have a good grasp of Pre Calculus from Semester 1 Pre Calculus course. The course is calculus-free and has an emphasis on Combinatorics, Geometry, Functions and Proof. It will also seek to develop Mathematical thinking and problem-solving skills with an emphasis on understanding and logical reasoning. Material will be used with real world applications.

title: Foundation Statistics
description: The Statistics course in Semester 2 is a first course in probability and statistics using examples drawn from the Humanities and Social Sciences. The Course introduces types of data and Excel tools for statistical calculations. It then looks at sampling and observational studies as well as the representation and summary of data. Probability distributions will be covered. Material will be used with real world applications and students will be encouraged to develop modelling and problem solving skills within this context.

title: Foundation 'Statistics'
description: The Statistics course in Semester 2 is a first course in probability and statistics using examples drawn from the Humanities and Social Sciences. It is designed for students who plan to study in the social sciences where the capture, processing and analysis of data is of central importance. The course introduces types of data and Excel tools for statistical calculations. It then looks at sampling and observational studies as well as the representation and summary of data. Probability distributions will be covered. Material will be used with real world applications and students will be encouraged to develop modelling and problem solving skills within this context.

title: Mathematics for Life Sciences (Biology And Chemistry)
description: The semester 2 foundation course, “Mathematics for Life Sciences,” builds on what the students learned in Foundation Pre-Calculus and develops their knowledge and understanding of more advanced mathematical concepts and techniques. Students will also further develop skills in solving a variety of problems with an emphasis on the application of mathematics to Life Science problems.

title: Mathematics for Physical Sciences
description: The semester 2 foundation course, “Mathematics for Physical Sciences,” requires that students have a good grasp of Pre-Calculus from Semester 1. The structure and content of the course is based on the competencies, knowledge and skills set out for Level Zero in the European Framework for Mathematics Curricular in Engineering Education. This course builds on what the students learned in Pre-Calculus and develops their knowledge and understanding of more advanced mathematical concepts and techniques. Students will also develop skills in solving a variety of problems with an emphasis on the application of mathematics to Engineering and Physical Science related problems. The topics covered include; matrices and systems of linear simultaneous equations, trigonometric functions, coordinate geometry, conic sections, rates of change, applications of differentiation, integration and its applications, vectors and complex numbers.

title: Foundation Mathematics 2
description: This course starts with further mathematical topics such as matrices, vectors and complex numbers. The second part of this course deals with introductory probability and statistics.

title: Introduction to Physics
description: This physics course is conceptual in its nature. It aims to draw the larger picture of physics as a unique discipline of science by identifying its main branches, fundamental concepts, and the basic laws that govern them.

title: Foundation 'Physics 2'
description: “Foundation Physics 2” continues the work started in “Foundation Physics 1.” The course extends the range of topics covered to oscillations and waves, thermodynamics, electricity and magnetism, and requires progressively more advanced mathematical skills. Students complete a series of eight laboratory practicals that use state-of-the-art, purpose-designed apparatus. These practicals are designed to reinforce lecture material and continue developing students’ experimental skills, while giving students practice at compiling laboratory reports. Discussion of conceptual aspects and more individual attention to students is provided through active-learning seminars and via drop-in support sessions that guide individuals through problem solving. Student performance is assessed through lab reports and brief formative quizzes, an online (Moodle) test under exam conditions and heavier weighted mid-term and final exams.

title: Beginning French II
prerequisite: FRE 101 Beginning French I (246) (C- and above)

title: Intermediate French I
prerequisite: FRE 102 Beginning French II (454) (C- and above)

title: Intermediate French II
prerequisite: FRE 201 Intermediate French I (667) (C- and above)

title: Introduction to French and Francophone Studies
prerequisite: FRE 102 Beginning French II (454) (C- and above)

title: French for Oral Proficiency
prerequisite: FRE 201 Intermediate French I (667) (C- and above)

title: Advanced Expression
description: In this French advanced expression course, students fine-tune their speaking and writing skills through intensive class discussion, oral presentations, pronunciation drills, linguistic lessons, and other activities.
prerequisite: FRE 201 Intermediate French I (667) (C- and above)

title: Advanced French Grammar and Composition
description: This course covers two main components: advanced study and practice of structures of French grammar, and the development of effective skills, focused on various writing genres.
prerequisite: FRE 202 Intermediate French II (1122) (C- and above)

title: Contemporary French Civilization
description: Advanced written and spoken expression trough issues of modern French and francophone society and culture.
prerequisite: FRE 202 Intermediate French II (1122) (C- and above)

title: French Linguistics
description: The course deepens the understanding of the French language, its structures, and its use in real speech situations, covering the major aspects of phonology, morphosyntax and global variation, also discussing the French-based creoles.
prerequisite: FRE 102 Beginning French II (454) (C- and above) AND LING 131 Introduction to Linguistics (1394) (C- and above)

title: Foundation Chemistry and Biology
description: ‘Chemistry & Biology’ is a Semester 2 course that provides good grounding in both these two key subjects. The module has a strong practical component with students completing a wide variety of experiments and practical skills development. Numerical skills are sharpened in regular ‘problem solving classes’. Topics include: Atomic Structure, Bonding, Periodicity, Cell Growth, Structure & function, Kinetics, Enzymes, Acids-Bases, Organic Chemistry, Microbiology, Homeostasis, Genetics, Photosynthesis, Atmospheric Chemistry, Ecology, Evolution. Assessment is carried out through exams, lab reports, case studies, courseworks and online tests.

title: Foundation Computer Science
description: The Web programming module is an elective, primarily for NUFYP students studying Physics. The module is divided into three main blocks of study (1) The design and implementation of web pages. (2) Gathering and analysis of data using EXCEL spreadsheets and graphs. (3) Using JavaScript in web page development. It introduces students to computer-based tools and methods that will be useful throughout their university training and professional careers. Students will develop knowledge and understanding of the protocols and technology underlying the Internet, web pages, spreadsheets, graphs, and programming. Skills are developed in gathering data, performing routine analysis, and correctly presenting the results in a professional manner in documents, presentations, and web pages.

title: Foundation 'Physics'
description: The semester 2 module ‘Physics’ builds on students’ previous understanding of kinematics, forces and momentum, while introducing basic calculus. It then covers key laws of electricity and magnetism, before finishing with introductory chemistry-slanted topics. Students complete a series of laboratory practicals that parallel the lecture material while their calculation skills are sharpened in weekly ‘problem solving classes’. Topics include: Kinematics, Calculus, Vectors & Forces, Energy Interconversion, Circular Motion, Static Equilibrium, Rotational Dynamics, Electrical Forces & Fields, Chemical Bonding, Materials, Organic Chemistry and Chemical Thermodynamics. Assessment is carried out through exams, lab reports and online tests.

title: Essential Biology and Chemistry 2
description: “Essential Biology & Chemistry 2” is the sequence to “Essential Biology & Chemistry 1.” The course highlights the central role that chemistry and biology play among the sciences and their relevance to industry and to daily life. The course has a strong practical component with students completing 10 laboratory practicals that cover a wide variety of experiments and learning styles. Practical skills are developed, as are planning and investigation strategies, through discovery-based learning. Students will also analyze case studies to develop critical thinking and practice their scientific writing skills. Students also undertake a team-based investigation project related to an environmental issue affecting Kazakhstan. Practice in chemistry calculations is sharpened in regular ‘problem solving classes’ which involve student teams and a problem-based learning approach. More individual attention to students is provided in seminars and through drop-in support sessions.

title: Sciences
description: This foundation course provides students with topics in science.

title: Introduction to Geology
description: This introductory course to Geology will cover the following topics: the Solar System; formation, differentiation, and present structure of the Earth; the mantle, the oceanic crust and plate tectonics; the continental crust; rivers and oceans; origins and evolution of life; climate change; natural resources.

title: Mineralogy
description: This course in mineralogy will provide the students with the necessary fundamentals which are required for following courses in petrology and geology of ore deposits.
prerequisite: GEOL 101 Fundamentals of Geology (4774) (C- and above)

title: Geologic Maps and Cross-Sections
description: This course on geologic maps and cross-sections will introduce the students to the reading of topographic and geologic maps, to the identification of geologic structures on geologic maps, as well as to the construction of cross-sections.
prerequisite: GEOL 101 Fundamentals of Geology (4774) (D and above) OR GEOL 102 Fundamentals of Geology (4772) (D and above)

title: Sedimentology and strartigraphy
description: The content of this course is the following: (1) sedimentary processes and depositional environments; (2) sedimentary facies and paleoenvironments; (3) lithostratigraphic units, biostratigraphy, chronostratigraphy, and correlations; (4) introduction to sequence stratigraphy. This course will provide the students with a solid background in sedimentology, in particular concerning the formation and evolution of sedimentray rocks in the context of the rock cycle, the concepts of stratigraphy and the relation between sedimentary processes and geologic time, and the importance of sedimentology and stratigraphy in petroleum exploration.
prerequisite: GEOL 101 Fundamentals of Geology (4774) (D and above) OR GEOL 102 Fundamentals of Geology (4772) (D and above) AND GEOL 202 Geologic Maps and Cross-Sections (5123) (D and above)

title: Paleontology
description: This course is a necessary complement to the course on Sedimentology and Stratigraphy. It will cover the major groups of organisms preserved as macrofossils and microfossils in the geologic record. During the laboratory, the characteristic fossils for each time period will be treated. It will also illustrate the applications of paleontology to such important fields as paleoclimate reconstruction or petroleum exploration. The aims of this paleontology course are: (1) to introduce the students to the major groups of macrofossils and microfossils; (2) discuss the occurrence of fossils in the geologic record in terms of the origins and the evolution of life in general as well as in each major fossil group, as well as of the mass extinction events which have affected the planet.
prerequisite: GEOL 101 Fundamentals of Geology (4774) (D and above) OR GEOL 102 Fundamentals of Geology (4772) (D and above)

title: Field Geology 1
description: This course consists of ten days of field work in the Karatau region. The students will learn how to use geological equipment on the field. They will generate their own stratigraphic columns and geologic maps.
prerequisite: GEOL 202 Geologic Maps and Cross-Sections (5123) (C- and above)

title: Geomorphology
description: The main aim of the course is understanding of landforms and the processes that produce and modify them. The course considers some of the practical aspects of reading a geomorphological, map, recognized the landforms and understanding the natural processes.
prerequisite: GEOL 101 Fundamentals of Geology (4774) (C- and above) OR GEOL 102 Fundamentals of Geology (4772) (C- and above)

title: Igneous and metamorphic petrology
description: The content of this course is the following: • Igneous petrology: Composition and properties of magmas, magmatic differentiation, cooling and textures, modal compositions of the major types of igneous rocks, IUGS classification, CIPW norm calculations. Laboratories: Macroscopic and microscopic description procedures for the major types of igneous rocks. Classification based on modal abundances and normative calculations. Metamorphic petrology: Temperature-pressure conditions of regional and contact metamorphism, major types of metamorphic rocks, notion of metamorphic facies, characteristic minerals, metamorphic reactions and isograds, P-T diagrams. Laboratories: exercises constructed around macroscopic and microscopic observations, identification of metamorphic reactions, and interpretation of chemical and thermometric data.
prerequisite: GEOL 101 Fundamentals of Geology (4774) (D and above) OR GEOL 102 Fundamentals of Geology (4772) (D and above)

title: Thermodynamics and Geochemistry
description: This course will cover the fundamentals of geochemistry and geochemical thermodynamics, and demonstrate with the aid of examples their usefulness in magmatic and metamorphic petrology. The content is the following: • Fundamentals of thermodynamics and their application in the Earth Sciences; • Phase diagrams for igneous and metamorphic petrology; Trace element and isotope geochemistry for igneous and metamorphic petrology.
prerequisite: GEOL 101 Fundamentals of Geology (4774) (D and above) OR GEOL 102 Fundamentals of Geology (4772) (D and above)

title: Structural Geology and Tectonics
description: This course will introduce the students to the mechanics of rock deformation, the recognition and interpretation of faults, folds, foliation, lineation, shear zones, mylonites, and other kinematic indicators, as well as to the regional structural geology.
prerequisite: (GEOL 101 Fundamentals of Geology (4774) (D and above) OR GEOL 102 Fundamentals of Geology (4772) (D and above)) AND GEOL 202 Geologic Maps and Cross-Sections (5123) (D and above)

title: Geophysics
description: This course will introduce the fundamentals in the three main disciplines of geophysics – gravimetry, seismology, and geomagnetism. The theory will be illustrated with applications in the geological sciences, in particular in mineral and petroleum exploration, and in groundwater resource assessment. An introduction to the interpretation of seismic profiles will be given, and the techniques of measurement in gravimetry and geomagnetism will be explained.
prerequisite: GEOL 204 Sedimentology and strartigraphy (5475) (D and above)

title: Geology of ore deposits
description: The course has been organized by ore deposit type with an effort to integrate aspects of geodynamics, tectonics, petrology, mineralogy and physical chemistry which are important to establish genetic models for ore deposits. Examples from Kazakhstan are used as case studies for the laboratories when this is possible.
prerequisite: GEOL 101 Fundamentals of Geology (4774) (D and above) OR GEOL 102 Fundamentals of Geology (4772) (D and above) OR GEOL 201 Mineralogy (5122) (D and above)

title: Geodynamics
description: This course will explore in details the dynamics of the Earth, including the core, the mantle, and the crust.
prerequisite: GEOL 101 Fundamentals of Geology (4774) (D and above) OR GEOL 102 Fundamentals of Geology (4772) (D and above)

title: Geographic Information Systems
description: Geographic Information Systems (GIS) are routinely used in a wide range of geological studies, including geological mapping and exploration projects.

title: Environmental Geochemistry
description: This course will cover fundamental aspects of physical chemistry relevant to heavy metal dispersion, radionuclide migration, and oil spill contamination.

title: Hydrogeology
description: This course will cover the fundamentals of physics required in hydrogeological studies as well as in groundwater resource management.

title: Field Geology 2
description: This course will consist of two weeks of field work in the Altai Mountains of East Kazakhstan. It will give the opportunity to the students to put into practice what they will have learned in igneous and metamorphic petrology, structural geology, geodynamics, geology of ore deposits, and geographic information systems.
prerequisite: GEOL 303 Structural Geology and Tectonics (5874) (D and above) OR GEOL 301 Igneous and metamorphic petrology (5886) (D and above)

title: Petroleum Geology and Geochemistry
description: This introductory course to petroleum exploration will discuss the theories on the origin of petroleum, the composition and properties of petroleum.

title: Water Resource Management
description: This course will focus on the scientific basis for water resource management, including watershed delineation, hydrologic budget, contamination sources and water quality, water resource carrying capacity, wetlands protection, and the impact of climate change on the evolution of water resources. A local case study will be investigated by the students.

title: Geostatistics
description: This course introduces the practical applications of basic and advanced statistical methods. It will introduce different data collection, exploratory analysis and quality assurance methods. Deterministic and geostatistical interpolation methods will also be demonstrated.
prerequisite: MATH 161 Calculus I (118) (C- and above)

title: Research Project I
description: This unit represents the first part of the final undergraduate research project of the students, who will produce a review of the bibliography related to their own research project. This review of the bibliography will be made under the guidance of their supervisors. At the end of the semester, the students will give a presentation in front of the professors of the department.

title: Research Project II
description: This unit represents the second part of the final undergraduate research project of the students, who will now concentrate on the Projects itself. At the end of the semester, the students will give a presentation in front of the professors of the department.
prerequisite: GEOL 404 Research Project I (6423) (C- and above)

title: Exploration Geology & Geophysics
description: This course will introduce the students to the principles behind the geological and geophysical methods applied in exploration for mineral, hydrocarbon, and water resources.
prerequisite: GEOL 101 Fundamentals of Geology (4774) (C- and above)

title: Remote Sensing of the Earth
description: This course introduces students to satellite-based analysis for solving geoscience and environmental problems.
prerequisite: GEOL 402 Water Resource Management (6422) (C- and above)

title: Photography for Geosciences
description: In this digital photography course students will learn to understand what different types of cameras and lenses exist, how to work properly with the camera, including smart phone, understanding and making full use of the various camera settings.
prerequisite: GEOL 101 Fundamentals of Geology (4774) (D and above)

title: Advanced Hydrogeology
description: This course will cover the fundamentals of physics required in hydrogeological studies as well as in groundwater resource management.
prerequisite: GEOL 309 Hydrogeology (6152) (C- and above)

title: Advanced Economic Geology
description: This course will start with an introduction, classification, distribution, and characteristics of ore deposits, particularly metallic ores. It will also link types of ore deposits with particular plate tectonic settings along with their genesis.

title: Advanced Petroleum Geology
description: This course includes an introduction to the theory of petroleum formation and occurrence as well as state-of-the-art tools and techniques used in petroleum exploration and reservoir development.

title: Advanced Sedimentology
description: This course provides a state-of-the-art review of sedimentary systems including those formed in fluvial, lacustrine, deltaic, tidal, shoreline, and deep marine settings. Lectures include discussions, exercises, core and field studies, and consideration of modern and outcrop studies as an aid to subsurface activities.

title: Advanced Geochemistry
description: This course provides advanced theoretical knowledge of high-temperature geochemistry required for data interpretation and integration in geosciences.

title: Advanced Geophysics
description: This course provides theoretical foundations that are required for the understanding and critical interpretation of modern geophysical concepts and in-depth knowledge of basic mathematical methods like multidimensional analysis, optimization, and approximation theory as well as physical modeling.

title: Advanced Petrology
description: This course provides all the information about igneous and metamorphic rocks including their important geochemical and isotopic systematics. The igneous part will start with the classifications and textures of igneous rocks and structures of bodies.

title: Exploration Geoscience
description: This course offers an in-depth exploration of the geological, geochemical, and geophysical techniques that are crucial for understanding the Earth's lithosphere and its mineral and energy resources. The course is structured into modules that address exploration methods frequently applied in minerals and energy exploration.

title: Advanced Structural Geology and Microtectonics
description: This course provides the student with an advanced level understanding of structural geology, stress and strain, brittle and ductile rock deformation mechanisms, and geometries at micro-, meso- and macro-scale and trains 3D thinking to help solve more complex tectonic problems.

title: Advanced Field Geology
description: Application of geological field methods to produce a geological map, cross-sections, a report, and an oral presentation describing the local geological structure and history in a structurally or sedimentologically complex area in sedimentary, metamorphic, or magmatic rocks

title: Advanced Tectonics and Geodynamics
description: This course provides an advanced level understanding of large-scale scale deformation processes that shaped the Earth, including plate tectonics (e.g. evolution of subduction zones, spreading ridges) and other deformation processes at the scale of the entire crust and mantle such as the dynamics of mantle plumes, hotspots and the effect of large-scale meteorite impacts.

title: Advanced Hydrogeology
description: This course provides a rigorous foundation in groundwater flow processes, aquifer characterization, groundwater–surface water interactions, and hydrogeochemistry.

title: Carbonate Systems, Processes and Deposits
description: The course will provide the students with a solid background in sedimentology, in particular concerning the formation and evolution of carbonate sedimentary rocksю
prerequisite: PETE 502 Petroleum Geology (4478) (C- and above)

title: Integrated Geoscience and Engineering for Exploration and Energy System Transition
description: The course (limited to 5 students) is designed for students to evaluate as a team a geophysical and geological dataset. The data set consists of seismic, well data, geochemical information, and geophysical logs. The class provides students with an insight into the petroleum exploration and energy system transition.

title: Thesis I
description: This course aims to train the students to identify relevant research problems, perform a continuous literature review on a research problem, and develop and implement an original methodology to investigate possible solutions to this problem.

title: Thesis II
description: This course aims to train the students to identify relevant research problems, perform a continuous literature review on a research problem, and develop and implement an original methodology to investigate possible solutions to this problem
prerequisite: GEOL 689 Thesis I (8595) (P)

title: Geology and Resources of Central Asia
description: This course will provide PhD students with advanced knowledge about the geology and natural resources of Central Asia, as well as emerging prospects. The course comprises a series of modules taught by all geoscience instructors and includes topics related to their ongoing research in the region, which allows students to get familiar with potential supervisors and areas of interest.

title: Thesis Research
description: The thesis research course fulfills the requirement for continuous registration and is designed to support the student in taking ownership of their research progress.

title: Beginning German
description: This course is for beginners. During the course we will focus on all 4 main skills of language-learning: reading, listening, writing and speaking as well as a 5th skill: audio-visual comprehension.

title: Beginning German II
description: Continuation of GER 101.
prerequisite: GER 101 Beginning German (3173) (C- and above)

title: Intermediate German I
description: Continuation of GER 102.
prerequisite: GER 102 Beginning German II (3335) (C- and above)

title: Intermediate German II
description: Continuation of GER 201.
prerequisite: GER 201 Intermediate German I (3722) (C- and above)

title: Financial Accounting
description: This course provides students with an understanding of the construction and interpretation of corporate financial reports, which are used by external parties (including investors, creditors, and regulators).

title: Managerial Accounting
description: The course focuses on planning, decision-making, and control, and covers two main topics: cost management systems and management control systems.

title: Thesis/Global Practicum
description: This course provides EMBA students with an opportunity to apply concepts and tools learned during the program to improve their own companies.

title: Managerial Economics
description: This course is designed to introduce students to the economic viewpoint of managerial decisions. It is not designed as an alternative to other managerial views, but instead should be viewed as complementary.

title: Team Building and Business Communications
description: This course combines the essentials of effective team building with the essentials of effective business communication, which is a critical component for personal career and organizational success. There will be a component of group work so that students can practice the leadership skills of empowering others, leading with integrity, dealing with conflict, and leveraging the power of diversity at both an individual and cultural level.

title: Financial Data Analytics I
description: This course will introduce you to basic concepts and methods of statistics and data analysis in a practice-oriented way. We will train you to use statistical software (Stata and R) to discover and understand patterns, regularities, correlations and dependencies, but also randomness in economic and financial cross-sections and time series

title: Principles of Finance
description: The course examines the theory of financial decision-making by firms and examines the behavior of the capital markets in which these decisions are taken. The underlying concept is the concept of value and value creation. Upon the completion of the course the students will be able to build a spreadsheet model of a typical business project and analyze it from the financial perspective.

title: Financial Data Analytics II
description: In this (GSBF513) course we will dig deeper into the models and methods of data analytics that we started discovering in the sibling course Financial Data Analytics I (GSBF 511).

title: Corporate Finance
description: This course develops a theoretical framework for understanding and analysing major financial challenges of a modern firm in the contemporary global market environment. In doing so it aims to provide the conceptual background for corporate financial analysis from the point of corporate value creation. The course provides necessary knowledge in evaluating different management decisions and their influence on corporate performance and value.

title: Investments I
description: The course covers the basic principles and techniques of investment analysis and portfolio selection and management. Topics include diversification, asset allocation, portfolio optimization, factor models, the relation between risk and return, trading, passive (e.g., index-fund) and active (e.g., hedge-fund, long-short) strategies, mutual funds and performance evaluation.

title: Investments II
description: The course covers the advanced principles and techniques of investment analysis and portfolio selection and management. Topics include diversification, asset allocation, portfolio optimization, factor models, the relation between risk and return, trading, passive (e.g., index-fund) and active (e.g., hedge-fund, long-short) strategies, mutual funds and performance evaluation.
prerequisite: GSBF 515a Investments I (4106) (C- and above)

title: Financial Markets and Institutions
description: The course builds an understanding of the economics of global financial markets and the global economic context in which managers make decisions. The approach in the course is to view the entire financial system as being comprised of four important markets: money, bond, stock, and foreign exchange.

title: Macroeconomics for Finance
description: The objective of this course is to undertake a rigorous study of the theoretical foundations of modern financial economics. The course will cover the central themes of modern finance including individual investment decisions under uncertainty, stochastic dominance, mean-variance theory, capital market equilibrium and asset valuation, arbitrage pricing theory, option pricing and the potential application of these themes.

title: Risk Management
description: Risk Management. This course covers qualitative and quantitative approaches to managing risk. We cover market risk, credit risk, liquidity risk, settlement risk, model risk, volatility risk, kurtosis risk and other types of financial risks

title: Financial Reporting and Analysis
description: The first part of the course focuses on the construction and interpretation of corporate financial reports, which are used by external parties (including investors, creditors, and regulators). The second part of the course deals with financial statement analysis by financial analysts. We learn how to estimate and interpret a firm’s performance indicators using liquidity, efficiency, profitability, solvency and valuation ratios

title: Empirical Asset Pricing
description: This course covers empirical research of asset pricing models. Topics include structural and reduced-form econometric tests, empirical patterns of return predictability in the time-series and the cross-section, and common data preprocessing operations for handling large panel data sets of firm-level market data and accounting data.

title: Ethics, Governance and Regulation
description: This course deals with the written and unwritten rules for analysts, portfolio managers, investment officers, managers, directors and shareholders. We give an overview of the legal structure of corporate governance and theories of corporate governance

title: Entrepreneurial Finance
description: This course is designed to introduce students to the ways in which entrepreneurs in western capital markets raise money to launch businesses

title: Special Topics in Corporate Finance
description: This course is designed to enhance students’ analytical and critical thinking skills so that they are able to effectively: • Address advanced and specific challenges of corporate financial management. • Analyze a real-world advanced corporate finance case. • Solve advanced quantitative and qualitative corporate finance problems.

title: Active Portfolio Management
description: This course provides a systematic and applied approach to active portfolio management

title: Islamic Banking and Finance
description: The course explains the differences between a traditional and an Islamic finance and banking. The operation of bank accounts under Sharia conditions will be explored

title: Insurance and Actuarial Science
description: This course will cover traditional actuarial models and theory of life contingencies with computational techniques, and with an emphasis on the practical context for survival models and valuation methods

title: Global Finance Experience Residency (I)
description: A study program organized by the National Bank of Kazakhstan in which experts and managers of financial institutions and organizations, as well as representatives of the regulator of the financial markets are actively involved

title: Global Finance Experience Residency (II)
description: In order to link the academic learning to the challenges of real-life situations in the international environment, students will undertake a two-week trip to one of the global financial centers

title: Master’s Thesis
description: The final course in the curriculum is the Thesis, which provides students with exposure to the theory and practice of finance in domestic and/or international markets. This capstone course is intended to represent a synthesis of the MSc in Finance program learning outcomes and demonstrate competence in finance in terms of both theory and practice, as well as effective communication skills, all of which will be considered in the evaluation of deliverables: a paper and an oral defense.

title: Master’s Thesis
description: The final course in the curriculum is the Thesis, which provides students with exposure to the theory and practice of finance in domestic and/or international markets. This capstone course is intended to represent a synthesis of the MSc in Finance program learning outcomes and demonstrate competence in finance in terms of both theory and practice, as well as effective communication skills, all of which will be considered in the evaluation of deliverables: a paper and an oral defense.

title: Foundations of Finance
description: The course examines the theory of financial decision-making by firms and examines the behavior of the capital markets in which these decisions are taken. The topics covered are goals and governance of a firm, TVM (time value of money), the basics of valuing bonds and stocks, NPV (net present value), IRR (Internal Rate of Return) and other investment criteria, and capital budgeting.

title: Corporate Finance
description: This course takes the perspective of financial managers responsible for making significant investment and financing decisions. It covers financial tools and applications, e.g. discounted cash flow analysis as well as equilibrium risk and return tradeoffs.

title: Financial Analysis
description: The course provides a framework to analyze and interpret financial statements, exposes students to the publicly available sources of financial information used in capital markets, and develops important Excel modeling skills pertaining to financial planning and analysis.

title: Management and Organizations
description: To be an effective manager and leader requires both a broad understanding of how organizations function as well as personal skills for managing people and relationships. This course addresses fundamental issues at both levels. At both the individual and team level, we help build the skills that effective managers need to implement their insights and decisions

title: Quantitative Tools for Managers
description: This course is about understanding, analyzing and using data and uncertain information in management. More technically, it is a statistics course with an emphasis on the applications of statistical tools and the interpretation of their results to management problems

title: Strategy
description: The purpose of the course in strategy is to make participants familiar with the core concepts and techniques that function as foundations for formulating and implementing successful strategies. However, its basic intent is not on mastering specific analytical tools but rather on using strategic thinking and the development of a managerial attitude to guide actions in the face of uncertainty and complexity. So the main focus of the course is to learn how to use and apply these skills when judging complex management situations.

title: Supply Chain Management
description: A supply chain is a network of organizations that are involved in the different processes and activities that produce value in the form of products and services. Effective supply chain management can enable companies to increase market shares, reduce costs, and improve customer service.

title: Entrepreneurship
description: This course is designed to address the needs of students who hope to pursue startup opportunities, join a new venture as early employees, lead new ventures in established firms, or pursue careers where the ability to evaluate startups would be helpful (e.g., venture capital, mergers and acquisitions). It provides students with tools and information for evaluating entrepreneurial projects, negotiating with business partners, and developing strategies for starting their ventures.

title: Decision Models
description: Decision problems involving uncertainty or many variables are difficult to grasp intuitively. In these cases we may benefit from using a computer-based model to explore and evaluate the possibilities in a systematic fashion.

title: Advanced Leadership
description: This course will not draw a sharp distinction between “managers” and “leaders” because success in organizations means having a full repertoire of skills and knowing when to use them. That is, leaders need to be effective at communicating a vision, building relationships, and designing larger systems that are fair and efficient. Thus, the Advanced Leadership course builds on the key principles covered in the Management and Organizations course, but with a focus on leadership challenges around diversity, innovation, and change.

title: Operations Management
description: Operations management involves planning and controlling the processes used to produce the goods and services provided by an organization. In essence, it is the management of all activities related to doing the actual work of the organization. Increased competition, expanding product variety and more demanding consumers require more efficient supply chains.

title: Negotiation
description: This course will help students understand the theory and processes of negotiation as practiced in diverse settings, recognize the components of an effective negotiation, and analyze the individuals own behavior in negotiations.

title: Raising Capital
description: The course explains how venture capitalists arrange the financing for a company; what they look for in a business plan; how they value a business; and how they structure the terms of an agreement. Using informative case studies, and exercises, the course discusses the basic principles of the venture capital method, strategies for raising capital, methods of valuing the early-stage venture, and proven techniques for negotiating the deal.

title: AI and Emerging Technologies in Business
description: A 9-day EMBA residency at HKUST Hong Kong covering emerging technologies (blockchain, 5G, fintech) and Artificial Intelligence — equipping business leaders with the strategic knowledge to navigate and lead in the digital age.

title: Emerging Markets Strategy
description: The course will explore why and how strategies in emerging markets differ in both kind and intensity

title: Capstone Project
description: The capstone project requires the students to converge and leverage learnings from the previous courses by undertaking a strategic assignment in an organization. The course gives students a chance to bring their upgraded leadership and management skills alive and understand the consequences of their decisions and actions related to the strategic initiative undertaken. The capstone project allows students to study an inter-disciplinary issue, problem, or opportunity of strategic significance in an organizational or entrepreneurial context.

title: International Immersion Experience
description: International Immersion Experience is a 10-day international study tour that gives students firsthand exposure to global business environments. Through classroom learning, company visits, meetings with business and government leaders, and cultural immersion, students develop a deeper understanding of international business, diverse markets, and cross-cultural management, strengthening their ability to think and lead in a global context.

title: Marketing Management
description: The concepts and skills earned in this course will enable the students to develop a coherent marketing strategy for an organization. The course aims at enabling students to develop a robust understanding of marketing strategy for an organization. The students will gain insight into the role of marketing within the organization and the process which shapes the marketing strategy.

title: Marketing Strategy
description: The course is concerned with how to manage customers to maximize firm profits, i.e. how to select, acquire, retain, and profit from customers. The course builds on the core marketing class and the core strategy class.

title: Orientation
description: Orientation includes four elements: 1) Team building activities designed to strengthen leadership skills and the ability to work in teams; 2) Ethics - Ethics in academia instills values, guiding ethical behavior in research and practice, cultivating awareness, responsibility, and critical thinking for students to apply ethical principles in real-world scenarios, fostering a culture of integrity and professionalism. ; 3) Business math to develop functional literacy with a basic set of Excel and or other business tools; and 4) pre-term accounting - students will gain familiarity with the financial accounting process and the four major financial statements.

title: Foundations of Social Science Research
description: This course serves as a basis for understanding social science research by helping students understand and defend their own choices regarding knowledge and beliefs. Emphasizing the influence of these choices on research design and methodology, the course introduces both theoretical concepts and practical considerations in selecting and designing research methods.

title: Qualitative Research Methods
description: This module is designed to help students gain an understanding of qualitative research methods in the field of business and management. It covers the collection, analysis, and representation of qualitative data, as well as their integration into mixed methods research. The module explores the relationships between research design, data collection, ethics, analysis, representation, reflexivity, and theorization. It introduces students to the theoretical and methodological foundations of qualitative inquiry, including current debates in the field. Students will have hands-on experience with various qualitative research methods and will be expected to understand qualitative research's role in business and management, philosophical and methodological debates, research design, data generation and analysis, and writing up research findings. They will also conduct their small-scale qualitative research as part of the assessment using publicly available documents as data sources. This module aims to enhance students' qualitative research skills and practical experience.

title: Quantitative Research Methods
description: This course is designed for individuals with a background in statistics and econometrics. It covers various data analysis techniques for business and business economics research, including cross-sections, surveys, repeated and hierarchical cross-sections, time series, and panel data. It also explores causal inference, emphasizing the importance of understanding model assumptions and their testability. Practical assignments and data sets are provided to illustrate real-world research. The course encourages students to write an empirical paper that could potentially become part of their first academic research project.

title: Core Research Skills I
description: This course introduces students to business research, focusing on theory, ethics, and various research methods. It covers research design, data collection, basic data analysis, and report writing. The course emphasizes practical knowledge to prepare students for their research projects and to evaluate others' research. It serves as a foundation for advanced research methods in their respective fields.

title: Subject Specific Course I
description: This course provides essential training for success as a researcher in areas such as Accounting, Business Economics, Finance, Management, Organizations, and Strategy. Its primary objective is to enhance the quality of your research projects and publications by fostering good research practices and improving writing skills. Additionally, the course offers opportunities to practice teaching by developing and presenting a course in your chosen business research area.

title: Subject Specific Course II
description: This course introduces foundational studies in business research areas like Accounting, Business Economics, Finance, Management, Organizations, and Strategy. It focuses on understanding key studies, identifying important research issues, and learning research design, rather than covering the entire literature or recent studies. These skills are valuable for conducting and evaluating research.

title: Subject Specific Course III
description: This course equips students with the skills to design and conduct rigorous empirical research in business areas such as Accounting, Business Economics, Finance, Management, Organizations, and Strategy. It also trains students to critically evaluate empirical findings in academic articles and the media, identifying strengths, weaknesses, and potential biases.

title: Core Research Skills II
description: This course is designed to introduce students to business research and to develop student’s research and analytical skills

title: PhD Qualifying Exam
description: Qualifying examinations will be in a written format and examine a student’s ability to demonstrate competence in solving questions related to her field of PhD studies

title: Thesis Research Progress
description: This course guides students in advancing their thesis research, focusing on refining research questions, methodology, and analysis. By the end, students will have a solid draft and a clear plan for completing their thesis.

title: Thesis Proposal Presentation
description: The thesis proposal presentation is a comprehensive presentation of the student’s existing work toward his/her thesis as well as a proposal of the remaining steps to complete the thesis.

title: Mathematical Economics
description: This course offers a hands-on introduction to statistics and data analysis. You'll learn to use Stata and R to explore patterns, correlations, and randomness in economic and financial data.

title: Microeconomics I
description: This course offers rigorous training in microeconomic theory relevant to finance. Topics include consumer optimization, choice under uncertainty, no-arbitrage, information economics, game theory, and market microstructure. Students will learn to derive formal results, model effectively, and explain key outcomes.

title: Year 1 Summer Paper Submission and Presentation
description: Students develop and present an individual research paper grounded in economic reasoning, applying core research skills such as literature review, research design, and basic data analysis. The course emphasizes feasibility, clarity of the research question, and coherence between theory, methodology, and findings.

title: Year 2 Summer Paper Submission and Presentation
description: Students produce and present an advanced independent research paper demonstrating higher academic rigor, methodological precision, and critical engagement with literature. The course emphasizes originality, robust analysis, and the ability to generate and defend well-supported conclusions.

title: Introduction to World Environmental History
description: The course is an introduction to Environmental History. It uses case-studies from different continents and devotes a special attention to the modern environmental history of Central Asia.

title: Introduction to the History of Science and Technology
Introduction to the History of Medicine
description: This course surveys the most important developments, issues, accomplishments and problems in the history of medicine from the beginnings of human civilization to the present. Our focus in this class will be on the healing traditions of both non-Western and Western civilizations.

title: History of Magic
description: A history of magical and divinatory practices and their prosecution

title: The Mongol Empire
description: Chinggis Khan and his descendants built and ruled the largest land empire in history – the Mongol Empire that left a profound imprint on Eurasia and the world.
prerequisite: Subject "HST" BETWEEN 100 and 199 OR Subject "" BETWEEN 100 and 199 OR Subject "" BETWEEN 100 and 199 OR Subject "" BETWEEN 100 and 199

title: The Age of the Dragon Throne: Chinese Civilizations from the Mongols through the Qing
description: This course is a history of Chinese civilizations from the 13th to 20th centuries that emphasizing change and continuity as well as an understanding of the foundations of modern China.

title: Coins, cotton, and cocoons: Global trade and Eurasian materiality (ca. 1500-1850)
prerequisite: Subject "HST" BETWEEN 100 and 199

title: Public Health, Society, and the State
description: This course investigates the historical experience of health and illness from a population perspective. Surveying the development of governmental responsibility for the maintenance of public health from the industrial revolutions of the 18th century through the fears of global plagues that characterize the contemporary moment, it reveals how public health theories and practices are the result not only of scientific advances, but also, of social, cultural, economic, and political concerns.
department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, Political Science and International Relations

title: An Introduction to Comparative History: The Eurasian Steppes and Great Plains of North America
description: This course will introduce the idea of comparative history. We will compare, and contrast, the history of two regions in different parts of the world, but with some similarities as well as differences in their histories. We will study the transformation of the steppes of Eurasia and Great Plains of North America between the 16th and 20th centuries. Large parts of these grasslands and the lives of their inhabitants -- steppe nomads, such as Kazakhs, and Plains Indians, for example the Sioux -- were changed forever. Their lands were conquered and annexed by larger states: the Russian Empire, later the Soviet Union, and United States of America. The Russian and American states sponsored scientific studies of these lands, encouraged outsiders to settle or colonize them, and suppressed resistance. The settlers supported themselves partly by plowing up the land and growing crops. Their agricultural way of life partly replaced that of the native peoples who had relied more heavily on herding and hunting animals. The settlers reaped large harvests in good years, when the rains came, but experienced crises in years of drought. From the late nineteenth century there were attempts to develop more sustainable ways of farming and to conserve samples of the former natural environment of the grasslands. The changing ways of life in the grasslands were reflected in the cultures of the two societies.

title: India 1757-1947: Empire, Nationalism and Independence
prerequisite: Subject "HST" BETWEEN 100 and 199

title: The Atlantic World
description: Moving across a range of historical subjects, students will examine how exchange, communication, empire, and globalization shaped the history of this region.
prerequisite: HST 172 Middle Eastern History II (from 1800) (1194) (C- and above) OR HST 100 History of Kazakhstan (172) (C- and above) OR HST 103 Central Asian History I (to 1700) (197) (C- and above) OR HST 131 European History I (to 1700) (201) (C- and above) OR HST 122 World History II (from 1500) (1162) (C- and above) OR HST 121 World History I (to 1500) (1193) (C- and above) OR HST 123 Introduction to the History of Science and Technology (1376) (C- and above) OR HST 199 Freshman Seminar: Western Intellectual History (1509) (C- and above) OR HST 182 East Asian History II (from 1500) (213) (C- and above) OR HST 151 US History I (to 1877) (668) (C- and above) OR HST 104 Central Asian History II (1700 - 1991) (1192) (C- and above) OR HST 132 European History II (from 1700) (139) (C- and above) OR HST 199 Freshman Seminar (241) (C- and above) OR HST 152 US History II (from 1877) (465) (C- and above)

title: History of Medical Ethics
description: This course surveys the history of medical ethics from Ancient Greece through contemporary times. It deals with subjects such as human and animal experimentation, abortion, euthanasia, and vaccination.
prerequisite: Subject "HST" BETWEEN 100 and 199

title: Cannibalism and Civilization
description: A global history of human behaviour and human bodies viewed through the lens of cannibalism.
department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, Sociology and Anthropology

title: WWI and the World: Causes, conduct and the consequences of WWI
description: In this course in addition to covering the more conventional aspects of the historiography on the war, we will also focus on the conduct and impact of the war in the East which was radically different than the Western experience.
department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, Kazakh Language and Turkic Studies

title: World War II
prerequisite: HST 172 Middle Eastern History II (from 1800) (1194) (C- and above) OR HST 100 History of Kazakhstan (172) (C- and above) OR HST 103 Central Asian History I (to 1700) (197) (C- and above) OR HST 131 European History I (to 1700) (201) (C- and above) OR HST 122 World History II (from 1500) (1162) (C- and above) OR HST 121 World History I (to 1500) (1193) (C- and above) OR HST 123 Introduction to the History of Science and Technology (1376) (C- and above) OR HST 199 Freshman Seminar: Western Intellectual History (1509) (C- and above) OR HST 182 East Asian History II (from 1500) (213) (C- and above) OR HST 151 US History I (to 1877) (668) (C- and above) OR HST 104 Central Asian History II (1700 - 1991) (1192) (C- and above) OR HST 132 European History II (from 1700) (139) (C- and above) OR HST 199 Freshman Seminar (241) (C- and above) OR HST 152 US History II (from 1877) (465) (C- and above)

title: Soviet Central Asia in WWII
description: This course will examine the role and place of Soviet Central Asia and its communities in World War II. It will look at the war through the eyes of Muslim soldiers from Central Asia, its women and its minorities, including the deported peoples and Gulag prisoners. The course will also focus on how the Great Patriotic War shaped Soviet Central Asia and the impact and legacy it had on the post-war Central Asian societies.
prerequisite: REL 110/HST 110 Introduction to World Religions (142) (B and above) OR REL 120 Religion and Science (457) (B and above) OR REL 140 Religion in the Modern World (1623) (B and above) OR REL 160 Lived Religion (1347) (B and above) OR HST 100 History of Kazakhstan (172) (B and above) OR HST 103 Central Asian History I (to 1700) (197) (B and above) OR HST 104 Central Asian History II (1700 - 1991) (1192) (B and above) OR HST 105 Introduction to World Environmental History (4424) (B and above) OR HST 121 World History I (to 1500) (1193) (B and above) OR HST 122 World History II (from 1500) (1162) (B and above) OR HST 123 Introduction to the History of Science and Technology (1376) (B and above) OR HST 124 Introduction to the History of Medicine (3000) (B and above) OR HST 125 History of Magic (5668) (B and above) OR HST 131 European History I (to 1700) (201) (B and above) OR HST 132 European History II (from 1700) (139) (B and above) OR HST 151 US History I (to 1877) (668) (B and above) OR HST 152 US History II (from 1877) (465) (B and above) OR HST 172 Middle Eastern History II (from 1800) (1194) (B and above) OR HST 182 East Asian History II (from 1500) (213) (B and above) OR HST 199 Freshman Seminar (241) (B and above) OR HST 199 Freshman Seminar: Western Intellectual History (1509) (B and above)

title: Modern Britain:Culture,Politics, and Society since 1750
description: This course explores the rise and fall of this superpower through the 18th to the 20th centuries through a series of major themes and events, focusing on culture, politics and society.
prerequisite: Subject "HST" BETWEEN 100 and 199

title: Russian History from Riurik to Catherine the Great
description: This course will examine the political and cultural antecedents to the Russian Empire.

title: The Russian Empire from Catherine the Great to the Bolshevik Revolution
description: This course examines the sweep of Russian history, beginning with the expansion of the Empire and engagement with European thought under Catherine II. The course pays particular attention to the political, social, and artistic experimentation of Russia’s “long 19th century,” ending with the outbreak of the First World War.
prerequisite: Subject "HST" BETWEEN 100 and 199

title: The Soviet Experiment: Citizenship, Nationality, and Violence in the USSR, 1917-1991
prerequisite: HST 100 History of Kazakhstan (172) (C- and above) OR HST 103 Central Asian History I (to 1700) (197) (C- and above) OR HST 104 Central Asian History II (1700 - 1991) (1192) (C- and above) OR HST 121 World History I (to 1500) (1193) (C- and above) OR HST 122 World History II (from 1500) (1162) (C- and above) OR HST 131 European History I (to 1700) (201) (C- and above) OR HST 132 European History II (from 1700) (139) (C- and above) OR HST 151 US History I (to 1877) (668) (C- and above) OR HST 152 US History II (from 1877) (465) (C- and above) OR HST 172 Middle Eastern History II (from 1800) (1194) (C- and above) OR HST 182 East Asian History II (from 1500) (213) (C- and above) OR HST 199 Freshman Seminar (241) (C- and above)

title: Peter the Great (1682-1725): First Emperor of Russia and “Father of the Fatherland”
description: In 1721 the Russian Senate granted tsar Peter the titles: “Emperor”; “the Great”; and “Father of the Fatherland”. Over his reign he transformed Russia’s image to emulate the states of western Europe. The most famous symbol is his new capital city of St Petersburg. He founded the city several hundred kilometers northwest of the old capital of Moscow and hired foreign architects to design it: St. Petersburg was built to impress. Peter carried out reforms in many areas: the armed forces; government and administration; the economy and society. He sent Russians to study abroad and promoted secular education inside Russia. He overhauled the relationship between the state and Russian Orthodox Church. Throughout his reign he pursued an imperial vision, fighting wars with Russia’s enemies - Sweden (successfully), the Ottoman Empire (unsuccessfully) - and promoted contacts further afield, including Central Asia. In this course we will examine the motivation behind Peter’s reforms, and assess whether he radically transformed Russia, or continued, with greater vigor, the policies of previous tsars. Students will have the opportunity to evaluate Peter’s reign on the basis of contemporary primary sources and to compare Peter’s new capital city with Kazakhstan’s new capital city of Astana.

title: Eurasian revolutions, 1905-1949
description: Two assumptions lie at the heart of this course: first, that Revolution represents a particularly modern phenomenon and second, that various revolutions, circumscribed by time and geography as they are, are profoundly interconnected. The discussion of upheavals on the Eurasian continent in the first half of the Twentieth Century would allow us to elaborate on those assumptions by substantiating them with concrete details and by teasing out some of the most consequential corollaries.

title: European Dictators
prerequisite: HST 100 History of Kazakhstan (172) (C- and above) OR HST 103 Central Asian History I (to 1700) (197) (C- and above) OR HST 104 Central Asian History II (1700 - 1991) (1192) (C- and above) OR HST 121 World History I (to 1500) (1193) (C- and above) OR HST 122 World History II (from 1500) (1162) (C- and above) OR HST 131 European History I (to 1700) (201) (C- and above) OR HST 132 European History II (from 1700) (139) (C- and above) OR HST 152 US History II (from 1877) (465) (C- and above) OR HST 172 Middle Eastern History II (from 1800) (1194) (C- and above) OR HST 182 East Asian History II (from 1500) (213) (C- and above) OR HST 199 Freshman Seminar (241) (C- and above)

title: Clash of Civilizations: Communities, Confessions and Empires in Central Europe, 1000-1890
description: A survey of Central Europe from Christianization to the Enlightenment with an emphasis on interethnic and interfaith coexistence on the borderland between Catholic, Orthodox and Islamic civilization.

title: Modernizing the Periphery: Nationalism, Communism, and Empire in Central Europe, 1890-Present
prerequisite: Subject "HST" BETWEEN 100 and 199

title: Representations of Nature in the Early Modern World
description: This course examines how the arts and the sciences collaborated to gain insight into nature in the early modern world. This course takes a thematic approach, informed by a close examination of visual and textual sources to see how questions of creation, morphology, scale, growth, and deformity, were investigated in the early modern world, and how we can retrace their scientific and artistic logic today.
prerequisite: HST 100 History of Kazakhstan (172) (C- and above)

title: History of Sexuality
description: This course surveys the history of sexuality from antiquity to the present. Examining the ways in which social institutions such as medicine, religion, government, and the law have shaped constructions of “normal” and “deviant” sexuality, it compares and contrasts patterns of sexual desire and behavior, sexual identity formation, and sexual regulation across a variety of chronological and geographical areas.

title: History of the Soviet Union: Politics, Society, Culture
description: This course adopts a three-pronged approach to the history of the Soviet Union. First, we will look at the political history of “the first socialist state,” assuming a bird’s eye-view of the Soviet statesmen. Shifting gears in the middle of the term, we will explore the Soviet society, constructing our discussion around key themes of “utopia,” “nation,” “dissent,” “gender,” “consumption” and “memory.” Finally, we will turn our attention to Soviet culture, especially its “popular manifestations,” which had spawned out a language tying disparate parts of that multifaceted experience together

title: Soviet History Through Film
