description: This course explores the history of the Soviet Union through cinema, treating films both as historical documents and as interpreters of the past. By tracing the arc of Soviet history, from revolution to collapse, through cinema, the course examines how narratives and myths about the USSR were created, challenged, and remembered. With special attention to Central Asia and films by non-Russian directors — including both documentary and fiction films, and both more “artistic” productions and popular genre movies — students will learn to critically analyse film as a historical source and reflect on cinema’s role in shaping historical memory.

description: This course will trace the political, cultural, and intellectual history of Russia’s Orthodox Church over the 19th and 20th centuries. Through a close reading of primary sources and scholarly literature, it will examine the place of Orthodox Christianity in the reform, reaction and eventual collapse of the Tsarist regime. It will explore the opposition to radical socialism of Orthodox intellectuals, and the Christian utopian visions proposed by those same thinkers. The course will conclude with a study of the Orthodox Christian component of the Soviet and post-Soviet ideology of “Eurasianism.” Ultimately, the course will question whether Orthodox Christianity has served more to facilitate cooperation or to exacerbate divisions, both within Russia and in Russia’s relations with the world.

title: Exploring Eurasian Environmental History
description: The lands of Eurasia have proved an extraordinarily rich field for environmental historians. The lands have diversity of environments, from Arctic tundra, through forests and steppes to deserts and mountains in Central Asia. Their inhabitants have had a variety of lifeways, such as nomadic pastoralism, settled farming, extracting mineral resources and fossil fuels, and many branches of industry. And these lands have been governed by different political systems, including empires ruled by khans/tsars, Communist-Party regimes, and managed democracies, amongst others. Eurasia contains many ecosystems important for science, a wealth of natural resources that have been exploited, beautiful landscapes and wildlife attractive for tourists. Eurasia has also been the location of catastrophic environmental disasters caused by humans, most notably perhaps the drying up of the Aral Sea and the explosion at the Chernbyl nuclear power station in Ukraine.

prerequisite: KAZ 202 Academic Kazakh II (4562) (C- and above) OR KLL "[C1.1] Advanced"

title: Kazakh Literature
description: In this course students will get familiar with the history of Kazakh Literature.

title: Language and Globalization
description: The course is specifically designed to facilitate students' understanding the processes and functioning of the kazakh language within the context of the globalization of English in Kazakhstan.
prerequisite: KAZ 202 Academic Kazakh II (4562) (C- and above) OR KLL "[C1.1] Advanced"

title: Kazakh for Civil Service
description: This course will concentrate on knowledge of Official Kazakh language standards that students began to learn in the Upper-Intermediate and Advanced levels of Kazakh language.
prerequisite: KAZ 202 Academic Kazakh II (4562) (C- and above) OR KLL "[C1.1] Advanced"

title: Abai’s World
description: The purpose of the course is deepening student learning Abai’s literary legacy.
prerequisite: KAZ 202 Academic Kazakh II (4562) (C- and above) OR KLL "[C1.1] Advanced"

title: Kazakh Language for Engineers
description: Students will be trained to understand professionally qualified speech, conduct business meetings and talks.
prerequisite: KAZ 202 Academic Kazakh II (4562) (C- and above) OR KLL "[C1.1] Advanced"

title: Practical Cultural Kazakh Language
description: The course “Practical Cultural Kazakh language” is designed for learners who are interested in learning about Kazakh language, culture and cuisine of Kazakh people who have no previous knowledge of Kazakhstan

title: Onomastics: History and Function of Names
description: The course of onomastics gives basic knowledge on Kazakh onomastics. The juridical documents on onomastics in Kazakhstan are going to be compared with documents of other states. The course will widely discuss the onomastic units. Students will deal with scientific researches of geographical and administrative objects of their native or current living places. They will learn how to make scientific conclusions through the analysis of given information.
prerequisite: KAZ 202 Academic Kazakh II (4562) (C- and above) OR KLL "[C1.1] Advanced"

title: Scientific Style in Kazakh Language
description: In this course students will explore the scientific style in Kazakh language.
prerequisite: KAZ 202 Academic Kazakh II (4562) (C- and above) OR KLL "[C1.1] Advanced"

title: Kazakh for Career Development
description: The course Kazakh for Career Development is designed for students in a advanced level, who are interested in advancing their careers in the global marketplace.
prerequisite: KAZ 202 Academic Kazakh II (4562) (C- and above) OR KLL "[C1.1] Advanced"

title: Contemporary Kazakh Literature
description: It is important to analyze the effects of the historical and social changes on the development of society of the second half of the twentieth century, which contributes to the special part of the national history. In addition the importance of providing the characteristics for the general conditions of the literature at that time and explaining its main traits in details to the young students is quite significant. The major directions of the word art, life and creativity of writers and poets, the title and genre and other objectives in the duration between 1950 and 2000 of the Kazakh land are discussed in a wide range in this course.
prerequisite: KAZ 202 Academic Kazakh II (4562) (C- and above) OR KLL "[C1.1] Advanced"

title: Language and ethnicity
description: This course studies the connection between language and ethnos from the scientific viewpoint and considers the ethno cultural lexis as a tool to study the nation.
prerequisite: KAZ 202 Academic Kazakh II (4562) (C- and above) OR KLL "[C1.1] Advanced"

title: Kazakh Terminology
description: This course is developed to expand students’ knowledge about Kazakh terminology. The course’s content covers topics from the history of Kazakh terminology’s development to the current situation. Future specialists will learn about enhancing terminology quality, experts who devoted themselves to the field, phases of the terminology evolution.
prerequisite: KAZ 202 Academic Kazakh II (4562) (C- and above) OR KLL "[C1.1] Advanced"

title: Kazakh Diplomacy
description: The content of Kazakh diplomacy course consists of international relations of Kazakhstan and includes diplomatic negotiations, diplomatic protocols, diplomatic documentation, the formation of the state border.
prerequisite: KAZ 202 Academic Kazakh II (4562) (C- and above) OR KLL "[C1.1] Advanced"

title: Cultural Studies and Kazakh Culture
prerequisite: KAZ 202 Academic Kazakh II (4562) (C- and above) OR KLL "[C1.1] Advanced"

title: Language and Culture
description: The purpose of this course is to teach Kazakh culture through linguistic units.
prerequisite: KAZ 202 Academic Kazakh II (4562) (C- and above) OR KLL "[C1.1] Advanced"

title: Intercultural Communication through Film
description: This course aims to develop students' Kazakh language skills and cross-cultural communicative competence through film. Films are considered as very valuable tool not only for developing language skills, but also for facilitating intercultural learning, as they communicate through their characters, story, context, dialogues and audio-effects at several levels to students. Films help students to internalize situations connect with various theories and concepts.
prerequisite: KAZ 202 Academic Kazakh II (4562) (C- and above) OR KLL "[C1.1] Advanced"

title: Kazakh for Social Science
description: Kazakh for the Social Sciences is a comprehensive professional language course that prepares students to excel in the fields of Sociology, Anthropology, and Political Science, while fostering cross-cultural understanding. The course encourages active engagement with diverse social science topics, enhances research skills, and promotes the exchange of diverse perspectives among students.
prerequisite: KAZ 202 Academic Kazakh II (4562) (C- and above) OR KLL "[C1.1] Advanced"

title: Kazakh Cinema
description: The course explores the historical, cultural, and aesthetic development of Kazakh cinema from its inception to the present day.
prerequisite: KAZ 202 Academic Kazakh II (4562) (C- and above) OR KLL "[C1.1] Advanced"

title: Dramatic Reading (CPS 1)
prerequisite: KLL "[C1.1] Advanced"

title: Kazakh literature of the XV-XIX centuries
description: Kazakh literature of the XV-XIX centuries is a course covering significant periods in the history of the national art of speech. In the content of the course the issues of artistic and stylistic continuity of traditional Zhyrau and poetic poetry are explained orally in a scientific and theoretical way.
prerequisite: Subject "KAZ" BETWEEN 300 and 399 OR Subject "KAZ" BETWEEN 300 and 399

title: Shoqan Studies: A Decolonialist Discourse
description: The course explores the historical, cultural, and aesthetic development of Kazakh cinema from its inception to the present day.
prerequisite: Subject "KAZ" BETWEEN 300 and 399

title: Scientific Discourse of Alash
description: This course explores how scientific discourse developed in Kazakh language at the beginning of the 20th century. Starting with Baitursynuly’s Alippe, students will examine books on language, history, natural sciences, and more. They will study the works of Alash intellectuals, many of whom were later repressed, and reflect on how Kazakh scientific terminology was formed a century ago.
prerequisite: Subject "KAZ" BETWEEN 300 and 399

title: Elementary Kazakh as a Foreign Language I
description: Beginning Kazakh as a foreign language.

title: Elementary Kazakh as a Foreign Language II
description: Elementary Kazakh as a foreign language II.
prerequisite: KFL 101 Elementary Kazakh as a Foreign Language I (4889) (C- and above)

title: Intermediate Kazakh as a Foreign Language I
description: Intermediate Kazakh as a foreign language I.

title: Intermediate Kazakh as a Foreign Language II
description: Intermediate Kazakh as a foreign language II.
prerequisite: KFL 201 Intermediate Kazakh as a Foreign Language I (4887) (C- and above)

description: A first semester of Advanced Kazakh as a foreign language.

title: Advanced Kazakh as a Foreign Language II
description: A second semester of Advanced Kazakh as a foreign language.
prerequisite: KFL 301 Advanced Kazakh as a Foreign Language I (4886) (C- and above)

title: Beginning Korean I
description: This course is for beginners. During the course we will focus on all 4 main skills of language-learning: reading, listening, writing and speaking.

title: Beginning Korean II
description: Continuation of KOR 101.
prerequisite: KOR 101 Beginning Korean I (4672) (C- and above)

title: Intermediate Korean I
description: Continuation of KOR 102.
prerequisite: KOR 102 Beginning Korean II (4791) (C- and above)

title: Intermediate Korean II
description: Continuation of KOR 201.
prerequisite: KOR 201 Intermediate Korean I (5059) (C- and above)

title: Advanced Korean I
description: KOR 301 will provide Academic Korean for those who plan to study Korean at higher educational institutions in the future or for those who want to obtain academic knowledge of the language and to develop academic language skills such as making presentations, participating in group discussions, listening to lectures, note-taking, summarizing lectures, reading and writing academic papers.
prerequisite: KOR 202 Intermediate Korean II (5060) (C- and above)

title: Linguistics for non-majors
description: This course is intended to introduce students to the fundamentals of linguistic analysis, i.e. the analysis of natural human language using scientific methods, data analysis, and interdisciplinary thinking. The course will equip students with the knowledge and skills necessary to explain how language is structured, how it is used, and how humans communicate. The course offers an introduction to linguistics for non-majors where the students will also learn that linguistics doesn’t study language in isolation – it connects with many other areas of science to understand how language works, evolves, and functions in human life.
antirequisite: LING 131 Introduction to Linguistics (1394) ( and above)

title: Introduction to Language and Communication
description: The course offers a description of the communicational functions of language, the pragmatics of language and language variation. The course also covers the basics of discourse and conversation analyses.

title: Language Variation and Change: the Story of English
description: The course offers an introduction to comparative-historical linguistics by identifying and describing variation and change of the English language. The course will focus on sound change, history of words and the evolution of grammar of the English language. Within the course the students will also become aware of language variation and discuss the role of English as the global language.

title: Computer Programming for the Humanities and Social Sciences
description: The course equips Humanities and Social Science students with Computational literacy and Python skills they need for various kinds of academic and real-world applications.

title: Introduction to Sociolinguistics
description: This first year introductory course is meant to establish students’ understanding of central themes and topics in the field, in order to support their continued coursework in upper division sociolinguistics courses. Language is not just a static repository of grammar rules and vocabulary, but rather a diverse and ever-changing means of expression for individuals, communities, countries, and global networks. In this course we explore the nature of variation both within and across languages – how different ways of using language(s) can be meaningful and essential for our ever-shifting politics, cultures, and an increasingly interconnected world.
prerequisite: LING 130 Introduction to Language and Communication (4014) (C- and above) OR LING 131 Introduction to Linguistics (1394) (C- and above)

title: Languages of Eurasia
description: The course undertakes to provide a concise survey of the main language families of Eurasia, including Altaic, Uralic, Indo-European, Sino-Tibetan, Tungus-Manchu, and Paleo-Asiatic.

title: Introduction to Cognitive Linguistics
description: The course provides an introduction to Cognitive Linguistics – an actively developing interdisciplinary branch of language study, comprising knowledge and research from cognitive science and different domains of linguistics. Cognitive methods are widely acclaimed in linguistics. Cognitive Linguistics is represented by a family of theories that explore all domains of language using a range of theoretical and experimental methods. Cognitive linguistics is based on the assumption that linguistic phenomena are rooted in general cognitive capacities and therefore, linguistic research should be informed by and accord with what is known about the mind and brain from other disciplines. The course acquaints the students with the main principles and notions of cognitive linguistics. The students practice applying cognitive methods to the analysis of linguistic phenomena in English, Russian, and Kazakh languages. The forms of instruction include lectures, article presentations and discussions, and practical linguistic analysis.
prerequisite: LING 131 Introduction to Linguistics (1394) (C and above)

title: Language and the Mind
description: The course will focus on how language is represented and processed in the human brain.

title: Survey of Research Methods in Linguistics
description: This course examines the manner in which language data and linguistic knowledge is produced and analyzed.
prerequisite: LING 131 Introduction to Linguistics (1394) (C- and above)

title: Introduction to Applied Linguistics
description: This is an introductory course for undergraduate students specializing in WLL or in any area of specialization. No previous coursework in this field of inquiry is assumed.

title: Second Language Acquisition Theory and Research I
description: This course is the first half of a year-long course that deals with second language acquisition (SLA) theories and research methods.

title: Language Diversity and Language Universals
description: The course teaches students about the linguistic diversity in the world and explains the differences and similarities among the world languages.
prerequisite: LING 131 Introduction to Linguistics (1394) (C and above)

title: Sounds of the World’s Languages
description: This course is an introduction to the fundamentals of phonetics and phonology. It will examine the range of sounds used in the major world’s languages (e.g. English, Spanish, Russian, etc) and the ways they are used. The course will be useful for students interested in linguistics and foreign languages.

title: Introduction to Turkic Historical and Comparative Linguistics
description: This course offers an intensive introduction to Turkic philology and the major problems in the diachronic and synchronic study of the Turkic languages. Students with adequate preparation in Turkic languages will find this course a useful introduction to reading approximately a dozen major Turkic languages of Central Asia and elsewhere.
department: Kazakh Language and Turkic Studies, Languages, Literature and Linguistics

title: Corpus Linguistics
description: This course introduces Corpus Linguistics, one of the two most essential data gathering techniques in linguistics. A corpus allows us to directly observe language usage and evaluate it qualitatively and quantitatively. With a sufficiently large corpus, one can explore morpho-syntax and semantics while exclusively relying on context. Smaller corpora still provide a strong basis for subsequent elicitation. In this course, we will look at different types of corpora, how they can be created and used from existing materials or from scratch, and at different ways of searching these corpora.
prerequisite: LING 131 Introduction to Linguistics (1394) (D and above)

title: Introduction to Generative Syntax
description: This course is designed for students interested in broadening and deepening their knowledge of theoretical approaches in linguistics. It outlines the core principles and tenets of generative syntax and teaches students to analyze and model syntactic phenomena using generative theoretical machinery.
prerequisite: LING 131 Introduction to Linguistics (1394) (C and above)

title: Methods of Teaching Foreign Languages
description: The course introduces students to contemporary methods of teaching foreign languages and to principles of task-based instruction course consists of lectures, workshops, guest teaching, and service learning. Assessments include classroom observations, reflection papers, a textbook comparison paper, and a technology presentation, as well as practical assignments in lesson planning, the design of activities and tests and a final portfolio.

title: Practicum in Teaching Foreign Languages
description: This is a practical course in developing teaching skills, consisting of supervised student teaching, tutoring, as well as instructor-led weekly group practicums. Assessments include designing lessons and activities, weekly teaching reports, and a final portfolio.

title: Advanced Topics in Linguistics
description: This 300-level course is designed to allow LLL faculty and visiting scholars to teach courses in the domain of their research interests. The course is designed to meet the important element of NU’s overall goal to promote research-integrated and research-informed teaching. The topics of this course will vary in accordance with the specific professor’s preferences, but they will consistently imply and involve deep analysis of chosen topic in the general realm of theoretical and applied linguistics.
prerequisite: LING 131 Introduction to Linguistics (1394) (C- and above)

title: Language Contact in Central Asia
description: This course will explore contacts between languages from the perspective of general linguistics and social linguistics. In this course, students will learn core concepts in language contact. We will also consider specific case studies from languages all over the world, and reflect on cases studies in Central Asian language contact. This course focuses on developing the students’ abilities to formulate research questions and proposals as well. Students will examine their hypothesis by field work.
prerequisite: LING 131 Introduction to Linguistics (1394) (C- and above)

title: The Art and Science of Analyzing Languages: Morphosyntax of the World's Languages
description: The course teaches the methods for analyzing morphosyntax of the world’s languages with an ample range of linguistic examples and practical exercises.
prerequisite: LING 131 Introduction to Linguistics (1394) (C- and above)

title: Psycholinguistics
description: Psychology of Language is an interdisciplinary field in which it covers the perception and production of language, reading written language, processing sentences, mental lexicon and first /second plus language acquisitions.
prerequisite: LING 131 Introduction to Linguistics (1394) (C- and above) OR LING 272 Language and the Mind (1847) (C- and above) OR LING 273 Survey of Research Methods in Linguistics (2158) (C- and above)

title: Historical Linguistics
description: This course provides an introduction to Historical Linguistics, i.e. to how sounds, morphemes and patterns develop over time, on the ways how languages can be related to each other. It acquaints the students with different types of changes, techniques by which these can be identified, and the ways in which these changes entitle us to postulate certain genetic or contact relations between those languages.
prerequisite: LING 131 Introduction to Linguistics (1394) (C- and above) AND (LING 240 Introduction to Sociolinguistics (6838) (C- and above) OR LING 270 Languages of Eurasia (2485) (C- and above) OR LING 273 Survey of Research Methods in Linguistics (2158) (C- and above) OR LING 277 Language Diversity and Language Universals (3834) (C- and above) OR LING 278 Sounds of the World’s Languages (3850) (C- and above) OR LING 280/TUR 280 Introduction to Turkic Historical and Comparative Linguistics (3175) (C- and above) OR LING 375 The Art and Science of Analyzing Languages: Morphosyntax of the World's Languages (6237) (C- and above) OR LING 470 Multilingualism and Language Contact (3339) (C- and above) OR LING 374 Language Contact in Central Asia (3047) (C- and above) OR LING 140 Language Variation and Change: the Story of English (4835) (C- and above))

title: Discourse and Grammar
description: The course provides an introduction to Discourse and Grammar – an interdisciplinary branch of language study, comprising research from typology, syntax, interactional linguistics, and cognitive science. Discourse and Grammar is an interdisciplinary framework that looks at the development of grammatical constructions from the point of view of language use. Discourse and Grammar is based on the assumption that speakers make functional choices at every level of structure and that, as such, grammatical constructions arise from the functions they serve for language users. The course will cover the two major direction of the interface between grammar and interaction: (1) how grammatical structures arise from fluid patterns of language use; (2) how stable structures of grammar provide templates for linguistic action. The course acquaints the students with the main principles and notions of Discourse and Grammar, as well as with the different qualitative and quantitative methods used to carry out research in the discipline. The students practice applying these methods to the analysis of linguistic phenomena in Kazakh languages. The forms of instruction include lectures, article presentations and discussions, and practical linguistic analysis.
prerequisite: LING 131 Introduction to Linguistics (1394) (C and above)

title: Statistics and computational methods in Linguistics
description: This course is a hands-on primer to quantitative/statistical methodology in linguistics. In the first part of the course (until week 6), we introduce fundamental concepts of quantitative analysis (variables and hypothesis), discuss the logic of quantitative studies, and cover the basics of a programming language (R or Python). We discuss a variety of descriptive graphs, measurements (frequency and dispersion), and tests (tests for independence, distribution) for monofactorial analysis. We end the module by implementing these concepts trough popular corpus-linguistics techniques (frequency lists, key words, collocations). We then move on to the second section of the course (until week 11) , where we explore techniques for multifactorial analysis that are frequently in linguistics (linear and generalized linear regression modeling, classification trees, and random forests). In the last weeks of the course we discuss and implement best practices for dataset preparation and data visualization. We study these topics on linguistic datasets.
prerequisite: LING 131 Introduction to Linguistics (1394) (C- and above) AND Subject "LING" BETWEEN 200 and 299

title: Experimental semantics
description: The aim of the course is an in-depth study of semantics, primarily with the help of empirical and in particular, corpus and experimental methods. It aspires to explore the existing discussions, points of contention and different viewpoints on major semantic issues. During the course, students become familiar with the main theoretical issues of semantics, and through the study of selected research articles, form an idea of the various experimental research accounts of these issues. They test different research methods, conducting their own experiments related to the main course topics. They critically examine different research and identify points of contention and potential gaps. They formulate their own suggestions for further research, design and conduct an experiment. Thus, the outcome of the course is the design and realization of a full independent research project in semantics: the students must formulate the research question, choose the experimental method and tasks, develop the stimuli, upload the experiment on PCIbex online platform, conduct the experiment, download and process the results, interpret the data, and make a presentation including discussion of the results. The results of the experiment could potentially be developed into a qualitative paper if they are substantive and represent an advancement in the study of the respective field.
prerequisite: LING 130 Introduction to Language and Communication (4014) (C- and above) OR LING 131 Introduction to Linguistics (1394) (C- and above)

title: Multilingualism and Language Contact
description: This course studies phenomena related to multilingualism and language contact, and its consequences.
prerequisite: LING 131 Introduction to Linguistics (1394) (C- and above) OR LING 270 Languages of Eurasia (2485) (C- and above) OR ANT 277/WLL 271 Language and Society (1027) (C- and above) OR LING 272 Language and the Mind (1847) (C- and above) OR LING 273 Survey of Research Methods in Linguistics (2158) (C- and above) OR LING 274 Introduction to Applied Linguistics (2486) (C- and above) OR LING 275 Second Language Acquisition Theory and Research I (4473) (C- and above)

title: Language Ideologies
description: How do beliefs and perceptions about what language is or should be structure our use and understanding of individual speakers and speech communities? What is the relationship between language and structures of power? This course introduces students to the study of Language Ideology, one of the primary topics of study in linguistic anthropology, which connects the semiotic study of sign forms not only to the cohesion and coherence of language in its various modalities (spoken, written, signed), but also to the social and historical relations structuring our categories and understanding of the object ‘language’ in itself.
prerequisite: LING 131 Introduction to Linguistics (1394) (C- and above)

title: Advanced Empirical Methods in Linguistics
description: This course is designed for the senior undergraduate WLLC majors and graduate students, and attends to theoretical and practical aspects of collecting and analyzing natural human language data within two main empirical methodological domains: (i) field linguistics and language documentation, and (ii) corpus linguistics.
prerequisite: LING 131 Introduction to Linguistics (1394) (C and above)

title: Discourse, Grammar, and Interaction
description: This course examines the manner in which language data and linguistic knowledge is produced and analyzed, what modern linguistics considers data, evidence, explanation.
prerequisite: LING 131 Introduction to Linguistics (1394) (C- and above) OR ANT 277/WLL 271 Language and Society (1027) (C- and above) OR LING 272 Language and the Mind (1847) (C- and above)

title: Tense, Aspect, Modality and Evidentiality
description: This course is designed to give students an overview of the study of tense, aspect, modality and evidentiality (TAME) and their interrelatedness. The course covers a selection of approaches, with literature ranging from classical texts, via overview texts, to research articles. It concludes with a term paper.
prerequisite: LING 273 Survey of Research Methods in Linguistics (2158) (C- and above) AND (LING 375 The Art and Science of Analyzing Languages: Morphosyntax of the World's Languages (6237) (C- and above) OR LING 377 Historical Linguistics (7972) (C- and above) OR () ( and above) OR LING 473 Advanced Empirical Methods in Linguistics (6244) (C- and above))

title: Language and Worldview
description: This senior level course in linguistic anthropology will cover the topics of linguistic relativity, Deaf communities and the ‘culture’ concept, language socialization and sociolinguistic indexicality, storytelling and environmental change, soundscapes, and ontologies of language. The purpose is to explore how the pragmatic qualities of language shape and are shaped by cultural experience, and in turn, how a ‘worldview’ may be created (and changed) through language. Students will be tasked with exams and presentations, but also with a series of short creative projects, in order to explore the central theoretical concepts of each topical unit.
prerequisite: LING 131 Introduction to Linguistics (1394) (C and above) OR LING 272 Language and the Mind (1847) (C and above)

title: Advanced Independent Study
description: Students design and undertake an individual program of study on an advanced topic in linguistics under the supervision of a faculty member.

description: This course will explore contacts between languages from the perspective of general, historical, socio- and contact linguistics. Its goal is to offer the participants a solid understanding of language contact all over the world which can then be applied to the Central Asian contact. Students acquire basic concepts of the study of language contact, such as lexical borrowing, code-switching, multilingualism, language maintenance and language shift. They will study the patterns along which qualitatively new language varieties may evolve as the results of language contact. Students will have the opportunity to plan and conduct research on language contact phenomena.

title: Advanced Empirical Methods in Linguistics
description: This course is designed for graduate students conducting research in languages and linguistics. It attends to theoretical and practical aspects of collecting and analyzing natural human language data within two main empirical methodological domains: (i) field linguistics and language documentation, and (ii) corpus linguistics.

title: Language Contact in Central Asia
description: This course will explore contacts between languages from the perspective of general, historical, socio- and contact linguistics. Its goal is to offer the participants a solid understanding of language contact all over the world which can then be applied to the Central Asian contact. Students acquire basic concepts of the study of language contact, such as lexical borrowing, code-switching, multilingualism, language maintenance and language shift. They will study the patterns along which qualitatively new language varieties may evolve as the results of language contact. Students will have the opportunity to plan and conduct research on language contact phenomena.

title: Tense, Aspect, Modality and Evidentiality
description: This course is designed to give students an overview of the study of tense, aspect, modality and evidentiality (TAME) and their interrelatedness. The course covers a selection of approaches, with literature ranging from classical texts, via overview texts, to research articles. It concludes with a term paper.

title: Language and Worldview
description: This senior level course in linguistic anthropology will cover the topics of linguistic relativity, Deaf communities and the ‘culture’ concept, language socialization and sociolinguistic indexicality, storytelling and environmental change, soundscapes, and ontologies of language. The purpose is to explore how the pragmatic qualities of language shape and are shaped by cultural experience, and in turn, how a ‘worldview’ may be created (and changed) through language. Students will be tasked with exams and presentations, but also with a series of short creative projects, in order to explore the central theoretical concepts of each topical unit.

title: Discourse and Grammar
description: The course provides an introduction to Discourse and Grammar – an interdisciplinary branch of language study comprising research from typology, syntax, interactional linguistics, and cognitive science. The course takes Discourse and Grammar as the label for a unified field which looks at discourse from the perspective of grammar, and grammar from the perspective of discourse. The Discourse and Grammar approach is interested in finding functional explanations behind the emergence of grammar. Discourse is understood as the domain of language use, with speakers making functional choices at all levels of structure, whether across sentence and larger unit boundaries, inside clauses and phrases, or even within words. Grammar provides the structures for linguistic action, and functionally motivated linguistic action in turn produces the recurrent patterns that ultimately grammaticize, giving rise to linguistic structure. The course will cover the two major directions of the interface between grammar and interaction: (1) how grammatical structures arise from fluid patterns of language use (discourse); (2) how stable structures of grammar provide templates for linguistic action. Research questions in the domain of Discourse and Grammar can be addressed through a variety of methods, including quantitative (corpus linguistics, psycholinguistics experiments) and qualitative (Conversation Analysis, discourse analysis, structural analysis).

title: Computer Aided Design
description: Computer Aided Design is a core course for 2nd-year students with the main focus on the fundamentals of engineering design: visualization, sketching, drawing, modeling, prototyping, assembling, and testing.

title: Environmental Science
description: This course is designed to equip students with a foundational understanding of environmental science and sustainable engineering. It will cover the latest developments in climate change, explore effective mitigation strategies and energy transitions, and examine the application of sustainable, green engineering principles for future advancements.

title: Material and Manufacturing I
description: This course primarily intends to introduce the students to a wide variety of materials and relevant theories. This course covers ferrous & non-ferrous materials and three other major categories of non-metallic materials namely ceramics, polymers and composite. Students will be introduced to the idea of production processes required for various materials. Different types of heat treatment processes such as annealing, normalizing, quenching, tempering, surface modification methods to improvise material properties further will be introduced.

title: Engineering Dynamics I
description: The key focus areas are: a) Model and analyze the kinematics of systems of rigid bodies. b) Model and analyze dynamic interactions of rigid bodies. c) Apply the principle of work and energy for rigid bodies in complex motion. d) Apply the principle of impulse and momentum for rigid bodies in complex motion. e) Model and analyze three dimensional rigid body systems (introduction).

title: Fluid Mechanics I
description: The course is concerned with the static and dynamics of liquids and gases. The analysis of the behavior of fluids is based upon the fundamental laws of applied mechanics that relate to the conservation of mass, energy and momentum equations. The triad of integral, differential, and experimental approaches is being employed throughout the entire course.
prerequisite: PHYS 161 Physics I for Scientists and Engineers with Laboratory (116) (D and above)

title: Engineering Thermodynamics
description: This course covers all the standard essentials of engineering thermodynamics as is found in most standard university courses. The course has a bias towards the essentials for mechanical engineering students.

title: Machine Elements Design
description: The module aims to impart the necessary knowledge and skills for mechanical engineering students to analyse and design machine elements and simple machines
prerequisite: MAE 205 Material and Manufacturing I (5534) (D and above)

title: Control Systems
description: The course aims to provide a solid background for the understanding of classical controller, its analysis and design techniques. It will help students in developing hardware and software packages.

title: Fluid Mechanics II
description: The module focuses on the fundamental concepts, principles and theories of external flows, boundary layers, compressible flows, and turbomachinery.
prerequisite: MAE 300 Fluid Mechanics I (5926) (D and above) OR EME 275 Fluid Mechanics I (1988) (D and above)

title: Computer Aided Engineering
description: The course is aiming to introduce the fundamentals of the Finite and Boundary Element methods (FEM / BEM) and guide students in the development and usage of such methods in the engineering profession. Focus will be given in solving specific engineering problems ranging from solid mechanics, to heat transfer and fluid flows using both student-developed and commercial analysis software packages.
prerequisite: ENG 202 Numerical Methods in Engineering (5506) (D and above) AND MAE 201 Computer Aided Design (5011) (D and above)

title: Mechanics of Machines
description: The course consists of analysis of machines and mechanisms operation with application of statics and dynamics principles. Application of these principles with analysis of operation of mechanisms provides background for design of machine elements. Also gear theory will be introduced, balancing of shaking forces and crank effort diagram and flywheels. Finally, mechanical vibration in machine elements will be explained to define the natural frequency, transient and steady state responses.
prerequisite: MAE 206 Engineering Dynamics I (5535) (D and above)

title: Aerodynamics
description: Familiarization of students with the basic principles of the concepts, techniques, and theory for the analysis of aerodynamic forces; Development of various relevant skills and competences through the application of aerodynamics to the design of engineering components and systems; Introduction to computational aerodynamics and panel methods codes for analysis of forces for general aircraft
prerequisite: MAE 300 Fluid Mechanics I (5926) (D and above)

title: Structural Mechanics II
description: Structural mechanics II aims to study plasticity, brittle vs ductile failure modes, composite materials, fast fracture, fatigue, creep, and instability of structures such as buckling of columns. A theoretical introduction to the finite element method will be delivered. Students shall be able to develop critical thinking skills and identify the failure mode of a structure
prerequisite: MAE 200 Structural Mechanics I (5010) (D and above) OR CEE 200 Structural Mechanics I (5005) (D and above)

title: Vehicle Propulsion Systems
description: Introduction of the most important concepts of mathematical system modelling using vehicle propulsion problems as examples, both with traditional energy sources and clean-energy sources. Presentation of several model classes of propulsion systems and components will be given. Application of modern system components and control tools to vehicle propulsion systems will be included.
prerequisite: MAE 301 Engineering Thermodynamics (5927) (D and above) OR BENG 226 Engineering Thermodynamics (1553) (D and above)

title: Summer Internship
description: The course aims to provide an opportunity for students willing to develop their professional skills and gain work experience during the summer term of their studies. Students having completed their 2nd or 3rd year of studies are eligible for this elective course which allows placement in a discipline-related organization or company with the aim of applying and developing their skill in a real world engineering environment. Internship programs are coordinated in collaboration with the institutional Career and Advising Center – CAC.

title: Heat Transfer
description: The course covers the heat transfer phenomena including conduction, convection and radiation. Boiling and condensation, and heat exchangers are treated as well. By learning the basis of all these phenomena and techniques, the students will develop advance knowledge and understanding of heat transfer. The module will assist students to gain an understanding of heat transfer concepts and their applications.
prerequisite: MAE 300 Fluid Mechanics I (5926) (D and above) AND MAE 301 Engineering Thermodynamics (5927) (D and above)

title: Mechanical Systems Design
description: The course will consist of application and enhancement of previously studied principles of machine elements design (MAE 302 course) to design complex mechanical systems and machines. Teaching methods will include group assignments, peer learning.
prerequisite: MAE 302 Machine Elements Design (5928) (D and above)

title: Additive Manufacturing
description: This course aims to present & study Additive Manufacturing (AM) technologies such as Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM), Stereolithography (SLA) and Selective Laser Melting (SLM), as well as an overview of AM and industry 4.0. The module includes a presentation of the different materials available for use with these technologies, such as photopolymer resins, plastic filaments for FDM printing and metal powders for metal AM, i.e., SLM. The production and properties of metal powders will be studied in detail. Topology optimization for 3D printing will be also covered in this module. Project-based learning is a major component in this course and therefore project assignments, lab experimentation and practical sessions will be used to develop student skills in designing for AM, critical thinking in reviewing models for AM and assessing the pros and cons of each applicable approach and technique. Formal assessment is carried out via 2 mini-projects (25 and 50%) and a final examination (25%).
prerequisite: MAE 205 Material and Manufacturing I (5534) (D and above)

title: Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Design
description: Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) Design is a design course that covers the aspects of modern aircraft design for small unmanned and autonomous vehicles. It covers the design of fixed wing and multi-rotor aerial vehicles that can be used for a variety of applications such as parcel delivery, surveillance, environmental monitoring, and mapping. The course integrates the students’ knowledge of aerodynamics and control and introduces the concepts of static and dynamic stability. Students design, build and test conceptual models to affirm the concepts of flight and control.
prerequisite: (MAE 303 Control Systems (5929) (D and above) AND MAE 340 Aerodynamics (6576) (D and above)) OR MMAE 603 Modern Control Engineering (4500) (C- and above)

title: Computer Aided Geometric Design
description: CAGD, which stands for Computer Aided Geometric Design, is the discipline concerned with the computational and geometric aspects of free-form curves, surfaces and volumes as they are used, for example, in CAD/CAM (Computer Aided Design / Computer Aided Manufacture), scientific visualization and computer graphics. It is safe to say that CAD revolutionized modern day engineering. CAD allows for the easier development of products and product management integration and CAGD is its main pillar. Having thorough knowledge of the internal mathematical representations and modelling is a significant asset for every engineer that is willing to be involved in engineering projects.
prerequisite: MAE 201 Computer Aided Design (5011) (D and above)

title: Fire Engineering
description: The Fire Engineering course aims to: 1) Provide a general understanding of the principles of enclosure fire dynamics, 2) Help the students to appreciate their applications to building fires and smoke analysis, 3) Familiarize the students with the basic design methods for fire-fighting systems.
prerequisite: MAE 305 Fluid Mechanics II (6173) (D and above) AND MAE 301 Engineering Thermodynamics (5927) (D and above)

title: Flight Performance and Mechanics
description: By the end of the course the student will be expected to be able to: 1) Understand airplane flight conditions and stability. 2) Analyze airplane flight performance in various conditions. 3) Relate the various physical elements and environmental parameters which govern the design and performance of airplane. 4) Appreciate space flight and hypersonic vehicles.
prerequisite: MAE 340 Aerodynamics (6576) (D and above) OR MAE 305 Fluid Mechanics II (6173) (D and above)

title: Materials and Manufacturing II
description: This course is designed to provide students with an overview of a wide variety of manufacturing processes (additive, forming & subtractive) and system including assembly. It will also provide the insight of fundamental principle behind the manufacturing processes. This course includes project work which requires student to generate G coding and fabricate part product using computer numerical controlled (CNC), machine.

title: Feasibility Analysis of Clean Energy Technologies
description: This module gives the student an introduction to the preparation of pre and feasibility studies of clean energy technologies , which includes: energy efficiency measures and technologies based on renewable energies.

title: Advanced Topics in Computational Fluid Dynamics
description: 1. Review fundamental governing differential equations in incompressible fluid dynamics and energy conservation, both in Vector and Cartesian-tensor notation. 2. Introduce concept of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and learn computational hardware & software and space-time discretization schemes generally associated to it by programming own small codes and by using commercial software widely used for engineering applications. 3. Introduce some advanced topics in CFD, such as turbulence modelling, radiation and combustion modeling, multiphase modeling, computational fluid structure interaction and most popular methods used in engineering applications.
prerequisite: MAE 300 Fluid Mechanics I (5926) (D and above) AND ENG 202 Numerical Methods in Engineering (5506) (D and above)

title: Multiphase Systems
description: This course will identify the industrial occurrence of the simultaneous flow of more than one phase and highlight the implications for design. The course will cover the basic principles, engineering models and equations of multi-phase flows and selected multi-phase systems.
prerequisite: MAE 300 Fluid Mechanics I (5926) (D and above) AND MAE 305 Fluid Mechanics II (6173) (D and above)

title: Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems and Microsystems technology
description: The course aims to introduce MEMS devices, microsystems and their applications. The course will start with an introduction to the working principles of microsystems. It will follow up with the microsystems design and fabrication. Some representative sensors (pressure, toque and flow) will be presented to demonstrate the application and advantages of such miniaturized devices.

title: Mechanics of Soft Materials
description: This course provides a brief background on materials chemistry and will then shift toward the chemical and physical properties of polymers, with a focus on mechanical properties. Effects of chemical structure and morphology on thermal and mechanical properties as well as the behavior of materials under stress, will be discussed in depth. A fundamental understanding of the corresponding characterization techniques (DMA, DSC, TGA, Mass Spectrometry, and FTIR) will be covered.
prerequisite: ENG 102 Engineering Materials I (4708) (D and above)

title: Introduction to Maintenance Engineering
description: The aim of the course is to introduce students to the fundamentals of maintenance engineering. The students will learn the importance of maintenance and the dangerous consequences of the lack of maintenance in modern engineering and industrial settings. The students will be able to learn concepts such as maintenance management and control, preventive maintenance, corrective maintenance, reliability-centered maintenance, human error, quality and safety, reliability, cost efficiency, and maintainability. In addition, students will study the mathematical tools necessary to perform risk and maintenance analysis such as failure data analysis, maintenance cost analysis, and optimal experiment design.
prerequisite: ENG 201 Applied Probability and Statistics (5505) (D and above)

title: Application of Optimization in Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering.
description: The course aims to introduce students to the fundamentals of optimization theory. Specifically, the course aims to introduce students to the dynamic field of finding the local and/or global extrema of functions. The students will be able to learn concepts such as unconstrained and constrained optimization, convex and nonconvex optimization, gradient-based, stochastic, and mixed optimization, single shooting, multiple shooting, collocation, differential inclusion methods, homotopy optimization, direct and indirect methods, dynamic programming, linear and quadratic programming problems, etc.
prerequisite: ENG 202 Numerical Methods in Engineering (5506) (D and above) AND MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (D and above)

title: Heating, Ventilating and Air Conditioning
description: Heating, ventilating, and air conditioning of indoor environment are mandatory in modern society. It provides human comfort and enhances human health. These two factors lead to an increase in safety and productivity. Moreover, controlled environments for various public and health-care buildings including hospital and data centers are necessary. The topics includes air-conditioning systems, moist air properties and conditioning processes, comfort and health, heat transmission, solar radiation, heating and cooling loads & air diffusion.
prerequisite: MAE 301 Engineering Thermodynamics (5927) (D and above)

title: Introduction to Aerospace Propulsion.
description: The course aims to introduce students to the fundamentals of optimization theory. Specifically, the course aims to introduce students to the dynamic field of finding the local and/or global extrema of functions. The students will be able to learn concepts such as unconstrained and constrained optimization, convex and nonconvex optimization, gradient-based, stochastic, and mixed optimization, single shooting, multiple shooting, collocation, differential inclusion methods, homotopy optimization, direct and indirect methods, dynamic programming, linear and quadratic programming problems, etc.
prerequisite: MAE 300 Fluid Mechanics I (5926) (D and above) AND MAE 301 Engineering Thermodynamics (5927) (D and above)

title: Fundamentals of Space Flight Dynamics
description: This course is designed to provide students with fundamental knowledge and modeling techniques in the most important fields of space flight dynamics, namely, orbital mechanics, rocket vehicle dynamics, and spacecraft attitude dynamics. The whole course will be delivered through a mathematical software package capable of performing symbolic and numerical calculations. With a strong emphasis on scientific problem-solving using programming, this course equips students with the knowledge and skills necessary to become specialists in the field of space engineering.

title: Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Design
description: Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) Design is a design course that covers the aspects of modern aircraft design for small unmanned and autonomous vehicles. It covers the design of fixed wing and multi-rotor aerial vehicles that can be used for a variety of applications such as parcel delivery, surveillance, environmental monitoring, and mapping. The course integrates the students’ knowledge of aerodynamics and control and introduces the concepts of static and dynamic stability. Students design, build and test conceptual models to affirm the concepts of flight and control.
prerequisite: MMAE 603 Modern Control Engineering (4500) (C- and above)

title: Ambulatory Internal Medicine Clerkship
description: 4-week Ambulatory Internal Medicine clerkship. The location for the Ambulatory Medicine is the Diagnostic Center, UMC and the National Referral Hospital for Oncology and Transplantation.

title: Pediatric Ambulatory Medicine Clerkship
description: The Pediatric Ambulatory Medicine Clerkship is oriented around key areas that have been identified as essential for medical school graduates to know. Clinical rotations will last for 4 weeks. The location for the PAMC is the UMC NRCMCH, RDC.

title: Anesthesiology Clerkship
description: This 2-week clerkship overview covers the disciplines of general anesthesiology. The course is primarily designed to prepare students to assume the role of a primary care physician and to become familiar with the clinical presentations and management of common problems in anesthesiology.

title: Mathematical Discovery
description: This course is to explore applications of mathematics in real life, including social choice and management science, showing that math is more than a set of formulas.
antirequisite: MATH 161 Calculus I (118) (C- and above)

title: Pre-Calculus
antirequisite: CPS "MATH" BETWEEN 60 and 100 OR MATH 161 Calculus I (118) ( and above)

title: Calculus II
prerequisite: MATH 161 Calculus I (118) (C and above)

title: Discrete Mathematics
prerequisite: MATH 161 Calculus I (118) (C and above)

title: Calculus III
prerequisite: MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (C and above)

title: Linear Algebra with Applications
prerequisite: MATH 161 Calculus I (118) (C and above)
corequisite: MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (C and above)

title: Introduction to Differential Equations
prerequisite: MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (C and above)

title: Mathematics for Artificial Intelligence
description: This course provides a rigorous mathematical foundation for Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML). Students will explore key mathematical concepts, including linear algebra, probability theory, optimization that form the backbone of modern AI techniques. The course will include theoretical lectures and practical exercises applying these concepts to AI models.
prerequisite: MATH 161 Calculus I (118) (C- and above) OR CSCI 151 Programming for Scientists and Engineers (192) (C- and above)

title: Introduction to Number Theory
prerequisite: MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (C and above) AND MATH 251 Discrete Mathematics (85) (C and above)

title: Abstract Algebra I
prerequisite: MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (C and above) AND MATH 251 Discrete Mathematics (85) (C and above)

title: Applied Statistical Methods
description: Descriptive statistics, measures of location and spread,graphic methods,basic probability properties, Bayes’ rule, probability distributions, expected value and variance, binomial and normal distributions, point and interval estimation,hypothesis testing,one-sample and two-sample t-tests,chi-square tests,linear regression, quality measures, and assumption verification, ANOVA and multiple comparisons.
prerequisite: MATH 161 Calculus I (118) (C and above)
antirequisite: MATH 321 Probability (482) (C and above)

title: Probability
prerequisite: MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (C and above)
antirequisite: ECON 211 Economic Statistics (2280) (C- and above) OR PLS 211 Quantitative Methods (221) (C- and above)

title: Mathematical Statistics
description: The course starts where Probability ends and considers point estimation, method of moments, maximum likelihood estimation, unbiasedness, consistency, sampling distributions, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, power of tests.
prerequisite: MATH 321 Probability (482) (C and above) OR ECON 211 Economic Statistics (2280) (C and above)

title: Actuarial Mathematics I
description: This course covers the standard topics for the Financial Mathematics (FM) exam recommended by the Society of Actuaries (SDA)
prerequisite: MATH 321 Probability (482) (C and above) OR ECON 211 Economic Statistics (2280) (C and above) OR (MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (C and above) AND MATH 310 Applied Statistical Methods (82) (C and above))

title: Research Methods
description: This course is designed to teach students basic skills that are essential in research work in mathematical sciences.
prerequisite: MATH 321 Probability (482) (C and above)

title: Numerical Methods with Applications
prerequisite: MATH 274 Introduction to Differential Equations (484) (C and above) AND MATH 263 Calculus III (81) (C and above)
antirequisite: ENG 202 Numerical Methods in Engineering (5506) (C and above)

title: Introduction to Proofs
description: The course develops skills required to prove mathematical statements, familiarizes students with various forms of mathematical statements (tautologies, contradictions, conditionals and their variants, etc.)
prerequisite: MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (C and above) AND MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (C and above)

title: Advanced Calculus with Differential Forms
description: The course covers total derivatives, Taylor formula in several variables, inverse and implicit function theorems as well as applications. The main goal is to prove Stokes theorem with differential forms.
prerequisite: MATH 263 Calculus III (81) (C- and above) AND MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (C- and above)

title: Real Analysis I
prerequisite: MATH 263 Calculus III (81) (C and above) AND MATH 251 Discrete Mathematics (85) (C and above)

title: Introduction to Mathematical Biology
description: This course covers single species models, interacting models, infectious disease models, and molecular interactions, neural and biological oscillators.
prerequisite: MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (C and above) AND MATH 274 Introduction to Differential Equations (484) (C and above)

title: Internship
description: MATH 399 Internship is an elective 6 ECTS workload, which provides an opportunity for a student to gain practical hands-on work experience in a related field of interest.

title: Abstract Algebra II
description: This course covers topics from coding theory, Galois Theory, multilinear algebra, advanced group theory, and advanced ring theory.
prerequisite: MATH 302 Abstract Algebra I (620) (C and above)

title: Topics in Algebra
prerequisite: MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (C and above)

title: Graph Theory
prerequisite: (MATH 301 Introduction to Number Theory (613) (C and above) OR MATH 251 Discrete Mathematics (85) (C and above)) AND MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (C and above)

title: Linear Programming
description: The course starts with formulation of real problem into a linear program (LP), geometric interpretation of linear optimization, integer programming and LP relaxation, duality theory, simplex method, sensitivity analysis, robust optimization, ellipsoid and interior point methods, and semidefinite optimization, applications (e.g., game theory and network optimization).
prerequisite: MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (C and above) AND MATH 263 Calculus III (81) (C and above)

title: Nonlinear Optimization
description: This course covers an introduction into convex sets and convex functions, unconstrained and constrained optimization, existence of solutions (Weierstrass' theorem) as well as various types of optimality theorem.
prerequisite: MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (C and above) AND MATH 263 Calculus III (81) (C and above)

title: Cryptography
prerequisite: MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (C and above) AND (MATH 251 Discrete Mathematics (85) (C and above) OR MATH 301 Introduction to Number Theory (613) (C and above) OR MATH 355 Introduction to Proofs (86) (C and above))

title: Actuarial Mathematics II
description: Life insurances, survival distributions and models, life tables, life annuities, contingency models, insurance benefits, premium and reserve calculations, multiple life and multiple decrement models.
prerequisite: MATH 321 Probability (482) (C and above) OR ECON 211 Economic Statistics (2280) (C and above)

title: Mathematical Finance
description: The course aims to cover knowledge of basic financial actuarial models with applications and to prepare students pass the actuarial financial economics (MFE) exam.
prerequisite: MATH 321 Probability (482) (C and above) OR ECON 211 Economic Statistics (2280) (C and above)

title: Stochastic Processes
description: This course covers discrete-time and continuous-time Markov chains.
prerequisite: MATH 321 Probability (482) (C and above) OR ECON 211 Economic Statistics (2280) (C and above)

title: Regression Analysis
prerequisite: MATH 322 Mathematical Statistics (1165) (C and above)
antirequisite: SOC 203 Quantitative Methods in Sociology (1377) (C and above) OR PLS 211 Quantitative Methods (221) (C and above)

title: Design of Experiments
description: The course begins with one-way and two-way ANOVA for fixed effects, diagnostics and remedial measures, multiple comparisons.
prerequisite: MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (C and above) AND (MATH 310 Applied Statistical Methods (82) (C and above) OR MATH 322 Mathematical Statistics (1165) (C and above))

title: Nonparametric Methods
description: A large part of this course is dedicated to considering nonparametric analogs of parametric tests.
prerequisite: MATH 322 Mathematical Statistics (1165) (C and above)

title: Time Series Analysis
prerequisite: MATH 322 Mathematical Statistics (1165) (C and above)

title: Statistical Programming
description: Introduction to the basics of programming and algorithms in statistics. Exploration data of storage, manipulation, plotting, and analysis. Modularization, conditional execution, looping, and function construction are covered along with program debugging techniques.
prerequisite: MATH 322 Mathematical Statistics (1165) (C and above)

title: Stochastic Calculus
description: This class introduces stochastic calculus and its applications. In the first half of the class, the course introduces the measure theoretic probability concepts. Next, we move to Ito lemma and stochastic differential equations. Examples of stochastic differential equations with explicit solutions are provided.
prerequisite: MATH 321 Probability (482) (C and above) OR ECON 211 Economic Statistics (2280) (C and above)

title: Introduction to Lie Groups and Representations
description: The course material consists of a review and expansion of some topics of calculus of several variables; especially the inverse and implicit function theorems, which are essential tools. Then the classical matrix groups and their properties will be studied, along with their Lie algebras. Finally, representations of SO(3) and SL(n,C) will be studied, among others.
prerequisite: MATH 361 Real Analysis I (483) (C and above) AND MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (C and above) AND MATH 274 Introduction to Differential Equations (484) (C and above)

title: Topology
description: A course in topology which covers the topics on metric spaces, topological spaces and their properties.
prerequisite: MATH 361 Real Analysis I (483) (C and above)

title: Real Analysis II
description: This course is a continuation of MATH 361, beginning with differentiation and ending with the Lebesgue integral.
prerequisite: MATH 361 Real Analysis I (483) (C and above)

title: Advanced Linear Algebra
description: This course is designed to introduce some advanced topics not included in MATH 273 and study some concepts in MATH 273 more deeply. This course is theorem-proofs style course, emphasizing theories
prerequisite: MATH 251 Discrete Mathematics (85) (C and above) AND MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (C and above)

title: Introduction to Differential Geometry
description: This course explores the geometry of curves and surfaces, blending concepts from calculus and linear algebra. It begins with the study of curves, covering their length, curvature, and reparametrization. The focus then shifts to surfaces, including their definitions, smoothness, and types such as quadric and ruled surfaces. Key topics include calculating lengths and curvatures on surfaces, examining isometries and conformal mappings, and understanding intrinsic properties through the second fundamental form and Gauss-Weingarten maps. Advanced topics address geodesics, Gaussian curvature, and significant theorems like Gauss' remarkable theorem, providing tools to analyze and solve geometric problems.
prerequisite: MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (C and above) AND MATH 361 Real Analysis I (483) (C and above)

title: Nonlinear Continuum Mechanics
description: This course is concerned with the mathematical foundations of nonlinear continuum mechanics and theory of elasticity. Mathematically, the course is centered on a key concept of a tensor, frequently used in continuum mechanics. Mathematical preliminaries of the course are focused on tensor algebra. After dealing with mathematical preliminaries, the course will proceed to core topics of the course: kinematics of a deformable body, equilibrium and balance equations, and constitutive equations for hyperelastic materials. The course will be completed by showing examples of constitutive modelling for solids, fluids and fiber-reinforced materials.
prerequisite: MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (C and above) AND MATH 263 Calculus III (81) (C and above)

title: Matrix Analysis
prerequisite: MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (C and above)

title: Nonlinear Differential Equations
prerequisite: MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (C and above) AND MATH 274 Introduction to Differential Equations (484) (C and above)

title: Numerical Methods for Partial Differential Equations
description: The course is a blend of conceptual and practical aspects of numerical solutions of partial differential equations, and aims at students of senior level.
prerequisite: MATH 351 Numerical Methods with Applications (1166) (C and above) AND MATH 481 Partial Differential Equations (1168) (C and above)

title: Applied Finite Element Methods
description: Computer-aided Introduction to Finite Element Methods for solving initial/boundary value problems in science and engineering with industrial applications, implementation techniques.
prerequisite: MATH 351 Numerical Methods with Applications (1166) (C and above)

title: Complex Analysis
prerequisite: MATH 263 Calculus III (81) (C and above)

title: Partial Differential Equations
prerequisite: MATH 274 Introduction to Differential Equations (484) (C and above)
corequisite: MATH 480 Complex Analysis (618) (C and above)

title: Fourier Analysis
description: This course introduces the topics of Fourier series and Fourier transform, with applications to differential equations and orthogonal polynomials.
prerequisite: MATH 263 Calculus III (81) (C and above) AND MATH 274 Introduction to Differential Equations (484) (C and above)

description: Selected topics in mathematics not included in existing courses.

title: Special Topics in Mathematics II
description: Selected topics in mathematics not included in existing courses.

title: Special Topics in Mathematics III
description: This course treats selected topics in mathematics not included in existing courses.

title: Directed Study in Mathematics I
description: Under the supervision of a faculty advisor, a student pursues independent research on a topic in, or related to, Mathematics.

title: Directed Study in Mathematics II
description: Under the supervision of a faculty advisor, a student pursues independent research on a topic in, or related to, mathematics.

title: Linear Algebra with Applications
description: This course covers systems of linear equations, matrices and inverses, determinants, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, inner product spaces and orthogonal matrices, and an introduction to vector spaces as the theoretical portion of the course.

title: Measure Theory and Applications
description: This course is an introduction to the subject of measure theory and Lebesgue integration, and its applications in probability.

title: Optimization Methods and Techniques
description: The course covers an introduction to optimization methods and techniques. Lectures will discuss the main theoretical results, the most relevant algorithms and show how to use them for solving real case studies. Relevant optimization software will be introduced as well.

title: Operations Research
description: Operations research helps in solving problems in different environments that needs decisions. This course covers topics that include: mathematical programming, stochastic optimization, fuzzy optimization, dynamic programming, deterministic and stochastic optimal control, multi-criteria decision aid, and application to engineering, finance, management.

title: Theory of Probability
description: The graduate-level course starts with the probabilistic measure and integration theory and elaborates on conditional expectations. Further topics include: random variables, distributions, moments, and characteristic functions in an abstract setting, convergence modes of random variables along with Gaussian processes.

title: Scientific Modeling and Simulation with Mathematics
description: This course will use scientific principles in physics, biology and engineering in combination with mathematical methods to formulate and design mathematical models to study real life problems.

title: Applied Finite Element Analysis
description: Computer-aided Finite Element Analysis for initial/boundary value problems in science and engineering with industrial applications; implementation techniques in Matlab/Octave.

title: Scientific Computing
description: Algorithm design motivated by problems in physics, engineering, epidemiology, chemistry, and biology; implementation techniques in MATLAB; elements of shell programming under Unix/Linux and use of modern software packages for numerical computations; preparation of reports in the scientific style and maintain scientific software.

title: Statistical Learning
description: The course covers theoretical foundations and applications of machine learning models. Topics include supervised methods for regression and classification (linear models, trees, neural networks, ensemble methods, instance-based methods), Bayesian parametric learning, density estimation and clustering, sequential models. Programming projects covering a variety of real-world applications are assigned.

title: Data Analysis and Statistical Learning
description: The course begins with the general formulation of the supervised learning problem and proceeds with the model assessment/selection issues, the comparison of models. We proceed to covering regularization, kernels, design of neural networks and, finally, based on Vapnik-Chervonenkis theory, we discuss how sample size affects the generalization power.
prerequisite: MATH 540 Statistical Learning (2340) (B- and above)

title: Statistical Programming
description: The course deals with data analysis using advanced statistical programming such as R or SAS. Students will learn syntax, how to read fixed and free format data, use built-in and user-written functions, optimization and graphical capabilities. The applied statistical problems considered include linear and nonlinear regression, experimental design, and others.

title: Advanced Numerical Methods
description: This course covers advanced numerical methods that are used in large scale scientific and engineering computations and simulations. The topics include Krylov subspace methods and preconditioning, conjugate gradient method and BiCGstab, iterative methods for eigenvalue computation, and advanced numerical methods for initial value problems.

title: Stochastic Analysis
description: Stochastic analysis covers stochastic integration, stochastic differential equations, and related topics. Students are required to have a background in measure theory. Topics include but are not limited to: Ito integrals, Martingales, stochastic differential equations, and some applications in finance.
prerequisite: MATH 510 Measure Theory and Applications (5685) (C and above)

title: Advanced Nonlinear Differential Equations
description: Advanced topics are presented on nonlinear ordinary and partial differential equations and their solutions. They are examined from the viewpoint of their critical points, phase space trajectories, Poincare maps, periodic and quasiperiodic solutions. The Poincare-Bendixson theorem, stability analysis, perturbation methods and bifurcation theory are described. Applications to Physics and Biology are introduced.

title: Numerical Methods for Partial Differential Equations
description: Finite difference, volume, and element methods; explicit/implicit methods for time integration; Convergence, consistency, stability; the Poisson equation, heat equation, wave equation, advection-diffusion equation, and Stokes equation.

title: Modeling and Numerical Analysis for Incompressible Fluids
description: Model equations for incompressible fluids; stable numerical schemes based on finite element discretizations; stabilization methods for convection-dominated transport problem; basic functional analytic tools for analysis of Navier-Stokes equations; solver implementation; simulations for incompressible fluids
prerequisite: MATH 519 Scientific Computing (4685) (B- and above)

title: Advanced Complex Analysis
description: This course introduces Complex Analysis at the graduate level. Topics include (but are not limited to) Cauchy’s theorem, Runge’s approximation theorem, meromorphic functions, Paley-Wiener theorem, infinite products, Hadamard’s factorization theorem, analytic continuation, etc.

title: Mathematical Biology
description: Exponential, logistic, and Gompertz growth, Harvest models, Stochastic birth and death processes, discrete-time models, delay models, predator-prey models, chemostat models, competition models, mutualism models, spatially structured models, age structured models.

title: Research Seminar
description: This course provides graduate students with a broader view of the latest research in Mathematics. Seminar speakers are faculty members, PIs of research institutes and visiting academics. Students are required to attend all seminars, to participate in the weekly discussion sessions and to submit via TurnitIN reports on three of the seminars.

title: Thesis Research Preparation
description: This course is designed to facilitate during the Summer Term of first Academic Year the preparation for the Thesis Proposal Research and Thesis Research in the second Academic Year.

title: Analytic Number Theory
description: This course introduces techniques from the theory of functions of a real or complex variable to investigate properties of numbers.

title: Asymptotic Analysis
description: This course presents techniques for approximating functions defined by integrals or solutions to differential equations.

title: Advanced Partial Differential Equations with Applications
description: Laplace and heat equations, wave equations, fundamental solutions, maximum principles, Sobolev spaces, embedding theorems, weak solutions, energy methods, regularity of solutions, existence and uniqueness of solutions, general linear elliptic, parabolic and hyperbolic equations, and applications.

title: Introduction to Nonlinear Dispersive and Wave Equations
description: The aim of this course is to provide students an introduction to nonlinear dispersive and wave equations, and the methods used to study the qualitative properties of their solutions. These equations arise as fundamental models of a wide variety of physical systems, including the propagation of waves and the study of nonlinear optics, and are closely related to models of fluids, as well as a number of aspects of statistical and quantum mechanics.

title: Potential Theory and Polynomial Approximation
description: Numerical approximation with polynomials, both theory and practice. The emphasis is on Chebyshev polynomials on an interval, but some other topics will be covered. Expertise in numerical and theoretical sides of the topic will be expected.

title: Applied Functional Analysis
description: Banach and Hilbert spaces; linear operators; Frechet derivative; approximate solution to operator equations; generalized Fourier series; applications in mathematical physics and engineering

title: Thesis Proposal
description: This course is designed to monitor progress and develop understandings and skills to plan and conduct independent research at the MSc level.
prerequisite: MATH 592 Research Seminar (5760) (C- and above)

title: Thesis
description: Student will conduct independent work under the direction of a supervisor on a research problem in the student's designated area of research. The student will prepare and defend the thesis.
prerequisite: MATH 691 Thesis Proposal (5769) (P)

title: Doctoral Thesis
description: This course is designed to monitor progress and develop understandings, skills, and outlooks to conduct original, independent research at the PhD level. The student will develop (with the advisor’s guidance) a research plan at the beginning of the semeste

title: Thesis Research
