description: This module is a continuation of ‘Beginning Persian 1’ and ‘Beginning Persian 2’. It aims to enhance and solidify students’ command of the Persian language and further develop their listening, reading, writing, and communication skills.
prerequisite: PER 102 Beginning Persian II (4790) (C- and above)

title: Intermediate Persian II
description: This module is a continuation of ‘Intermediate Persian I’. It aims to enhance and solidify your command of the Persian language and further develop your listening, reading, writing, and communication skills.
prerequisite: PER 201 Intermediate Persian 1 (4987) (C- and above)

title: Fluid Mechanics and Thermodynamics
description: This course aims to introduce students to the fundamentals fluid mechanics and its applications in petroleum engineering. The focus will be on solving fluid flow problems and design of pipeline and equipment for fluid transport. It also provides an introduction to the essential theoretical basis of engineering thermodynamics and its application to a range of problems of relevance to practical engineering and aims to equip students with basic tools and methodologies for carrying out thermodynamic analyses of engineering systems.
prerequisite: MATH 161 Calculus I (118) (C- and above)

title: Transport Phenomena
description: The physical processes of momentum, heat and mass transfer will be covered under the term Transport Phenomena. The focus of this course is momentum transfer, mass transfer, and energy transfer. Differential and integral balance equations for conservation of mass, energy and momentum will be derived and used to solve a wide range of fluid flow problems.
prerequisite: ENG 200 Engineering Mathematics III (Differential Equations and Linear Algebra) (5009) (C- and above)

title: Drilling Engineering with Laboratories
description: The course introduces the basic concepts, theory and practices in drilling engineering. Topics include an introduction to drilling engineering, rotary drilling systems and operations, well control and monitoring systems. Specifically, drilling fluids, drilling hydraulics, formation pore and fracture pressure estimation, design of mud weight and kick evaluation are discussed.
prerequisite: PETE 201 Fluid Mechanics and Thermodynamics (5120) (C- and above)

title: Reservoir Rock and Fluid Properties with Lab
description: This course covers fundamental and basic topics related to rock and fluid in reservoirs. In the rock section, basic petrophysical properties of reservoir rocks are covered including porosity, permeability, fluid saturation, electrical conductivity, mechanical properties, capillary pressure, and relative permeability. In the fluid section, the phase behavior of hydrocarbon systems as related to petroleum recovery is introduced.

title: Numerical Methods for Petroleum Engineers
description: This course covers the introduction of numerical methods and their applications in solving petroleum engineering problems. Topics cover numerical solutions of linear and nonlinear equations, ordinary differential equations, systems of equations, various solution techniques, interpolation and curve fitting, computer applications, numerical differentiation and integration, the principles of finite difference method to ordinary differential equations, and error and stability analyses. Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to set up mathematical models for typical petroleum engineering problems with certain complexity and solve them numerically with MATLAB®.
prerequisite: ENG 200 Engineering Mathematics III (Differential Equations and Linear Algebra) (5009) (C- and above) OR ENG 101 Programming for Engineers (4517) (C- and above)

title: Reservoir Engineering I with Laboratory works
description: Introduction to fundamental concepts in reservoir engineering, Defining reserves, Different methods to estimate oil and gas reserves, Material balance equations for different types of oil and gas reservoirs, Definition and classification of water aquifers and basic concepts for water influx, Well performance behavior and calculation of productivity index, Decline curve analysis, Improved oil recovery methods and Enhanced oil recovery methods.
prerequisite: PETE 204 Reservoir Rock and Fluid Properties with Lab (5487) (C- and above)

title: Well Logging and Formation Evaluation
description: The course introduces the student to conventional open hole well logging techniques and log interpretation methods. The objective is to provide insight into basic well logging methods that are employed in formation evaluation and petrophysical analysis.
prerequisite: GEOL 101 Fundamentals of Geology (4774) (C- and above)

title: Well Completion and Stimulation
description: This course provides the completion system with theoretical background in each section. The completion practices and equipment are designed along with perforating techniques for both onshore and offshore. Formation damage and treatment are also introduced. The use of artificial lift is discussed. Stimulation, fracturing and sand control technique are explained.
prerequisite: PETE 203 Drilling Engineering with Laboratories (5486) (C- and above)

title: Well Test Analysis
description: Well testing is powerful tool to assess the reservoir and well performance. Analysis and evaluations of well conditions and reservoir characterization by using different well testing techniques are the main focus of this course. To be familiar with this subject, both the theory and field examples will be covered in the course content. In summary this course will include an introduction to well testing, Basic diffusivity equation for radial flow, transient pressure analysis, gas deliverability test and derivative type curves.
prerequisite: PETE 302 Reservoir Engineering I with Laboratory works (5955) (C- and above)

title: Reservoir Engineering II
description: Concepts and importance of water flooding, theories and derivations of fractional flow equations from Darcy’s law for two-phase flow, theories and derivations of frontal advance equations from continuity equations for water displacing oil, water flooding patterns and characteristics, areal sweep efficiency and influential factors, well injectivity calculation, reservoir heterogeneity and its impact on water flooding processes, vertical and volumetric sweep efficiency, water flooding performance assessment, oil recovery calculations, water flooding design, and strategy optimization.
prerequisite: PETE 302 Reservoir Engineering I with Laboratory works (5955) (C- and above)

title: Production Engineering
description: Design and Operation of Production Systems using Nodal Analysis.
prerequisite: PETE 201 Fluid Mechanics and Thermodynamics (5120) (C- and above) OR PETE 302 Reservoir Engineering I with Laboratory works (5955) (C- and above)

title: Reservoir Simulation
description: Numerical simulation principles and tools for hydrocarbon reservoir modeling.
prerequisite: PETE 301 Numerical Methods for Petroleum Engineers (5881) (C- and above) AND PETE 302 Reservoir Engineering I with Laboratory works (5955) (C- and above)

title: Capstone Design Project I
description: The final year students will work with one of the faculty members and will conduct research work in one of the areas of petroleum engineering. At the end of this course the students will submit an initial report and will orally present their work which will be examined by a team of faculty members. The students will continue their research work in Capstone Design Project II.
prerequisite: PETE 302 Reservoir Engineering I with Laboratory works (5955) (C- and above) AND PETE 203 Drilling Engineering with Laboratories (5486) (C- and above)

title: Production Enhancement
description: We will cover different aspects of methods to increase production from a well. Main production related problems will be discussed and methods to overcome them and improve production will be analyzed. Operations such as well stimulation and artificial lift will be introduced and covered during the course.
prerequisite: PETE 307 Production Engineering (6146) (C- and above)

title: Petroleum Geomechanics
description: The course introduces the student to principles of rock mechanics and its application in petroleum engineering domain including exploration, drilling, and production. The objective is to provide insight into basics of rock mechanics that are employed in petroleum engineering with practical examples, case studies, after laying a theoretical foundation.
prerequisite: GEOL 101 Fundamentals of Geology (4774) (C- and above) OR GEOL 102 Fundamentals of Geology (4772) (C- and above)

title: Enhanced Oil Recovery
description: Mechanisms involved during different enhanced oil recovery techniques are discussed in this course. Also different methods such as gas injection, thermal methods, chemical EOR, low salinity water flooding, mobility control methods, and nanofluid injection are explained and analyzed in this course.
prerequisite: PETE 204 Reservoir Rock and Fluid Properties with Lab (5487) (C- and above)

title: Capstone Design Project II
description: The Capstone Design Project aims to develop the student’s research skills toward building foundation knowledge on a particular petroleum industry related problem or a research topic, and further investigating the problem and proposing possible methods or solutions.
prerequisite: PETE 400 Capstone Design Project I (6424) (P)

title: Gas Engineering
description: This elective course focuses on basic applications of reservoir and production engineering of gas fields. Definition and components, properties of natural gases, hydrate formation, and inhibition, equation of states (EoS), and special topics in gas reservoirs will be covered. Drilling and well completion of gas wells, well flow performance and recovery, problems in gas wells, natural gas processing, gas gathering and transport, underground gas storage, and health and safety (HSE) regulations in gas fields will also be discussed.
prerequisite: PETE 302 Reservoir Engineering I with Laboratory works (5955) (C- and above) AND PETE 307 Production Engineering (6146) (C- and above)

title: Surface Facilities
description: The first part of the course covers the basic concepts and techniques necessary to design, specify, and manage oil field surface production facilities. It clearly explains the equipment and processes used in joint separation, such as two-phase oil and gas or oil and water, oil and water treating systems, and the selection of piping and pumps. The second part of the course focuses on areas that primarily concern gas handling, conditioning, and processing facilities. Specific areas included are the process of dehydration, acid gas treatment, gas processing, the mechanical design of pressure vessels, compressors and pressure relief. Last but not least, the safety system topic is also covered.
prerequisite: PETE 307 Production Engineering (6146) (C- and above) AND PETE 203 Drilling Engineering with Laboratories (5486) (C- and above)

title: Introduction to Data Science and Machine Learning
description: This undergraduate course offers a foundational understanding of data science and machine learning. It covers essential concepts, techniques, and tools for extracting meaningful insights from data. Students will learn data preprocessing, exploratory data analysis, machine learning algorithms, and the ethical implications of these technologies. The course emphasizes practical applications and hands-on experience, preparing students to tackle real-world data challenges.
prerequisite: MATH 161 Calculus I (118) (C- and above)

title: Advanced Technologies in Drilling
description: This elective course focused on advanced topics in drilling engineering to make students familiar with new technologies applied in fields.
prerequisite: PETE 203 Drilling Engineering with Laboratories (5486) (C- and above) AND PETE 304 Well Completion and Stimulation (5883) (C- and above)

title: Foundations of Petroleum Engineering
description: In this course, fundamental sections of upstream petroleum engineering is introduced. These fundamental subjects will be used in other courses of the program. Fundamental aspects of reservoir and rock properties, reservoir fluid properties and E&P processes will be presented in this course.

title: Petroleum Geology
description: This course follows the classical ‘source-to- trap’ treatment by covering the following topics: hydrocarbon source rocks (mineralogy, organic carbon content), kerogen (formation, composition, types and evolution during diagenesis), petroleum and gas generation from kerogen, expulsion from source rock, and migration to reservoirs, reservoir rocks (mineralogy, formation water chemistry, diagenesis, and petrophysical properties), petroleum (composition, physical properties, changes upon maturation, biomarkers, maturity indicators), traps and seals, sedimentary basins, notion of petroleum systems, methods of petroleum exploration, reserve estimations, petroleum provinces of the world.

title: Fluid Flow Through Porous Media
description: In this course, fluid flow types and mechanisms in the porous media will be discussed. Classifications of flow and descriptions of fluid flow in porous media will be studied. Conservation laws, constitutive relations of fluid flow, and equation of transient fluid flow in porous media will be analyzed in details. Different types of fluid flow such as steady, pseudo-steady, and transient flow in linear, radial and spherical systems will be discussed and analyzed.

title: Advanced Formation Evaluation
description: The main aim of this course is to review of conventional and contemporary well logging and core analysis methods and technologies. These techniques will be used to determine reservoir parameters. Also by these methods, it is possible to integrate the log, core and other well data to produce a consistent interpretation of a given reservoir.

title: Advanced Drilling Engineering
description: The main idea in this course is to present conventional technologies in drilling engineering, and main parameters to be considered in design such as drilling fluid properties, and pressure control. Also, methods will be analyzed to optimize the drilling operation for a specific reservoir.

title: Advanced Well Testing and Evaluation
description: Well testing methods are used to estimate parameters of reservoirs such as permeability, skin factor, and drainage area. Different methods of well testing for oil and gas reservoirs are discussed and analyzed in this course. Hence, students will be able to design a well test operation and analyze data obtained from tests to improve the knowledge from hydrocarbon formations.

title: Thesis I
description: Master students in petroleum engineering work on their thesis in the second year. In this course, students will work on their research thesis, submit their thesis after successful completion of the work, and present their finding in an oral defence session.

title: Petroleum Data Analytics
description: The content of this course will focus on analyzing datasets generated in oil and gas industry using various analytical techniques. Students are expected to understand the fundamental principles and master different data analytics techniques after attending this course. Knowledge and skills will enable students to quickly adapt to petroleum engineer or researcher roles in both industry and academia.

title: Research Seminar
description: After completion of the research and before the thesis defence, each student will present his/her findings as a seminar to supervisors and course instructor. Feedback and comments will be collected to improve the quality of presentation. Also these comments will help the student to improve technical aspects of the work and become ready for the final defence.

title: Advanced Reservoir Geomechanics
description: This course covers different aspects of Geomechanics in petroleum engineering and the application of Geomechanics in different disciplines such as drilling, formation stability, fracturing, reservoir compaction, and underground storage.

title: Research Proposal Preparation
description: Master students in petroleum engineering work on their thesis in the second year. In this course, students will prepare details of their proposal and methodology and also present the progress of their work for other students and faculties. Feedbacks from faculties will improve the quality of their work.

title: Unconventional resources drilling
description: This study aims to summarize the thinking process or main considerations when developing the exploration drilling strategy in unconventional resources, which accommodate subsurface, environmental, drilling and construction perspectives.

title: Introduction to Geospatial, Earth Observation and Surveying Technologies for Onshore and Marine Petroleum and Mining Industry
description: This course introduces geodetic surveying, geospatial and earth observation technologies applied for marine and onshore petroleum and gas & mining industry.

title: Advanced Petroleum Exploration
description: The IBA is a hands-on opportunity for students to experience the creative process and the high-tech science that is the foundation of the Energy Industry today.
prerequisite: PETE 502 Petroleum Geology (4478) (C- and above)

title: Thesis II
description: Master students in petroleum engineering work on their thesis in the second year. In this course, students will work on their research thesis, submit their thesis after successful completion of the work, and present their finding in an oral defense session.

title: Advanced Well Engineering
description: Main topics required in drilling and production engineering will be covered in this course. In the production section, major applications of production engineering to design, estimate, and optimize production from oil and gas wells will be covered.

title: Current Research Literature
description: This course will help PhD students to become more familiar with the literature of the research direction and research topic they choose as their PhD thesis. This course will help students to prepare their research proposal.

title: Advanced Reservoir Engineering
description: This course covers different aspects of primary and secondary recovery in reservoir engineering. Also advanced topics such as fractured reservoirs will be covered for PhD students. Individual project will be offered to each PhD student during the semester.

title: Advanced Reservoir Simulation
description: Different aspects and methods of discretization of fluid flow in porous media equations and methods to solve them will be discussed in this course. Simulation of reservoirs by black oil and compositional approached will be analyzed and procedure and steps of methods are discussed during the course. Specific simulation project will be assigned to PhD students in this course to develop advanced codes.

title: Fluid Flow Through Porous Media
description: In this course, fluid flow types and mechanisms in the porous media will be discussed. Classifications of flow and descriptions of fluid flow in porous media will be studied. Conservation laws, constitutive relations of fluid flow, and equation of transient fluid flow in porous media will be analyzed in details. Different types of fluid flow such as steady, pseudo-steady, and transient flow in linear, radial and spherical systems will be discussed and analyzed.

title: Advanced Enhanced Oil Recovery
description: Enhanced oil recovery course focuses on different methods used in oil industry to improve and increase the production of oil from reservoirs. Different oil recovery mechanisms are discussed in this course to describe parameters affecting sweep efficiency in porous media. Specific design and modeling projects and assignments will be designed and delivered to PhD students during the course.

title: Special Topics in Petroleum Engineering: Data Analytics
description: The content of this course will focus on analyzing datasets generated in oil and gas industry using various analytical techniques. PhD students are expected to understand the fundamental principles and master different data analytics techniques after attending this course. Knowledge and skills will enable students to quickly adapt to petroleum engineer or researcher roles in both industry and academia.

title: Advanced Special Core Analysis
description: Introduction to fundamental concepts in conventional core analysis, and measurement techniques. Also, it provides introduction to coring techniques, challenges and pitfalls. This course provides detailed information about advanced core analysis, measurement techniques of relative permeability, advancement in the techniques with their advantages and drawbacks. Also, it provides complete information on measurement techniques for capillary pressure, advantages of different process and their drawbacks. This course also covers measurement techniques for wettability studies, in addition to measurement of electrical and acoustic properties of rock. This course also provides knowledge on quality control of laboratory generated data, planning a SCAL program and integration of SCAL data into reservoir models. Also, the role of SCAL data in recovery calculations and simulation modeling.

title: Thesis Research
description: A research plan is developed by the student in collaboration with the Program Advisor or Research Supervisor at the start of the semester outlining the research goals to be accomplished. At the end of the semester the student files a research report which is graded (P/F) by the Program Advisor or Research Mentor (when selected). The “in-progress” grade is submitted and maintained on the student’s transcript; credit is awarded on successful completion of thesis requirements.

title: Special topics in Petroleum Engineering: Unconventional Resources Drilling
description: This study aims to summarize the thinking process or main considerations when developing the exploration drilling strategy in unconventional resources, which accommodate subsurface, environmental, drilling and construction perspectives.

title: Thesis Research
description: For the research thesis students are expected to conduct research leading to new discoveries under the supervision of a faculty member. In the course of the 4 years, students are expected to become independent researchers able to design and conduct their

title: Thesis Research
description: For the research thesis students are expected to conduct research leading to new discoveries under the supervision of a faculty member. In the course of the 4 years, students are expected to become independent researchers able to design and conduct their own research.

title: Molecular Basis of Health and Disease
description: In this course the molecular basis of different diseases will be discussed. The course will be held as a seminar in which peer-reviewed original papers and reviews concerned with molecular basis of a variety of different diseases will be discussed.

title: Molecular basis of health and disease
description: In this course the molecular basis of different diseases will be discussed. The course will be held as a seminar in which peer-reviewed original papers and reviews concerned with molecular basis of a variety of different diseases will be discussed.
prerequisite: PHDBS 702a Molecular Basis of Health and Disease (5837) (P)

title: Biomedical Research Analysis and Design of Experimentation
description: In this course students will learn about good experimental design and start to analyse data obtained in practical experiments. The course will be held as a discussion group, where results from different ongoing experiments in NUSOM are analysed and problems and further possible research directions are discussed.

title: Biomedical Research Analysis and Design of Experimentation
description: In this course students will learn about different experimental designs and start to analyse data obtained in practical experiments. The course will be held as a discussion group, where results from different ongoing experiments in NUSOM are analysed and problems and further possible research directions are discussed.
prerequisite: PHDBS 703a Biomedical Research Analysis and Design of Experimentation (5836) (P)

title: NUSOM seminar (final semester)
description: This course will teach students to critically discuss research results. Presentations will be given by national and international experts on different topics. Students will also be given the opportunity to orally present and discuss their own results.

title: NUSOM seminar
description: This course will teach students to critically discuss research results. Presentations will be given by national and international experts on different topics. Students will also be given the opportunity to orally present and discuss their own results.

title: Biosafety, Animal Welfare and Ethics
description: In this course students will learn about ethical considerations as well as animal welfare and biosafety aspects that have to be taken into account when designing and conducting biomedical research.

title: Advanced Biomedical Research Analysis and Design of Experimentation
description: In this course the students will learn to analyse scientific data and design experiment. The course will be held as a discussion group, where results from different ongoing experiments in NUSOM are analysed and put into context with existing literature

title: Advanced Biomedical Research Analysis and Design of Experimentation
description: In this course the students will learn to analyse scientific data and design experiment. The course will be held as a discussion group, where results from different ongoing experiments in NUSOM are analysed and put into context with existing literature
prerequisite: PHDBS 703a Biomedical Research Analysis and Design of Experimentation (5836) (P) AND PHDBS 703b Biomedical Research Analysis and Design of Experimentation (8552) (C and above) AND PHDBS 706a Advanced Biomedical Research Analysis and Design of Experimentation (5835) (P)

title: Publication Analysis
description: In this course students will learn to critically analyse peer-reviewed publications. The course will be held as a seminar in which peer-reviewed original papers are discussed regarding their merits and weaknesses as well as their impact on the different PhD projects.

title: Publication Analysis
description: In this course students will learn to critically analyse peer-reviewed publications. The course will be held as a seminar in which peer-reviewed original papers are discussed regarding their merits and weaknesses as well as their impact on the different PhD projects.
prerequisite: PHDBS 702a Molecular Basis of Health and Disease (5837) (P) AND PHDBS 702b Molecular basis of health and disease (8551) (C and above) AND PHDBS 707a Publication Analysis (5840) (P)

title: Writing for Biomedical Sciences
description: This course teaches students in the Biomedical Sciences program to become more effective genre specific writers. This course highlights key characteristics of science writing and emphasizes the importance of organizing writing around research outcomes, communicating difficult discipline and statistical concepts clearly and effectively for scientific and general audiences. Focused on the writing stages of planning, drafting, and revising tests, this course teaches through engagement with scientific literature and activities based on practical examples and exercises. Students will analyze and produce common scientific writing genres while considering the rhetorical, ethical, and technical aspects of developing and producing texts. This course will also prepare students for the writing of their interim and final PhD theses. Topics include effective writing principles, writing process and anxiety-reduction methods, and the science-specific genres of IMRAD (research reports), grant writing, peer review, ethics in science writing, and writing for general audiences.

title: Molecular Basis of Infection
description: Infectious diseases accompanied humans throughout evolution. From early days to modern times infection is tirelessly challenging our defense systems with old and new mechanisms, ultimately modifying our species by leaving traces in our genome and phenotype. This course intends to provide a broad vision on those major infectious diseases that hit humanity, covering historical aspects on discovery, understanding and therapeutic challenges, from early interventions to up to date prevention and treatment. A significant portion of this course will be dedicated to the molecular mechanisms behind infection, the key to understand and act against it. The course will be taught by a team of infectious disease experts, covering different topics and aspects of infection and molecular medicine.

title: Molecular Pathology of Cancer
description: The main focus of the course is on the studies, which advance fundamental knowledge of the molecular mechanisms of tumour initiation, progression and metastasis. The course helps the students to systematize information on molecular biology of cancer, cancer pathology, and genetics. The following topics will be covered: • Oncogenes and tumour suppressors • Signal transduction and cancer • Cell cycle control and apoptosis in cancer • Abnormalities in DNA repair in cancer • Tumour biology • Invasion-metastasis cascade • Angiogenesis • Introduction to oncoimmunology

title: Molecular Basis of Genetic Disease
description: The course examines and discusses the application of molecular genetics in the understanding of human health and diseases, to decipher how gene expression is regulated and how it is mis-regulated, which may be associated with medical problems. We will discuss how scientists apply the genetics knowledge to help develop interventions and new therapies to treat and to prevent diseases. The expanding knowledge of genetics and its impact in medicine, together with the increasing discoveries of human coding and non-coding genes in the human genome, is also helping scientists to invent new approaches to study single gene and multifactorial genetic disorders. We will weigh the impact of next generation sequencing with its ever decreasing cost and increasing fidelity of how this will impact precision/personalized medicine in the present, in fields such as pharmacogenomics and cancer treatment and also its future implications. We examine how epigenetics bridge the nexus between our genes and the environment and why this has significant impact not only to human health in this generation but also in the next 2 generations. With genome editing moving at a fast pace we are now able to make targeted changes to our genome at the embryonic stage, with very low off target errors and negligible mosaics, this will bring gene therapy and stem cell therapy much closer to bedside application in the near future.

title: Molecular Immunology
description: The Molecular Immunology course will cover the molecular and cellular interactions of the immune response to pathogens and tumor cells as well as mechanisms involved in immunological. The immune system as a target for therapeutic intervention will also be explored.

title: From the Bench to the Bedside: Drug Development and Clinical Trials
description: Overview of the complex pathways that lie between hypothesis regarding pharmaceutical therapies, and the end goal, regulatory approval of a new chemical entity for therapeutic use, and beyond.

title: Molecular Basis of Chronic Inflammation
description: Molecular cuases for chronic inflammatory diseases will be discussed
prerequisite: PHDBS 712 Molecular Immunology (6518) (C+ and above)

title: Molecular Basis of Neurological Disorders
description: Neurological disorders remain among the most devastating diseases affecting mankind for several reasons including the unavailability of effective treatment. Often affected patients will loose several of the qualities that we most strongly associate with being human. In the last decades molecular genetics approaches have greatly advanced our understanding of the pathological processes operating in many of these diseases. This course will introduce students to the principle of nerve cell biology in the context of several clinically relevant neurological disorders. The main aspect is to demonstrate how defects at cellular and molecular levels will give rise to the features of the disorders, as we know them from clinical presentation. How do alterations like for instance a gene mutation, an allelic variance, the over- or under-expression of genes or environmental changes affect cells, structures and circuits. The disorders that will be covered in this course include inherited and acquired conditions affecting neurons as well as glial cells. We will also cover the most recent advances in diagnosing and treating the diseases as well as required additional research required to further deepen our understanding of the underlying molecular mechanisms.

title: Recombinant Drugs
description: The early days that witnessed the bridging of genetics and microbiology led to the advent of molecular biology, an authentic revolution of the human power to interact with and modify biological systems. Among other aspects, this giant revolution formed the platform to develop novel strategies in the field of biomedicine, with the possibility to integrate medicinal chemistry with a completely innovative source of drugs, those based on the recombinant DNA technology. The history and impact of recombinant drugs started with the first FDA-approved case (an E. coli-produced recombinant insulin) and the immediate setting of new paradigms for the pharmaceutical world. Many different recombinant protein drugs followed this first success. A parallel milestone in the field of molecular biology coupled to immunology is represented by the establishment of the monoclonal antibody production. While the endless and extremely diversified application of this technology goes without mentioning, the drug market is constantly fueled with new monoclonal antibody drugs. Gene therapy, vaccine development and synthetic biology are other arms of the therapeutic and prophylactic intervention based on genetic engineering.

title: Organ System and Common Diseases
description: Pathophysiology –is the study of the disturbed physiological processes that cause, result from, or are otherwise associated with a disease or injury. Pathology is the medical discipline that describes conditions typically observed during a disease state, whereas physiology is the biological discipline that describes processes or mechanisms operating within an organism. Pathology describes the abnormal or undesired condition, whereas pathophysiology seeks to explain the functional changes that are occurring within an individual due to a disease or pathologic state. The course will introduce students to the pathogenesis of different diseases and potential pharmacological targets. Subject includes physiology and pathophysiology of cardiovascular, pulmonary, renal, gastrointestinal systems, neuroscience, immunology.

title: Principles of Pharmacology and Toxicology
description: In this course students will learn about the basic principles and mechanisms of commonly used drugs and how they exert their actions. Students will learn about drug Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism and Excretion (ADME) and drug pharmacodynamics including drug-receptor dynamics. Students will learn and apply commonly used pharmacological and toxicological terminologies including agonist, antagonist (reversible, irreversible, competitive etc.), drug half-life, volume of distribution, bioavailability, elimination rate, area under the curve and many other relevant terms. In addition, as part of the toxicology component of the course, students will learn about poisons, venoms and their antidotes. They will also be briefed about applied toxicology in research and practice such as forensic toxicology.

title: Systemic Pharmacology
description: In this course the effects of different drugs on the human system will be discussed.

title: Drug Discovery I
description: Drug discovery is a long, complex and expensive process. Despite the technological advancement, a new medicine will take an average of 10 to 15 years from target identification through approval for marketing with an approximate average cost of more than two billion dollars. The course will introduce students to the drug discovery world, particularly the preclinical stage. The course is designed to enhance the knowledge and practice of preclinical evaluation of drugs with a specific focus on the key elements of the multi-disciplinary component of drug discovery and development. Subjects include Target identification, drug design, HTS development, lead identification and optimization and pre-clinical testing, drug delivery and regulatory requirements.

title: Drug addiction and toxicology
description: In this course the biological basis of the development of drug abuse will be discussed

title: Thesis Research
description: This course comprises the main work of the PhD in Global Health. In this course, students learn to independently conduct and plan research, review the literature, reflect on the direction of the project and conduct the research independently. Students ela

title: Thesis Research
description: This course comprises the main work of the PhD in Global Health. In this course, students learn to independently conduct and plan research, review the literature, reflect on the direction of the project and conduct the research independently. Students elaborate a semester plan of action that will be reviewed at the end of the semester. For the successful completion of this course, the student will submit a PhD Thesis, in which the student will demonstrate an original contribution to knowledge that is deemed to have high quality and international impact.

title: Foundations of Global Health
description: This course will provide students with advanced knowledge on major global health issues and challenges. Global health problems will be explored from the perspective of the broad social and environmental determinants of health and disparities, and the Sustainable Development Goals. Up-to-date original, peer-reviewed papers will be used as a basis for discussions.

title: Health Policy and Systems in Global Health
description: This course will provide students with advanced knowledge on the evidence regarding global health interventions, including relevant actors and institutions shaping global health, and the challenges of measuring the burden and impact of those problems as well as assessing the benefits of global health interventions. The gap between evidence and practical policy-making and the interplay between both worlds will be examined. Ethical issues in global health research will also be discussed. Up-to-date original, peer-reviewed papers will be used as a basis for discussions.

title: NUSOM Seminar in Global Health
description: This course will run for the whole duration of the program. In this course, internal and external researchers will give presentations about their research. Students are expected to discuss and analyze the research results presented in the different talks.

title: NUSOM Seminar in Global Health
description: This course will run for the whole duration of the program. In this course, internal and external researchers will give presentations about their research. Students are expected to discuss and analyze the research results presented in the different talks. Students’ attendance is required as well as their active participation in the seminars. Students will also elaborate a report reflecting on the topics discussed during each semester seminars. They will also present and defend the results they obtain in the course of their research. This is also the platform for students to learn to present their work at conferences.

title: Global Health into Action
description: This course will provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the processes involved in translating research discoveries into practices that effective and efficiently, promote health and prevent disease in the global health arena and with a special focus in Central Asian countries. Upon completion of this course, students will identify factors that may facilitate or impede the translation “into action” of the scientific evidence identified in their individual research projects.

title: Methods in Global Health Research
description: This course will provide students with solid and practical skills to investigate in global health. This course is designed to allow students to reflect on the scientific basis of global health research to generate valid and relevant knowledge. Students will discuss the strengths and limitations of different methods so they could advance in their individual research projects.

title: Implementation Science in Global Health
description: This course will provide students an opportunity to understand the core concepts, theories and frameworks of implementation research in global health setting, and what research methods of implementation science can be applied in tackling key global health challenges, with an emphasis on Central Asian countries.

title: Advanced Methods in Global Health Research
description: Students will learn to identify key findings and apply models in global health research. The results will be put into context with existing and newly emerging scientific knowledge. Based on this the students will be expected to develop future scientific proposals to determining the direction in which his/her thesis is leading. The students will present the results they are obtaining in their research projects.

title: Critical Appraisal in Global Health
description: In this course, literature relevant to the PhD program will be introduced by supervisors as well as the PhD students. Critical appraisal skills to identify strong and weak points of the papers will be discussed as well as the implication a paper has on the PhD project to which it is linked. Students are expected to present an in-depth analysis of papers relevant to their thesis.

title: Writing for Health Sciences
description: This course teaches students in Health Sciences to become more effective genre-specific writers. Topics include effective writing principles, the writing process and anxiety-reduction methods, the science-specific genres of IMRAD (research reports), peer review, ethics in scientific writing, health communication, and writing for general audiences.

title: Writing for Health Sciences
description: This course teaches students in the Global Health program to become more effective writers. This course highlights key characteristics of science writing and emphasizes the importance of organizing writing around research outcomes, communicating effectively for scientific and general audiences. This course will also prepare students for the writing of their interim and final PhD theses.

title: Introduction to Global Health
description: This course will provide students with advanced knowledge on major global health issues and challenges, these global health problems are addressed through health systems, policies, and international governance structures, and examine implementation frameworks and translational research models that enable the scaling of effective interventions in diverse contexts.

title: Scientific Communication and Critical Thinking in Health Sciences
description: This course develops the scientific writing and critical appraisal skills necessary for doctoral research in health sciences.

title: The Good Life in Practice
description: The course aims to give students an understanding of course-relevant philosophical argumentation. Students should also acquire the skills to present and critically respond to arguments in written form. Generally students should become more skilled at reason giving, providing arguments, engaging with novel ideas, exploring intellectual problems in depth, and writing clearly. The course will also encourage the development of intellectual virtues, such as open-mindedness, intellectual courage, fair-mindedness, intellectual charity, and inquisitiveness.

title: Classical Chinese and Indian Ethic
description: Students will read and discuss from the classic works of Chinese and Indian philosophy, refining their ability to reason about how to live and familiarizing themselves with ideas that continue to shape the lives of billions of people.

title: Knowledge and Reality
description: We examine the relationship between our minds and our bodies; our knowledge of our own minds, of other minds, and of the world at large; the nature of personhood; whether we have free will; and whether there is a God.

title: Introduction to Contemporary Political Philosophy
description: This course introduces students to the main ideas, problems, and positions in contemporary political philosophy. Positions to be considered include utilitarianism, liberalism, libertarianism, Marxism, communitarianism, and Feminism. We will focus on how each position understands fundamental notions in political philosophy, like justice, rights, and freedom, to address specific moral dilemmas that arise within the context of socially coordinated action and social cooperation.

title: Critical Thinking
description: This course will teach you how to get better at reasoning and arguing. Topics covered include evaluating arguments, constructing arguments, reconstructing arguments, formalizing arguments, clarifying meaning and identifying common mistakes in argument (fallacies). At the end of the course you should be able to (1) identify the structures of real-life arguments in order to decide if they are good or bad, and (2) argue logically about things that matter to you. This course is specifically designed to improve writing, thinking and oral presentation skills that are applicable to all areas of academic study and relevant to working life. Careful application in this course will deepen your capacity to critically evaluate everyday practical scenarios and will help you ‘think outside the box

title: Philosophy of Religion
description: This course covers major arguments for and against theism, and philosophical examination of other issues concerning religion.

title: Environmental Philosophy
description: In this course, we will discuss many environmentally related topics, from ecological ethics to contemporary arguments for cultural and economic change.

title: Introduction to Islamic Philosophy and Theology
description: This course introduces key trends, concepts, and debates in Arabic/Islamic philosophy, focusing on its development in the medieval period and the interplay between philosophy and theology, the nature of God, creation, causality, and the limits of human knowledge.

title: Ethics
description: This course will give you an introduction in some of the fundamental problems in ethics.

title: Bioethics
description: This course examines ethical challenges that arise from the possible applications of science and technology to living organisms, while drawing mainly on Marianne Talbot's Bioethics: An Introduction.

title: Philosophy of Science
description: We will examine the question how science evaluates hypotheses and chooses between competing theories; read about what scientific explanations consist in; and consider whether our best scientific theories are to be interpreted merely as effective instruments for predicting the future, or rather, as true descriptions of the hidden structure of the universe.

title: Truth and Reality
description: This course is about the pursuit of truth, what it means for something to be “real”, and how the two are related. Topics include: trust, cognitive bias, self-deception, and objectivity, as well as reality and truth themselves.

title: Religion and Democracy
department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, Political Science and International Relations

title: Global Justice
department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, Political Science and International Relations

title: Philosophy of Law
description: In this course we will consider some of the philosophical questions raised by law and legal systems. By the end of the semester, students will have a better understanding of some of the fundamental issues in the philosophy of law.

title: Formal Logic
description: Formal logic is fundamental to philosophy, mathematics, linguistics, and computer science. It can also improve one’s everyday reasoning skills. This introductory course uses specialized software tools to teach model theory and proof theory for propositional and first order logic.

title: Beyond Common Sense: An Introduction to Paradox
description: A paradox is an argument that leads by apparently impeccable reasoning from premises that appear to be indisputably true to a conclusion that seems patently false. Solving a paradox therefore involves rejecting something that seems commonsensically indisputable (one of the premises, the reasoning or the denial of the conclusion). That rejection can teach us something surprising and valuable about the topic of the paradoxical argument. Paradoxes covered may include Moore’s paradox (theory of knowledge and philosophy of language), the surprise exam paradox (theory of knowledge), the two-envelope paradox (decision theory) , the Cable Guy paradox (decision theory), the preface paradox (theory of knowledge), the lottery paradox (theory of knowledge and philosophy of probability) , the paradox of confirmation (philosophy of science), the Ship of Theseus (metaphysics), Thompson’s lamp (philosophy of physics), Achilles and the Tortoise (metaphysics), Newcombe’s choices (decision theory), the paradox of omnipotence (philosophy of religion), and the paradox of fiction (philosophy of literature).

title: Philosophy of Cognitive Science
description: Cognitive Science is the multidisciplinary investigation of mind and intelligence that includes psychology, philosophy, artificial intelligence, neuroscience, linguistics, and anthropology. In this course, we explore the philosophical underpinnings of cognitive science and the central debates that have characterized its development and evolution.

title: Becoming a Sage: Introduction to Daoism
description: Daoist sages were said to merge with the changes of the cosmos. Ideally, they would be able to live without the friction of misfortune. Can we apply their principles to life today? How can we understand the world from the perspective of a sage?
department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, History, Philosophy and Religious Studies

title: Free Will and Moral Responsibility
description: This course examines free will and moral responsibility. Topics include: causal determinism; incompatibilism; libertarianism; resentment, blame and other moral responses; whether responsibility is impossible; whether agency is personal, causal, or non-causal.

title: Philosophy of Agency
description: This course examines core topics on the philosophical study of human agency. In investigating this topic, we will examine the nature of reasons for action, the kinds of psychological states involved in intentional agency, and the question of practical irrationality.

title: Philosophy of History
description: This course will introduce students to classic and contemporary answers to questions about historical knowledge and its object
department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, History, Philosophy and Religious Studies

title: Truth, Knowledge and Belief
description: The course will examine central issues in contemporary epistemology. These issues include explaining what knowledge is, whether we can know anything, and what value knowledge has. An aspect of the course will be addressing how central issues in epistemology have been treated in other cultures. This will involve discussion of experimental philosophy and aspects of Chinese and Indian philosophy.

title: Social Contract Theory
prerequisite: PLS 120 Introduction to Political Theory (512) (C- and above)

title: Does Equality Matter?
description: In this course, we will survey debates about whether equality matters, and if so, equality of what?

title: Truth, Lies, Media, and Propaganda
description: This course examines issues in applied epistemology. Applied epistemology is concerned with how epistemic practices can be altered so as to improve cognitive attainment. To this end the course draws on David Coady's recent book, What To Believe Now, and examines the relationship between experts and non-experts, the blogosphere and traditional media, propaganda, and other similar areas with which applied epistemology is concerned.

title: History of 19th and 20th Century Philosophy
description: This course concerns topics in the history of philosophy, from the 19th and early 20th centuries. Major figures studied might include Hegel, Marx, Nietzsche, Frege, Russell, Wittgenstein, Moore, Kierkegaard, Husserl, Merleau-Ponty, and Heidegger. Major movements might include existentialism, early “analytic” philosophy, and phenomenology.

title: Sex, Life, and Death: The Philosophy of Biology
description: Biology often investigates subjects at the interface between mechanism and function, as well as between matter, mind, and behavior. What is the significance of evolution by natural selection in the origin of new life forms, of seemingly purposeful adaptations, and of purposeful behavior?

title: Philosophy of Artificial Intelligence
description: Artificial intelligence will likely change our lives, our jobs, and our societies. How will AI computers and robots function, what powers will they have, and how can we ensure that they will not destroy us, but rather, improve our lives?

title: Philosophy of Mind
description: How can a thought fit inside a brain? How does a thought represent the real world, and how does it represent plans, possibilities, and dreams? How do we get to have conscious feelings and sensations? And what does this mean for our place as persons in the physical world?

title: Aristotle’s Theoretical Philosophy
description: An introduction to Aristotle’s views on how the world is and how we come to know it.

title: Philosophy and Tragedy
description: This course is labeled Philosophy AND Tragedy to reflect a dual concern with art and human life. First, we shall study the philosophy of the art of tragedy, examining the nature of tragic works as such and inquiring into the cognitive, emotional, moral, and political values distinctive of tragedy. Second, the course will look to tragedy to inform philosophical problems of human existence. These include such problems as human agency amid weakness of will; the conflict between moral and political values; the limits of rationality and the liberation of liminal experiences (such as religious and ritual ecstasy). Both our aims require a substantive engagement with tragedy; to that end, tragic works themselves will figure on the syllabus (e.g., by Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides, or perhaps other authors); we hope to include more contemporary literary works. Philosophers on the syllabus include, variously, Plato, Aristotle, Hume, Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Nussbaum.
department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, Languages, Literature and Linguistics

title: Kant’s Critique of Pure Reason
description: A survey of Kant’s Critique of Pure Reason.

title: Independent Study
description: This class allows students to pursue a focused exploration of a topic that is not offered in conventional classes, while under the supervision of a faculty member.

title: Special Topics in Philosophy
prerequisite: PHIL 101 Introduction to Philosophy (242) (C- and above) OR PHIL 210 Ethics (459) (C- and above) OR PHIL 320 Truth, Knowledge and Belief (470) (C- and above) OR PHIL 230/PLS 230 Religion and Democracy (671) (C- and above)

title: Human Rights and Cultural Differences
department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, Political Science and International Relations
prerequisite: Subject "PHIL" BETWEEN 100 and 199 OR Subject "PHIL" BETWEEN 200 and 299 OR Subject "PHIL" BETWEEN 300 and 399 OR Subject "PHIL" BETWEEN 400 and 499 OR Subject "" BETWEEN 100 and 199 OR Subject "" BETWEEN 200 and 299 OR Subject "" BETWEEN 300 and 399 OR Subject "" BETWEEN 400 and 499 OR PLS 120 Introduction to Political Theory (512) (C- and above) OR PLS 328/REL 328 Confucianism and the Development of Chinese Politics (2396) (C- and above) OR PLS 437 Nationalism and Multi-Ethnic Governance (99) (C- and above)

title: Philosophy of Art
description: This course surveys topics in philosophical aesthetics and the philosophy of art. Topics include: aesthetic judgment, aesthetic concepts, the aesthetic and the non-aesthetic, artistic value, the nature of representation (especially across painting, photography, and cinema), interpretation (especially literary interpretation), art and knowledge, art and morality, and definitions of art. In reviewing extra place forms, the instructor will give special consideration to practitioners of the fine arts (music, painting, poetry, sculpture, architecture) and their extensions (e.g., literature, drama, cinema).

title: Philosophy and Tragedy
description: This course is labeled Philosophy AND Tragedy to reflect a dual concern with art and human life. First, we shall study the philosophy of the art of tragedy, examining the nature of tragic works as such and inquiring into the cognitive, emotional, moral, and political values distinctive of tragedy. Second, the course will look to tragedy to inform philosophical problems of human existence. These include such problems as human agency amid weakness of will; the conflict between moral and political values; the limits of rationality and the liberation of liminal experiences (such as religious and ritual ecstasy). Both our aims require a substantive engagement with tragedy; to that end, tragic works themselves will figure on the syllabus (e.g., by Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides, or perhaps other authors); we hope to include more contemporary literary works. Philosophers on the syllabus include, variously, Plato, Aristotle, Hume, Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Nussbaum.
department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, Languages, Literature and Linguistics

title: Physics I for non-majors with Lab
Physics II for non-majors with Lab
Introductory Physics I with Lab
corequisite: MATH 161 Calculus I (118) ( and above) OR CPS "MATH" BETWEEN 60 and 100
antirequisite: PHYS 161 Physics I for Scientists and Engineers with Laboratory (116) ( and above) OR PHYS 171 Physics I for Physics Majors with Laboratory (1401) ( and above)

title: Introductory Physics II with Lab
prerequisite: (MATH 161 Calculus I (118) ( and above) OR MATH 162 Calculus II (170) ( and above) OR MATH 263 Calculus III (81) ( and above) OR MATH 169 Accelerated Calculus (3) ( and above)) AND (PHYS 151 Introductory Physics I with Lab (649) (C- and above) OR PHYS 161 Physics I for Scientists and Engineers with Laboratory (116) (C- and above))
antirequisite: PHYS 162 Physics II for Scientists and Engineers with Laboratory (173) ( and above) OR PHYS 172 Physics II for Physics Majors with Laboratory (1402) ( and above)

title: Physics I for Scientists and Engineers with Laboratory
description: This is an introductory calculus-based course covering Mechanics and Thermodynamics.
corequisite: MATH 161 Calculus I (118) (C and above)
antirequisite: PHYS 171 Physics I for Physics Majors with Laboratory (1401) (C- and above)

title: Physics II for Scientists and Engineers with Laboratory
description: This is an introductory algebra-based course covering Electricity, Magnetism and elements of Optics.
prerequisite: PHYS 161 Physics I for Scientists and Engineers with Laboratory (116) (C- and above) OR PHYS 151 Introductory Physics I with Lab (649) (C- and above)
antirequisite: PHYS 172 Physics II for Physics Majors with Laboratory (1402) (C- and above)

title: Physics I for Physics Majors with Laboratory
corequisite: MATH 161 Calculus I (118) (D and above) OR CPS "MATH" BETWEEN 60 and 100
antirequisite: PHYS 151 Introductory Physics I with Lab (649) (C- and above) OR PHYS 161 Physics I for Scientists and Engineers with Laboratory (116) (C- and above)

title: Physics II for Physics Majors with Laboratory
prerequisite: PHYS 171 Physics I for Physics Majors with Laboratory (1401) (C- and above) OR PHYS 161 Physics I for Scientists and Engineers with Laboratory (116) (C- and above)
corequisite: MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (D and above)
antirequisite: PHYS 162 Physics II for Scientists and Engineers with Laboratory (173) ( and above)

title: Introductory Astronomy I
description: This course presents an overview of introductory-level astronomy for general science and non-science majors. It will broadly cover our present understanding of the Universe. The topics covered are: (i) the methods and tools used in astronomy, (ii) a brief history of astronomy, (iii) the content of the universe from ‘small’ to ‘large’ scales, namely from the solar system, to stars, interstellar medium, galaxies and the universe as a whole.

title: Introductory Astrophysics
description: This course presents an overview of introductory-level astrophysics for general science and non-science majors.
prerequisite: PHYS 162 Physics II for Scientists and Engineers with Laboratory (173) (C- and above)

title: Classical Mechanics I
description: Classical mechanics I can be considered as a first course in theoretical physics. The course deals with the formulation of the laws of mechanics describing the motion of massive bodies under the presence of external forces. This formulation is related to the mathematical structure of space and time and requires several advanced mathematical tools. The relevant mathematical background is to be introduced during the course when required. The course covers Newton’s Laws, Reference frames, Gravitation, Oscillations, Central Motion, Lagrangian and Hamiltonian Dynamics. The topics learned in Classical Mechanics constitute the natural starting point for all other branches of theoretical physics including Astrophysics, Quantum Mechanics, Fluid Dynamics, Thermodynamics, Dynamical systems and Relativity.
prerequisite: (PHYS 162 Physics II for Scientists and Engineers with Laboratory (173) (C- and above) OR PHYS 172 Physics II for Physics Majors with Laboratory (1402) (C- and above)) AND MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (C- and above)

title: Classical Mechanics II
description: The course will deal with some advanced topics in classical mechanics. The main topics covered will include (i) an introduction to non-linear dynamical systems and chaos, (ii) continuous media, starting from rigid body motion and inertia tensor to stress and strain, D’Alembert equation, continuity equation and Euler equation for fluids, (iii) the basics of Special Relativity from the point of view of mechanics, including Lorentz transformations, symmetry groups, special relativistic kinematics and dynamics.
prerequisite: PHYS 221 Classical Mechanics I (652) (C- and above)
corequisite: MATH 274 Introduction to Differential Equations (484) (D and above)

title: Introduction to Nuclear Science and Technology
description: The course provides a comprehensive and pedagogical introduction to nuclear science and technology. The course considers topics such as nuclei and nuclear interactions, nuclear structure and reactions, nuclear decay, radioactivity and fission as well as nuclear applications and technologies such as nuclear power plants, nuclear medicine, fusion, radioactive dating, food and agriculture and space science. Students will develop a strong foundation in nuclear physics and gain insight into real-world cutting-edge technologies and applications in the nuclear and energy production industrial sectors in Kazakhstan and around the world.

title: Modern Physics with laboratory
prerequisite: MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (C- and above) AND (PHYS 152 Introductory Physics II with Lab (1176) (C- and above) OR PHYS 162 Physics II for Scientists and Engineers with Laboratory (173) (C- and above) OR PHYS 172 Physics II for Physics Majors with Laboratory (1402) (C- and above))

title: Intermediate Physics Lab I
prerequisite: PHYS 162 Physics II for Scientists and Engineers with Laboratory (173) (C- and above) AND MATH 162 Calculus II (170) ( and above)
corequisite: PHYS 261 Modern Physics with laboratory (125) (C- and above)

title: Intermediate Physics Lab II
prerequisite: PHYS 265 Intermediate Physics Lab I (126) (C- and above) AND PHYS 261 Modern Physics with laboratory (125) (C- and above)
corequisite: PHYS 270 Introduction to Scientific Computing and Data Analysis (488) (C- and above)

title: Introduction to Scientific Computing and Data Analysis
description: This course covers computational and data analysis techniques for scientific and engineering problems, including numerical methods, system simulations, statistical analysis, and machine learning basics.
prerequisite: (CSCI 150 Fundamentals of Programming (1501) (C- and above) OR CSCI 151 Programming for Scientists and Engineers (192) (C- and above) OR CSCI 115 Programming Fundamentals (5257) (C- and above)) AND MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (C- and above)
corequisite: MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (D and above)

title: Applied Methods of Computational Physics with Laboratory
description: In this course basic methods developed for numerical solutions of math physics problems are used for solutions of real-life applications. First part of the course teaches the methods such as graphing, finding roots, numerical interpolation, extrapolation, numerical differentiation and integration, numerical diagonalization of matrices and others.
prerequisite: MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (C- and above) AND MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (C- and above)
antirequisite: PHYS 270 Introduction to Scientific Computing and Data Analysis (488) (C- and above)

title: Thermodynamics and Statistical Physics
description: This course covers macroscopic and microscopic description of thermal phenomena.
prerequisite: MATH 263 Calculus III (81) (C- and above) AND (PHYS 162 Physics II for Scientists and Engineers with Laboratory (173) (C- and above) OR PHYS 172 Physics II for Physics Majors with Laboratory (1402) (C- and above))

title: Introduction to Quantum Technologies
description: This course offers broad introduction into emerging quantum technologies. The first part of the course covers past century of “the first quantum revolution”: the foundations, principles, and paradoxes of q.-(quantum) mechanics, from superposition and Schrodinger cats, to tunneling and interference of particles, uncertainty, entanglement, qubits, teleportation, etc. The second part of the course introduces “the second quantum revolution”, emerging in the last 25 years, where foundations of q.-mechanics is put to work in rapidly developing technologies. We discuss the major trends in q.-science, such as q.-information, q.-communication and cryptography, q.-computing and simulations, q.-metrology, sensing, and imaging. The state of the art and future challenges of q.-technologies will be illustrated with recent examples, such as extremely fast q.-computers, extremely precise q.-clocks, and extremely secure q.-communication lines. The course will conclude with brief discussion of our expectations for q.-technologies, public perceptions and market needs.

title: Research project and internship
description: Summer internship or research project supervised by an NU Physics Department faculty member or by a scientist not belonging to the NU Physics Department.

title: Applied Mathematical Methods
description: This introductory undergraduate course offers a student-friendly overview of essential mathematical techniques in science and engineering. Students will learn general-purpose methods such as linear algebra, differential equations, and Fourier transforms, gaining practical analytical skills valuable in fields like biology, economics, engineering, and data science.
prerequisite: (PHYS 172 Physics II for Physics Majors with Laboratory (1402) (C- and above) OR PHYS 162 Physics II for Scientists and Engineers with Laboratory (173) (C- and above)) AND MATH 274 Introduction to Differential Equations (484) (C- and above)

title: Classical Electrodynamics I
description: This course elaborates the interaction of electrostatic and magnetostatic fields with different types of matter and formulates mathematical methods for solving problems in various geometries. The connection is drawn of the observed and analyzed effects with applications at the static regime. The electromagnetic waves are introduced in unbounded space for signal propagation.
corequisite: PHYS 315 Applied Mathematical Methods (653) (D and above) OR PHYS 411 Advanced Mathematical Physics (3142) (D and above)

title: Classical Electrodynamics II
prerequisite: PHYS 361 Classical Electrodynamics I (651) (C- and above)

title: Optics with Laboratory
prerequisite: PHYS 361 Classical Electrodynamics I (651) (C- and above)

title: Research Methods
description: This course is designed to introduce students to basic research methods in physics that are essential in everyday research work in modern academic, industrial, and government environments. Physics Faculty will share their experiences in theoretical, computational, observational, and experimental methods. The topics may include characteristics of good research, science ethics, science funding, research proposals, gathering and critical evaluation of scientific information, various tools and software, bibliometrics and scientometrics, writing scientific reports and white papers, publication process in peer-reviewed journals, preparing technical oral presentations, dissemination of research results, proprietary vs open science, science policies and advocacy, public outreach, and others.

title: Physics Research Project
description: Research project approved and supervised by an NU Physics Department faculty member.

title: Advanced Mathematical Physics
description: In this course students advance in problem analysis involving partial differential equations, tensors, complex-valued functions and Fourier transforms.
prerequisite: MATH 274 Introduction to Differential Equations (484) (C- and above) AND PHYS 162 Physics II for Scientists and Engineers with Laboratory (173) (C- and above)

title: Parallel Computing
description: This course provides an introduction to parallel programming with an emphasis on applications in scientific computing. Topics include an overview or relevant aspects of the hardware for parallel computer systems and parallel programming models (shared memory, distributed memory, and GPU-based computing), performance considerations, parallel algorithms, scalability, and code optimization techniques. Practical exercises will involve hands-on experience with using common libraries and software stacks for parallel computations, such as OpenMP (multithreading), MPI (message passing), and CUDA/OpenCL (GPU computing) in high-performance computing environments. The course is suitable for students interested in computational science and data-intensive research.
prerequisite: PHYS 270 Introduction to Scientific Computing and Data Analysis (488) (C- and above) OR CSCI 151 Programming for Scientists and Engineers (192) (C- and above) OR CSCI 115 Programming Fundamentals (5257) (C- and above)

title: Quantum Mechanics I
description: In this course, students learn the basics of non-relativistic quantum mechanics. The course introduces the concept of the wave function, its interpretation, and covers the topics of potential wells, potential barriers, quantum harmonic oscillator, and the hydrogen atom. Next, a more formal approach to quantum mechanics is taken by introducing the postulates of quantum mechanics, quantum operators, Hilbert spaces, Heisenberg uncertainty principle, and time evolution. The course ends with topics covering the addition of angular momenta, spin, emergence of energy bands in periodic systems, and some basic aspects of many-body quantum mechanics, such as the indistinguishability of identical particles and electron orbitals in atoms.
prerequisite: PHYS 221 Classical Mechanics I (652) (C- and above) AND PHYS 361 Classical Electrodynamics I (651) (C- and above)

title: Quantum Mechanics II
description: This course covers several widely used approximate methods of quantum mechanics: the variational method (including the Hartree-Fock approach), stationary and time-dependent perturbation theory, semiclassical approximation, and adiabatic approximation. In the framework of these methods some important applications will be considered, such as the fine structure of atomic energy levels, chemical bonding, theory of alpha-decay, selection rules for dipole transitions, Rabi oscillations, etc. Students will also learn the basics of quantum scattering theory. If time permits, some elements of relativistic quantum mechanics and/or the formalism of second quantization may be considered.
prerequisite: PHYS 451 Quantum Mechanics I (1415) (C- and above)

title: Field Theories in Physics
description: The course deals with field theories in physics as obtained via a Lagrangian approach through the variation of the action. The main focus is on Newtonian gravity, thermodynamics, Maxwell’s electromagnetism, quantum mechanics, scalar fields and relativity.
prerequisite: MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (C- and above) AND PHYS 221 Classical Mechanics I (652) (C- and above)
corequisite: PHYS 451 Quantum Mechanics I (1415) (C- and above)

title: Astrophysics and General Relativity
description: The course on star formation and evolution, supernovae, general relativety, including cosmology and black holes and high energy phenomena
prerequisite: MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (C- and above) AND PHYS 221 Classical Mechanics I (652) (C- and above) AND MATH 274 Introduction to Differential Equations (484) (C- and above)

title: Advanced Experimental Physics
description: This is an advanced laboratory course in the real research laboratory setting. Students will gain experience in setting up and conducting experiments and analyzing acquired data in various areas of physics including but not limited to condensed matter physics, nanotechnology, thermodynamics, laser optics, accelerator physics, semiconductor devices, photovoltaics.
prerequisite: PHYS 370 Optics with Laboratory (1405) (C- and above)

title: Introduction to Optoelectronics
description: This course aims to teach basics of semiconductor physics and optoelectronic devices based on semiconductors.
prerequisite: PHYS 261 Modern Physics with laboratory (125) (C- and above) OR PHYS 473 Introduction to Solid State Physics (1423) (C- and above) OR CHEM 331 Physical Chemistry I (634) (C- and above) OR MAE 301 Engineering Thermodynamics (5927) (C- and above) OR CHME 201 Chemical Engineering Thermodynamics (5007) (C- and above) OR ELCE 204 Solid State Devices (5508) (C- and above)

title: Introduction to Solid State Physics
description: This course covers the fundamentals of solid-state physics spanning structural, binding, mechanical, vibrational, thermal, electrical, magnetic and optical properties of crystalline, defected and non-crystalline solids (metals, semiconductors and insulators). The properties and phenomena in solids are studied as a result of their interaction with external radiation, fields and particles. Take all the fundamentals of physics, including classical and quantum mechanics, electromagnetism, thermodynamics and statistical physics, and put them all together to study a piece of matter. Critical applications in material science, nanotechnology, solid-state devices, thermal and electrical energy transport & conversion, and materials characterization techniques will also be addressed. A grasp of fundamental and advanced principles and techniques in solid-state physics is very important in much of modern applied physical sciences, high-technology as well as fundamental research.
prerequisite: PHYS 261 Modern Physics with laboratory (125) (C- and above) OR CHEM 331 Physical Chemistry I (634) (C- and above) OR MAE 301 Engineering Thermodynamics (5927) (C- and above) OR CHME 201 Chemical Engineering Thermodynamics (5007) (C- and above) OR ELCE 204 Solid State Devices (5508) (C- and above)

title: Lasers and Photonics
description: This course covers topics of lasers, photonics and the broader subject of the interaction of laser radiation with matter. The topics may include an overview of research and industrial applications of photonics.
prerequisite: PHYS 370 Optics with Laboratory (1405) (C- and above)

title: Statistical Mechanics
description: Statistical Mechanics provides a microscopic description of macroscopic phenomena using probability theory and statistical methods. Due to the large number of particles in a physical system (thermodynamic limit), the related probability distributions are very sharp so that macroscopic observables are sufficiently represented by averaged microscopic quantities. The applicability of the concepts of Statistical Mechanics is very broad spanning from thermodynamics and condensed matter as well as to chemistry, biology, economics, and engineering science.
prerequisite: PHYS 280 Thermodynamics and Statistical Physics (1179) (C- and above)

title: Directed Study of Advanced Physics Topics
description: Directed study of advanced physics topics supervised by an NU Physics Department faculty member.

title: Teaching Practicum in Physics
description: Students will teach laboratory and recitation classes for first-year physics courses under the supervision of a Physics Department faculty member.

title: Honors Thesis Research
description: The course is designed to monitor progress and develop understandings and skills to plan and conduct independent research at the Bachelor of Sciences level. The student will perform a research project under supervision of Physics Faculty. Honors Thesis Research constitutes a partial fulfillment and pre-requisite for the Honors Thesis course. The research plan will be used as a basis for the assessment of the student's research progress.

title: Honors Thesis
description: This is a substantive research project assigned by a Physics Faculty supervisor. The project is to be concluded with a written Honors thesis, which is a comprehensive report on the research problem, background, experimental or theoretical results and analysis. The thesis is to be presented by the student in an open public setting and to be evaluated jointly by the project's supervisor and by another Physics Department faculty member.

title: Teaching Practicum
description: The course introduces students to the pedagogical structures and methods of teaching and learning, beginning with program structure and curricular requirements to the elucidation of learning objective and learning outcomes, the selection of student assessment methods, and the quality assurance life cycle processes.

title: Classical Mechanics
description: The course covers Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations of classical mechanics, rigid body motion and classical scattering theory.

title: Quantum Mechanics
