description: The course covers nonrelativistic quantum mechanics and introduces elements of relativistic quantum theory. The focus of the course is on the applications of quantum mechanics to experimentally relevant physical settings.

title: Scientific Computing and Data Analysis
description: This course covers advanced computational and data analysis methods for solving complex scientific and engineering problems. Topics include numerical methods, system simulations, algorithm efficiency, statistical modeling, signal processing, and machine learning, with real-world applications.

title: Classical Electrodynamics
description: The course systematically covers electromagnetic fields in vacuum and matter in non-relativistic and relativistic limits.

title: Statistical Physics
description: The course covers grad-level topics of statistical physics. Possible choices may include fluctuations, susceptibilities and transport in the linear-response regime near thermodynamic equilibrium, Landau theory of second-order phase transitions, critical phenomena, Boltzmann kinetic equation and its applications to nonequilibrium phenomena.

title: Parallel Programming for Scientific Computing
description: This course introduces parallel programming techniques with a focus on applications in computational science and large-scale numerical simulations. Topics include the architecture of parallel computing systems, parallel programming models (shared memory, distributed memory, and GPU-based computing), performance optimization, load balancing, and scalability. Emphasis is placed on practical implementation using industry-standard parallel computing frameworks, including OpenMP (multithreading), MPI (message passing), and CUDA/OpenCL (GPU computing). Students will gain hands-on experience running and optimizing parallel code on high-performance computing systems, with applications relevant to computational sciences.
prerequisite: PHYS 511 Scientific Computing and Data Analysis (3169) (C- and above) OR CSCI 501 Software Principles and Practice (2408) (C- and above) OR DS 501 Fundamentals of Data Science (5218) (C- and above)

title: Solid State Physics
description: This course covers the fundamentals of solid-state physics spanning structural, binding, mechanical, vibrational, thermal, electrical, magnetic and optical properties of crystalline, defected and non-crystalline solids (metals, semiconductors and insulators). The properties and phenomena in solids are studied as a result of their interaction with external radiation, fields and particles. Take all the fundamentals of physics, including classical and quantum mechanics, electromagnetism, thermodynamics and statistical physics, and put them all together to study a piece of matter. Critical applications in material science, nanotechnology, solid-state devices, thermal and electrical energy transport & conversion, and materials characterization techniques will also be addressed. A grasp of fundamental and advanced principles and techniques in solid-state physics is very important in much of modern applied physical sciences, high-technology as well as fundamental research.

title: Advanced Instrumentation Methods
description: This is an advanced laboratory course. Students will master assembling and designing experiments

title: Analytical Methods in Science
description: This course covers essential mathematical techniques for solving practical problems in science and engineering. Topics include Fourier analysis, which is handy for signal processing and imaging, and differential equations, essential for modeling biological and economic systems. Students gain practical skills using computational software, making this course valuable for diverse scientific careers.

title: Field Theories
description: The course deals with field theories in physics as obtained via a Lagrangian approach through the variation of the action. The main focus is on Newtonian gravity, thermodynamics, Maxwell’s electromagnetism, quantum mechanics, scalar fields and relativity.
prerequisite: PHYS 505 Classical Mechanics (2261) (D and above)

title: General Relativity
description: The course deals with Einstein’s theory of gravity. From differential geometry and the formulation of the theory to the most important solutions and their interpretation.

title: Advanced Physics Laboratory
description: This is an advanced laboratory course in the real research laboratory setting. Students will gain experience in setting up and conducting experiments and analyzing acquired data in various areas of physics including but not limited to condensed matter physics, nanotechnology, thermodynamics, laser optics, accelerator physics, semiconductor devices, photovoltaics

title: Introduction to Optoelectronics
description: This course aims to teach basics of semiconductor physics and optoelectronic devices based on semiconductors.

title: Directed Study of Advanced Topics in Modern Physics
description: An independent study course on an advanced physics topic, chosen in consultation with a faculty supervisor. The student engages in self-directed learning through reading and regular discussions. A final report summarizes the material studied and key insights. The supervisor provides a brief evaluation and grade recommendation.

title: Research Methods
description: This course deals with the methodology in research.

title: Thesis study
description: This course is designed to monitor progress and develop understandings, skills, and outlooks to conduct original, independent research at the MS level. The student will develop (with the advisor’s guidance) a research plan at the beginning of the semester that will state a research problem/question/hypothesis, its background, outline a research strategy and experimental approach, method of data collection, interpretation and validation, and method of communication of the project results to others. The research plan is used as the basis for assessment of the student’s research progress.

title: Thesis Research
description: Offered in the Fall, this course bridges Thesis Study (PHYS 600) and Thesis (PHYS 692). It helps MSc Physics students refine their research skills, develop their thesis project and outline, and prepare for their final defense.

title: Thesis
description: Students will conduct research work under the direction of a supervisor on a novel research problem in a designated area of research. At the end of the semester, the student will prepare and defend the thesis.

title: Doctoral Thesis
description: This course is designed to facilitate before the end of the prescribed program period or approved degree deferral period the writing and submission of the doctoral thesis for review by the thesis examiners. The thesis must be completed according to the Format and Style Guidelines of the Physics Department.

title: Thesis Research
description: This course is designed to monitor progress and develop understandings, skills, and outlooks to conduct original, independent research at the PhD level. The student will develop (with the advisor’s guidance) a research plan at the beginning of the semester that will state a research problem/question/hypothesis, its background, outline a research strategy and experimental approach, method of data collection, interpretation and validation, and method of communication of the project results to others. The research plan is used as the basis for assessment of the student’s research progress.

title: Current Research Literature
description: This course is designed to provide students a directed focus on preparing a literature review on the topic of their interest in coordination with a faculty supervisor. The students are expected to develop a comprehensive review of the state of the art and identify the major gaps in the field of research. They also develop critical assessment and comparison of the past literature, and present the work in the form of the term paper.

title: Classical Mechanics
description: This course aims to provide the students with knowledge of the fundamental laws of classical mechanics, mathematical methods for the solution of equations of motion, application of the laws and motion and mathematical methods to mechanical systems.

title: Quantum Mechanics
description: This course aims to provide mastery of graduate level quantum mechanics.

title: Scientific Computing and Data Analysis
description: This course covers advanced computational methods and data analysis techniques for solving complex scientific and engineering problems, emphasizing numerical methods, high-fidelity simulations, and algorithm efficiency. Students will also explore data-driven modeling, statistical inference, signal processing, and machine learning with research-oriented applications.

title: Classical Electrodynamics
description: This is the Electrodynamics course covering advanced treatment of electromagnetic phenomena.

title: Statistical Physics
description: In this course, students learn advanced and modern techniques for computational modeling and simulations.

title: Solid State Physics
description: This course covers the fundamentals of solid-state physics spanning structural, binding, mechanical, vibrational, thermal, electrical, magnetic and optical properties of crystalline, defected and non-crystalline solids (metals, semiconductors and insulators). Critical applications in material science, nanotechnology, solid-state devices, thermal and electrical energy transport & conversion, and materials characterization techniques will also be addressed. A grasp of fundamental and advanced principles and techniques in solid-state physics is very important in much of modern applied physical sciences, high-technology as well as fundamental research.

Students gain practical skills using computational software, making this course valuable for diverse scientific careers.

prerequisite: PHYS 505 Classical Mechanics (2261) (D and above)

title: General Relativity
description: The course deals with Einstein’s theory of gravity. From advanced differential geometry and the formulation of the theory to the derivation and interpretation of the most important solutions.

title: Advanced Physics Laboratory
description: This is an advanced laboratory course in the real research laboratory setting. Students will gain experience in setting up and conducting experiments and analyzing acquired data in various areas of physics including but not limited to condensed matter physics, nanotechnology, thermodynamics, laser optics, accelerator physics, semiconductor devices, photovoltaics

title: Introduction to Optoelectronics
description: This course aims to teach basics of semiconductor physics and optoelectronic devices based on semiconductors.

title: Lasers and Photonics
description: This advanced-level course will introduce PhD students to the important field of light-matter coherent interactions, coherent optics, laser physics and engineering, fundmentals of photonics and introduction to nonlinear optics.

title: Directed Study of Advanced Modern Physics Topics
description: An independent study course on an advanced physics topic, chosen in consultation with a faculty supervisor. The student engages in self-directed learning through reading and regular discussions. A final report summarizes the material studied and key insights. The supervisor provides a brief evaluation and grade recommendation.

title: Research methods and ethics
description: This course will help PhD students to learn the skill of planning and development of research work. This includes reading the current literature and identifying open research questions as well as communicating scientific and technical knowledge and ideas to the peer community. This course is designed to introduce students to basic research methods in physics that are essential in everyday research work in modern academic, industrial, and government environments as well as the associated ethical issues.

title: Introduction to Public Administration
department: Political Science and International Relations, Sociology and Anthropology

title: Introduction to the Politics of Central Asia
description: The course will introduce key concepts and theories in political science that will be useful for the study of Kazakhstani and Central Asian politics such as the state structure and legal and political systems. In particular, we will discuss the different aspects of contemporary politics such as institution-building, political economy, gender and religion, civil society dynamics, etc.

title: The Political Challenges of Technologies and Science: An Introduction
description: This is an introductory class on the ethical challenges associated with science and contemporary technologies

title: Quantitative Methods
antirequisite: ECON 211 Economic Statistics (2280) (C- and above)

title: Public Opinion and Elections
description: This course will teach public opinion and election behavior.
prerequisite: PLS 211 Quantitative Methods (221) (C- and above) OR ECON 211 Economic Statistics (2280) (C- and above)

title: Political Game Theory
description: Game Theory is the study of strategic interactions. It is a collection of techniques designed to model strategic interactions and formulate predicted outcomes.
prerequisite: PLS 211 Quantitative Methods (221) (C- and above) OR ECON 101 Introduction to Microeconomics (379) (C and above)

title: Ancient Political Theory
prerequisite: PLS 120 Introduction to Political Theory (512) (C- and above)

title: Modern Political Theory
prerequisite: PLS 120 Introduction to Political Theory (512) (C- and above)

title: Contemporary Political Theory
description: The third in the historical political theory series.
prerequisite: PLS 120 Introduction to Political Theory (512) (C- and above)
antirequisite: PHIL 131 Introduction to Contemporary Political Philosophy (4032) (C- and above)

title: Confucianism and the Development of Chinese Politics
description: This course will examine how Confucian texts have been selectively interpreted during each important historical juncture of China. As we will see, the various interpretations provide us with a window into the political development of China. This course is important for students who are interested in Chinese politics.
department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, Political Science and International Relations

title: Anarchy
prerequisite: PLS 120 Introduction to Political Theory (512) (C- and above)

title: Politics and Governance of Eurasia
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: U.S. Government and Politics
description: This course provides an overview of the institutions, processes, and content of politics in the United States.
prerequisite: (PLS 140 Introduction to Comparative Politics (223) (C- and above) OR PLS 101 Introduction to Political Science (513) (C- and above)) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Politics of East Asia
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Politics of Development
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Political Corruption
description: In this module, students will study the phenomenon of political corruption from the perspective of countries, governments, businesses, citizens, and the people within these entities and discuss the cross-cutting nature of political corruption and its impact on social and economic development. This module will also foster students’ awareness of the latest international developments related to integrity and anti-corruption and of how these instruments can be employed to work in different contexts.
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Politics of Sub-Saharan Africa
description: The course is designed to introduce students to the politics of contemporary Sub-Saharan Africa. The first part of the course reviews Africa’s recent political history, focusing on the impacts of colonization and on the types of states that have emerged from the continent’s colonial experience and evolved in the subsequent decades. The second part examines the challenges that postcolonial governments face as they attempt to manage the interests of diverse societies and reform economies and political institutions. The course pays particular attention to Africa’s diversity and to the substantial cross-country and sub-national variation observed on the continent.
prerequisite: PLS 140 Introduction to Comparative Politics (223) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Revolutions, Social Movements, and Contentious Politics
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: International Political Economy
description: This course examines the political foundations of international economic relations and how these relations influence and are influenced by domestic politics of states. Our focus will be on international trade, investments and capital flows, and issues of economic development. The primary goal of this course is to give students a broad understanding of the global economy through grasping political and economic theories explaining state behavior in economic relations and economic policies states pursue.
prerequisite: PLS 150 Introduction to International Relations (511) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above) AND PLS 211 Quantitative Methods (221) (C- and above)

title: International Relations Theory
description: This course is designed to provide a detailed introduction to International Relations theory. This course examines the major theories of International Relations and explores practices and problems of international politics in a global context. Key themes addressed include power, con cooperation and interdependence, and political economy. Our primary goal throughout this course will be to lay the theoretical and analytical foundations for the study of international politics. In order to do so, we shall examine several theoretical approaches in IR that seek to answer important research questions and puzzles in international politics.
prerequisite: PLS 150 Introduction to International Relations (511) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: European Integration Politics
prerequisite: (PLS 140 Introduction to Comparative Politics (223) (C- and above) OR PLS 150 Introduction to International Relations (511) (C- and above)) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Introduction to International Law
prerequisite: PLS 150 Introduction to International Relations (511) (C- and above) AND PLS 140 Introduction to Comparative Politics (223) (C- and above) AND PLS 120 Introduction to Political Theory (512) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: European Union: Institutions and Policies
description: European Union: Institutions and Policies is a 300 level undergraduate course aimed at introducing students to the politics of the European Union (EU). The core objective of this course is to familiarize students with one of the most advanced instances of regional integration.
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: International Politics of the Korean Peninsula
description: The Korean Peninsula is the last place where the Cold War politics remains dominant today: two Koreas remain divided with substantial hostility. However, the past quarter century witnessed fluctuating moods between long-standing adversaries. What can explain the variation in inter-Korean relations, and what can be said about the future of Korea? This course is designed to investigate the inter-Korean relations through different theories of IR and to provide historical knowledge about the case. The focus will be on changing strategies of two Koreas over time and the theoretical implications of Korean cases to the broader literature of conflict and international politics. This course is a writing intensive course, which requires a term paper no shorter than 5,000 words.
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above) AND PLS 150 Introduction to International Relations (511) (C- and above)

title: United Nations
description: The course will delve into the international relations theories on cooperation along with evaluating global issues the Untied Nations seeks to address.
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Foreign Policy Analysis
prerequisite: PLS 150 Introduction to International Relations (511) (C- and above)

title: Memory Politics in East Asia
description: This course investigates the impact of past events on present politics among countries in East Asia. By reading a wide range of scientific literature, from philosophical arguments of apologies and forgiveness to memory politics and public apologies in IR contexts, students will learn about various theoretical arguments over the past in East Asia. Major cases to be covered in this course include the comfort women issue between Japan and neighboring countries, civilian killings during the Vietnam War, memory politics stemmed from Cold War politics, and the history textbook controversies between Japan, China, and South Korea.

title: Science, Technology and International Affairs
description: This course aims to examine how scientific development and technological innovations shape relations among nations, understand how technological progress can help to advance sustainable development and promote peace in the world, and why new technologies can create risks and uncertainties for the global community.
prerequisite: PLS 150 Introduction to International Relations (511) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Visual Politics
description: The purpose of this course is to examine this “visual turn” in global politics. Why visuals matter? What role does visual content play in people’s everyday life? What is the political power of images? How international events are being shaped by them? We will devote considerable time to exploring visual dimension of politics within the Central Asian context.
prerequisite: PLS 140 Introduction to Comparative Politics (223) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Civil-Military Relations
prerequisite: PLS 211 Quantitative Methods (221) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Law, Politics and Society
description: This introductory course examines how law intersects with politics and society; how, when, and why law works or fails to work in regulating social behavior, exercising social control, resolving disputes, and creating social change in Kazakhstan and countries around the world.
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Comparative Welfare States
description: At the beginning of the 21st century the welfare state deserves more attention than ever before. The current economic crisis, accompanied by significant social and demographic challenges, has put welfare state reforms on the agenda of many North American, Western European, Latin American, East Asian and post-communist countries. The controversy surrounding the modern welfare state involves a large variety of issues: How can we define and analyze welfare states, what is social justice, what factors contributed to welfare state crisis, what actors are involved in the struggle for welfare reforms, what is the nature of the connection between the welfare state, the economy and the labor market, how do we account for cross-national differences of welfare state regimes, and what are the specific challenges those regimes face respectively? In this course, we will address these questions in order to gain some insight into the functioning of modern welfare states in different parts of the world and assess current government efforts of reforming them.
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Comparative Public Policy
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Moot Court in Public International Law
description: This course trains students to analyze international legal texts, draft legal opinions, and present arguments in moot courts that simulate the work of international tribunals such as the International Court of Justice.
prerequisite: PLS 120 Introduction to Political Theory (512) (C- and above) AND PLS 150 Introduction to International Relations (511) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Intermediate Special Topics in Comparative Politics
description: This 300-level course is designed to allow PSIR faculty and visiting faculty to teach courses related to their research interests and to introduce students to those topics and the process by which research on that topic is done.
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Politics of China
description: This course offers a conceptual framework for understanding Chinese politics that highlights the intersection of politics and economics. It shows and analyzes how rather than develop into a market economy and liberal democracy, China today represents a major alternative model of development and needs to be studied not as a historical anomaly but as a real challenger to what has been considered the norm.
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Modern Korean Politics
description: This course examines South Korea’s rapid economic development, democratic transition, and prospects for reunification. Topics include the government’s role in industrialization, the institutions and culture shaping Korean democracy, and key issues related to North Korea, including division and the nuclear question.
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C and above) AND PLS 211 Quantitative Methods (221) (C and above)

title: Independent Study
description: This class allows students to pursue a focused exploration of a topic that is not offered in conventional classes, while under the supervision of a faculty member. Interested students will need to have maintained60 hours of previous coursework, be in good academic standing, and be able to demonstrate the ability to work independently of the supervising faculty member, as the faculty role will be one of guidance as opposed lecturer. Both the topic and a study plan must be approved by the faculty member prior to enrollment.
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above) AND PLS 211 Quantitative Methods (221) (C- and above)

title: Maximum Likelihood Models
description: The course will teach generalized linear models, which covers models for binary data, count data, and duration.
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above) OR PLS 211 Quantitative Methods (221) (C- and above)

title: Experimental Political Science
description: This upper level seminar is designed to introduce students to experimental literature in political science. We will learn key concepts, applications, practical issues of experimental research in political science.
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above) AND PLS 211 Quantitative Methods (221) (C- and above)

title: Scientific Research in Political Science
description: This course will introduce students to the quantitative study of political science, with a special emphasis on research designs and methods.
prerequisite: PLS 150 Introduction to International Relations (511) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above) AND PLS 211 Quantitative Methods (221) (C- and above)

title: AI from a Social Science Perspective
description: This course examines artificial intelligence from the perspective of the social sciences.
prerequisite: PLS 120 Introduction to Political Theory (512) (C- and above)

title: Theories of Political Obligations
description: A theory of political obligation explains why individuals have a moral duty to obey the state or advocate policies contrary to governmental decisions. This course will examine various approaches in the literature including arguments from gratitude, consent, natural duty, fair play, nationalism, feminism, as well as Islamic and Confucian traditions.
prerequisite: PLS 325 Ancient Political Theory (675) (C- and above) OR PLS 326 Modern Political Theory (1131) (C- and above)

title: Just War Theory
description: This course examines the moral reasons that allow the use of violence (jus ad bellum), the ones that should regulate the conduct of a war (jus in bello) as well as principles that should lead to a just peace (jus post bellum). This class also focuses on the contemporary ethical issues that have arisen since the beginning of the 21st Century which are associated with the War on Terror and the development of technologies.
prerequisite: PLS 120 Introduction to Political Theory (512) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Immigration Theory
description: This class will provide students with an overview of normative arguments and ethical consideration to various aspects of immigration theory overtime, from the classical to contemporary period.

title: Issues in the Philosophy of Social Science
description: This course is designed to address a range of issues in the philosophy of social science from positivist inquiries how to differentiate between facts and values to the post-positivist occupation with the role of academic knowledge and research in a broad system of power relationships.
prerequisite: PLS 120 Introduction to Political Theory (512) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Feminist Political Theory
description: This is a class about feminist political theory. We will explore utilitarian, Marxist, Black, and Islamic feminist traditions (among others).
prerequisite: PLS 120 Introduction to Political Theory (512) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Hannah Arendt on Power, Violence, and Revolution
description: This is a class on the political philosophy of Hannah Arendt. We will explore such themes as: totalitarianism, revolution, violence, mass society, and political belonging.
prerequisite: PLS 120 Introduction to Political Theory (512) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Science, Politics and the State in Comparative Context, c.1850-1980
description: By comparatively exploring these processes in the US, Britain, Germany and Russia we will chart the powerful relationship between science and governance that has emerged in modern history, and find ways of examining science policy within its cultural context.
department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, Political Science and International Relations
prerequisite: Subject "HST" BETWEEN 200 and 299 OR Subject "HST" BETWEEN 300 and 399

title: Politics and Governance of the Russian Federation
description: This course is designed to provide students with an in-depth understanding of Russian politics from the late Soviet era to the present (i.e. from Gorbachev to Putin).
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Comparative Democratization
description: In this course, we will raise central questions that motivate social scientists and policymakers the world over.
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Homeland Security
description: This is an upper level undergraduate course which focuses on a variety of topics related to unconventional domestic security challenges.
prerequisite: PLS 140 Introduction to Comparative Politics (223) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Text Analysis and Political Communication in the Information Age
description: This course offers working knowledge and hands-on experience in political communication research, with special attention to the methodology of quantitative text analysis. Students will learn critical questions in the political communication literature and how those questions can be studied through text analysis. Students will also have an opportunity to develop their own text analysis project to collect and analyze political communication datasets.
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above) AND PLS 211 Quantitative Methods (221) (C- and above)

title: Political Polarization in Democracies
description: This course is designed to provide an in-depth exploration of the fundamental aspects of political polarization in democracies, as well as theories and debates about its causes and consequences.
prerequisite: PLS 140 Introduction to Comparative Politics (223) (C and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C and above) AND PLS 211 Quantitative Methods (221) (C and above)

title: Nationalism and Multi-Ethnic Governance
description: This course considers both the theories of group identity and group rights in the political context of the nation-state as well as policy choices governments make to implement certain theoretical perspectives. Toward this goal, we will consider both liberal and non-liberal approaches to addressing multiethnic populations and assess the successes and breakdowns of governance in a number of cases.
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above) AND PLS 140 Introduction to Comparative Politics (223) (C- and above)

title: Advanced Topics in Comparative Politics
description: This course allows students to take topical courses from professors who are teaching courses on their primary areas of interest. These seminars are meant to broaden student understanding of particular issue areas in comparative politics. Potential topics include immigration, nationalism, federalism, voting, party behavior, regional studies, institutions, judicial politics, interest groups, and more. This course draws on the research expertise of professors in the department and gives students the opportunity to read, discuss, and write about core subject areas in greater depth in preparation for their thesis work.
prerequisite: PLS 140 Introduction to Comparative Politics (223) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Political Violence
description: This course is designed to provide students with an overview of the various ways in which violence relates to the conduct of politics.
prerequisite: (PLS 140 Introduction to Comparative Politics (223) (C- and above) OR PLS 150 Introduction to International Relations (511) (C- and above)) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: The Politics of Immigration Control
description: In order to fulfill capstone requirements, this course will apply core concepts of comparative politics (i.e. state capacity, national identity, state-society relations, models of the welfare state, state management of economies) to the policy area of immigration.
prerequisite: PLS 140 Introduction to Comparative Politics (223) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Comparative Political Parties
description: This seminar will deals generally with the topic of political parties. Specifically, models, roles, and changes in political parties and party systems
prerequisite: PLS 140 Introduction to Comparative Politics (223) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Comparative Electoral System
description: Elections are core instruments as well as defining feature of representative democracy. This course is designed to introduce students to the key features of various electoral systems, including how votes are casted, counted and translated into seats, and theories and debates on political and economic consequences of electoral system. To this end, a series of theoretical, conceptual, and empirical issues to studying electoral systems will be taught and discussed.
prerequisite: PLS 140 Introduction to Comparative Politics (223) (C- and above)

title: Politics and Governance of the Gulf
description: This is a class on the politics and governance of the Gulf. It will explore a range of domestic and foreign policy issues facing the region.
prerequisite: PLS 140 Introduction to Comparative Politics (223) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Advanced Topics in International Relations
description: This course is meant to broaden student understanding of particular issue areas in international politics.
prerequisite: PLS 150 Introduction to International Relations (511) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above) AND PLS 211 Quantitative Methods (221) (C- and above)

title: The United Nations System
description: This course delves into the organizational framework and operational significance of the United Nations system, including the United Nations --- the premier intergovernmental entity. The course will introduce students to the theories of cooperation and the role of the United Nations in fostering collaboration in economic development, human rights, and security affairs. The course will conclude by discussing the difficulties associated with multilateralism and the future of intergovernmental organizations, including the United Nations.
prerequisite: PLS 150 Introduction to International Relations (511) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above) AND PLS 211 Quantitative Methods (221) (C- and above)
antirequisite: PLS 458 International Organization (1870) (C- and above)

title: The Politics of Arms in International Relations
description: This class will examine arms in international relations from a number of perspectives and at different levels of analysis.
prerequisite: PLS 150 Introduction to International Relations (511) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above) AND PLS 211 Quantitative Methods (221) (C- and above)

title: International Security and Conflict
description: This course will explore issues of international security including interstate war, ethnic conflict, terrorism, and low-level conflicts.
prerequisite: PLS 150 Introduction to International Relations (511) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above) AND PLS 211 Quantitative Methods (221) (C- and above)

title: International Organization
description: This course examines interstate cooperation through the various “isms” used to explain this international relations outcome and specific empirical cases of cooperation.
prerequisite: PLS 150 Introduction to International Relations (511) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: International Conflict Processes
description: This course is designed to introduce students to the scientific study of conflict, in areas related to the bargaining theory of war, deterrence and the security dilemma, alliances, arms races, the democratic peace, and other areas of scholarly inquiry. Thus this class is not about any particular conflict but rather about the notion of conflict and why/how it occurs.
prerequisite: PLS 150 Introduction to International Relations (511) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above) OR PLS 211 Quantitative Methods (221) (C- and above)

title: Environmental Politics
description: This course is a comprehensive overview of the international and comparative politics and policy dimensions of the natural environment. We will examine the political forces that shape how government, organizations, and citizens across the globe respond to environmental problems and the consequences of those approaches.

title: NGO Politics
description: This course will examine the growing and changing roles of nongovernmental organizations in both domestic and international politics.
prerequisite: PLS 150 Introduction to International Relations (511) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Politics of International Finance
description: This course aims to provide students with a strong analytical understanding and empirical survey of the major debates in the field such as the analysis of exchange rate policies, capital movements, international financial institutions such as the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund, currency crises etc.
prerequisite: PLS 150 Introduction to International Relations (511) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: International Relations of Asia
description: This course will analyze the increasing complexity of international relations in Asia. It will emphasize the strategic aspects in interstate relations related to growing tensions from security and economic concerns.
prerequisite: PLS 150 Introduction to International Relations (511) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: International Relations of Eurasia
description: The course investigates the international politics surrounding the wider Eurasian space, including great power rivalries, conflict patterns, regional governance, transportaition infrastructures, and foreign policy adaptations.
prerequisite: PLS 150 Introduction to International Relations (511) (C- and above) AND PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: Negotiation, Cooperation and Strategy
description: This course provides a game theoretic approach to strategic decision situations in politics, economy, business, and public administration.
prerequisite: ECON 302 Game Theory and Economic Analysis (1378) (C- and above) OR PLS 315 Political Game Theory (704) (C- and above)

title: Public Choice and Public Policy
description: Public choice and public policy is a course designed to acquaint students with a sub-discipline of economics and political science that attempts to explain (and improve) the public policy process via economics. Students will learn about the origins of public choice and the key theories of the public choice school, as well as actively engage in the debates on “how to govern.”
prerequisite: PLS 140 Introduction to Comparative Politics (223) (C- and above) AND PLS 211 Quantitative Methods (221) (C- and above)

title: Research Practicum in PSIR
description: The purpose of this course is to give graduate and undergraduate students practical and in-depth experience with any number of research methods by involving them in the projects of PSIR faculty.
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above) AND PLS 211 Quantitative Methods (221) (C- and above)

title: Research Practicum in PSIR
description: The purpose of this course is to give graduate and undergraduate students practical and in-depth experience with any number of research methods by involving them in the projects of PSIR faculty.
prerequisite: PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above) OR PLS 211 Quantitative Methods (221) (C- and above)

title: Nietzsche
description: A capstone seminar in political theory.
prerequisite: PLS 325 Ancient Political Theory (675) (C- and above) OR PLS 326 Modern Political Theory (1131) (C- and above)

title: Capstone Course in Comparative Politics
prerequisite: PLS 101 Introduction to Political Science (513) (C- and above) AND PLS 140 Introduction to Comparative Politics (223) (C- and above) AND Subject "PLS" BETWEEN 200 and 299 AND Subject "PLS" BETWEEN 300 and 399

title: Quantitative Research Methods
description: This course will teach you about quantitative research methods and give you a chance to practice conducting and analyzing your own research. Through readings and class discussions, you will become familiar with the basic tools and concepts of quantitative social research. You will design and conduct your own research to examine the question that you select.

title: Qualitative Methods in Political Science
description: This course will teach you about qualitative research methods and give you a chance to practice conducting and analyzing your own research. Through readings and class discussions, you will become familiar with the basic tools and concepts of qualitative social research. You will design and conduct your own research to examine the question that you select.

title: Maximum Likelihood Models
description: The course will teach generalized linear models, which covers models for binary data, count data, and duration.
prerequisite: PLS 510 Quantitative Research Methods (1946) (C- and above)

title: Experimental Political Science
description: This upper level seminar is designed to introduce students to experimental literature in political science. We will learn key concepts, applications, practical issues of experimental research in political science.
prerequisite: PLS 511 Qualitative Methods in Political Science (1631) (C- and above)

title: Scientific Research in Political Science
description: This course will introduce students to the quantitative study of political science, with a special emphasis on research designs and methods.

title: Global Economic Governance
description: This graduate seminar examines the institutions, rules, and practices that structure the global political economy, with a focus on the dynamics of global economic governance. While International Political Economy (IPE) broadly explores the interaction of markets and politics, this course places particular emphasis on the mechanisms of governance: the legal, institutional, and informal arrangements through which cooperation and contestation occur in the global economy. The course is organized into thematic clusters that progress from theory to application. We begin with conceptual debates on why states and non-state actors cooperate in the absence of a global government, drawing on theories of power, institutions, and transnational expertise.

title: AI from a Social Science Perspective
description: This course examines artificial intelligence from the perspective of the social sciences.

title: Human Rights and Cultural Differences
description: In this course you will acquire the tools to analyze rights-talk and learn to appreciate the relevance of history for our understanding of human rights as well as the purpose and relevance of normative theories.

title: Theories of Political Obligations
description: A theory of political obligation explains why individuals have a moral duty to obey the state or advocate policies contrary to governmental decisions. This course will examine various approaches in the literature including arguments from gratitude, consent, natural duty, fair play, nationalism, feminism, as well as Islamic and Confucian traditions.

title: Just War Theory
description: This course examines the moral reasons that allow the use of violence (jus ad bellum), the ones that should regulate the conduct of a war (jus in bello) as well as principles that should lead to a just peace (jus post bellum). This class also focuses on the contemporary ethical issues that have arisen since the beginning of the 21st Century which are associated with the War on Terror and the development of technologies.

title: Immigration Theory
description: This class will provide students with an overview of normative arguments and ethical consideration to various aspects of immigration theory overtime, from the classical to contemporary period.

title: Hannah Arendt on Power, Violence, and Revolution
description: This is a class on the political philosophy of Hannah Arendt. We will explore such themes as: totalitarianism, revolution, violence, mass society, and political belonging.
antirequisite: PLS 426 Hannah Arendt on Power, Violence, and Revolution (5398) (C- and above)

title: Politics and Governance of the Russian Federation
description: This course is designed to provide students with an in-depth understanding of Russian politics from the late Soviet era to the present (i.e. from Gorbachev to Putin).

title: Comparative Democratization
description: In this course, we will raise central questions that motivate social scientists and policymakers the world over. Students will analyze, critique, and apply theories and concepts that political scientists have developed in response to these questions.
prerequisite: PLS 540 Core Seminar in Comparative Politics (1374) (C- and above)

title: Homeland Security
description: This is a graduate course which focuses on a variety of topics related to unconventional domestic security challenges.

title: Text Analysis and Political Communication in the Information Age
description: This course offers working knowledge and hands-on experience in political communication research, with special attention to the methodology of quantitative text analysis. Students will learn critical questions in the political communication literature and how those questions can be studied through text analysis. Students will also have an opportunity to develop their own text analysis project to collect and analyze political communication datasets.
prerequisite: PLS 510 Quantitative Research Methods (1946) (C- and above) AND PLS 511 Qualitative Methods in Political Science (1631) (C- and above)

title: Political Polarization in Democracies
description: This course is designed to provide an in-depth exploration of the fundamental aspects of political polarization in democracies, as well as theories and debates about its causes and consequences.
prerequisite: PLS 510 Quantitative Research Methods (1946) (C and above) AND PLS 540 Core Seminar in Comparative Politics (1374) (C and above)

title: Nationalism and Multiethnic Governance
description: This course considers both the theories of group identity and group rights in the political context of the nation-state as well as policy choices governments make to implement certain theoretical perspectives

title: Politics of the Internet
description: The course investigates the distribution and exercise of political power in the digital sphere; contestation—involving corporations, governments and other political organizations, and civil society actors—over the architecture of and control over digital networks; the distinctive properties, advantages, and limitations of political activities undertaken on the internet; and the political ramifications of digitalization. Students in the course review the social science literature on the politics of technology and the internet, reflect on scholarly accounts of the political changes brought about by digitalization in class discussions, and advance their own perspectives through presentations and written assignments.

title: Advanced Topics in Comparative Politics
description: This course is meant to broaden student understanding of particular issue areas in comparative politics.

title: Political Violence
description: This course is designed to provide students with an overview of the various ways in which violence relates to the conduct of politics.

title: The Politics of Immigration Control
description: In order to fulfill capstone requirements, this course will apply core concepts of comparative politics (i.e. state capacity, national identity, state-society relations, models of the welfare state, state management of economies) to the policy area of immigration.

title: Comparative Political Parties
description: This seminar will deals generally with the topic of political parties. Specifically, models, roles, and changes in political parties and party systems

title: Comparative Electoral System
description: Elections are core instruments as well as defining feature of representative democracy. This course is designed to introduce students to the key features of various electoral systems, including how votes are casted, counted and translated into seats, and theories and debates on political and economic consequences of electoral system. To this end, a series of theoretical, conceptual, and empirical issues to studying electoral systems will be taught and discussed

title: Politics and Governance of the Gulf
description: This is a class on the politics and governance of the Gulf. It will explore a range of domestic and foreign policy issues facing the region.

title: Advanced Topics in International Relations
description: This course is meant to broaden student understanding of particular issue areas in international politics.

title: The United Nations System
description: This course delves into the organizational framework and operational significance of the United Nations system, including the United Nations --- the premier intergovernmental entity. The course will introduce students to the theories of cooperation and the role of the United Nations in fostering collaboration in economic development, human rights, and security affairs. The course will conclude by discussing the difficulties associated with multilateralism and the future of intergovernmental organizations, including the United Nations.
antirequisite: PLS 558 International Organization (1871) (C- and above)

title: The Politics of Arms in International Relations
description: This class will examine arms in international relations from a number of perspectives and at different levels of analysis.

title: International Security and Conflict
description: This course will explore issues of international security including interstate war, ethnic conflict, terrorism, and low-level conflicts.

title: International Organization
description: This course examines interstate cooperation through the various “isms” used to explain this international relations outcome and specific empirical cases of cooperation.
prerequisite: PLS 550 Core Seminar in IR (1372) (C- and above)

description: This course prepares MA students for conducting independent research in political science and international relations.

description: This course helps students to conceptualize a thesis project and create an initial plan for data collection.

title: Research for Thesis
description: Students will work on tasks in support of their thesis in consultation with thesis advisers.

title: MA Thesis I
description: This course prepares students to write the MA Thesis with the goal of defending the thesis at the end of the academic year.

title: MA Thesis II
description: This course prepares students to write the MA Thesis with the goal of defending the thesis at the end of the academic year.

Through readings and class discussions, you will become familiar with the basic tools and concepts of quantitative social research. You will design and conduct your own research to examine the question that you select.

title: Qualitative Research Methods
description: This course offers an in-depth introduction to qualitative research methods, covering essential concepts, methodologies, and applications across various disciplines, including data collection techniques like interviews, ethnographic fieldwork, and focus groups, and analysis methods such as coding, thematic, and narrative analysis. By the end, students will understand the philosophical foundations of qualitative research and be equipped to apply these methods effectively in their own projects.

title: Experimental Political Science
description: The use of experiment and experimental data is no longer a privilege of natural scientists or psychologists, but increasingly common among social scientists in general. This upper level seminar is designed to introduce students to experimental literature in political science.

title: Scientific Research in Political Science
description: This course will introduce students to the quantitative study of political science, with a special emphasis on research designs and methods.

title: Immigration Theory
description: The purpose of this class is to explore the normative dimensions of immigration theory. It is not always appreciated in contemporary ethical discourse that the issue of accepting and entertaining strangers and foreigners is one of the oldest ethical challenges facing human communities. One often finds in classical literature reflections on the extent and nature of one’s duty to be hospitable.

title: Issues in the Philosophy of Social Science
description: This course is designed to address a range of issues in the philosophy of social science from positivist inquiries how to differentiate between facts and values to the post-positivist occupation with the role of academic knowledge and research in a broad system of power relationships.

title: Hannah Arendt on Power, Violence, and Revolution
description: Hannah Arendt wrote on some of the most pressing political issues of the twentieth century: totalitarianism, revolution, and the ailments of mass society. This class will be dedicated to understanding Arendt’s approach to politics, which was quite novel.

title: Politics and Governance of the Russian Federation
description: The purpose of this course is to acquaint students with the (geo)politics of the Russian Federation

title: Comparative Democratization
description: Democratization is one of the key areas of study in comparative politics. In the last fifty years, authoritarian regimes around the world have been replaced—sometimes in evolutionary fashion, sometimes practically overnight—with governments that are responsive to their citizens and committed to the rule of law.

title: Core Seminar in Comparative Politics
description: This course is meant to introduce graduate students to the field of Comparative Politics (CP), a diverse and core sub-field of Political Science. CP is both a methodological approach and a core set of concepts that are used together to create generalizable knowledge about politics in one or more countries.

title: Advanced Topics in Comparative Politics
description: This course allows students to take topical courses from professors who are teaching courses on their primary areas of interest. These seminars are meant to broaden student understanding of particular issue areas in comparative politics.

title: Political Violence
description: This course is designed to provide students with an overview of the various ways in which violence relates to the conduct of politics

title: Comparative Electoral System
description: Elections are core instruments as well as defining feature of representative democracy, as elections are links that connect the preferences of citizens to the composition of government. In order for representative democracy to work, a set of rules to determine who gets elected – how votes are casted, counted and translated into seats - should be well-defined.

title: Core Seminar in IR
description: The purpose of this course is to provide students with a firm foundation of the sub-field of international relations and prepare them for advanced study in this sub-field. International Relations concerns itself with explaining the behavior of states and other actors in the international system

description: This course delves into the organizational framework and operational significance of the United Nations system, including the United Nations --- the premier intergovernmental entity.

The course will rely on readings from international relations and political science journals for theoretical and empirical examination of these issues.

We will examine the political forces that shape how government, organizations, and citizens across the globe respond to environmental problems and the consequences of those approaches.
