Students will learn about the origins of public choice and the key theories of the public choice school, as well as actively engage in the debates on “how to govern.”

title: Beginning Polish
description: This course is for beginners. During the course we will focus on all 4 main skills of language-learning: reading, listening, writing and speaking. One of the main goals is to introduce students to the Polish language, culture and history and to encourage them to explore the linguistic and cultural space on their own.

title: Beginning Polish II
description: This course is for beginners. During the course we will focus on all 4 main skills of language-learning: reading, listening, writing and speaking. One of the main goals is to introduce students to the Polish language, culture and history and to encourage them to explore the linguistic and cultural space on their own.
prerequisite: POL 101 Beginning Polish (7641) (C- and above)

title: Intermediate Polish I
description: This course is an introduction to the Polish language’s intermediate level. It is designed for those who are willing to continue their Polish language learning after completing it at beginner and elementary level. In this course, students will continue to increase proficiency with emphasis on oral communication with grammar and vocabulary taught in the context of Polish culture presented through interactive activities, discussion, multimedia resources, and reading assignments. The course focuses on expanding vocabulary, improving grammatical accuracy, and enhancing communication in various real-life situations. Students will practice speaking, listening, reading, and writing with authentic materials. Special attention is paid to introducing the students to complex grammatical structures, idiomatic expressions, and cultural aspects of Poland.
prerequisite: POL 102 Beginning Polish II (8214) (C- and above)

title: Principles of Public Health Problem Solving
description: This course is an introduction to public health problem solving skill sets as applied to the multi-disciplinary fields of public health, including problem identification, measurement and characterization, and finding solutions.

title: Inferential Biostatistics
description: Inferential Biostatistics course introduces the major concepts of modern statistics as applied to problems in public health. The course continues discussing concepts learnt from MMMM 505 while advancing to more complex ideas around inferential reasoning and simple regression. Evaluation is based on individual and group problem sets, quizzes and an examination.
prerequisite: MMMM 505 Inferential Biostatistics (3839) (C and above)

title: Inferential Biostatistics
description: This course introduces the major concepts of modern statistics as applied to a broad range of problems in the multidisciplinary field of public health, from concepts and application of probability and distributions, continuing through fundamental methods of inferential reasoning and simple regression modeling.

title: Biostatistical Modeling and Sampling
description: This course builds on the concepts and applications of modern concepts in biostatistics covered in the inferential statistics course, as applied to a broad range of problems in the multidisciplinary field of public health. The course introduces practical concepts and applications for simple and multivariate regression modeling using various link functions and sampling scheme development, sample size calculations and power analysis. The course provides opportunities for real life case applications. Evaluation is based on individual and group problem sets (including computer quizzes, and examinations.

title: Principles of Analytical Epidemiology
description: Principles and methods of analytical epidemiology provides a quantitative toolkit to investigate infectious and non-infectious (including genetic) diseases, mental and physical health disorders, related behaviors and complications, and health systems and health policies.

title: Advanced Analytical Epidemiology
description: This course builds upon the courses Principles of Analytical Epidemiology, Social and Behavioral Sciences and both Biostatistics courses. Students learn advanced methods to further assessing the impact of bias, confounding and interaction and acquire advanced techniques for mitigating those effects.

title: Qualitative Research Methods
description: This course will teach students about qualitative research methods. It will introduce students to the theoretical foundations of qualitative research as well as give them a chance to practice conducting and analyzing their own research.

title: Emerging Infectious Diseases
description: This course addresses important emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases and their public health impact globally and in Kazakhstan, including those diseases that have developed drug resistance.

title: Health Services Management, Health Economic and Health Policy
description: This course provides the practical and theoretical underpinnings of the organization and management of health organizations, health economics and health policy. Specific emphasis is placed on evaluation of health services and systems, individual leadership, management and policy development skills development. Evaluation is based upon examinations and student projects.

title: Principles of Heath Economics and Policy
description: This course is a continuation of PUBH 551 Principles of Health Administration and Economics, expanding on and focusing more on the diverse basics of health economics and health policy. The course covers general issues in economics and policy of the health care system and emphasizes the development of essential skills in critical thinking and team work.
prerequisite: PUBH 551 Health Services Management, Health Economic and Health Policy (3696) (C and above)

title: Graduate Research Seminar I
description: This course begins a structured emphasis on application of core knowledge and critical thinking skills. Students will critically review, discuss and provide written evaluations of relevant international peer-reviewed scientific journal articles in public health areas with a variety of study designs and methods.

title: Global Nutrition and Sustainability
description: This course provides students with basic concepts in nutritional science and public health, including nutrition strategies and technology to improve health, well-being and to sustain food ecosystems. Students will be able to apply knowledge gained in understanding how diet influences health to inform national, global food policies and dissemination of evidence-based information.

title: Health Education and Promotion
description: This course covers fundamental communications concepts and basic methods for developing and evaluating effective health education and health promotion programs, focusing on areas of behavioral change and health interventions for prevention. The course covers why health educational and promotion programs fail, how to assess effectiveness of different approaches to inform program, project and policy design, and how to design and conduct monitoring and evaluations for improving health communications and health promotion programs. Evaluation will be based on project design and evaluation.

title: Social and Behavioral Sciences in Public Health
description: This course introduces a framework for analyzing the behavioral and socio-cultural-economic determinants and risk factors for public health problems and the role of the individual, family, and community in addressing these problems. The course introduces survey methods, design and applications.

title: Methods in Public Health
description: The course focuses on advanced specialized methods and applications used for evaluation and assessments, especially as they relate to chronic diseases. The course covers a range of specialized applications designed to supplement and enhance methods and applications from previous MPH courses that are utilized in public health professions, including metanalysis, econometrics, program evaluation techniques and others. Assessment will be determined by three projects, each representing a third of the grade.

title: Problem Investigations in Environmental Health
description: This course presents the broad concepts and principles used in organizing and assessing the major environmental and occupational health problems in low/middle income and in industrialized countries and reviews interventions in the control and prevention of environmental health conditions. Student evaluation is based on quizzes, examinations and paper.

title: Risk Management in Health Care
description: This course is an introduction to the diverse basics of risk management methods used in healthcare field. The course covers general issues of safety culture in the healthcare facility, risk identification and assessment and concepts of governance of health care organizations in regard with risk management system. The overall aim of the course is to develop skills in understanding and applying a broad range of methods of risk management in healthcare field.

title: Applied Methods in Health Services Research
description: The course provides insight in the various research questions, designs, and analytical methods used in Health Services Research, as well as how to use them as an input into health policy making, emphasizing the necessary links between the production of scientific knowledge and the complexities of the decision making arena. HSR addresses issues such as access and quality of health care delivery, financing and use of health care services, disparities in access, the overall functioning and performance of health care systems, and implementation of change. The overall goal of the course are for students to be able to competently work providing scientific support into the health policy decision making, identifying the effective and efficient ways to organize, manage, finance, and deliver high quality care, and to be able to support and stimulate policy changes to strengthen health care systems based on the best available evidence. The course is organized around lectures, to set out key ideas, followed by student presentations, and some form of group exercise- this might take the form of brainstorming and group discussion. Students will give 2-3 presentations to the class on the assigned readings. They will also give 1 presentation to class on a health services and policy topic which have significant relevance for Kazakhstan. Students will also be asked to work in groups to identify a policy relevant question, outline a research strategy to address this problem with a scientific rigorous methodology, and make a brief presentation to a mock funding panel in the last session.

title: Graduate Research Seminar II
description: This course begins a structured emphasis on application of core knowledge and critical thinking skills. Students will critically review and discuss a number of relevant peer-reviewed journal articles with a more focused orientation toward application of these insights to the health context and challenges in Kazakhstan and Central Asia.

title: Master’s Project Planning
description: This course allows students to formulate a preliminary project proposal for their MPH Project. Students will apply the knowledge and skills acquired during the first year curriculum to shape and focus a tentative project proposal and implementation plan. Evaluation is based upon successful completion of intermediate milestones and the final goal of producing a final Master’s Project proposal. Group and individual exercises and facilitated discussions on proposed projects will be conducted.

title: Master’s Project Implementation
description: Under the guidance of a faculty mentor and advisory team, students will concentrate on implementing and completing the Master’s Project defined and planned during the Master’s Project Planning course. Assessment is based upon successful completion of intermediate milestones and the final goal of implementing and completing a Master’s Project, which includes professional PowerPoint presentation which is scored and commented on by judges and a finalized thesis. (Pass/Fail).

title: Introduction to World Religions
description: This course offers an introduction to the major religious traditions in the world.
department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, History, Philosophy and Religious Studies

title: Religion in the Modern World
description: This course is designed to offer students an introduction to some of the vast diversity and complexity of religion in the contemporary world.

title: Buddhist Religious Traditions
description: This course offers a survey of Buddhism from its origins to the present.

title: War and Peace in Religious Thought and Practice
History of Sufism in the Middle East and Central Asia
description: This course will provide a broad survey of Sufism and the Islamic mystical traditions, with a particular focus on the history of Sufism and the Sufi orders in the Middle East and Central Asia.
department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, History, Philosophy and Religious Studies
prerequisite: Subject "HST" BETWEEN 100 and 199

title: The Crusades
department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, History, Philosophy and Religious Studies
prerequisite: Subject "HST" BETWEEN 100 and 199

title: Buddhism in Central Asia
description: This course will explore the diffusion and evolution of Buddhism within Central Asia and along the Silk Road.
prerequisite: Subject "REL" BETWEEN 100 and 199

title: Religions in the Soviet and Post-Soviet Eras
description: Based on recent historiographic debates of leading religious scholars, as well as specialists in Russian, Soviet and Central Asian studies, this course examines both the Soviet state policies of the 20th century towards religions, and the dynamics and peculiarities of the revival of Orthodox Christianity, Islam, Buddhism, indigenous and New Age religious movements in the former Soviet republics in the 21st c.
department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, History, Philosophy and Religious Studies
prerequisite: Subject "REL" BETWEEN 100 and 200 OR Subject "REL" BETWEEN 100 and 200 OR Subject "HST" BETWEEN 100 and 200

title: Religion and Power in Islamic Central Asia
description: This course will examine the relationship between religious and political institutions within Central Asia from the 8th to the 19th century. The course will meet with HST/REL 350.
department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, History, Philosophy and Religious Studies

title: History of Sufism in the Middle East and Central Asia
description: This course will provide a broad survey of Sufism and the Islamic mystical traditions, with a particular focus on the history of Sufism and the Sufi orders in the Middle East and Central Asia.
department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, History, Philosophy and Religious Studies

title: Beginning Russian
description: This course is for students with very little or no previous classroom instruction in Russian. Proficiency-based approach will stress the development of communicative abilities in- and outside the classroom.

title: Beginning Russian II
description: Intensive Elementary Russian II class for students who have been studying Russian for one semester.

title: Kazakhstan - history, culture, traditions, society, modernity
description: This course provides foreign students with an acquaintance with Kazakhstan - its political and administrative system, landscape and climatic features, the main stages of historical development, material and spiritual cultural heritage, customs and traditions, national values, religion and ecology, current problems of political reform, social economic modernization of modern Kazakhstan.

title: Intermediate Russian
description: In this class, which is roughly equivalent to a college-level second-year Russian course, students will further develop their language skills in all four modalities (listening, speaking, writing and reading) through communicative activities in and outside the classroom.

title: Intermediate Russian II
description: Intensive Intermediate Russian II class for students for students who have been studying Russian for three semesters.

title: East in Soviet Russian-language culture: origin and fate
description: In my course, I propose to study Russian-language texts and films created in the Soviet era in which the Eastern person appears as an object of representation. In the chosen texts, the Eastern person for the Russian-language reader is a representative of the peoples of Central Asia and Kazakhstan. The texts will be analyzed in light of the political and cultural situation in which they were created. We will discover the processes through which the image of the Eastern people was shaped in Soviet Russian-language culture, study the main features of their portrayal, and see the purposes behind the creation of this image by Russian-language writers.

title: Soviet Everyday Life through Cinema
description: This course will focus on the history of Soviet cinema and the representation of Soviet everyday life in films made between the 1920s and the early 1990s. Cinematic images immersed in a broad historical context will be our primary tool for defining and understanding the specifics of Soviet way of life. Drawing on various historical sources and critical analysis of films, we will discuss how cinema helps us to reconstruct the worldview of Soviet (wo)men and explain the causes of dramatic tension between the personal and the public in the Soviet discourse.

title: What is Islam? Anthropological Perspectives
description: Anthropology of Islam as a part of Anthropology of Religion can be a valuable source of theoretical advances. This course uncovers the main stages of Anthropology of Islam as a special area of research and the ways of describing what Islam is. We will consider how studies of Islam are conducted in general and local contexts and which key points of the discussions we can find.

title: Advanced Russian
description: Entering with intermediate mid or intermediate high level of Russian proficiency, students will work on increasing their level to intermediate high and advanced low or mid.

title: Advanced Russian II
description: Intensive Advanced Russian II class for students who have been studying Russian for five semesters.

title: Academic Writing in Russian
description: This course will focus on the main aspects of academic writing in Russian. The basic principle of the course is maximum practice with the necessary theory. We will write academic texts of various genres and try to improve them. We will find out the proper way to conduct academic correspondence in Russian, observing both language and ethical standards. And most importantly, learning mysteries of academic writing in Russian, we will rely on your research interests.

title: Russian Literature in the Context of Eurasia
description: This course will study texts of Russian literature in the context of mastering and understanding the space of a huge country, of which Kazakhstan was once a part. Travel and wandering are one of the most important themes in Russian literature. Studying this topic allows one to better understand the mentality of the Russian person, and the deep philosophical and historical problems of Russian life. The biography and creativity of such great writers as Alexander Pushkin, Leo Tolstoy, Fyodor Dostoevsky, Anton Chekhov, Andrey Platonov are connected with Kazakhstan and the space of Asia.

title: Soviet Female Writers and Poets
description: The program of the course consists of texts by Soviet female writers and poets written in Russian. The course aims to broaden the 20th-century literary canon which has traditionally focused more on male than female authors. Rather than analyzing “female images” in literature, we will talk about texts created by female writers and the writing strategies that they employed. During the course, we will address a variety of texts studying them within the Soviet cultural and historical context, with close reading being the primary method of analysis. The main aspects of the course will be the examination of several cases that illustrate different literary strategies of female writers.

title: Kazakh Music History
description: This course focuses on the creation and development of Kazakh music from its very beginning up to the present. Peculiarities of Kazakh music development in various periods, musical genres, new musical streams, different styles of music transformation, instrumentation, and Kazakh composers and singers from the various periods of Kazakh history, traditional and contemporary music will be emphasized during the course. Kazakh Music History course enables students to enrich the vocabulary, knowledge, and develop analytical skills in terms of identifying music from different contrasting periods, etc. The course will be delivered in Russian.

title: Advanced and Superior Composition and Conversation Russian
description: This course is intended for students who have already achieved advanced proficiency in Russian.

title: Advanced and Superior Composition and Conversation Russian II
description: Intensive Advanced and Superior Composition and Conversation Russian II, equivalent to eighth-semester Russian

title: Social Problems and Issues of Eurasia
description: This is a survey course which aims to look into contemporary social problems in Eurasia with a sociological lens (i.e., using social theory and social science research). Over the past two decades or so, societies in post-Soviet Eurasia have been confronted with new and old social issues affecting well-being of diverse social groups. In addition, there have been shifts in public attitudes and perceptions of social problems and of how to address them. We will look into old and emerging issues and policy responses in the socioeconomic and political context of the region. Some of the issues of interest include rising inequality and polarization, changing demographics and family structure, health and gender issues, ethnic and race issues, migration, and environmental problems. We will also discuss how the post-Soviet transformation has affected the way social issues are perceived and addressed and how certain issues have come to be constructed as important social problems, while other social phenomena were moved to the periphery of the public discourse. It relies on discussions in class, language of delivery, readings, and assessments is Russian.

title: International relations of Eurasia
description: The course investigates the international politics surrounding the wider Eurasian space, including great power rivalries, conflict patterns, regional governance, transportaition infrastructures, and foreign policy adaptations.

title: Mechanics: Statics and Dynamics
prerequisite: MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (C- and above) AND (PHYS 161 Physics I for Scientists and Engineers with Laboratory (116) (C- and above) OR PHYS 171 Physics I for Physics Majors with Laboratory (1401) (C- and above))

title: System Dynamics and Modeling
prerequisite: MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (C- and above) AND (PHYS 162 Physics II for Scientists and Engineers with Laboratory (173) (C- and above) OR PHYS 172 Physics II for Physics Majors with Laboratory (1402) (C- and above))

title: Electrical and Electronic Circuits I with Lab
prerequisite: MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (C- and above) AND (PHYS 162 Physics II for Scientists and Engineers with Laboratory (173) (C- and above) OR PHYS 172 Physics II for Physics Majors with Laboratory (1402) (C- and above) OR (PHYS 141 Physics I for non-majors with Lab (1437) (C- and above) AND PHYS 142 Physics II for non-majors with Lab (1438) (C- and above)))

title: Electrical and Electronic Circuits II with Lab
prerequisite: ROBT 203 Electrical and Electronic Circuits I with Lab (62) (C- and above)

title: Signals and Sensing with Lab
prerequisite: MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (C- and above) AND (PHYS 162 Physics II for Scientists and Engineers with Laboratory (173) (C- and above) OR PHYS 172 Physics II for Physics Majors with Laboratory (1402) (C- and above))

title: Microcontrollers with Lab
prerequisite: CSCI 150 Fundamentals of Programming (1501) (C- and above) OR CSCI 151 Programming for Scientists and Engineers (192) (C- and above) OR ENG 101 Programming for Engineers (4517) (C- and above)

title: Mechanical Design I with CAD Laboratory
description: This course focuses on the fundamentals of mechanical design which lays the analytical foundation needed for the design of machine elements. Laboratory sessions of the course teach students basic skills of computer-aided design (CAD) and exposes them to different manufacturing processes with major emphasis on additive and subtractive manufacturing technologies.
prerequisite: ROBT 201 Mechanics: Statics and Dynamics (475) (C- and above)

title: Mechanical Design II with Machining Laboratory
description: This course presents the design of machine elements in context as parts of a whole machine. Topics include introduction to design of shafts, bearings, spur gears, helical, bevel, and worm gears, springs, screws and fasteners, clutches and brakes. Machining laboratory focuses on machining methods of metals and plastics and the resultant issues of design, fabrication and manufacturability of parts or components. The topics included are drilling, cutting, bending, turning, milling, grinding, and CNC machining. Machine shop safety instructions are presented at the very beginning of laboratory sections.
prerequisite: ROBT 301 Mechanical Design I with CAD Laboratory (622) (C- and above)

title: Linear Control Theory with Lab
prerequisite: ROBT 202 System Dynamics and Modeling (68) (C- and above)

title: Electromechanical Systems with lab
prerequisite: ROBT 203 Electrical and Electronic Circuits I with Lab (62) (C- and above)

title: Embedded Systems
prerequisite: ROBT 206 Microcontrollers with Lab (476) (C- and above)

title: Power Electronics
description: Deals with switching issues in switch mode power supplies and high power converters and inverters.
prerequisite: ROBT 204 Electrical and Electronic Circuits II with Lab (491) (C- and above)

title: Industrial Automation
description: Introduction to automation and plants, programmable logic controllers (PLCs), industrial sensors, industrial communication buses (CAN, ASI, Fieldbus), G-Code for CNC machines, operation with industrial robotic manipulators, pneumatic and hydraulic components.

title: Image Processing
prerequisite: MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (C- and above) AND MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (C- and above)

title: Robotics I: Kinematics and Dynamics
description: This course covers classical topics in robotics with particular emphasis on the kinematics, and dynamics of industrial manipulators. Different kinematics architectures are introduced together with classical modeling techniques based on homogeneous transformations. Analysis of velocities, static forces, and kinematic singular configurations is carried out by means of differential kinematics. The equations of motion of a manipulator are derived using Newton-Euler and Lagrange methods.
prerequisite: ROBT 201 Mechanics: Statics and Dynamics (475) (C- and above) AND MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (C- and above)

title: Research methods
description: The course covers both the fundamentals of critical reading, writing and research document analysis as well as composition of scientific papers.

title: Internship
description: All students in Robotics and Mechatronics are required to complete an internship, from the second year onwards, to provide them a practical problem-solving experience as a bridge between coursework and professional life.

title: Robot Dynamics and Control
description: Rotational and translational linear transformations, common robot configurations, robot forward and inverse kinematics, manipulator dynamics, trajectory generation for robot manipulators, position and force control of robotic manipulators, robot visualization.
prerequisite: ROBT 303 Linear Control Theory with Lab (623) (C- and above)

title: Robotic/Mechatronic System Design
description: This course brings together aspects of design in mechanical and electrical/electronic systems so that students will have a good idea of the range of advanced techniques available in designing robotic and mechatronic systems integrating tools and skills developed in previous courses.
prerequisite: ROBT 204 Electrical and Electronic Circuits II with Lab (491) (C- and above) AND ROBT 206 Microcontrollers with Lab (476) (C- and above)

title: Robotics II: Control, Modeling and Learning with Laboratory
description: This course introduces control, modeling and learning techniques applied to industrial robot-manipulators and mobile robots. The theoretical concepts will be tested with the support of different robot modeling and simulation environments, such as MATLAB/Simulink, V-REP and Gazebo using a widely applied in robotics Robot Operating System (ROS) software framework for control and learning algorithm implementation.
prerequisite: ROBT 303 Linear Control Theory with Lab (623) (C- and above) AND ROBT 312 Robotics I: Kinematics and Dynamics (5263) (C- and above)

title: Machine Learning with Applications
description: This course is targeted at students who need to learn about modern techniques available for designing intelligent decision-making machines.
prerequisite: MATH 273 Linear Algebra with Applications (84) (C- and above) AND MATH 321 Probability (482) (C- and above) AND CSCI 152 Performance and Data Structures (489) (C- and above)

title: Human-Robot Interaction
description: This course is designed to provide an overview of Human-Robot Interaction field in practice and research with topics including social signal processing, multi-modal communication, natural language interaction, robot-assisted therapy, human perception tools and technologies, smart environments, interaction design for robots, ethics, and many others.
prerequisite: CSCI 152 Performance and Data Structures (489) (C- and above)

title: Capstone Project I
description: This capstone project course serves as the culmination of students' academic journey in their major, providing an opportunity to integrate and apply their knowledge and skills within the robotics and mechatronics engineering field. The Fall semester's capstone project course marks the beginning of an intensive, hands-on experience in robotics and mechatronics engineering. Students work in teams on research and development (R&D) solutions that address current needs in the field.
prerequisite: ROBT 391 Research methods (7418) (C- and above)

title: Capstone Project II
description: Building on the foundational work of the Fall semester, the Spring graduation project course continues to advance students' proficiency in robotics and mechatronics engineering. In this semester, students will take their R&D projects to the next level by implementing and testing their designs, ensuring they meet the specified requirements.
prerequisite: ROBT 491 Capstone Project I (1896) (D and above)

title: Robot Perception & Vision
prerequisite: ROBT 501 Advanced Robot Kinematics (2263) (C- and above)

title: Research Methods
description: This course firstly introduces students to research methodologies including surveys, interviews, experimentation, and case studies. Then, different topics such as research design, and data collection and analysis of data are covered.

title: Robotic Motion Planning
description: Second year graduate level course in motion planning with a focus on robotic systems.
prerequisite: ROBT 501 Advanced Robot Kinematics (2263) (C- and above) AND CSCI 501 Software Principles and Practice (2408) (C- and above)

title: Intelligent Robot Manipulation
prerequisite: ROBT 501 Advanced Robot Kinematics (2263) (C- and above)

title: Brain-Machine Interfaces
description: This course is an introduction to the fundamentals in BMI technology and discusses its applications including both invasive and non-invasive BMI systems for controlling user interfaces, prosthetic arms, wheelchairs, and robotic exoskeletons.

title: Optimal Control and Estimation
description: This course aims to provide the state-of-the-art concepts relative to optimal control, in particular with application to robot motion planning.
prerequisite: ROBT 503 System Dynamics and Control (2264) (C- and above)

title: Thesis Proposal
description: Students are led through the processes required to plan and initiate an independent research project that will make an original contribution to engineering knowledge. Students are required develop a research proposal based on literature analysis, and begin to execute the proposal.

title: Thesis
description: The student will conduct independent work under the direction of a supervisor on a research problem in the student's designated area of research. The project will involve a substantial amount of work in one of the NU research laboratories.
prerequisite: ROBT 691 Thesis Proposal (5930) (P)

title: Thesis Research
description: This course is designed to monitor progress and develop understandings, skills, and outlooks to conduct original, independent research at the PhD level. The student will develop (with the advisor’s guidance) a research plan at the beginning of the semeste

title: Thesis Research
description: This course is designed to monitor progress and develop understandings, skills, and outlooks to conduct original, independent research at the PhD level. The student will develop (with the advisor’s guidance) a research plan at the beginning of the semester that will state a research problem/question/hypothesis, its background, outline a research strategy and experimental approach, method of data collection, interpretation and validation, and method of communication of the project results to others. The research plan is used as the basis for assessment of the student’s research progress.

title: Advanced Optimal Control and Estimation
description: This course aims to provide the state-of-the-art concepts relative to optimal control, in particular with application to robot motion planning.

title: Advanced Dynamic Systems and Control
description: The course aims to introduce the doctoral students to the state-of-the-art analytical tools and methods used for control system design. The course will start with the modeling of physical systems in the frequency and state space domains. The student will master analytical tools such as Bode plots, root locus diagrams and phase plots. The second part of the course include frequency domain based control design (mainly focused on PID controllers) and then covers control system design in state space (linear quadratic regulators, servo-controllers, etc.). In the last part, students will glimpse to different advanced control algorithms such as model predictive control, adaptive control and soft-computing based control. The students will read and analyze advanced literature on the topic regularly.

title: Current Research Literature
description: This course is designed to provide students a directed focus on preparing a literature review on the topic of their interest in coordination with a faculty supervisor. The students are expected to develop a comprehensive review of the state of art and identify the major gaps in the field of research. They also develop critical assessment and comparison of the past literature, and present the work in the form of the term paper.

title: Laboratory Practicum
description: Students will apply educational and instructional methodologies from the pre-requisite courses SST 501 and 502 in laboratory and practical sessions
prerequisite: SEDS 502 Teaching Practicum (2824) (P)

title: Teaching and Laboratory Practicum I
description: Teaching and Practicum I offers MSc students in engineering disciplines hands-on experience in teaching and learning environments under the guidance of a faculty mentor. Students will participate in instructing and supervising undergraduate labs, practicum sessions, and classroom activities, gaining practical skills for both instructional and leadership roles. The course emphasizes the development of instructional materials, assessment strategies, and reflective teaching practices. By the end of the course, students will be able to design and implement instructional sessions, assess student performance, and critically evaluate their own experience. Ultimately, the course equips students with essential pedagogical skills for their professional development as educators in academic and laboratory settings.

title: Teaching and Laboratory Practicum II
description: Teaching and Practicum II offers MSc students in engineering disciplines hands-on experience in teaching and learning environments under the guidance of a faculty mentor. Students will participate in instructing and supervising undergraduate labs, practicum sessions, and classroom activities, gaining practical skills for both instructional and leadership roles. The course emphasizes the development of instructional materials, assessment strategies, and reflective teaching practices. By the end of the course, students will be able to design and implement instructional sessions, assess student performance, and critically evaluate their own experience. Ultimately, the course equips students with essential pedagogical skills for their professional development as educators in academic and laboratory settings.

title: Research Methods
description: This course introduces students to representative research methodologies such as surveys, interviews, experimentation, and case studies.

title: Mathematics for Humanities/Social Sciences: Problem Solving and Logic
Resource Economics
description: This course introduces students to analysis of natural resource industries. Students learn the fundamentals of economic valuation of mining and petroleum projects. They proceed to discussing resource markets and government regulation. The course concludes with a discussion of impacts of the business cycle, economic growth, emerging technologies, and climate policies on the resource industries.
prerequisite: MATH 161 Calculus I (118) (C- and above) OR MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (C- and above)
antirequisite: ECON 201 Intermediate Microeconomics (133) (C- and above) OR ECON 202 Intermediate Macroeconomics (207) (C- and above)

title: Strength of Materials
description: This course provides an introduction to the fundamental aspects of stress and deformation analysis of basic structural materials subjected to different types of loads.
prerequisite: SMG 100 Introduction to Natural Resources Extraction (4773) (C- and above) AND MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (C- and above) AND PHYS 161 Physics I for Scientists and Engineers with Laboratory (116) (C- and above)

title: Engineering Economics
description: This course provides a systematic framework for analyzing costs, benefits, and other economic aspects of alternative approaches in engineering.
prerequisite: SMG 200/ECON 220 Resource Economics (6197) (C- and above) OR ECON 120 Managerial Economics (1852) (C- and above) OR MATH 161 Calculus I (118) (C- and above) OR MATH 162 Calculus II (170) (C- and above)

title: Research Methods
description: On successful completion of this subject, students will be able to: 1. 1-Demonstrate an ability to effectively conduct preliminary research on a topic of interest in a chosen field of study. 2. 2-Perform preliminary work to extend this topic. 3. 3-Show a high level ability to communicate in writing by producing a detailed literature review and project proposal on the topic. 4. 4-Employ high level oral communication skills through the delivery of a seminar presentation speaking to a captive audience.

title: Research Methods and Statistics
description: Statistics course will focus on the statistical and data analytics techniques applied for onshore and marine petroleum and gas & mining industry. This course will provide PhD students with the practical skills and theoretical knowledge on how to collect, analyze, interpret and present different types of data and research results for onshore and marine petroleum and gas & mining industry.

title: Introducing Kazakhstan: from the Past to the Future
description: The course provides an introduction to the issues of the complex and dynamic historical, cultural, economic and social development of Kazakhstan.

title: Social Science Research Methods
description: Social Science Research Methods is designed as an introduction to basic concepts in both quantitative and qualitative research such as research design, measurement, sampling, and analysis.

title: Social Justice in a Global Society
Food and Society
department: Sociology and Anthropology, Sociology and Anthropology

title: Sociology of Race and Ethnicity
description: This course is a general introduction to the sociology of race and ethnicity. We will begin to understand how race and ethnicity shape our social life and how they intersect with other systems of inequality and significant social institutions. Various theoretical approaches to the sociological study of race and ethnicity will be explored.

title: Science, Technology, and Society
description: The aim of this course is to present an overview of the relationship between science, technology, and society: from the practice of science, to the production of scientific truth, to the development of technologies, and to the impact of technologies on social life.

title: International Migration
description: This course reviews the main theories, and explanations of international migration. Throughout the course, theoretical approaches and empirical studies from different disciplinary traditions are discussed, explaining migration and the integration of first-generation immigrants at micro, meso, and macro-levels of analysis.

title: Social Movements: How People Make Change
description: This course builds a critical analysis of social movements or organized attempts by disempowered groups to demand and enact social change. We read and discuss interdisciplinary theoretical frameworks that will help us to better understand the dynamics shaping historical and contemporary social movements, how social movements are formed and why they meet with varying levels of success.

title: Environment and Society
description: This course will investigate the interaction between various environmental and social problems, as well as many political and economic problems that have continuously redefined how we think of nature and environment.

title: Classical Sociological Theory
prerequisite: SOC 101 Introduction to Sociology (508) (C- and above) OR SOC 115 Global Social Problems (1032) (C- and above) OR ANT 110 Introduction to Sociocultural Anthropology (501) (C- and above)

title: Decolonizing Social Theory: Can Women and Non-Europeans Think?
description: In this course, we will explore the gendered colonial foundations of social scientific theory, particularly in sociology, questioning what these foundations mean for current sociological practice informed by these theories and for sociological methods of inquiry. We will employ the lens of decolonization as a process, a theoretical tool and a method of sociological inquiry.

title: Social Inequality
prerequisite: SOC 101 Introduction to Sociology (508) (C- and above) OR SOC 115 Global Social Problems (1032) (C- and above)

title: Social Foundations of Education
prerequisite: SOC 101 Introduction to Sociology (508) (C- and above) OR SOC 115 Global Social Problems (1032) (C- and above)

title: Organizations and Society
prerequisite: SOC 101 Introduction to Sociology (508) (C- and above) OR SOC 115 Global Social Problems (1032) (C- and above)

title: Economy and Society
description: The aim of this course is to present an overview of the relationship between economy and society: from the production of goods and services, to their distribution, and their consumption. Additionally, the course aims to provide students with a sociologically informed understanding of the structure of the economy more generally: networks, markets, and institutions.
prerequisite: SOC 101 Introduction to Sociology (508) (C- and above) OR Subject "SOC" BETWEEN 200 and 299 OR Subject "SOC" BETWEEN 200 and 299 OR ECON 102 Introduction to Macroeconomics (503) (C- and above) OR PLS 120 Introduction to Political Theory (512) (C- and above) OR PLS 150 Introduction to International Relations (511) (C- and above)

title: Sexuality and Gender in a Transnational World
description: This course explores contemporary understandings of gender and sexuality from a feminist perspective. We will examine how understandings of sexuality and gender impact and are impacted by colonialism, global capitalism and what this means for gender- and sexuality-based rights activism in a global and interconnected world.
prerequisite: SOC 101 Introduction to Sociology (508) (C- and above) OR SOC 115 Global Social Problems (1032) (C- and above) OR SOC 210 Gender and Society (226) (C- and above)

title: Organized Crime and Corruption
description: This course provides a thorough grounding in the scholar literature on organized crime and an introduction to its links with corruption. The course engages case studies of organized crime groups from around the world. It analyses anti-organized crime and anti-corruption policies and provides case studies of these from the former Soviet Union.
prerequisite: SOC 101 Introduction to Sociology (508) (C- and above)

title: Digital Media Research Methods
description: Recent advancements in communication technologies and the rise of digital platforms, databases, and networks have opened new opportunities for social scientific research. This course aims to explore these new opportunities and to provide a theoretical foundation as well as practical approaches to digital media data collection, analysis, and presentation. Students will explore specific examples of how empirical research in the field of digital media produces valuable insights into a variety of contemporary social and cultural issues. Big Data analysis, Internet-based surveys, data mining, digital ethnography, predictive analytics with social media data are among the topics that will be discussed in this course.
prerequisite: SOC 201 Social Science Research Methods (1341) (C- and above) OR SOC 203 Quantitative Methods in Sociology (1377) (C- and above) OR ECON 211 Economic Statistics (2280) (C- and above) OR PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above)

title: COVID-19: The sociocultural aspects of a pandemic
description: In addition to being a global medical pandemic, COVID-19 has done much to lay bare the ways in which we as human beings sharing a single planet view ourselves in terms of nation-states, races, ages, institutions, political ideologies, social classes, and, indeed, members of a shared humanity. While the pandemic has brought humanity together in some noteworthy ways, it has also laid bare many of the systemic inequalities that lay at the foundation of our global society. This course will draw on the work of social scientists from a broad range of disciplinary backgrounds including sociologists, anthropologists, psychologists, political scientists, historians, economists, scholars of race and ethnicity, sex and gender, class and inequality, and a broad range of those committed to social justice. The aim of the course is to better understand the causes, impacts, and consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic from a social scientific perspective.
prerequisite: SOC 101 Introduction to Sociology (508) (C- and above)

title: Art and Society
description: This course offers an introduction to the social history and sociology of art, encompassing both traditional high culture and contemporary cultural industries (e.g., cinema and popular music). We will explore questions such as: How do we determine what counts as "real" art and what does not? How did different social groups exploit art, and what did they consider to be refined or inferior taste? What insights can artistic creations provide about the societies in which they were produced? What types of data can we obtain about art production and consumption? How has the role and social standing of artists evolved across different historical periods, and what did it mean to be an artist in various times and places? How was the creation of art organized in diverse cultural and historical contexts, and how did those structures influence the nature of artistic output?
prerequisite: SOC 201 Social Science Research Methods (1341) (C- and above) OR ANT 214/SOC 214 Qualitative Methods (1033) (C- and above)

title: Digital Deviance
description: This course explores the concept of digital deviance, focusing on how deviant behaviors manifest, are facilitated and are resisted in digital spaces. The course begins by defining key concepts such as digital deviance, cybercrime, online violence, technology-facilitated abuse, highlighting the complex and often blurred boundaries between crime and deviance in digital environments. The course introduces foundational theories of deviance and their application in the digital realm.
prerequisite: SOC 201 Social Science Research Methods (1341) (C- and above) OR SOC 203 Quantitative Methods in Sociology (1377) (C- and above) OR SOC 210 Gender and Society (226) (C- and above) OR SOC 211 Social Justice in a Global Society (162) (C- and above) OR SOC 213 Work and Society (453) (C- and above) OR SOC 215 Sociology of Race and Ethnicity (3647) (C- and above) OR SOC 217 Sociology of the Family (1324) (C- and above) OR SOC 220 Science, Technology, and Society (2512) (C- and above) OR SOC 221 International Migration (2516) (C- and above) OR SOC 223 Social Movements: How People Make Change (3357) (C- and above) OR SOC 301 Classical Sociological Theory (683) (C- and above) OR SOC 310 Social Inequality (1031) (C- and above) OR SOC 314 Organizations and Society (1328) (C- and above) OR SOC 317 Economy and Society (2513) (C- and above) OR SOC 318 Sexuality and Gender in a Transnational World (3648) (C- and above)

title: Special Topics in Sociology
description: The exact topic of this course will change each time it is offered. It is used to explore new or unusual topics for which another course does not already exist.

title: Research Assistance in Sociology
description: The aim of this course is to allow students to assist in the research projects of faculty in the Sociology and Anthropology Department. The precise area and nature of research assistance will vary between faculty and their research projects. It is envisaged that students will participate in one or more of the following: the preparation of research materials; the collection of data; the management of databases; the analysis of data; the writing of research output. This course is aimed primarily at advanced anthropology majors who wish to gain experience in the research process.

title: Violence Against Women: An Intersectional Approach
description: The course provides an understanding of violence against women, the dynamics and effects of violence against women, and the contributions of gender, culture, race/ethnicity, socioeconomic and migratory status to the experiences of violence survivors
prerequisite: Subject "SOC" BETWEEN 200 and 299 OR Subject "SOC" BETWEEN 200 and 299 OR Subject "SOC" BETWEEN 300 and 399 OR Subject "SOC" BETWEEN 300 and 399

title: Citizenship in Eurasia: Political Sociology of Civic Belonging
description: In the mid-20th century Hannah Arendt famously called citizenship “the right to have rights.” Citizenship turns humans into modern political subjects by enlisting them into demos and polity. This is why it stands at the center of political sociology. Citizenship has four dimensions: membership status, human rights, political participation, and civic identity. In this course we follow the recent developments in Eurasian citizenship and identify key forces shaping it: state-building, nationalism, migration and population transfers, foreign policy, patriarchy, economic transition, etc. We discuss how today we can keep to the ancient ideal of being a “good citizen” and a “good human” at the same time?
prerequisite: SOC 101 Introduction to Sociology (508) (C- and above) OR SOC 115 Global Social Problems (1032) (C- and above) OR SOC 180 Introducing Kazakhstan: from the Past to the Future (5063) (C- and above) OR SOC 201 Social Science Research Methods (1341) (C- and above) OR SOC 301 Classical Sociological Theory (683) (C- and above)

title: Social Problems and Issues in Eurasia
description: Throughout the course of the semester we will examine contemporary social problems in Eurasia with a sociological lens.
prerequisite: SOC 101 Introduction to Sociology (508) (C- and above) OR SOC 115 Global Social Problems (1032) (C- and above) OR SOC 218 Introduction to Social Policy (1326) (C- and above)

title: Applied Policy Analysis: Tools and Perspectives
description: This course will provide an offer an overview of perspectives on the policy making process and supply students with practical tools and methods that can be used to undertake the analysis of policy.
prerequisite: SOC 101 Introduction to Sociology (508) (C and above)

title: Modern Sociological Theory
description: The course provides a historical introduction to modern sociological theory, covering the period from what is typically qualified as the end of the "classical" era (the 1920s) to the mid-1980s.
prerequisite: SOC 301 Classical Sociological Theory (683) (C and above)

title: Sociology of Consumption
description: This course explores major sociological theories of modern consumption. Since the early development of sociology, scholars have examined why people consume and with what consequences for society and the environment. Theories addressed in the course include status-driven consumption (Veblen), the influence of mass culture and ideology (Frankfurt School, Baudrillard), identity formation through consumption (consumer culture theories), social distinction (Bourdieu), political expression (politicized consumption), and acts of resistance (cultural studies). Students will critically engage with these perspectives to understand the complex nature of consumer behavior.
prerequisite: Subject "SOC" BETWEEN 200 and 299

title: Statistics and Machine Learning for Social Reform
description: Social reform is an organized collective effort to restructure culturally accepted norms and improve various spheres of society often focusing on issues like inequality, poverty, education, labor rights, and family violence. Since the onset of industrialization in Europe, reform groups have employed statistical data to expose the social conditions they aspired to eradicate. Further urbanization, economic and population expansion, internal migration and the increasing public interest to social issues all make it essential today to understand statistics and machine learning from a sociological perspective. This course offers an overview of most popular statistical and machine learning methods including exploratory data analysis, model diagnostics, comparative and longitudinal modeling, dimensionality reduction and clustering techniques. With the use of R notebooks and log files, students will engage in hands-on data exploration and feature engineering, apply code, fit and critically evaluate models, and interpret the results through a sociological lens.
prerequisite: (SOC 201 Social Science Research Methods (1341) (C- and above) AND SOC 203 Quantitative Methods in Sociology (1377) (C- and above)) OR (PLS 210 Political Science Research Methods (129) (C- and above) AND PLS 211 Quantitative Methods (221) (C- and above)) OR (SOC 101 Introduction to Sociology (508) (C- and above) AND ECON 301 Econometrics I (664) (C- and above))
antirequisite: CSCI 235 Programming Languages (638) (C- and above) OR ECON 318 Applied Econometrics (6078) (C- and above) OR CSCI 344 Data Mining and Decision Support (1916) (C- and above) OR PETE 410 Introduction to Data Science and Machine Learning (8128) (C- and above) OR CSCI 447 Machine Learning: Theory and Practice (4828) (C- and above) OR MATH 449 Statistical Programming (2104) (C- and above) OR ELCE 455 Machine Learning with Python (6365) (C- and above)

title: Capstone Seminar Part I
description: SOC 498 is the first part of the year-long capstone seminar taught to senior students majoring in Sociology. During this course students will design their research projects, develop research instruments, review relevant literature, obtain ethics review approval from the SHSS ethics review committee, and start data collection. There will be two types of capstone projects: Track One: An independent academic research and undergraduate thesis. Track Two: Community-engagement participatory research project and project report.

title: Capstone Seminar II
description: SOC 499 is the second part of the year-long capstone seminar taught to senior students majoring in Sociology. The goal of this course is to help students consolidate your analytical, writing, communication, and presentation skills as well as learn new practical skills that allow students to communicate their work to both academic and nonacademic audiences. Students will engage in systematically analyzing data, writing their findings, and revising their work through feedback and comments with the guidance of the teaching faculty member, peers, research advisor, and other experts brought into assist in the process of constructing an original product.
prerequisite: SOC 498 Capstone Seminar Part I (3043) (C- and above)

title: Social Inequality
description: Societies around the world are characterized by the unequal distribution of wealth, prestige and power. In this course we will examine how societies are socially stratified and the ways in which inequality is shaped by class, race/ethnicity and gender, among other social divisions. We will also look at how social institutions, including the family, the educational system, the economy and workplace, and the media are key in both creating and reproducing inequalities. Finally, we will examine the role of the state, non-governmental organizations, and individuals in reducing social inequality.

title: Citizenship in Eurasia: Political Sociology of Civic Belonging
description: In the mid-20th century Hannah Arendt famously called citizenship “the right to have rights.” Citizenship turns humans into modern political subjects by enlisting them into demos and polity. This is why it stands at the center of political sociology. Citizenship has four dimensions: membership status, human rights, political participation, and civic identity. In this course we follow the recent developments in Eurasian citizenship and identify key forces shaping it: state-building, nationalism, migration and population transfers, foreign policy, patriarchy, economic transition, etc. We discuss how today we can keep to the ancient ideal of being a “good citizen” and a “good human” at the same time?

title: Qualitative Research Methods
description: This course will teach you about qualitative research methods and give you a chance to practice conducting and analyzing your own research. Through readings and class discussions, you will become familiar with the basic tools and concepts of qualitative social research. You will design and conduct your own research to examine the question that you select.
department: Area Studies, Political Science and International Relations, Sociology and Anthropology

title: Social Problems and Issues in Eurasia
description: Throughout the course of the semester we will examine contemporary social problems in Eurasia with a sociological lens.

title: Gender, Power and Social Change in South Asia
description: This course explores contemporary understandings of gender and sexuality in South Asia from a post-colonial feminist perspective. We will examine how understandings of sexuality and gender impact and are impacted by colonialism, global capitalism and the peculiarities of NGO activism for social change in the global South.
department: Sociology and Anthropology, Sociology and Anthropology

title: COVID-19: The sociocultural aspects of a pandemic
description: In addition to being a global medical pandemic, COVID-19 has done much to lay bare the ways in which we as human beings sharing a single planet view ourselves in terms of nation-states, races, ages, institutions, political ideologies, social classes, and, indeed, members of a shared humanity. While the pandemic has brought humanity together in some noteworthy ways, it has also laid bare many of the systemic inequalities that lay at the foundation of our global society. This course will draw on the work of social scientists from a broad range of disciplinary backgrounds including sociologists, anthropologists, psychologists, political scientists, historians, economists, scholars of race and ethnicity, sex and gender, class and inequality, and a broad range of those committed to social justice. The aim of the course is to better understand the causes, impacts, and consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic from a social scientific perspective.

title: Contemporary Central Asia
description: In this course the students will learn about the five Central Asian countries – Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan.

title: Literature and The Spanish Civil War
description: This course will analyse different cultural representations that took place during or after the war from poets such as Pablo Neruda, Miguel Hernández, César Vallejo, Rafael Alberti, novelists, including Ramón Sender, Max Aub, Agustín de Foxá, Ernest Hemingway and Javier Cercas and films such as Las bicicletas son para el verano directed by Jaime Chávarri.

description: This course introduces students to the rich short story tradition of Spanish America, through the writings of Jorge Luis Borges, Juan Rulfo, Isabel Allende, Horacio Quiroga, Gabriel García Márquez, and Julio Cortázar. title: Colloquial Spanish
description: The Colloquial Spanish course will continue developing the level of Spanish as a foreign language, with the methodology task approach although the content of the course will be focused on colloquial language, especially on the lexical aspect. Also, to a much lower degree, we will be working on some phonetic and grammatical characteristics typical of colloquial speech.

title: Advanced Spanish Grammar and Composition
description: The main objective of this course is to review and strengthen some of the major concepts of Spanish grammar and likewise to develop effectivewriting skills in Spanish, primarily for academic writing.

description: This course introduces students to the rich short story tradition of the Spanish-speaking world. Students will write short critical essays in Spanish to strengthen their language skills.

description: Students will apply educational and instructional methodologies from the pre-requisite courses SST 501 and 502 in laboratory and practical sessions of their respective disciplines under the supervision of an experienced faculty member, maintaining a regular log of activities, and summarizing observations and experiences in a final report.

Literary and Cultural Theories: Reading the Past: Historicism, Presentism, Hauntology
description: “I began with the desire to speak with the dead”, Stephen Greenblatt famously wrote in his Shakespearean Negotiations (1988), a seminal text of the New Historicism. The course will be concerned with questions raised by this quotation: How can we address the past? How should we read literary and cultural texts of previous centuries? Is this dialogue with the past always shaped by our present perspectives and concerns? Is there any reason why we should try to acknowledge the alterity of earlier periods? Are the ghosts of the past still haunting our present age and impacting the future? We will discuss different theoretical positions that address these issues, including New Historicism, Presentism, and Hauntology. Our readings of theoretical texts will be complemented by an assessment of their usefulness for literary and cultural analysis, not least in the fields of Gender, Queer, and Postcolonial Studies.

title: Communications and Networks with Lab
description: The Communications and Networks with Lab course combines theoretical knowledge with practical laboratory experience in modern communication systems and computer networks. Students perform hands-on experiments using Python, Jupyter Notebook, and NVIDIA Sionna to analyze link-level performance, including BER/SER, Eb/N0, and intersymbol interference (ISI). The laboratory component also introduces medium access control (MAC) concepts through simulations of random access protocols, providing practical skills in communication system analysis and network performance evaluation.

title: Electromagnetic Field and Wave
description: Electromagnetic Field and Wave provides a comprehensive introduction to the theory and applications of electromagnetic fields and waves. The course covers Maxwell’s equations, electromagnetic wave propagation, transmission lines, waveguides, radiation, and wave behavior in different media. Emphasizing both analytical methods and physical understanding, it equips students with the knowledge needed to analyze electromagnetic phenomena and their applications in wireless communications, radar, optics, fiber-optic systems, and other modern engineering technologies.

Development and Management of the Yellow River Basin
description: This course examines the geographical, historical, and policy dimensions of the Yellow River Basin and its role in China’s development. It explores water management, environmental challenges, and the link between natural processes and governance decisions in river basin management.

title: Financial Instruments and Markets
description: This course introduces the main financial instruments and markets, including fixed-income and equity instruments, derivatives, and international and sustainable finance. It develops students’ skills in analysing, valuing, and managing financial instruments and portfolios using practical tools such as Excel.

title: Introduction to Accounting
description: This course introduces basic accounting principles, concepts, and terminology. It covers business transactions, acquisition and use of resources, production and sale of goods and services, and related financial activities. The course combines theoretical concepts with practical exercises and business cases.

title: Microeconomics
description: This course introduces the basic concepts and principles of microeconomics. It covers production functions, costs of firms, factor markets, market structures, perfect competition, monopoly, and price discrimination. The course combines theoretical concepts with practical exercises and applications to real-world economic situations.

title: Introduction to Sustainable Development
description: This course examines the conflicts and challenges of sustainable development at national and global levels, focusing on issues such as climate change, energy transition, and food and nutrition. It explores practical solutions across different contexts to support long-term planetary sustainability.

title: Logistics & Supply Chain Management
description: This course examines key concepts and analytical tools used in the design and management of modern logistics and supply chains.

title: Comparative Governance and Development Practices
description: This interdisciplinary course explores global governance and development through cutting-edge research and real-world applications. It features a series of lectures by distinguished international scholars and practitioners.

title: International Organizations and Global Governance
description: This course offers an in-depth exploration of international organizations, spanning their history, typologies, roles, and operations.

title: From Tributary System to Post-Cold War Architectures: Evolving Visions of Asian Order
description: This course traces the evolving visions of Asian Order from ancient times to present, namely ancient order based on China-centered tributary system, colonial order based on unequal treaties, the proposed wartime order based on Japan’s war expansion, Cold War order based on U.S.-Soviet rivalry, and current explorations for a post-Cold War Asian order.

title: POSTCOLONIAL LITERATURE: THEMES AND TROPES
description: This course focuses on literary narratives written by authors who live in countries which were colonised and who write in English. Students will explore how postcolonial ideas and issues discussed in class impact on their understanding of the contemporary world. The course is text-oriented but matters of history and context are also considered as essential.

title: READING AMERICAN LITERATURE
description: In this course, students will be exposed to some important American texts and writers They will read selected extracts from different genres as well as full-length texts. The course will encourage students to explore the development of the American literary tradition and the political, social and cultural forces which shaped the tradition.

title: INTRODUCTION TO POSTMODERN FICTION
description: This course will primarliy act as an introduction to the reading of postmodern fiction, whereby ideas and concepts such as the various constructions of reality, historicity, the metanarrative, as well as double encoding will have to be understood before students delve into the actual reading of the stories and novels. In addition to that, key postmodern theorists such as Baudrillard, Lyotard and Hutcheons will be mentioned alongside some of the works of the foundational postmodern writers like Becket, Borges, Ballard, Morrison and Eco.

The first is to familiarize students with anthropological approaches to a range of pressing contemporary concerns, as well as the ability to analyse socially anthropology’s place in social analysis. It is hoped that this will spark ideas and provide critical entry points into current anthropological conversations, debates and literatures that will help students develop, say, funding proposals, MRP and PhD projects. The second objective is to sharpen students’ critical reading, reasoning, debating and writing skills.

Buddhism and science: view and meditation in the light of physics and neuroscience
description: Buddhism and science have developed models of reality based on empirical evidence and logic. Eastern models of reality tend to be structured around mind, and one idealist current of Buddhist thought even reduces matter to mind on the presupposition that mind alone exists (cittamātra). Western scientific models, however, are inclined to privilege matter, to the extent that for extreme proponents of scientific materialism mind has no place in a naturalistic account of the world. Given this situation, the grounds on which Buddhism and science can meet are models of reality that do not attempt to reduce mind and matter to each other. The acceptance of such a view inevitably leads to the question of whether and, if yes, how mind and matter are capable of mutual interaction. Some models of quantum physics suggest that consciousness, or the act of observation, may play a fundamental role in determining the outcome of quantum events.

title: Mysteries of the Human Mind
description: The human mind is the foundation of society and culture, and it is something we are intimately acquainted with. But at the same time, its underlying nature is still shrouded in mystery and hard to explain. This course uses an interdisciplinary approach to explore the fascinating complexities of the mind. It involves philosophical analysis, scientific investigation, and an awareness of history and the broader social and moral implications of technology. A central issue is whether the mind is a computer. Can computers display intelligence, creativity, and emotions? Can the computer model of the mind explain the mysteries of consciousness and free will? Or do these mental phenomena require the existence of a soul? These issues are exciting not just because they are intellectually important, but also because to understand the mind is to understand ourselves better. We will see how the ideas in this course can help us become better thinkers, and improve our creativity and decision-making skills. We will also discuss how science and technology can challenge our conception of the self, and how they might affect future human evolution in radical ways.

title: Steel Structures
description: This course introduces the principles of steel structural behaviour and design, covering plastic analysis, steel members, plate girders, frames, connections, and composite structures. Students develop the skills required to analyze and design steel structural elements under various loading conditions.

title: Introductory Chinese
description: This course provides introductory Chinese language training in listening, speaking, reading, and writing, focusing on basic vocabulary, grammar, Pinyin, Chinese characters, and everyday communication. It is designed for students with no prior knowledge of Chinese.
