Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
description: This is an introduction course on the subject of artificial intelligence. Topics include: intelligent agents; search techniques for problem solving; knowledge representation; logical inference; reasoning under uncertainty; statistical models and machine learning.

title: Software Engineering
description: This course introduces the fundamental principles, methodologies and practices of modern software engineering. It covers the software process, and development activities including requirements engineering, software design, testing, deployment and evolution. The course emphasizes the use of contemporary tools, frameworks and techniques. It features a complete agile development project in which students work in teams to engineer and cloud-deploy a software service to satisfy their clients’ needs.

title: Modern Technologies on WWW
description: This course introduces fundamental web technologies and the core components of the World Wide Web. Students gain practical experience in designing and developing interactive web applications and learn to apply these technologies to solve real-world problems.

title: Interactive Mobile Application Design and Programming
description: This course introduces the fundamentals of mobile application development, including mobile device features, application types, and lifecycle. Students learn key design principles and gain hands-on experience building interactive mobile apps using modern tools, with a focus on user interface design, multimedia, networking, and testing.

title: Conflict Resolution Practice
description: Conflict is a natural part of life. All individuals are also equipped with certain conflict resolution skills. However, we still need to improve special abilities/skills allowing us to build relationships and form partnerships even under the most difficult circumstances to arrive at mutually satisfying outcomes in the conflicts we engage in. This course is an introductory skill- building course in conflict resolution. It aims to improve students’ understanding of why conflicts emerge as well as how we can peacefully manage/transform/resolve them.

title: Database Systems
description: This course introduces core concepts of database management systems, including data models, SQL, normalization, and transaction management, along with data structures such as indexing and hashing.

title: Software Engineering
description: This introductory course covers fundamental software engineering concepts, including requirements, system design, quality assurance, and software development processes, with practical use of modern tools.

title: Mobile Application Development
description: This course equips students with skills to develop mobile applications, including building and consuming web services. Students will learn to design, code, and deploy applications for mobile devices, as well as work with HTTP and web service integration.

title: Computer networks
description: This course introduces the basic principles of computer networks, including Internet architecture, protocol layers, and key technologies such as TCP/IP, routing, and Ethernet. Students learn how data is transmitted across networks, explore common applications (web, email, DNS), and understand performance, security, and modern networking concepts.

title: Artificial Intelligence
description: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a core area of Computer Science focused on designing intelligent agents capable of perceiving, reasoning, and acting in complex environments. This course provides a principled introduction to the foundations of AI, emphasizing problem-solving and decision-making under uncertainty. Topics include search algorithms and heuristics, constraint satisfaction problems, adversarial games, Markov decision processes and reinforcement learning, Bayesian networks for probabilistic reasoning, and temporal models such as hidden Markov models and filtering. Students will implement these methods in Python to build and evaluate intelligent systems across a range of problem domains.

title: Database Systems
description: This course is on the design and implementation of database management systems. Topics include relational model and relational algebra, database normalization, intermediate and advanced SQL, indexing and query optimization techniques, transaction management and concurrency, logging and recovery protocols and distributed databases. Case studies on open-source and commercial database systems are used to illustrate these techniques and trade-offs.

title: Machine Learning
description: This course will introduce the field of Machine Learning, focusing on the core concepts of supervised and unsupervised learning. In supervised learning we will discuss algorithms which are trained on input data labelled with a desired output, for instance an image of a face and the name of the person whose face it is and learn a function mapping from the input to the output. Unsupervised learning aims to discover latent structure in an input signal where no output labels are available, an example of which is grouping webpages based on the topics they discuss. Students will learn the algorithms which underpin many popular Machine Learning techniques, as well as developing an understanding of the theoretical relationships between these algorithms. The practicals will concern the application of machine learning to a range of real-world problems.

title: Additive manufacturing
description: This course introduces the principles, processes, materials, design considerations, and applications of additive manufacturing, with emphasis on fabrication workflows, quality, and emerging developments.

title: Data Science for Linguists
description: This practical introduction to data science is mainly intended for students of general linguistics who want to learn how to answer scientific questions based on large datasets, but will also be beneficial for students of computational linguistics who need to analyse and answer questions about data. It can also serve as a first introduction to Python for students who start during the summer semester, which can then be complemented by "Programming and Data Analysis" during the winter semester. After a quick tutorial on elementary Python for students who have never used it before (or would like to brush up on rusty skills), we start by introducing the standard toolbox of doing data science in Python (Jupyter notebooks, NumPy for numerical computations, Pandas for R-like data frames), and then dive into the bread-and-butter techniques of data analysis: data cleaning and preparation, linguistic preprocessing, data wrangling (joining, combining, reshaping), data aggregation and grouping, and visualisation.

title: Dependency treebanks and dependency parsing
description: This is a course on dependency analysis of natural language sentences. The course combines lectures on introductory topics; a practical com- ponent where participants work on treebank building and parsing; and seminar-style activities (reading, presentations, discussion) on some foundational and recent papers in the field. In essence, we will have a two-part course, where the first part is concerned with how to analyze natural language sentences using dependencies, and create treebanks containing dependency annotations. The second part is about training data-driven parsers on such treebanks.

Computer Organization and Systems

Students will gain an understanding of how hardware and software interact, providing a foundation for advanced studies in AI accelerators, embedded systems, and operating systems.

title: Systems and Control
description: This course introduces the fundamentals of feedback control, including physical system modeling, time- and frequency-domain analysis of open- and closed-loop systems, and controller design for stability, robustness, and performance.

title: Machine Intelligence and Applications
description: This course introduces the fundamental concepts and methodologies of machine intelligence with a focus on real-world applications. Students explore how machine intelligence techniques are applied to computer vision, robotics, recommender systems, routing, resource allocation, crowdsourcing, and image recognition.

title: Engineering Biochemistry
description: This course introduces key biochemical reactions in living organisms, covering topics such as proteins, enzymes, and bioenergetics.

title: Computational Methods for Chemical Engineering
description: This course covers basic numerical methods in bio and chemical sciences, with practical training in MATLAB, Mathematica, ChemDraw, and scientific databases like NCBI and SciFinder.

title: Chemical reaction Engineering
description: This course is designed to provide (1) an understanding of kinetics as it applies to chemical reactions from the microscopic viewpoint and (2) the basis required for designing chemical reactors for controlling chemical reactions.

title: Basic Microeconomics
description: This course introduces the fundamental principles of microeconomics, focusing on consumer behavior, demand and supply analysis, firm decision-making, market structures, and competitive equilibrium. Students will explore topics such as perfect competition, monopoly, oligopoly, game theory, welfare economics, and market failure, developing analytical skills to understand economic decision-making and market outcomes.

title: Intermediate Microeconomic Theory
description: This intermediate-level microeconomics course develops mathematical tools for systematically analyzing economic problems and builds economic intuition for understanding real-world issues and policy questions.

title: Econometrics
description: This course provides an introduction to econometric methods, with a strong emphasis on their application in applied economic research. Students who successfully complete the course will gain a solid understanding of the fundamental techniques of empirical economics, including linear regression, instrumental variable estimation, and limited dependent variable re- gressions.

title: Introduction to Econometrics
description: This is the first undergraduate course in econometrics, which introduces students the basic tools used in empirical research in economics. After an overview of probability and statistics that is necessary for econometrics, the course will introduce linear regression, which is the most widely used tool for a systematic examination of data. A significant emphasis will be placed on the estimation of linear regression parameters, hypothesis testing, and the interpretation of regression results.

title: Labor Economics
description: This course will examine a variety of topics in labor markets. First, we will develop theoretical models of labor supply, labor demand and the interaction of the two. These models will then be applied to understand issues such as wage determination, wage differentials, human capital investment, migration and discrimination, unemployment and labor policies, and unions.

title: Microelectronics I and Laboratory
description: This course covers the basics of microelectronics, from semiconductor device physics to analog circuit analysis techniques using nonlinear devices, i.e. transistors. This course has six labs where you can connect what you learn in lectures and hands-on practice.

title: Microelectronics I and Laboratory
description: This course covers the basics of microelectronics, from semiconductor device physics to analog circuit analysis techniques using nonlinear devices, i.e. transistors. This course has six labs where you can connect what you learn in lectures and hands-on practice.

title: Digital Signal Processing
description: This course introduces the fundamental concepts of signals and systems, focusing on both continuous-time and discrete-time analysis. Topics include sampling of continuous-time signals, the z-transform, and structures for discrete-time systems.

title: Power Electronics
description: This upper-level undergraduate course introduces the basics of power electronics for Electrical Engineering students. It combines lectures with hands-on design activities and projects using simulation software. Students learn the principles of power converters and gain practical experience in designing and building power hardware and control circuits, finishing the course with a clear understanding of real-world applications.

title: Microeconomics II
description: This course introduces key microeconomic theories, covering consumer behavior, demand, risk and uncertainty, production and costs, perfect competition, and government policies, with an emphasis on quantitative analysis and real-world applications.

title: Macroeconomics II
description: This course examines the determination of economic activity using different macroeconomic models and explores the main differences between these models. Students will also learn to analyze macroeconomic problems and identify appropriate economic policies to address them.

title: Foundation of Political Philosophy
description: This course explores major political philosophies and thinkers, focusing on key concepts such as freedom, justice, equality, and their influence on government and society.

title: Horror in English Literature and Film
English Creative Writing
description: This course introduces creative writing with a focus on prose, covering basic writing techniques and terminology, fiction writing, character development, dialogue, structure, and effective use of the English language.

title: Principles of Energy Engineering
description: This course introduces the fundamental principles of energy engineering, covering conventional and renewable energy conversion technologies, energy resources, and basic methods for analyzing energy systems. Students will explore the scientific and engineering principles underlying energy production, evaluate the advantages and limitations of different technologies, and develop an understanding of sustainable energy solutions for future applications.

title: Topics in European Studies Democracy and Dictatorship
description: This course provides an in-depth introduction to theories of democracy and dictatorship —including voluntarist and structural approaches to democratization and theories ofauthoritarian durability. We will focus in particular on current threats to democracy inEurope, including the rise of populism in the early 21st century.

title: Gateway Proseminar in European and Eurasian Studies
description: This course is a foundational graduate course that examines major historical and political transformations in Europe and Eurasia while developing students’ research, analytical, and interdisciplinary skills.

title: Financial Management
description: This course develops an understanding of the theoretical and practical issues related tofinancial management. The main objectives of the course are to introduce the students tothe financial markets and instruments, to expose the students to the quantitative tools andmethods of modern finance, and to help students gain competence in using these tools tomake sound financial decisions. Topics covered in the course include: the link betweenaccounting and finance, the time value of money, bond and stock valuation, investmentdecision criteria and capital budgeting, project analysis, risk-return relationship and costof capital.

title: Special Topics: Climate Change and Capital Markets
Learning and Teaching of German
description: The ultimate goal of this course is to introduce participants with little or no prior second languageteaching experience at post-secondary institutions to the theories and practices of second/foreignlanguage teaching and learning in postsecondary environments. Participants will gain a criticalunderstanding of the major teaching methods and techniques used in universities today.

title: Effective Oral Communication
description: This course develops effective oral communication skills through presentation planning, impromptu speaking, and practical communication strategies.

title: Treasure or Trouble: Managing Mineral Wealth
Organisational Failure & Public Policy Disasters
description: The subject is the analysis of organisational failure and public policy disasters from a variety of perspectives in an attempt to enable students to assess the risks of failure and to contribute to appropriate risk reduction and crisis management strategies.

title: The Political Economy of World Trade
description: This course examines organisational failures and public policy disasters from multiple perspectives, enabling students to assess risks and develop effective crisis management and risk reduction strategies.

title: Governance and Politics of Artificial Intelligence
description: This course is intended to give a next generation of policy makers a firm grasp of both the fundamentals of AI regulation – what is possible and what is not – and a survey of present-day political debates and governance strategies.

title: Data Science & Decision Making
description: This course explores decision-making in both theory and practice, combining classical decision theory with insights on human and machine cognition and bias. It also draws on real-world perspectives from professionals who make complex decisions in technical and policy contexts.

title: Energy Economics
description: Energy Economics is an introduction to the technology and economics of energy systems, power markets, and electricity networks. We study the economics of wind and solar energy and how renewables change energy systems and markets.

title: Contemporary Russian Politics
description: The idea of the course is to put current events in Russia in the context of the post-Soviet evolution of contemporary Russian politics.

title: Military Strategy, Operations & Technology
description: This course examines the use and preparation of military force to achieve political objectives, including strategies for addressing external threats and competing with adversaries. It introduces key concepts such as grand strategy, operations, tactics, and different approaches to warfare like attrition and maneuver.

title: History of a City II
description: Commencing with the conquest of Constantinople by Mehmed II in 1453, HIST 371 provides a comprehensive survey of the political, social, religious, and economic history of Ottoman Istanbul through the early 20th century. The course tracks the evolution of the city from an imperial capital to a modern metropolis, covering key themes such as the construction of the Ottoman urban landscape, imperial ceremonies, neighborhood [mahalle] life, immigration, the status of religious minorities, gender relations, justice administration, and the vibrant culture of public spaces like coffeehouses. In addition to these themes, the course explores Istanbul’s role in international diplomacy and commerce, as well as its manifold transformations from the classical age through the Tanzimat era and into the early 20th century. Designed as an undergraduate survey, the course combines lectures with class discussions. Students will engage with selected primary and secondary sources to understand the texture of daily life, urban dynamics, and the structural changes the city underwent over four centuries, rather than solely focusing on abstract historiographical debates.

title: Industrial Operations Management
description: This course covers data-driven operations management, including forecasting, production, quality, and supply chain management. It also explores the application of modern AI in designing and improving products and services.

title: S: Introduction to Literary Studies
description: Introduction to Literary Studies explores key literary genres—poetry, drama, and narrative—through close reading of texts such as Shakespeare’s Macbeth and Shelley’s Frankenstein, while developing analytical and academic writing skills.

title: European Foreign Policy
description: The objective of this course is to offer an all-round introduction into the nature of EU foreign policy, the actors, instruments and the interaction with the wider international context. The course will cover basic terminology, history, the institutional framework, and foreign policy issue areas. In addition, the topics of the EU’s identity as an international actor and of Europeanisation of foreign policies are addressed.

title: International Relations Theory and Asia-Pacific Regional Cooperation
Design of Machine Elements
description: This course covers the analysis and design of machine elements, including stress analysis, failure prevention, safety factors, experimental evaluation, and the use of modern engineering software tools.

title: Finite Element Analysis
description: This course covers the Finite Element Method for analyzing and solving solid mechanics problems, with emphasis on engineering design, simulation, and optimization using commercial FEA software.

title: Failure Analysis and Prevention
description: This course focuses on the analysis and prevention of engineering failures, including failure mechanisms, root-cause analysis, mitigation strategies, and material selection using engineering software.

title: International Law
description: This course is an introduction to the field of international law (IL). It is primarily designed for students of international relations and political science who have not previously studied the subject. It aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of how IL functions and provide an overall study of the basic concepts and issues of IL and how they relate to international relations and governance.

title: International Business and Global Responsibility
description: This course explores how businesses operate in the global arena and the challenges they face to be successful

title: Introduction to Marketing
description: This course provides an introduction to global marketing and what are considered effective marketing strategies, encouraging learners to recognize how customer value may be created and captured

title: Understanding LLMs
description: This course deals with language models (LMs), in particular (but not exclusively so) on transformer-based language models like GPT-x or LLama. It covers topics that will equip participants with a better conceptual and practical understanding of what LMs are, how they work, and how to understand them. In the course, we will look (among others) at LM architectures, training & fine-tuning, prompting, mechanistic interpretability of LMs, LM agents and different evaluation methods. Participants will be offered both a technical perspective and encouraged to critically think about important topics relevant to cognitive science and society in the context of LMs.

title: Poetics of Pollution: Literature and Environmental Waste
From Beowulf to Barrie – Elves and Fairies in English Literature
Ordinary Differential Equations
description: This course introduces the fundamental principles and methods of ordinary differential equations, covering first- and higher-order equations, systems of linear equations, Laplace transforms, nonlinear differential equations, and their applications.

title: Abstract Algebra I
description: This course provides an introduction to modern abstract algebra, covering groups, rings, fields, and their fundamental theories, and establishing a foundation for further study in related fields.

title: Calculus II
description: This course can roughly be divided into three parts. In the first part we will study the definite integral and its various applications. The second part will be devoted to the study of infinite sequences and series and their relation to the definite integral. Taylor series will also be studied. The final part of the course will deal with real valued functions of several variables that generalize the real valued functions of a real variable studied in Calculus 1 in several directions. Applications will be provided by means of different examples.

title: Ordinary Differential Equations
description: Natural phenomena involving change are commonly described by equations that relate variable quantities y(t) and their rates of change, i.e. derivatives y ′ (t), y ′′(t), ⋯; hence the name ordinary differential equations. This course introduces the theory of first-order and higher-order ordinary differential equations. It develops various standard methods of analytic solutions.

title: Numerical Analysis
description: Numerical analysis focuses on finding approximate solutions to complex problems by breaking them down into simpler arithmetic operations that computers can efficiently execute. Essentially, it involves solving challenging mathematical problems by performing a sequence of basic, manageable steps. The problems addressed in numerical analysis often originate from diverse areas of mathematics, especially algebra and analysis. Moreover, numerical analysis does not just produce raw numerical results; it also contributes significantly to the development of algebraic and analytic theories, enhancing our overall understanding of these disciplines.

title: Mathematical Foundations of Cryptography
description: This course introduces cryptographic algorithms and their applications for network security. Topics include implementation of security services, symmetric and public key crypto-algorithms, security services and secure network protocols.

title: Public Organizations and Management
description: This course examines public management by exploring managerial roles, values, and skills, while addressing challenges within institutional and democratic contexts.

title: Design and Manufacture
description: This course introduces the engineering design process, machine design principles, CAD-based design, prototyping, engineering analysis, and product development for mechanical systems.

title: CAD/CAM
description: This course introduces computer-aided design, product design methodologies, CAD modeling, digital engineering tools, and modern product development processes for engineering applications.

title: Energy conversion systems
description: This course provides an introduction to conventional and renewable energy sources, energy conversion technologies, and the operation of modern power plants.

title: Engineering & technology management
description: This course introduces the fundamentals of engineering economics and technology management, focusing on economic analysis, decision-making, problem-solving, and managerial models for engineering applications.

title: Entrepreneurship
description: This course examines how ongoing technological trends, particularly artificial intelligence, are transforming thefield of entrepreneurship. Students will learn how to identify opportunities in a tech-driven world, launch and growventures leveraging AI tools, and navigate new models like solopreneurship and platform-based startups. Thecourse also addresses the management challenges of starting and successfully running a new venture. The focuswill be on techniques and strategies that encourage innovation and entrepreneurship, as well as the criticalsuccess factors for entrepreneurs, including knowledge, skills, and abilities.Through a combination of interactive lectures, case studies, simulations, and practical exercises, students willdevelop an entrepreneurial mindset suited for the AI era.

title: Microeconomics
description: The objective of the course is to introduce the students to the main concepts and results of microeconomics, and the way how economists think.The course provides an in depth coverage of Microeconomics and is focused on Consumer Demand, Producer Behavior, Market Structure and Strategic Behavior, and General Equilibrium. Introductory microeconomics. How individuals and firms behave, and why we need a government.

title: Introduction to Marketing
description: This course is an introduction to the study of structure and functions of marketing systems inthe firm, economy, and society which will include analysis of the environment, targetmarkets, and managerial aspects of marketing. Role of marketing, consumer behaviour,business-to-business markets, marketing research, segmentation and targeting will also bedescribed and discussed. In addition, managerial aspects of marketing such as product andservice development, pricing, promotion, advertising, selling, and distribution will be covered.

title: Mathematics for Machine Learning III
description: This course covers fundamental concepts in probability and statistics essential for machine learning applications in computational linguistics. Building on the previous courses in Linear Algebra and Calculus, students will learn to apply probabilistic and statistical methods to language-related problems.

title: Global Development Finance Cooperation
description: This course explores major challenges in global development finance and how organizations address them through real-world case studies. It emphasizes practical skills in designing inclusive, sustainable solutions, supported by collaborative projects and interactive learning.

title: Culture, Creativity and Local Development
description: This course explores contemporary cultural, creative, and innovation policies, equipping learners with the skills to analyze, design, and implement frameworks that promote sustainable national and regional development. It emphasizes understanding the economic, social, and cultural impacts of creative industries and fostering leadership in policy-making.

title: Geopolitics of Energy Security in the Indo-Pacific Region
Population and Development
description: This course introduces demography, focusing on population growth and key areas - mortality, fertility, migration, and age structure - and their role in development.

title: Urban and Regional Development
description: This course explores how cities and regions grow or decline, introducing key urban concepts - such as sustainability, inequality, and smart cities - while developing skills to analyze complex policy issues across local and global levels.

title: Data Vizualization
description: This course introduces the fundamentals of data analysis and visualization, combining key design and statistical principles with hands-on practice using Python tools.

title: Ethics and Politics, East and West: an introduction to Philosophy
Philosophy of religion
description: There are several fields that study religion. Theology is the study of one’s own religion, through a religious lense. The theologian asks, “Given that my religion is true, what is the nature of God, morality, the afterlife, etc.?” Objective, secular studies of religion are called Religious Studies. These include, for example, the anthropology, history, psychology, and sociology of religion. Philosophy of religion, in particular, focuses on philosophically interesting questions surrounding religion, including such issues as the evidential value of religious experiences and testimony of miracles; the existence of God; and the dependence or independence of morality and meaning on religious foundations.

title: Classical Mechanics
description: This course introduces the fundamental principles of classical mechanics, including Newtonian mechanics, Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations, rigid body dynamics, oscillations, and central force motion. It provides the analytical foundation for advanced studies in physics and engineering

title: EDUCATION AND SOCIETY
description: This course is based on the framework of educational sociology. It will discuss the current issues and developments of formal and non -formal education in society, as well as analyse the role and impact of modern education based on sociological concepts and theories. Students also will develop, implement and report on field work programs as a socialization project of education in the community.

title: Capitalism and social justice
description: Who should get what? This is the fundamental issue in Political Theory. In this course, we will consider this and further crucial questions. Should we permit some people to possess great riches, while others live in poverty? Or should we seize the resources of the richest and redistribute them to the least advantaged? Should we give people freedom, or does their happiness matter more? The positions to be assessed span the political spectrum, including: • The liberal egalitarianism of John Rawls • The classical liberalism of F. A. Hayek • Robert Nozick’s libertarianism • John Stuart Mill’s utilitarianism • Contemporary defences of socialism

title: Public administration in China
description: This course aims to examine the context, structure, people and important issues in managing the public sector in contemporary China. The course provides students a basic understanding of China’s public administration system and its reforms. Several very important topics will be covered, including government structure and intergovernmental relations, and how to manage public employees, administrative reforms, and key issues in policy-making and implementation in contemporary China. This course encourages students to conduct group project, which will allow students to learn public policy analysis targeting real hot issues unfolding during China’s reform era. Sample policy areas include environmental governance, e-governance, and diversity and equity issues in public services. The newly emerged modes of public service delivery in China will also be discussed.

title: United States foreign policy
description: This course focuses on increasing understanding of U.S. foreign policy through an analysis of the different policy tools it frequently employs abroad. Accordingly, the course discusses a key component of American foreign policy -- the various ways in which the U.S. government tries to influence developments within other states by intervening in their domestic affairs. Interventions of various kinds, utilizing numerous tools, are frequently undertaken by the United States with major effects on the intervened country and subsequent U.S. foreign policy, as in the case of (to give one example of many) the covert overthrow of Iranian PM Mossadeq in 1953 and its effects on the anti- American tone of the Iranian Revolution (and the Iranian revolutionary government under Khomeini) 25 years later.

title: International relations of East Asia
description: This course is a survey of international relations in East Asia. In addition to historical patterns of international relations in the region, the course also addresses four issues here: What are major trends in regional IR? What is the source of conflict in the region? What are the common interests that unite peoples and states in East Asia? And how does the region organise itself? It explains dynamics and patterns of regional international relations in a broad geopolitical and geo-economic context. Topics in discussion include major powers’ role in the region, the Korean Peninsula, the Taiwan Strait, ASEAN, Southeast Asia and regional institution-building.

title: China and the world
description: This course will look at China’s position in the world – through its history and since the founding of the People’s Republic but with a heavy focus on developments and conditions since the economic opening in 1978. The aim is for students to tackle some of the big issues relating to China’s role in international politics and global affairs. Key questions include: What impact have the political, economic and social currents in Chinese history had on its contemporary foreign policies and relations? What has China’s economic transformation meant for the global economy? What are China’s main international relationships and how have their respective dynamics changed? In particular, what has been the nature of the China-United States relationship since the opening up of ties and diplomatic normalization in the 1970s? Are the global economy and the international order now essentially a “great power” competition between China and the US – and if so, what are the implications of such a framework for other countries and regions including the rest of Asia (particularly East Asia and India), Europe, Russia, the Middle East, Africa and what is called the Global South or the Global Majority? How has the global emphasis on economic and national security risks affected the outlook for the China-US relationship? Students should anticipate that the course will cover significant current developments in the China-US and China-global dynamic that will inevitably unfold during the semester. Topics for discussion in class and tutorial may therefore hinge on keeping abreast of and analyzing these events.

title: International development
description: The “Global South” has been highly marginalized yet strategically critical in international politics through- out modern history. This course examines the intersection of international politics and development in three parts: the major development bottlenecks faced by developing countries; the role of powerful states and international institutions in the developing world; and several new frontiers in international development including the rise of “emerging donors,” Chinese development finance, and the effects of pandemics on global development. The course will familiarize students with a wide range of political science, economics, history, and other social science research on global development. It will also introduce students to a diverse set of conceptual and methodological research approaches in political science and international relations.

title: Democratic theory
description: This course addresses crucial issues in contemporary democratic theory, broadly construed. We come across such terms as democracy, popular sovereignty, and collective self-governance in public discourse all the time. These terms and concepts are not only widely regarded as critical components of political legitimacy but serve as a rallying cry for political mobilization around the globe. They stir up controversies in public debates and agitate both friends and foes of democracy.

title: International Politics: The Rules of the Game
Education Economics and Policy
description: This course applies economic theory and empirical tools to analyze education and education policy, including its benefits and inequalities across different groups. It also explores key policy issues such as compulsory schooling and school choice through international examples and interactive learning methods.

title: Principles and Policies in Sustainability and the Environment
Economics of Developing Countries
description: This course examines key development challenges in areas such as public health, education, finance, and labor markets, with a focus on post-COVID-19 issues in developing countries. It equips students with empirical microeconomic tools to analyze policy problems through a blended learning approach.

title: Labour Market Issues and Public Policy
Pensions and Retirement Policies
description: This course examines pension systems and retirement income policies in Singapore and globally, covering social security models, government roles, and key challenges such as aging and fiscal sustainability. It focuses on designing financially resilient pension systems and understanding reform options through international comparisons.

title: Governing Cities of Tomorrow
description: This course explores the governance of emerging technologies in urban contexts, examining their environmental, social, and economic impacts. It equips students with analytical tools to design smart policies that maximize benefits while managing risks and unintended consequences.

title: Introduction to Coding for Public Policy
Prediction and Forecasting for Public Managers
International Economic Development
description: This course introduces international economic development with a focus on Asian economies, building analytical foundations to understand key macroeconomic policy issues. It explores how trade and financial flows have shaped Asia’s growth, alongside topics such as industrial policy, capital flows, and exchange rate regimes.

title: Biomedical Engineering
description: This course introduces the fundamentals of biomedical engineering, with a focus on biomedical devices, instrumentation, biosensors, physiological signal acquisition, and medical imaging. Students explore the engineering principles underlying modern biomedical systems and their clinical and research applications.

title: Advanced mobile system
description: This course introduces the principles of autonomous mobile robotics, focusing on perception, state estimation, navigation, and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM). Students learn the fundamental methods for enabling robots to localize, map, and navigate autonomously in real-world environments.

title: Deep Learning
description: This course introduces the fundamental theories and techniques of deep learning, with applications in robotics and artificial intelligence. Students explore image and natural language processing, generative and nonparametric models, and gain hands-on experience applying deep learning methods through practical exercises and a research-based final project.

title: Applied Econometrics
description: Applied Econometrics introduces the use of statistical and regression methods to analyze economic data, covering cross-sectional, time series, and panel data models, along with advanced techniques such as instrumental variables, simultaneous equations, and limited dependent variable models.

title: Elections and Political Behaviour
description: The course is divided roughly into two blocks: the first focuses on electoral behavior while the second examines electoral systems. The first half of the course presents the main theoretical approaches to voting behavior, as well as the most important empirical results. It also o!ers an overview of the major cross-national survey studies in the field. The second half of the course examines the characteristics of electoral systems, their prevalence in the world, ways to measure them, and their e!ects on party systems.

title: E-Governance
description: This course will overview recent developments in the realm of digital governance. It aims to provide a theoretical foundation for the analysis of practical cases. The course outlines technical solutions such as cloud services, online platforms, geographic information systems, internet of things, and digital twins. It will dive into digital governance in web, mobile, and hybrid online-o!ine contexts. It will look into such gov tech as e-health, e-public finance, digital-powered law enforcement, and smart cities. We will familiarise with the principles of government transparency via open data platforms and government accountability via such digital tools as e-tracker, e-audit, and e-oversight.

title: EU Law
description: This course examines the creation, legal nature and legal foundations of the EU; the fundamental rights and freedoms in the EU law; the general principles of EU law; the relationship between the national and EU law; the law-making procedures of the EU and member states' participation thereof; the implementation of the EU law in member states; the judicial system of the EU and actions and procedure in the Court of Justice of the EU. The course will deal to a large extent with the case law of the Court of Justice of the EU as the precedents have an essential role in the EU law-making.

title: Political Systems in Post-Soviet Space
description: The course begins by looking at the main patterns of political transformation in the region in the late 1980s - early 1990s, during and immediately after the collapse of the Soviet Union. In the second part, the typology of the evolution of political regimes in the following decades is introduced, and their current state is discussed. In doing that, the course relies upon the literature on democratization, as well as on the more recent works on the varieties of authoritarianism. The third part of the course consists of country cases that illustrate typical post-Soviet political trajectories and outcomes, ranging between oligarchical pluralism and authoritarian dictatorships. Topics considered for each country vary depending on the their relative importance for the specific case, but in most cases, the list includes constitution and the form of government, relations between the branches of power, political parties and interest groups, corruption, the state of fundamental rights and freedoms. Critical engagement with the concept of transition is a key element of all course sessions.

title: Graph Theory
description: This course introduces fundamental concepts and practical applications of graph theory, including Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs, trees, planarity, graph coloring, traffic systems, and matching problems. It also examines Japanese economic policies, their relationship to state interests and the international economy, and their contribution to Japan’s economic development.

title: Greater China: A multi-disciplinary introduction
description: This course adopts multi-disciplinary perspectives to examine significant and complex issues of China in the past and present. It is an introductory course required for majors and minors of China Studies in both the Arts Stream and the Social Sciences Stream. As a general survey of China, this course discusses China’s historical development, revolutionary past, cultural traditions, formal political structure, the market-oriented economic reform, and geographic, demographic and linguistic diversity, as well as contemporary issues of environment, resistance and mass media. Central themes throughout the course include China’s cultural identity, ethnicity, state-society relations, continuities and changes in China’s socio-political values, and China’s role in the global order. The purpose of this course is to provide students with a base of knowledge of China’s historical and contemporary experiences and contexts. It aims to help students understand how China’s historical legacy impacts today’s society, and how contemporary politics and economics transforms China in a comprehensive way.

title: Introduction to Russian Poetry and Poetics
description: The course introduces students to the basic concepts and traditions of Russian versification,and develops skills in analyzing poetic text. We will consider the formal featuresof Russian verse (meter, size, rhyme, stanza, phonetic and graphic techniques) and theirsignificance in creating and expressing the meaning of a poem. The main focus willbe on classical poetic forms. We will also consider the influence of the historical and culturalcontext on the semantic evolution of poetic forms.

title: PS: Structure and Meaning
description: This course introduces the fundamentals of syntax and semantics, focusing on how linguistic structures relate to meaning through theoretical frameworks and problem-based analysis of language data.

title: Power, Economy, and Society
description: Is money the only thing in the world that motivates people? Don’t we really need a regulatory mechanism like the state, or market is the miraculous mechanism to advance human lives? Do we have to work to live a normal life? Do we have to be tough, aggressive, and competitive to succeed in the neoliberal universe? What can we say about the culture of the new economy? How do we rationalize and normalize the socio-economic inequalities? This advanced sociology seminar departs from questions like these. It aims to provide students a general outlook on the workings of the current economy, i.e., deregulation, neoliberalism, platform capitalism, sharing economy, and its highly contested outcomes and costs like un- and under-employment, the shifting role of the state, poverty and inequality, personality issues and identity under precarization through exploring sociological and anthropological examples that are derived from the everyday life in different parts of the World.

title: Topics in Global Migration I
description: This course looks at global migration as a key area of sociological study, asking how the movement of people across borders is shaped by systems of power, inequality, and state control. We explore how migrants and refugees navigate identities and institutions shaped by race, bureaucracy, and citizenship, as well as by histories of war and colonialism. Topics include second-generation belonging and exclusion (Beaman, Shams), refugee resettlement in contexts of settler-colonialism and imperialism (Gandhi, Le Espiritu), and the micro-workings of asylum, legal practice, and non-citizenship in contemporary Europe (Tuckett, Cabot). Migration isn’t treated as a stand-alone topic here—it’s a lens for understanding deeper questions about power, belonging, and the global social order.

title: Introduction to sociology
description: Sociology is a systematic and critical study of human social life, groups, and societies. This introductory course aims to provide you with the key sociological concepts and perspectives in order to examine the intricate interplay between people and society. For example, how to make sense of our behaviour, how to comprehend the relationship we have with others, and how to understand the social world we live in. Topics include culture and norms, socialization and social interactions, social order and social structure, sex and gender, family and intimate relationship, deviance and crime, social stratification and inequality, media and information society, and globalization. At the end of the course, you will have a basic understanding of what sociology is: its main theorists, problems, methods, concepts, and its relevance to the contemporary world.

title: Intensive German Course for New Exchange Students of Bremen University – Complete Beginners A1.1 (Group A)
Introduction to Medicine
description: Introduction to Medicine is a one-semester introductory course that gives an overview of the Medical Sciences (Pre-Medicine) program and provides students with insight into various aspects of a physician profession.

title: Negotiating Gender: Queering the Sublime
description: This course examines the ways in which postmodern writers, thinkers and performers have rearticulated the binary oppositions of the traditional sublime as a form of queering, thus allowing different gendered and sexual identities to co-exist in ethical relation. Students will be asked to consider how these various revisions of the sublime, together with their resituating of the body/mind relation, affect conceptions of the political and the ethical, and how they engage with questions surrounding otherness, silence, presence, absence. They will be asked to consider how these texts reimagine selves engaging with the world, and with others in that world.

title: Negotiating Gender: Aesthetic Theory: Undoing Binaries
description: In the mid-eighteenth-century, German philosopher Alexander Baumgarten used the word ‘aesthetics’ to denote what he referred to as “the science of sensory knowledge”. On this understanding, the study of aesthetics is the study of something sensed, rather than something imagined or reasoned. In its most fundamental sense, aesthetics is about the experience of things in the world­ – one that relies on the interaction between the body and the mind to mediate this experience. As a means of re-presentation, aesthetic judgment can also be seen as a way of ordering the world, and the others in that world. In the eighteenth century, this was a process that was underwritten by binary oppositions (self/other, mind/body, culture/nature – ones that demarcated gender and sexuality in oppositional terms, thus reinscribing certain identity categories as fixed and unchangeable.

title: German A2.2 for Erasmus and Exchange Students
description: German A2.2 for Exchange Students develops intermediate German language skills, focusing on improving speaking, listening, reading, and writing for everyday communication in academic and social contexts.
