Languages, Cultures, and Communities of the Turkic World
description: This course offers an introduction to languages, cultures and communities of the Turkic World, their changes and continuities.

title: Introduction to Turkic languages
description: The course is designed to serve as a general reference source for all students with a keen interest in the Turkic family. The course aims to achieve a reasonable coverage of the differences and similarities of the modern Turkic languages and their dialects, focusing on key aspects of their linguistic structure.
department: Kazakh Language and Turkic Studies, Languages, Literature and Linguistics

title: Literatures of Central Asia
description: This course surveys Central Asian literature in translation.

title: Istanbul in Literature and Culture
description: This course will survey the changing social and historical configuration and complex relationships in the cosmopolitan of city Istanbul, from the time of Ottoman Empire through modern days.

title: Turkish Poetry in Translation
description: This course is a survey of Turkish poetry in translation.

title: Introduction to Old Turkic
description: This course offers an introduction to the Old Turkic literary languages in the runiform and Uyğur alphabets.
prerequisite: KAZ 202 Academic Kazakh II (4562) (C- and above) OR KLL "[C1.1] Advanced"

title: Introduction to Chagatay and Ottoman Turkish
description: This course offers an introduction to the pre-modern Turkic literary languages known as Chagatay Turkic and Ottoman Turkish.
prerequisite: KAZ 202 Academic Kazakh II (4562) (C- and above) OR KLL "[C1.1] Advanced"

title: Advanced Readings in Turkish Literature
description: The course is an introduction to Turkish literature through advanced readings in Turkish. Students should already have “Advanced Mid” level Turkish [CEFR B2].

title: Advanced Turkish in Media and Politics
description: Students will be introduced to the key problems of women and question of national identity in contemporary Turkey. They will explore scholarly articles as well as newspapers, documentaries, shows and films produced recently in Turkey. The course will be conducted in Turkish. Students should already have “Advanced Mid” level Turkish [CEFR B2].

title: The Turkish Novel
description: This course addresses social consequences of Pamuk’s role as an intellectual author who relates “national tradition” and “international canon”. Students will discuss the role of language and narration in shaping a person’s identity and perception of the external world during the semester.

title: Eurasian Environments
description: This course examines the relationship between humans and their environment across time and Eurasian space.

title: Selective reading of historical Turkic literature
description: The course offers an intensive linguistic analysis of historical Turkic literature, ranging from eighth-century Orkhun inscriptions to eighteenth-century Old Kazakh documents. The goal is to provide a relatively comprehensive morphosyntactic description of the various original texts in comparative perspective with modern Turkic languages, emphasizing linguistic convergence and divergence. Students with a strong interest in Turkic languages and historical linguistics may find the course informative.
department: Kazakh Language and Turkic Studies, Languages, Literature and Linguistics
prerequisite: LING 131 Introduction to Linguistics (1394) (C and above) OR LING 130 Introduction to Language and Communication (4014) (C and above) OR LING 140 Language Variation and Change: the Story of English (4835) (C and above) OR LING 240 Introduction to Sociolinguistics (6838) (C and above) OR LING 270 Languages of Eurasia (2485) (C and above) OR LING 273 Survey of Research Methods in Linguistics (2158) (C and above) OR LING 277 Language Diversity and Language Universals (3834) (C and above) OR LING 278 Sounds of the World’s Languages (3850) (C and above) OR LING 280/TUR 280 Introduction to Turkic Historical and Comparative Linguistics (3175) (C and above) OR LING 375 The Art and Science of Analyzing Languages: Morphosyntax of the World's Languages (6237) (C and above) OR LING 374 Language Contact in Central Asia (3047) (C and above) OR LING 470 Multilingualism and Language Contact (3339) (C and above)

title: Eurasian Environments
description: This course examines the relationship between humans and their environment across time and Eurasian space.

title: Advanced Topics in Turkic Studies
description: This course will be taught on a unique topic (i.e. not taught regularly) related to Turkic Studies. Students will complete a substantial project suitable international publication. This course can also be taught by visiting faculty. May be repeated for credit.

title: Doctoral Topic in Turkic Studies
description: This course will be taught on a unique topic (i.e. not taught regularly) related to Turkic Studies. Students will complete a substantial project suitable international publication. This course can also be taught by visiting faculty. May be repeated for credit.

title: Communication and Society
description: This course introduces principles and theories of communication applied in various contexts. Each area of communication introduced (Human Communication, Media Studies and Professional Communication) is examined through the lens of communication theory.

title: Introduction to Visual Communication
description: This course provides students with a practical introduction to visual communication. The course includes genres across print, audio, visual and video materials. Media-rich lectures examine visual genres including advertisements, packaging, video game worlds, pop videos, movies, comics, manga, anime and short pieces from YouTube, TikTok and Instagram.

title: Advanced English for Academic Purposes
description: Rhetoric and Composition is designed to develop students' abilities to think, organize and express their ideas clearly and effectively in writing.
department: Academic Success Centre, Communication and Composition

title: Introduction to Creative Writing
description: By introducing the genres, devices, techniques, and effects of creative writing, this course aims to help all writers write more creatively across genres.

title: Introduction to Public Speaking
description: This course focuses on extemporaneous speaking. It requires the development of rhetoric, research, and organizational skills to facilitate the delivery of information to specific audiences. Delivery is supported by advanced preparation, practice, and the use of outlines. This course is suitable for all majors. This course satisfies the Core Curriculum Year 2 Writing & Communication requirement.
prerequisite: WCS 150/ASC 100 Advanced English for Academic Purposes (2183) (C- and above)

title: Introduction to Journalism
description: This course will incorporate both practical and theoretical approaches in Journalism to equip students with a full understanding of the practice and principles of journalism. Specifically, students will be taught how to identify good reporting, research facts, and write news that are informative, engaging, and ethical.
prerequisite: WCS 101 Communication and Society (199) (C- and above) OR WCS 150/ASC 100 Advanced English for Academic Purposes (2183) (C- and above)

title: Interpersonal Communication
description: This course builds upon communication principles and theories introduced in WCS 101 Communication and Society, WCS 150 Rhetoric and Composition, and WCS 200 Introduction to Public Speaking. We will engage with various readings and research findings in interpersonal communication – an interdisciplinary subject which synthesizes findings in linguistics, psychology, biology, neuroscience, and communication. The course will examine how cultural perspectives and rhetorical situations influence the way we communicate and how we interpret the communication of others in personal and professional settings.
prerequisite: WCS 101 Communication and Society (199) (C- and above) OR WCS 200 Introduction to Public Speaking (175) (C- and above)

title: Gender and Communication
description: In this course, students will learn how to identify and analyze the forms of communication that enable and determine the construction of gender. Applying the tools of rhetoric that students studied in WCS 150, students will examine theories about how gender is communicated verbally and non-verbally in the everyday and in the virtual world.
prerequisite: WCS 101 Communication and Society (199) (C- and above) OR WCS 150/ASC 100 Advanced English for Academic Purposes (2183) (B- and above)

title: Intercultural Communication
description: In this course students will examine the barriers impeding successful communication between people with different cultural backgrounds, explore the relationship between culture and communication in various professional and personal contexts, and develop the necessary skills for enhancing self-reflection, flexibility, and sensitivity in intercultural encounters.

title: Health Communication
description: In this course, students will learn through a survey of theory and research in health communication. The course provides an overview of the interactions of people involved in the health-care process (parties and providers), communication in health care organizations, the public dissemination and interpretation of health-related messages, and cultural meanings of health and illness as they relate to physical, mental, and social health issues.
prerequisite: WCS 101 Communication and Society (199) (C- and above)

title: Academic Writing, Science Communication, and Media Literacy
description: This course presents students with practical information about communicating in different professional and technical discourse communities.
department: Academic Success Centre, Communication and Composition
prerequisite: ASC 100 Advanced English for Academic Purposes (9234) (C- and above) OR Test "IELTS" BETWEEN 6.5 and 9 OR WCS 150/ASC 100 Advanced English for Academic Purposes (2183) (C- and above)
antirequisite: WCS 200 Introduction to Public Speaking (175) (D and above) OR WCS 220 Science Writing (5686) (D and above) OR WCS 230 Say What you Mean: Clarity, Precision, and Style in Academic Writing (3026) (D and above) OR WCS 240 Writing for Digital Media (4421) (D and above) OR WCS 250 Advanced Rhetoric and Composition (3027) (D and above) OR WCS 260/WLL 235 Creative Writing: Introduction to Fiction Writing I (4000) (D and above) OR WCS 270 Academic and Professional Presentations (8409) (D and above)

title: Science Writing
description: This course teaches students in the Social and STEM sciences to become more effective science-genre specific writers. Building on the principles developed in SHSS 150, this course highlights key characteristics of science writing and emphasizes the importance of organizing writing around research outcomes, communicating difficult discipline and statistical concepts clearly and effectively for scientific and general audiences.
prerequisite: WCS 150/ASC 100 Advanced English for Academic Purposes (2183) (C- and above)
antirequisite: WCS 210/ASC 200 Academic Writing, Science Communication, and Media Literacy (4881) (C- and above)

title: Say What you Mean: Clarity, Precision, and Style in Academic Writing
description: In this course, students will build on the writing skills acquired in SHSS 150 and develop their voices in academic writing. They will learn to craft their own style of writing with an emphasis on clarity, audience, and purpose. Students will become familiar with the principles of strong and clear writing, e.g., cohesion, coherence, accuracy, and concision by reading selected texts across genres and time periods to identify how different writers express themselves while also effectively communicating with their audience. In analyzing the way these authors write, students will develop an eye for style and clarity, progressing from mere sentences to lengthier pieces of writing. Students will then be required to draw on this knowledge when producing their written works. This course is designed to appeal to students from any major who wish to focus on developing their writing voice. This course satisfies the Core Curriculum Year 2 Writing & Communication requirement.
prerequisite: WCS 150/ASC 100 Advanced English for Academic Purposes (2183) (C- and above)

title: Writing for Digital Media
description: In this course, students will learn how to build and break down arguments and information in a variety of different modalities including text, image, audiovisual and web. This course combines the application rhetorical analysis to design, focusing on expanding students’ communication abilities beyond text and speaking. Students will develop composition skills across media through individual and group projects. Writing for Digital Media is suitable for students from any major who want to learn how to present their ideas and their research effectively to different audiences in multimodal environments. Coding and/or advanced proficiency with computers are not requirements for this course. This course satisfies the Core Curriculum Year 2 Writing & Communication requirement.
prerequisite: WCS 150/ASC 100 Advanced English for Academic Purposes (2183) (C- and above)

title: Advanced Rhetoric and Composition
description: This course builds upon the research skills, rhetorical concepts, and thesis-driven writing introduced in SHSS 150, with an aim toward situating writing within the social sciences and humanities. Students will critically read and practice writing in various genres they are likely to encounter in the social sciences and humanities. Students will analyze and discuss genres and rhetorical strategies within and across disciplines. Through a process of planning, drafting, and revision, students will develop their writing voice and produce rhetorically aware texts that are appropriate to their field including essays, a literature review, and a research paper. This course satisfies the Core Curriculum Year 2 Writing & Communication requirement.
prerequisite: WCS 150/ASC 100 Advanced English for Academic Purposes (2183) (C- and above)

title: Creative Writing: Introduction to Fiction Writing I
description: This introduction to creative writing: fiction is primarily a seminar with a workshop emphasis. Students will work together as a group reading and critiquing not only the published fiction that will be assigned but also the exercises and short stories they will write. The course requires reading a significant amount of published fiction from the canonical to the contemporary with an eye on how these stories work and what students, as writers, can learn about the fundamentals of fiction from them. Students will also write exercises that will deepen their understanding of the basic elements of craft and hopefully develop their creative interests. By the end of the semester students will not only have a collection of exercises, but two fully edited and polished short stories that we will all have read and discussed in class. This course satisfies the Core Curriculum Year 2 Writing & Communication requirement.
department: Communication and Composition, Languages, Literature and Linguistics
prerequisite: WCS 150/ASC 100 Advanced English for Academic Purposes (2183) (C- and above)

title: Academic and Professional Presentations
description: This course teaches students basic skills in developing presentations appropriate for scientific and professional settings.
prerequisite: WCS 150/ASC 100 Advanced English for Academic Purposes (2183) (C- and above)
antirequisite: WCS 210/ASC 200 Academic Writing, Science Communication, and Media Literacy (4881) (C- and above)

title: Internship: Undergraduate Speaker Consultant I
description: Undergraduate speaker consultants in the Writing Center serve as peer consultants to support NU community members interested in practicing speeches and presentations and receiving feedback on crafting clear and effective messages, cultivating dynamic delivery, and reducing their public speaking anxiety.
prerequisite: WCS 200 Introduction to Public Speaking (175) (A- and above) OR WCS 270 Academic and Professional Presentations (8409) (A- and above)

title: Internship: Undergraduate Speaker Consultant II
description: Undergraduate speaker consultants in the Writing Center serve as peer consultants to support NU community members interested in practicing speeches and presentations and receiving feedback on crafting clear and effective messages, cultivating dynamic delivery, and reducing their public speaking anxiety.
prerequisite: WCS 300 Internship: Undergraduate Speaker Consultant I (8538) (P)

title: Argumentation and Debate
description: WCS 302, Argumentation and Debate, is designed to help students develop and hone skills in persuasion, debate, and advocacy.
prerequisite: WCS 200 Introduction to Public Speaking (175) (C- and above)

title: Multimodal Communication Internship I
description: Students will engage in real-world projects with campus or community partners, developing content and strategies that reflect the principles of effective multimodal design and communication. Emphasis is placed on reflective practice, foundational skill development, workplace communication, and professional goal setting.
prerequisite: WCS 240 Writing for Digital Media (4421) (A- and above)

title: Multimodal Communication Internship II
description: Students take on more complex projects, demonstrate increased independence, and refine their ability to adapt content for diverse audiences and platforms. A key component of this course is peer mentorship: students will mentor new interns and/or students currently enrolled in WCS 240: Writing for Digital Media, gaining leadership and collaborative experience.
prerequisite: WCS 304 Multimodal Communication Internship I (8702) (P) OR SSH 300 School of Sciences and Humanities Internship (712) (P)

title: Poetry Writing Seminar
description: This seminar is an advanced creative writing workshop-based course that focuses on the creation, research and revision of original student poetry as well as on the critical analysis of contemporary poetic theory and influential contemporary poets.
department: Communication and Composition, Languages, Literature and Linguistics

title: Advanced Fiction Writing
description: This is a workshop intensive class devoted to reading, analyzing, writing, and revision of creative writing and the study of the creative process. This course is intended for students already writing original creative work and interested in advanced techniques to refine writing though a process of repeated editing and analysis of their own works in progress. Students will finish the semester with submitting an edited piece of writing for publication.
prerequisite: WCS 260/WLL 235 Creative Writing: Introduction to Fiction Writing I (4000) (C- and above)

title: Screenwriting for Short Films
description: This course is a reading-and-writing intensive seminar focused on reading, analyzing and writing short film narratives. What that means is that students will work together as a group reading and critiquing not only the screenplays and films that will be assigned but also both of the screenplays students will write. Students will also do writing exercises that will deepen their understanding of the basic elements of craft and hopefully develop their creative interests and instincts. By the end of the semester, they will not only have a collection of exercises but two fully-edited and polished screenplays that will have been read and discussed by their peers and instructor.
prerequisite: WCS 260/WLL 235 Creative Writing: Introduction to Fiction Writing I (4000) (C- and above) OR WCS 240 Writing for Digital Media (4421) (C- and above)

title: Writing Fellows I – Composition and Collaboration in Theory and Practice
description: Writing Fellows improve their writing skills and discuss issues surrounding mentoring and tutoring writing.
prerequisite: WCS 150/ASC 100 Advanced English for Academic Purposes (2183) (B and above) AND (WCS 220 Science Writing (5686) (B+ and above) OR WCS 230 Say What you Mean: Clarity, Precision, and Style in Academic Writing (3026) (B+ and above) OR WCS 250 Advanced Rhetoric and Composition (3027) (B+ and above))

title: Writing Fellows II – Practicum in Composition & Collaboration
description: This course is a hands-on practicum that follows SHSS 390, in which writing fellows explored and discussed contemporary writing theories and writing center and research. Fellows will apply the knowledge they’ve gained in theory and research to help student writers in the Nazarbayev University community. Writing fellows will serve as peer writing tutors embedded in specific courses, allowing them to gain and reinforce their knowledge in discipline specific writing. Fellows will also participate in a weekly seminar meeting to discuss their service and learning and to stay current on writing center research.
prerequisite: WCS 390 Writing Fellows I – Composition and Collaboration in Theory and Practice (1969) (B and above)

title: Writing Fellows III - Research & Practice in Writing & Peer Mentorship
description: This is the third and optional segment in the Writing Fellows program. In this course, students will have the opportunity to continue working as a Writing Fellow embedded as a writing tutor in discipline courses as in SHSS 391. They will also mentor new Writing Fellows in their first year of study and practice while also conducting original research in specific topics within writing, pedagogy, peer mentorship, and other areas of Writing Center research.
prerequisite: WCS 391 Writing Fellows II – Practicum in Composition & Collaboration (3425) (B and above)

title: Internship: Undergraduate Writing Tutor I
description: Undergraduate tutors in the SSH Writing Center will serve as peer writing tutors to support NU students. Undergraduate tutors will be NU students in good standing who have successfully completed WCS 392 and are committed to continued development of their tutoring skills through tutoring, collaboration, and reflective practice.
prerequisite: WCS 392 Writing Fellows III - Research & Practice in Writing & Peer Mentorship (4472) (B and above)

title: Internship: Undergraduate Writing Tutor II
description: Undergraduate tutors in the SSH Writing Center will serve as peer writing tutors to support NU students. Undergraduate tutors will be NU students in good standing who have successfully completed WCS 392 and are committed to continued development of their tutoring skills through tutoring, collaboration, and reflective practice.
prerequisite: WCS 393 Internship: Undergraduate Writing Tutor I (7346) (P)

title: Independent Study in Creative Writing
description: This class allows students to pursue a focused exploration of a topic that is not offered on conventional classes, while under the supervision of a faculty member. Both the topic and a study plan must be approved by the faculty member prior to enrollment.
department: Communication and Composition, Languages, Literature and Linguistics

title: Science Communication
description: This graduate level course combines the application of rhetorical analysis to stylistic conventions of writing in the sciences and math with a focus on clarity, conciseness, and coherence. Students will write in their area of expertise in accordance with ethical and professional standards, prepare coherent reports of research findings, develop skills to author research publications, and present posters and/or oral presentations in conferences. They will learn to skillfully communicate scientific concepts and research findings using various modalities of communication with expert and lay audiences. This course trains students to deliver effective and appealing professional and scientific presentations with attention to best practices in the use of technical English and oral communication.

title: Rhetoric and Writing Pedagogy Across the Discipline
description: This course aims to introduce students to curriculum and instruction (pedagogy) affecting teaching and learning Rhetoric and Writing.

title: From Genre to Style and Back: Writing for PhD Students
description: This course aims to integrate genre-based writing instruction with the disciplinary concerns of graduate writers in PhD programs.

title: Introduction to Critical Issues in the Humanities and Social Sciences
Language, Experience, Culture
description: Students will be introduced to the ways in which humanistic study touches upon the issues of how human experience is formulated as a personal experience and how that experience is communicated interpersonally.
department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, Languages, Literature and Linguistics

title: Introduction to Theatre
description: This course presents an introduction to the different facets and disciplines which comprise Theatre Arts.

title: Introduction to the Comic Book
description: This course will introduce students to Japanese manga and American comic books and graphic novels. Students will learn the vocabulary and critical approaches to studying works of sequential art, as well as historical and cultural contexts for manga and the comic book in Japan and America.

title: Introduction to Linguistic Anthropology
description: In this course, we will examine the relationship between language (structure and usage) and social life. How does language affect our relationships with other people (on a small scale) or our social structure (on a large scale)? How do ideas about social life, or different groups of people, affect what we believe about language?
department: Languages, Literature and Linguistics, Sociology and Anthropology
antirequisite: ANT 277/WLL 271 Language and Society (1027) (C- and above)

title: Introduction to Translation Studies
description: This course will introduce the students to theoretical and practical issues in modern translation studies and provide elementary training in the practice of translation and interpreting.

title: World Literature II: from the 18th to the 20th century
Introduction to Poetry
description: This unit will train you in skills necessary for the critical appreciation of poetry. It introduces literary concepts such as genre, poetic form (stanzaic form, metre, rhyme, voice), textual criticism, and historical context.

title: Introduction to the Hispanic World
department: Languages, Literature and Linguistics, Languages, Literature and Linguistics

title: Renaissance in Italy and Beyond
description: How values and ideals are expressed in literary, artistic, and intellectual achievements of Renaissance Italy and beyond. We will survey the development of literature and arts in the 14th-16th century by looking at a selection of masterpieces.

title: Myth and Adaptation
description: This course examines classical myth in light of its appropriation by artists from antiquity to the 20th Century.

title: Creative Writing/Theatre
prerequisite: Subject "WLL" BETWEEN 110 and 125 OR Subject "WLL" BETWEEN 200 and 299 OR Subject "WLL" BETWEEN 300 and 399

title: Acting: Praxis, Theory and History
description: Acting theory and practice as explored through seminal texts in Western Realism, and reactions against Realism, as well as other acting and performance traditions in the world. Theorists and authors studied include Stanislavsky, Meyerhold, Chekhov, Vakhtangov, Artaud, Brecht, Grotowski, Suzuki and others.

title: Literature and Other Media
description: The course encourages students to reflect on the relationship and cross-fertilization between literature and other artistic media, old and new, such as visual arts, music, or computer games.

title: Western Theatre, Literature and History From Ancient Creece to 1800
prerequisite: WLL 101 Introduction to Critical Issues in the Humanities and Social Sciences (234) (C- and above) OR WLL 110 Introduction to Literary Studies (244) (C- and above) OR WLL 121 Introduction to Cultural Studies (243) (C- and above)

title: Survey of Contemporary Russian Literature and Culture
description: This course presents a survey of contemporary Russian and Russophone literature written after 1991 and explores various genres of prose and poetry (traditional novel, dystopias, postmodernist fiction, popular and detective literature, women’s prose, creative nonfiction) and other modes of cultural production (music, political and performance art). Discussions address the issues of politics, re-assessment of history, memory, gender, national identity, violence and terrorism, as well as the place of literature in the modern world.
prerequisite: Subject "WLL" BETWEEN 100 and 199 OR WCS 150/ASC 100 Advanced English for Academic Purposes (2183) (C- and above)

title: Survey of Soviet Literature and Culture
description: This course presents a survey of Soviet literature and culture and explores various genres of prose and poetry, as well as film, music, and visual arts. Discussions address the conflicts between progress and tradition, the individual and the collective, utopian and apocalyptic thought, writers and leaders, and Russia and the West.

title: Hong Kong Cinema
description: This course will examine Hong Kong cinema, primarily from the Golden Age of the 1990s. Students will be introduced to genres (comedy, action, ghost story/fantasy, etc.) and their particular historical, literary, and socio-economic contexts.

title: Western Theatre Literature and History: 1800-Present
antirequisite: WLL 321 Creative Writing/Theatre - Intermediate/Advanced (1398) (C- and above)

title: Superstition, Magical Realism, and Horror in Hispanic Culture
description: This course will provide an introduction to the Hispanic Culture through the prism of superstitious practices, magical realist writing, and tales of horror.
department: Languages, Literature and Linguistics, Languages, Literature and Linguistics
prerequisite: Subject "WLL" BETWEEN 100 and 499 OR Subject "HST" BETWEEN 100 and 499

title: The Comic Book in Japan and America
description: This course will introduce students to Japanese manga and American comic books and graphic novels.
prerequisite: Subject "WLL" BETWEEN 100 and 499 OR Subject "HST" BETWEEN 100 and 499

title: Fan Culture in the Age of Convergence
description: Whilst fandom traditionally carries negative connotations in contemporary society fans have become important cultural contributors. Far from being mindless consumers fans are active creators, who build their own (sub)culture on the basis of borrowed cultural material.

title: Survey of American Literature
description: The course is a chronologically organized survey of the literature of the USA from the late 18th century to the first decades of the 3rd millennium. It is centered on the students’ firsthand experience of methodical weekly reading of literary texts, mainly short stories, which are contextualized historically and discussed critically in class. The objective of the course is for each student to accumulate a fine and complex mental map of American literature and culture based on a nuanced and flexible understanding of how fiction is informed by individual and collective beliefs, social and regional milieus, and norms of ethics and aesthetics, which are all subject to historical change.

title: Literatures of South Asia
prerequisite: WLL 101 Introduction to Critical Issues in the Humanities and Social Sciences (234) (C- and above) OR WLL 110 Introduction to Literary Studies (244) (C- and above)

title: Dante's Inferno
description: In this course we will undertake a comprehensive and close reading of the entirety of one of the world’s literary masterpieces while using it as a springboard to readings that address some of the topics mentioned above.
prerequisite: Subject "WLL" BETWEEN 100 and 499 OR Subject "HST" BETWEEN 100 and 499

title: Petersburg Text in Russian Literature
description: Russian literature contains a body of texts, united by common themes, symbols and motifs that comprise a so-called "Petersburg Text".
prerequisite: Subject "WLL" BETWEEN 100 and 499 OR Subject "HST" BETWEEN 100 and 499

title: Shakespeare
description: Survey of the work of William Shakespeare. This includes representative examples from his lyric poems and plays (comedies, tragedies, and histories).
prerequisite: WLL 201 World Literature I (686) (C- and above) OR WLL 211 World Literature II: from the 18th to the 20th century (492) (C- and above) OR WLL 212 Introduction to Poetry (2167) (C- and above) OR WLL 240 Introduction to the Novel (687) (C- and above) OR WLL 241 Survey of Folk Tales (466) (C- and above) OR WLL 244 Survey of Nineteenth-Century Russian Literature (1395) (C- and above) OR WLL 349 Terrible Perfection: Women in 19th-Century Russian Literature (2488) (C- and above) OR WLL 246 Survey of Contemporary Russian Literature and Culture (3604) (C- and above) OR WLL 254/SPA 254 Superstition, Magical Realism, and Horror in Hispanic Culture (1851) (C- and above)

title: Literary Modernism: Tradition and Innovation
prerequisite: Subject "WLL" BETWEEN 200 and 299

title: Postmodern Fiction: Forms and Messages
description: The course addresses an open-ended range of fictions and methodological issues arising in the study of the so-called Postmodernism in Western (and) globalized literatures. By reading prose narratives from the second half of the 20th century in parallel with samples of contemporary critical theory, we reconstruct the free-flowing exchange of ideas between stories and philosophies of the period. The course enhances the students’ critical thinking about literature and reality and (re)introduces them to the many complexities and ironies of contemporary cultural experience.
prerequisite: Subject "WLL" BETWEEN 100 and 399

title: The image of the East in Russophone literature and culture: genesis and meaning
description: In my course, I propose to study Russian-language texts and films in which the Eastern person appears as an object of representation. The texts will be analyzed in light of the political and cultural situation in which they were created. Through analysis and discussion of texts and films of different genres and periods, the purpose of the course will be achieved: students will learn to understand how the image of the Eastern person was formed Russian-language culture and what features it included. This, in turn, will allow us to discuss the contribution of culture to cross-national relations between Russians and the peoples of Central Asia and Kazakhstan in the Soviet and post-Soviet periods.

title: Soviet Literature as Multinational Literature
description: This course presents a survey of Soviet literature and culture as a multinational unity, which consisted of the literatures and cultures of Soviet Republics. The point of this course is that Soviet culture is not equivalent to Russian; Russian literature will be studied only as a part of Soviet literature.

title: Deciphering the City in Modern Literature and Film
department: Languages, Literature and Linguistics, Languages, Literature and Linguistics
prerequisite: Subject "WLL" BETWEEN 100 and 499 OR Subject "HST" BETWEEN 100 and 499

title: Orientalism and Identity in Early Modern Western European Theatre
prerequisite: Subject "WLL" BETWEEN 100 and 499 OR Subject "HST" BETWEEN 100 and 499

title: Modern Japanese Literature
description: Students will be introduced to Japanese literature - primarily the short story and the novel - of the modern and contemporary periods.
prerequisite: Subject "WLL" BETWEEN 1 and 499 OR Subject "" BETWEEN 1 and 499 OR Subject "" BETWEEN 1 and 499 OR Subject "HST" BETWEEN 1 and 499 OR Subject "" BETWEEN 1 and 499 OR Subject "" BETWEEN 1 and 499 OR Subject "" BETWEEN 1 and 499

title: Contemporary Japanese Literature
description: Contemporary Japanese Literature is a companion course to the Fall 2015 the Modern Japanese Literature course, which examines a selection of important (and overlooked) short stories and novels spanning the Meiji, Showa, Taisho, and Heisei periods, the Contemporary Japanese Literature course will first address the debate concerning what constitutes “modern” and “contemporary,” or even “junbungaku (pure literature)” or “mass literature,” the value system that tends to mourn the death of socially invested, writer-as-activist/social critic/visionary model which some associate with the pre-1945 or even pre-1970 period.
prerequisite: Subject "WLL" BETWEEN 110 and 125 OR Subject "WLL" BETWEEN 200 and 299 OR Subject "WLL" BETWEEN 300 and 399

title: Elizabethan Theatre and Identity
description: This course will examine the construct of identity in a variety of Elizabethan theatre texts, focusing on the construct of gender, sexuality, religion and race.
prerequisite: Subject "WLL" BETWEEN 110 and 125 OR Subject "WLL" BETWEEN 200 and 299 OR Subject "WLL" BETWEEN 300 and 399

title: Terrible Perfection: Women in 19th-Century Russian Literature
description: This course will introduce you to some of the most fascinating female characters in classical Russian poetry and prose.

title: Contemporary Spanish Literature and Cinema: from the transition to the recent economic crisis
description: This course is dedicated to the most recent cultural and visual forms in Spain. We will consider how the democratic state has impacted on cultural practices in the last 50 years and the way in which these cultural practices have contributed to the consolidation of a democratic society. The reading and viewing of primary and secondary sources will allow us to discuss various aspects not only related to the artistic sphere, but also to the political, social and cultural context.
department: Languages, Literature and Linguistics, Languages, Literature and Linguistics

title: Graphic Narrative: Advanced Readings in Sequential Art
description: This course assumes a familiarity with the fundamentals of Comics Studies theory, history, and cultural context. Students are expected to exhibit fluency in the 'language' of sequential art - from terminology to modes of reading - and to be capable of situating a text within the larger framework of the genre and the medium. This course will expand upon analytical strategies developed at the beginner level in order to facilitate mature and informed discussions of graphic narratives that define or deconstruct the parameters of sequential storytelling.
prerequisite: WLL 155 Introduction to the Comic Book (3046) (C- and above) OR WLL 255 The Comic Book in Japan and America (1849) (C- and above)

title: Terror and Perfection: Soviet Female Writers and Poets
description: The program of the course consists of texts by Soviet female writers and poets written in Russian. The course aims to broaden the 20th-century literary canon which has traditionally focused more on male than female authors. Rather than analyzing “female images” in literature, we will talk about texts created by female writers and the writing strategies that they employed. During the course, we will address a variety of texts studying them within the Soviet cultural and historical context, with close reading being the primary method of analysis. The main aspects of the course will be the examination of several cases that illustrate different literary strategies of female writers.

title: Writing Speculative Fiction
description: This is an advanced creative writing seminar that will focus on reading, writing and discussing speculative fiction (science fiction, fantasy, magical realism and horror). Students will read and analyze contemporary authors; work with peers on collaboration and revision; and gain experience in flash fiction, interactive narrative, collaborative fiction and hybrid fiction.
department: Communication and Composition, Languages, Literature and Linguistics
prerequisite: WCS 260/WLL 235 Creative Writing: Introduction to Fiction Writing I (4000) (C and above)

title: Philosophy of Art
description: This course surveys topics in philosophical aesthetics and the philosophy of art. Topics include: aesthetic judgment, aesthetic concepts, the aesthetic and the non-aesthetic, artistic value, the nature of representation (especially across painting, photography, and cinema), interpretation (especially literary interpretation), art and knowledge, art and morality, and definitions of art.
department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, Languages, Literature and Linguistics

title: Research Assistance in Linguistics and Literature
description: The aim of this course is to allow students to assist in the research projects of faculty in the World Languages and Literature Department.

title: Advanced Topics in World Literature
description: This course broadens student understanding of particular areas in world literature. These areas may focus on geographical areas, time periods, language families, and/or theoretical topics related to the study of comparative literature.

title: Literary Theory
description: The course addresses a range of approaches in Literary Theory. It functions as a collaborative reading group committed to making sense of some allegedly difficult texts and testing their most counterintuitive ideas on familiar literary works. The course seeks to steer the class toward a better understanding of the benefits of critical thinking as contrasted with commonsensical assumptions about literature and culture by (re)visiting selected theorists from Aristotle to Larour.

title: Poetic Personae
description: The course introduces students to various lyric ‘personae’ that can be used by a poet to channel separate views of the world and artistic styles, problematizing the unity of consciousness.
prerequisite: Subject "WLL" BETWEEN 100 and 399

title: Oral Epic in Central Asia
description: This course examines the oral epics of Central Asia. Students will read selections of Turkic, Persian, and Mongolian epics, together with scholarship on the genre of epic and of oral literature more broadly.
prerequisite: Subject "WLL" BETWEEN 100 and 499

title: Contemporary Russian and Russophone Literature
description: This course is dedicated to the advanced study of contemporary Russian and Russophone literature written after 1991 and explores various genres of prose and poetry (traditional novel, dystopias, conceptualist poetry, postmodernist fiction, popular and detective literature, women’s prose, creative nonfiction) and other modes of cultural production (music, political and performance art). Discussions address the issues of politics, re-assessment of history, memory, gender, national identity, violence and terrorism, as well as the place of literature in the modern world.
prerequisite: Subject "WLL" BETWEEN 100 and 199

title: Media and Memory Politics in the Post-Soviet Space
description: This course will examine the relationship between media (historical texts, films, and other dramas) and memory politics, which attempt to construct a nation’s collective vision of the past.
department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, Languages, Literature and Linguistics

title: Laughter
description: This course examines how laughter functions as a social signal in real life and cultural artifacts.

title: The Call of the Evil: Unmasking the Villain(ness) in Popular Culture and Literature
description: This course aims to cast light on the reasons behind this deeply rooted fascination with the villains(nesses) who with their actions threaten and subvert the accepted social-cultural norms of their times. Specific attention will be paid to how the image of the villain(ness) has evolved over the years, reaching the point where villains/villainesses are being increasingly redeemed by the creative industries, through elaborate explorations of their backstories.

title: Creative Writing: Autofiction
description: This course is a reading and writing intensive seminar with a workshop component. It is devoted to analyzing, reading, writing and revision of our own and previously published autofiction longform writing within the scope of the study of the creative process. This course is intended for students already familiar with the techniques within creative writing and interested in exploring longer narrative elements within personal stories. In this class, we will compose original works and refine our writing though a process of workshop and revision. Students will finish the semester with a portfolio containing a students’ analysis of their writing and an edited and extended manuscript.

title: Philosophy and Tragedy
description: This course is labeled Philosophy AND Tragedy to reflect a dual concern with art and human life. First, we shall study the philosophy of the art of tragedy, examining the nature of tragic works as such and inquiring into the cognitive, emotional, moral, and political values distinctive of tragedy. Second, the course will look to tragedy to inform philosophical problems of human existence. These include such problems as human agency amid weakness of will; the conflict between moral and political values; the limits of rationality and the liberation of liminal experiences (such as religious and ritual ecstasy). Both our aims require a substantive engagement with tragedy; to that end, tragic works themselves will figure on the syllabus (e.g., by Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides, or perhaps other authors); we hope to include more contemporary literary works. Philosophers on the syllabus include, variously, Plato, Aristotle, Hume, Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Nussbaum.

title: Academic Communications for Graduate Studies I
description: This is the first half of a two-semester communications course which provides students with a structured opportunity to develop the linguistic knowledge and academic skills and strategies necessary to achieve their academic potential at graduate study in an English-medium higher education context. The aim of the course is to help students become competent oral users of English as well as critical learners.

title: Academic Communications for Graduate Studies II
description: This is the second half of a two-semester communications course which provides students with a structured opportunity to develop the linguistic knowledge and academic skills and strategies necessary to achieve their academic potential at graduate study in an English-medium higher education context. The aim of the course is to help students become competent oral users of English as well as critical learners.

title: Linear Algebra for Graduate Studies
description: This course provides NUZYP students with a basic understanding of linear algebra concepts and prepares them to solve problems that involve the basic linear algebra techniques. This includes the study of systems of linear equations, theory of abstract vector spaces and linear transformations. The goal of the course is to develop students’ understanding and use of basic linear algebra methods which are extensively employed in engineering and science studies.

title: Academic Reading for Graduate Studies I
description: This is the first half of a two-semester reading course which provides students with a structured opportunity to examine text structures assisting them to read effectively and critically and to focus on the language, thinking, and organization of English academic writing.

description: This course provides NUZYP students with a basic understanding of statistical concepts and prepares them to solve problems that involve the analysis of statistical data.
